Preface#

This book exists because the syntax is the easy part.

If you know C#, you can read Java code on your first afternoon. Both languages have curly braces, classes, interfaces, generics and lambdas. Both languages compile your code to an intermediate form. In Java, this form is called bytecode. In .NET, it is called IL. Both languages free unused memory with a garbage collector. C# took much of its design from Java, so the two languages are alike on purpose.

Everything around the language takes weeks. You have to learn these things:

  • which Java Development Kit (JDK) to install
  • why the build tool works so differently from MSBuild
  • why an annotation did nothing and reported no error (an annotation is like an attribute in C#)
  • why there is no await
  • why a method you did not mark virtual was overridden anyway

This book is about those things.

Who it is for#

You write C#, and you have used .NET 8. You are moving to Java, most likely to work on a Spring Boot service. You do not need to know any Java, and you do not need to have used C# 13 or C# 14. Every Java word is explained where a chapter first uses it.

The book also assumes that you forget things, and that you lose interest in a long book. So it gives each answer first, and it asks you questions instead of repeating itself.

How to read it#

Every chapter starts with a table. The table lists the differences between C# and Java for the topic of the chapter. Each row has a mark:

MarkMeansWhat to do
sameit works as it does in C#, so nothing changesread the row and move on
twistthe same idea as in C#, written differentlyread the row, and open the section only if you want the detail
trapyour C# habit gives the wrong resultRead the section. Most traps ask you to predict the result first.
newC# has nothing like it, so you have no C# habit to useread the section

Some traps show code with a question, such as "What does this print?". Decide on your own answer before you open the answer in the book. Being wrong for a moment helps you remember the right answer. Each chapter ends with one to three questions for the same reason.

The book has three reading modes and a Reference view. You choose one with the buttons in the sidebar:

ModeShowsTakes
Essentialsevery difference, and the explanation of the traps and the new ideas in the main chaptersabout 3 hours 45 minutes
Everydayalso the detail behind each twistabout 7 hours 25 minutes
Completeeverything, including legacy code and JVM internalsabout 10 hours
Referenceonly each chapter's table of differences, with the tours and the appendicesa quick pass

Start with Essentials. No reading mode hides anything. Folded material is shown as a one-line heading that you can open. Fourteen chapters cover things that you look up when you need them, such as Gradle, messaging and reactive code. Each of these chapters is marked as a look-up chapter, and Essentials shows only its table.

If you start work on a Spring Boot service on Monday, read the parts Day one and Language core. Then go directly to the chapter Spring Boot orientation. If your data is in Amazon DocumentDB, your data chapter is Document data. That chapter depends on a few sections of the relational chapter before it. The relational chapter says which sections.

To come back later, use the Refresh links in the sidebar. The links lead to three tours, and each tour is commented code. The three tours are Java in 19 minutes, Spring Boot in 17 minutes and Modern C# in 10 minutes. Review asks you the book's 163 questions one at a time. It asks a question again if you missed it. The Java tour, the Spring Boot tour and one pass of Review take about 1 hour 30 minutes together.

To find one fact, press ⌘K or Ctrl+K. Then type a C# name, or paste an error message. For example, IEnumerable, IOptions or the first line of a stack trace takes you directly to its answer. Some comparisons use a C# feature that you may have forgotten. Beside such a comparison, there is a one-line C# refresher. The refresher is marked with the C# version of the feature.

An appendix at the back says what the book targets, how its facts were checked, and what the book does not cover. See the appendix About this book.

Why Java feels familiar#

Day one · Chapter 01· 7 min read

C# and Java look alike. Curly braces, classes, interfaces, generics, lambdas and garbage collection all work in much the same way in both languages. That resemblance is real, and it is also the danger. The resemblance makes it easy to write Java as if it were C#.

KindC#JavaNote
samevar order = new Order(customer, lines)var order = new Order(customer, lines)classes, constructors, exceptions, generics and var all work the same way in Java
trapsealed classfinal classNothing may extend the class. Java has a sealed keyword too, and it means something else. Why
twistreadonly fieldfinal fieldassigned once, in the declaration or in the constructor Why
twistOrderService(IOrderRepository repository)a written-out constructorJava classes have no primary constructors Why
twistArgumentExceptionIllegalArgumentExceptionthe standard exception for a bad argument value Why
twistforeach (var line in lines)for (var line : lines)C# writes foreach and in, but Java writes for and a colon Why
newasync Task<Order> PlaceAsync()Order place(), run on a virtual threadblocking is cheap on a virtual thread, so there is no async Why
twistTotal { get; set; }getTotal() and setTotal()Java has no properties, but a record gives you accessors instead Why
trapno modifier means privateno modifier means package-privatevisible to the whole package, which surprises C# developers Why
newFile.ReadAllText(path), with nothing declaredthrows IOExceptiona checked exception must be caught, or listed after throws Why
twisttypeof(T)no equivalenttype arguments are erased when Java compiles, so a list does not know what it holds Why
trapVisual Studio's Build menu, with MSBuild hidden behind itMaven or Gradle runs the buildthe build is run by a separate tool, rather than by the IDE Why
trapprotectedprotectedThe keyword is the same, but protected in Java allows more callers than protected in C#. The next chapter asks which callers. Why
twist.NET, one product from one vendora specification, and a JDK from any of several vendorsthe web framework, the ORM and the test runner are third-party choices Why
twistIOrderRepositoryOrderRepositoryJava code drops the I prefix on interface names Why
twistnamespace Acme.Billingpackage com.acme.billingthe package should match the folder, and the file is named after its public class Why

One class, side by sidetwist#

C#
// The parameter list after the class name is a primary constructor.
public sealed class OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
{
    public async Task<Order> PlaceAsync(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines)
    {
        if (lines.Count == 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("An order needs at least one line.");
        foreach (var line in lines)
            if (line is null)
                throw new ArgumentException("A line is missing.");
        var order = new Order(customer, lines);
        await repository.SaveAsync(order);
        return order;
    }
}
Java 25
public final class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public Order place(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        if (lines.isEmpty())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("An order needs at least one line.");
        for (var line : lines)
            if (line == null)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("A line is missing.");
        var order = new Order(customer, lines);
        repository.save(order);
        return order;
    }
}
Reading the code
public final class OrderService

final on a class means the same as sealed on a class in C#. No other class may extend the class. Java has a sealed keyword too, but it means something else.

private final OrderRepository repository;

A final field is assigned once, in the constructor, like a C# readonly field.

public OrderService(OrderRepository repository)

Java classes have no primary constructors, so the constructor is written out. Most Java services use a framework called Spring. Spring passes the repository to the constructor, as the ASP.NET Core container would.

throw new IllegalArgumentException

IllegalArgumentException does the same as ArgumentException in C#.

for (var line : lines)

This loop does the same as foreach in C#. Java writes the keyword for, and it writes a colon in place of in.

var order = new Order(customer, lines);

var works as it does in C#.

repository.save(order);

There is no await, and the method returns Order, not Task<Order>. The call waits until the save has finished. For the reason, see the chapter Threads are cheap now.

The six things that will actually cost you timetrap#

This invoice class shows four of the six things. Its repository field is not shown.

C#
public class Invoice
{
    public Money Total { get; set; }

    // No modifier, so this is private by default.
    string LoadTemplate(string path) =>
        File.ReadAllText(path);

    public async Task SaveAsync() =>
        await repository.SaveAsync(this);
}
Java 25
public class Invoice {
    private Money total;
    public Money getTotal() { return total; }

    String loadTemplate(Path path) throws IOException {
        return Files.readString(path);
    }

    public void save() { repository.save(this); }
}
Reading the code
public Money getTotal() { return total; }

Java has no properties. A private field holds the value, and the method getTotal reads the field.

String loadTemplate(Path path)

In C#, a method with no modifier is private. In Java, a method with no modifier is package-private. This means that every class in the same package can call the method.

throws IOException

Files.readString can fail with IOException. IOException is a checked exception, so you must catch it or list it after throws.

public void save() { repository.save(this); }

The method has no async and no Task, so the call blocks. Blocking is cheap on a virtual thread, which is a lightweight thread.

The other two things are not in the class. The first is type erasure, which removes generic type arguments when Java compiles. The second is the build, which Maven or Gradle runs.

C# refresherReified generics: the type argument exists at run timeC# 2

In .NET, a generic type keeps its type argument at run time. So code can ask for typeof(T). Code can also test whether an object is a List<string>.

static string NameOf<T>() => typeof(T).Name;

NameOf<int>();                             // "Int32": T is known at run time

object xs = new List<int>();
Console.WriteLine(xs is List<string>);     // False: the type argument is checked

This table lists all six things, each with its chapter:

Your instinctThe Java realityChapter
Exceptions are all uncheckedChecked exceptions must be declared or caughtExceptions and resources
Generics are reifiedType arguments are erased at runtimeGenerics and type erasure
Properties are a language featureGetters and setters are just methodsFields, properties and immutability
Default access is privateDefault access is package-privateAccess modifiers and packages
I need async for scaleBlock on a virtual thread insteadThreads are cheap now
The build is part of the IDEMaven or Gradle runs the build, outside the IDEMaven vs csproj

These six links go to the chapters in the table, in the same order. They are exceptions, generics, properties, access, threads and the build.

protected is not the same keywordtrap#

Gotcha

protected does not mean what you think. In C#, protected means “this class and its subclasses”. In Java, protected allows more callers, and nothing warns you.

C#
public class Order
{
    protected void Recalculate() { }
}
Java 25
public class Order {
    protected void recalculate() { }
}

In C#, only Order and its subclasses can call Recalculate(). The Java method looks the same, but more classes can call it. To predict which classes can call it, see the chapter The week-one gotchas.

A mental model for the platform#

.NET is one product. Microsoft ships all of these parts, and versions them together:

  • the runtime
  • the base class library
  • the web framework
  • the object-relational mapper (ORM)
  • the dependency injection (DI) container
  • the test runner

Java is a specification plus a market. Oracle, Eclipse, Amazon, Azul and Red Hat all ship a Java Development Kit (JDK) built to the same specification. The web framework, the DI container and the ORM come from Spring or Quarkus, not from the JDK.

Each .NET piece has a Java counterpart, but the Java counterparts rarely come from the same vendor:

.NETJavaNote
CLRJVMboth compile bytecode to machine code as it runs
ILbytecodeone .class file per type, zipped into a JAR
BCL / System.*java.*, javax.*, jakarta.*the standard library, and much smaller than the BCL
NuGetMaven Centrala package is identified by group + artifact, not one name
.csproj + MSBuildpom.xml + MavenGradle and build.gradle.kts are the alternative
Assembly (.dll)JARa zip of compiled classes, and it is the unit you ship
SolutionMulti-module buildone parent pom lists the child modules
ASP.NET CoreSpring Bootnot shipped with Java, so it is a third-party dependency
Entity Framework CoreHibernate / Spring Data JPAalso a third-party dependency, because the JDK ships no ORM
xUnit + MoqJUnit 5 + Mockitoalso not shipped with Java, and Java has no built-in test runner
Note

The “not shipped with Java” rows are the real culture shock. There is no official web framework. Spring Boot is overwhelmingly the default in enterprise Java, and the largest part of this book is about Spring Boot. But Spring Boot remains a third-party choice. Quarkus and Micronaut are credible alternatives.

So a Java web service begins by choosing its framework. You list the framework as dependencies in the build file. ASP.NET Core arrives with the .NET SDK. But these dependencies are downloaded like any other library:

<!-- pom.xml: none of these ship with the JDK -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>       <!-- the ASP.NET Core role -->
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>  <!-- the EF Core role -->
</dependency>

Each <dependency> names a library by its group and its artifact. The group and the artifact are the two parts of a Maven name. spring-boot-starter-web is called a starter. It is one dependency that adds Spring's web framework and a web server. spring-boot-starter-data-jpa adds Hibernate, which is the most widely used ORM. No versions appear, because the Spring Boot parent file chooses them for you.

Conventions that differ#

Java code also looks different on the page, because the C# community and the Java community chose different conventions:

C#JavaExample
PascalCase methodscamelCase methodsGetName() to getName()
IFoo for interfacesno prefixIRepo to Repo
_camelCase fieldscamelCase, no prefix_name to name
Namespace need not match folderPackage should match folderthe build tools and the JVM expect it
One public type per file, looselyOne public type per file, strictlyfilename must match
PropertiesgetX() / setX()or a record component

Here is one interface and one class in each language, written in the style of each community:

C#: Acme/Billing/OrderService.cs
// The namespace need not match the folder.
namespace Acme.Billing;

// Interfaces start with I, methods use PascalCase.
public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Order? FindById(long id);
}

public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
{
    // Private fields use _camelCase, with a leading underscore.
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository = repository;
}
Java: com/acme/billing/OrderService.java
// The package matches the folder com/acme/billing/.
package com.acme.billing;

// No I prefix, and methods use camelCase.
public interface OrderRepository {
    Order findById(long id);
}

public class OrderService {
    // Fields have no underscore.
    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; }
}

The Java file starts with the line package com.acme.billing; and it is in the folder com/acme/billing/. The file name matches the public class inside the file. The interface name has no I prefix. Method names and field names start with a lower-case letter. The field name has no underscore.

LegacyThe Impl suffix

Older Java codebases pair every interface with a single implementation named OrderServiceImpl. You will see this naming often, especially in Spring code written before about 2015. This naming is no longer recommended. If there is exactly one implementation, you usually do not need the interface at all. If you do need the interface, name the implementation for what makes it different, such as JdbcOrderRepository or InMemoryOrderRepository.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksA C# file can be in any folder and hold several public types. What does Java expect of the file that holds com.acme.billing.OrderService, and why?
The file is named after its public class, so its name is OrderService.java. The file is in the folder that matches its package, which is com/acme/billing/. The build tools and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) find classes by that layout. So the freedom of a C# namespace does not apply in Java.
2
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
{
    public Order Place(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines)
    {
        if (lines.Count == 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("An order needs at least one line.");
        var order = new Order(customer, lines);
        repository.Save(order);
        return order;
    }
}
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public Order place(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        if (lines.isEmpty())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("An order needs at least one line.");
        var order = new Order(customer, lines);
        repository.save(order);
        return order;
    }
}

A Java class has no primary constructor, so the field and the constructor are written out. The field is final, which does the same as readonly in C#. So nothing can replace the repository later.

3
An expert asksA Java developer tells you that Java is a specification, not a product. What does that change for a service you build?
Several vendors ship a JDK built to the same specification, so you choose one JDK. The JDK holds no web framework, no object-relational mapper and no test runner. Spring Boot, Hibernate and JUnit are third-party libraries, and you list them as dependencies in the build file.

The week-one gotchas#

Day one · Chapter 02· 10 min read

Each item here is a few lines of Java where a C# habit fails. Most items behave differently from the same lines in C#. Two items behave the same, but the C# fix does not exist in Java. You do not need to know Java yet. Read each item as C#, and predict the result before you look.

The answers, in one tableopen it after you have predicted
KindC#JavaNote
trapa == b on stringsa.equals(b)== compares references in Java, even for String Why
trapa == b on two int or int? valuesa.equals(b) on two Integer valuesan Integer from -128 to 127 is a shared object, so == seems to work on small values Why
trapdecimalBigDecimalJava has no decimal type, and a double sum is inexact. Money is a BigDecimal, with methods in place of operators. Why
trapcounts["missing"]counts.getOrDefault("missing", 0)get returns null, which throws when unboxed to int Why
trapexpecting a copysubList, keySet and Arrays.asList return viewsa view shares the original's data, so a change to one shows in the other Why
trapa field with no modifiera private fieldJava's default is package-private, not private Why
trapprotectedprotected, which also opens the packageJava cannot say subclass-only, so the whole package gets access too Why
trapvirtual, to opt infinal, to opt outevery Java method can be overridden unless it is marked final Why
trapa nested classa static nested classwithout static, a nested class holds a hidden reference to its outer object Why
trapswitch on a null stringcase null -> ...a switch on a null String or enum throws unless it has case null Why
trapDateTimejava.time, never Date or SimpleDateFormatSimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe, and a Date can be changed after it is created Why
trapreturn in finally does not compilereturn in finally compilesit discards the exception that was leaving the try block, and reports no error Why
twistchecked(a + b)Math.addExact(a, b)Overflow wraps, as it does by default in C#. Java has no checked, so a method throws instead. Why
trapa lambda that throwsa lambda that wraps the exceptiona lambda passed to map cannot throw a checked exception such as IOException Why
sameobject[] o = new string[2]Object[] o = new String[2]both compile, and both fail only when the wrong type is stored Why

== on objectstrap#

The folded table before this section holds every answer. Open it after you have predicted, not before.

System.out.println does the same as Console.WriteLine in C#. Most of the short examples in this chapter run without changes in jshell. This is a prompt that runs each line as you type it. To start jshell, see the next chapter.

Predict== on two strings#
What does this print?
String a = "mug";
String b = readProductId();     // also "mug", read from an incoming order
System.out.println(a == b);
Show the answer
false

In C#, == on two strings compares their text. In Java, == asks whether the two variables point to the same object. This is true for every object type. Here b was built while the program ran, so it is a different object from a. The comparison often appears to work, because Java reuses one object for identical string literals.

Use a.equals(b), or Objects.equals(a, b) when either side may be null. See Equality, hashing and comparison.

The Integer cachetrap#

Integer is the object version of int. It is called the wrapper type of int. Java uses Integer wherever an object is needed, such as in a list. For more about wrapper types, see the chapter Numbers, money and time.

PredictTwo Integers with the same value#
What does this print?
Integer a = 127, b = 127;
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(c == d);
Show the answer
true false

Java shares one object for each boxed integer from −128 to 127. So a and b are the same object. But c and d are two separate objects, and == compares objects, not numbers. Tests with small numbers pass, and production fails. In C#, == on two int or int? values compares the numbers.

Compare boxed values with c.equals(d), which is true.

There is no decimaltrap#

PredictAdding 0.1 and 0.2#
What does this print?
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);
Show the answer
0.30000000000000004

C# prints the same result. The trap is that Java has no decimal type to use instead. A double cannot hold 0.1 exactly, so the sum is slightly wrong. For money, Java uses the class BigDecimal. C# uses operators on a decimal. Java calls methods on a BigDecimal.

C#
decimal total = 0.1m + 0.2m;   // 0.3 exactly
bool over = total > limit;
Java 25
BigDecimal total = new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2"));   // 0.3
boolean over = total.compareTo(limit) > 0;   // no > operator for BigDecimal

Build a BigDecimal from a string. Add with the method add. Compare with the method compareTo, which returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. Here limit is another amount. Using double for money is the most common correctness bug that a C# developer brings to Java. See Numbers, money and time.

A missing key in a maptrap#

In Java, a dictionary is called a map. The interface is Map, like IDictionary in C#. The class is HashMap, like Dictionary in C#.

The code below writes new HashMap<>() with empty angle brackets. The empty brackets are called the diamond. They tell the compiler to take the type arguments from the variable's declared type. For more about maps, see the chapter Collections.

PredictReading a missing key from a map#
What happens on the second line?
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
int n = counts.get("missing");
Show the answer
It throws NullPointerException.

get returns null for a missing key. Assigning null to an int unboxes it, and unboxing null throws. The exception comes from a line that shows no method call. In C#, counts["missing"] throws KeyNotFoundException, which is a clearer failure.

Use counts.getOrDefault("missing", 0).

Views are not copiestrap#

Arrays.asList makes a list from the values you pass to it. It is in the package java.util. You cannot use square brackets on a Java list. To change the first item, C# writes numbers[0] = 9. Java writes numbers.set(0, 9). For more about lists, see the chapter Collections.

PredictA list made from an array#
Which line fails?
var numbers = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3);
numbers.set(0, 9);
numbers.add(4);
Show the answer
numbers.add(4) throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Arrays.asList returns a view of an array, not a copy. So set changes the array itself. And add throws, because an array cannot grow.

These methods return views too:

  • subList
  • keySet, values and entrySet
  • reversed()

Changing a view changes its source. For an example, see the section subList and reversed. When you need a copy, make one with new ArrayList<>(view).

No modifier means package-privatetrap#

Gotcha

In C#, a member with no access modifier is private. In Java, a member with no access modifier is package-private. This means that every class in the same package can use it. A package is like a namespace in C#. So your C# habit gives the wrong result, and nothing warns you. See Access modifiers and packages.

public class Account {
    BigDecimal balance;        // package-private: any class in the package can write it
    private BigDecimal fee;    // what a C# field with no modifier means
}

Any class in the same package can read and change balance. Only fee is what a C# developer means by a field with no modifier.

Who can use a protected membertrap#

The two classes here are in two files of one package, com.acme.billing. A package is like a namespace in C#, and its name matches the folder.

Predictprotected, from a class that is not a subclass#
Does this compile?
// com/acme/billing/Invoice.java
public class Invoice { protected BigDecimal total; }

// com/acme/billing/Auditor.java: same package, not a subclass
class Auditor {
    void reset(Invoice i) { i.total = BigDecimal.ZERO; }
}
Show the answer
Yes.

In Java, protected gives access to subclasses and also to the whole package. Auditor is in the same package, so it can change total. In C#, protected means subclasses only. Java has no access level with that meaning.

Only private stops the other classes in the package, and it stops subclasses too. So the package is the boundary. Keep unrelated classes out of it. For the four access levels, see the chapter Access modifiers and packages.

Methods are virtual by defaulttrap#

In this code, extends names the base class. C# writes a colon there. @Override does the same as the override keyword in C#. It is an annotation, which is like an attribute in C#. For more about both, see the chapter Classes, constructors and initialisation.

PredictAn overridable method called from a constructor#
What does this print?
class Discount {
    Discount() { describe(); }
    void describe() { }
}
class SeasonalDiscount extends Discount {
    private String season = "winter sale";
    @Override void describe() { System.out.println(season); }
}

new SeasonalDiscount();
Show the answer
null

In C#, a method can be overridden only if it is marked virtual. In Java, every method can be overridden unless it is marked final. Here the base constructor calls describe, so the override in SeasonalDiscount runs. At that moment season has not been set yet, so it is null.

The same program in C# prints winter sale. C# sets the fields of a subclass before the base constructor runs. Java sets them after the base constructor runs.

If you make the field final with a constant value, the program prints winter sale. The reason is that the compiler copies a constant into the code that reads it. That hides the bug and does not fix it. A final field that is set from a method call is still null here.

Do not call an overridable method from a constructor. Mark a method final when overriding it would break the class.

Inner classes capture the outer instancetrap#

Gotcha

A C# nested class is always independent. In Java, a nested class is independent only if you write static. Without static, the class is called an inner class. Each object of an inner class holds a hidden reference to the outer object that created it. That reference keeps the outer object alive.

class Outer {
    class Inner { }           // holds a hidden reference to an Outer
    static class Nested { }   // independent, what C# gives you by default
}

new Outer().new Inner();      // an Inner needs an Outer first
new Outer.Nested();           // normal

Write static on every nested class, unless you want the outer reference on purpose. A missing static, as on Inner, is a common cause of memory leaks in listeners and callbacks.

switch and nulltrap#

This is the arrow form of switch. Each case runs the code after its ->. Here run and skip are two methods of the class. For more about the arrow form, see the chapter Switch expressions and statements.

PredictA switch on a null string#
What happens here?
String s = null;
switch (s) {
    case "a" -> run();
    default  -> skip();
}
Show the answer
It throws NullPointerException.

A switch on a null String or enum throws as soon as it sees the null. It throws before it looks at any case, so default does not catch the null. In C#, default catches a null, and so does the discard _.

From Java 21, write null as a case of its own: case null -> skip(); Java 21

Date and SimpleDateFormat are trapstrap#

Gotcha

Each of the old date classes has a problem. A java.util.Date can be changed after it is created. Calendar numbers months from zero. SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe. When several threads use one shared static instance, it produces wrong dates and reports no error. Use java.time only. See Numbers, money and time.

// shared across request threads: wrong dates under load
static final SimpleDateFormat OLD = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");

// immutable and thread-safe: share it freely
static final DateTimeFormatter ISO = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd");
String today = LocalDate.now().format(ISO);

SimpleDateFormat keeps working state inside itself, so two threads that format at the same time corrupt each other's dates. A DateTimeFormatter cannot change, so one shared instance is safe.

return inside finallytrap#

PredictA return inside finally#
What does this print?
int load() {
    try {
        throw new IllegalStateException("real problem");
    } finally {
        return 0;
    }
}

System.out.println(load());
Show the answer
0

A return inside finally replaces the value or the exception that was leaving the try block. The same happens for a catch block, and for a throw inside finally. So the exception is lost, and the caller never learns that anything went wrong. C# refuses to compile a return from a finally block.

Never return from finally. Java warns about it only when you compile with -Xlint:finally. See Exceptions and resources.

Integer overflowtwist#

Integer.MAX_VALUE is the largest int, like int.MaxValue in C#.

PredictAdding one to the largest int#
This prints -2147483648, as the same two lines do in C#. How do you make Java throw instead?
int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.println(big + 1);
Show the answer
Math.addExact(big, 1), which throws ArithmeticException: integer overflow

Java has no checked block. Integer overflow always wraps and reports no error, as it does by default in C#. You cannot make the + operator throw. Java also has no unsigned types, so there is no uint or ulong.

If overflow would be a bug, call Math.addExact. For unsigned arithmetic, use helpers such as Integer.divideUnsigned.

C# refresherchecked and unchecked: C#'s overflow controlC# 1
int big = int.MaxValue;
int wrapped = unchecked(big + 1);    // -2147483648
int safe = checked(big + 1);         // throws OverflowException

Checked exceptions and lambdastrap#

C# writes a lambda with =>. Java writes it with ->. A stream is like LINQ in C#. stream().map(...).toList() does the same as Select(...).ToList(). For more about lambdas, see the chapter Methods and parameters. For more about streams, see the chapter Streams vs LINQ.

PredictA lambda that reads a file#
Does this compile?
// files is a List<Path>; Files.readString reads a whole file as text
List<String> texts = files.stream()
     .map(f -> Files.readString(f))
     .toList();
Show the answer
No: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown

readString can throw IOException. IOException is a checked exception, which means that the compiler makes you catch it or declare it. A lambda passed to map cannot throw a checked exception, because the interface that map expects declares none. This is the gotcha that Java developers complain about most.

Catch the exception inside the lambda, and throw an unchecked exception in its place:

List<String> texts = files.stream()
     .map(f -> {
         try { return Files.readString(f); }
         catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
     })
     .toList();

See Exceptions and resources.

Arrays are covariant, in C# and in Java#

Both languages made this mistake, and both catch it only while the program runs, not when it compiles:

Object[] objects = new String[2];
objects[0] = 42;         // compiles; throws ArrayStoreException at runtime
Reading the code
Object[] objects = new String[2];

An array of String can be used as an array of Object. That compiles in both languages.

objects[0] = 42;

The array is really a String array, so it cannot hold an Integer. The error is caught only when the line runs, with ArrayStoreException.

Generics are invariant to avoid exactly this problem. That is why a List<String> is not a List<Object>.

Check yourself
1
Either of two Java strings may be null. How do you compare their text?
Objects.equals(a, b). a.equals(b) throws NullPointerException when a is null. == asks only whether a and b are the same object.
2
Why should a nested class be static unless you have a reason?
Without static it is an inner class. Each object then holds a hidden reference to the outer object that created it. The reference keeps the outer object alive, which is a common cause of memory leaks. A static nested class behaves like a C# nested class.
3
An expert asksA service keeps one static final SimpleDateFormat and formats dates on every request. What goes wrong, and what do you use instead?
SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe. It keeps working state inside itself, so two request threads that format at the same time produce wrong dates, with no error. Use java.time. A DateTimeFormatter cannot change, so one shared instance is safe.
Next · Day one03Getting a JDK, and the release train9 min

Getting a JDK, and the release train#

Day one · Chapter 03· 9 min read· Quick reference

To write Java, you install a Java Development Kit (JDK), which is like the .NET SDK. The JDK holds the compiler, the tools and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). The JVM runs compiled code. A Java Runtime Environment (JRE) has no compiler. There is no single Java, so you choose a version and a vendor.

KindC#JavaNote
twistthe dotnet-install scriptcurl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bashinstalls SDKMAN, the tool that installs a JDK and switches between several Why
twistseveral .NET SDKs, side by sidesdk install java 25.0.4-temSDKMAN installs and switches JDKs. The identifier is exact, so copy it from sdk list java. Why
twistdotnet new webapicurl https://start.spring.io/starter.tgz -d dependencies=webThe Spring Initializr generates the project. Its web page is start.spring.io, and IntelliJ has it built in. Why
twistdotnet run./mvnw spring-boot:runthe Maven wrapper is a script in the project that downloads Maven, so you never install it Why
samea Kestrel app runs on its ownthe JAR contains its own web serverthere is nothing to deploy into, on either side
twistC# Interactivejshella prompt that runs each line as you type it, in the JDK since Java 9 Why
twist[HttpGet("/hello")] in an [ApiController] class@GetMapping("/hello") in a @RestController classAn annotation is like an attribute in C#. Spring Boot listens on port 8080. Why
twist.NET 6, .NET 8, .NET 10Java 17, Java 21, Java 25These are the long-term support (LTS) releases. A Java release in between gets six months of updates, and a .NET release in between gets two years. Why
twist<TargetFramework><maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>the Java version the output must run on, whichever JDK runs the build Why
trap.NET Framework 4.8, fading awayJava 8, still in production in 2026Java 8 has no var, no records, no switch expressions and no text blocks Why
twist.NET 8, or .NET 10Java 21, or Java 25 for a new projectas of September 2026 most production Java runs on 21, and every library supports it Why
trapDOTNET_ROOTJAVA_HOMEThe mvn and gradle scripts use this JDK folder when the variable is set. An IDE compiles against the JDK in its project settings. Why
twistdotnet add package Xa <dependency> pasted into pom.xmlthere is no mvn add command, and the Spring Boot parent chooses the version Why
twistone .NET SDK, from MicrosoftTemurin, Corretto, Zulu and other builds of the JDKevery build comes from the same OpenJDK source, so take Temurin unless you have a reason Why
twisttop-level statements, then dotnet runvoid main() in Hello.java, then java Hello.javaThe feature is final in Java 25. Most real code still has public static void main(String[] args). Why

Five minutes to a running servicetwist#

Three steps install a JDK, generate a Spring Boot project and start it:

# 1. a JDK, without touching the system package manager
curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash
source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh"
sdk install java 25.0.4-tem      # the exact identifier comes from "sdk list java"

# 2. a project, generated from the command line
curl https://start.spring.io/starter.tgz \
     -d dependencies=web \
     -d type=maven-project \
     -d javaVersion=25 \
     -d artifactId=demo -d name=demo \
     | tar -xzf - -C . && cd demo

# 3. run it
./mvnw spring-boot:run
Reading the code
curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash

This line installs SDKMAN. SDKMAN is a tool that installs Java versions and switches between them.

sdk install java 25.0.4-tem

This line installs Temurin 25, which is a free build of the JDK.

curl https://start.spring.io/starter.tgz

This command asks the Spring Initializr for a new Maven project with the web starter. Then it unpacks the project into the folder demo.

./mvnw spring-boot:run

This line builds and starts the service with the Maven wrapper. The Maven wrapper is a script in the project that downloads Maven. Each library is a Java archive (JAR) file. Maven puts each JAR on the classpath. The classpath is the ordered list of folders and JARs that Java searches for a class. See The classpath is a search list.

The built JAR contains its own web server, as a Kestrel app does.

jshell: run one line of Javatwist#

The JDK includes JShell. JShell is a read-eval-print loop (REPL), which is a prompt where you type code and see the result immediately. JShell arrived in Java 9 Java 9. It does the same as C# Interactive, and it is the fastest way to check how a library behaves:

$ jshell
|  Welcome to JShell -- Version 25

jshell> var xs = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4)
xs ==> [1, 2, 3, 4]

jshell> xs.stream().filter(x -> x % 2 == 0).toList()
$2 ==> [2, 4]

jshell> Integer c = 128, d = 128
c ==> 128
d ==> 128

jshell> c == d
$5 ==> false

jshell> /exit

Each line is run as soon as you press Enter. In the line xs ==> [1, 2, 3, 4], jshell shows the value that it stored. filter(x -> x % 2 == 0) keeps the even numbers. C# writes a lambda with =>. Java writes it with ->. The last two lines are a trap from the week-one gotchas. Most of the short examples in that chapter run in jshell. /exit closes jshell.

One endpointtwist#

Add one file to that project, src/main/java/com/example/demo/Hello.java:

package com.example.demo;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
public class Hello {

    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "world") String name) {
        return "hello " + name;
    }
}
Reading the code
package com.example.demo;

This line names the package. A package is like a namespace in C#. The package name matches the folder that the file is in.

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

This line imports every class in that package, like a using directive in C#.

@RestController

This is an annotation, which is like an attribute in C#. This annotation tells Spring that the class handles HTTP requests, like [ApiController] on a controller.

@GetMapping("/hello")

This annotation sends GET /hello to this method, like [HttpGet("/hello")].

@RequestParam(defaultValue = "world") String name

Spring reads name from the query string, like [FromQuery] with a default value. When name is missing, Spring uses "world".

Call the endpoint from another terminal:

curl "http://localhost:8080/hello?name=java"
# hello java

The response is the text hello java. Spring Boot listens on port 8080 unless you configure another port.

The release traintwist#

Java ships a new version every six months, in March and September. Since Java 17, every fourth release is a long-term support (LTS) release, so an LTS release arrives every two years. The releases in between get six months of updates, and no updates after that.

ReleaseDateStatus.NET analogy
Java 82014LTS, still everywhere.NET Framework 4.8
Java 112018LTS, legacy.NET Core 3.1
Java 172021LTS, common.NET 6
Java 212023LTS, the usual default in September 2026.NET 8
Java 252025LTS, the newest in September 2026.NET 10

Each change to Java is described in a numbered JDK Enhancement Proposal (JEP). For example, JEP 444 added virtual threads in Java 21.

The JDK that runs the build and the Java version you target are separate settings, as they are in .NET. You can build on JDK 25 for Java 21:

<!-- pom.xml: compile for Java 21, whichever JDK runs the build -->
<properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
</properties>

<!-- under the Spring Boot parent, set this instead; the parent copies it across -->
<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
</properties>

maven.compiler.release tells the compiler which Java version the output must run on. It is like <TargetFramework> in a .csproj file.

Java 8 is still in productiontrap#

PredictA record and var, compiled for Java 8#
What does the compiler say?
// Snippet.java
public class Snippet {
    record Money(long cents) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var price = new Money(950);
        System.out.println(price);
    }
}
javac --release 8 Snippet.java     # compile it as a Java 8 codebase would
Show the answer
error: records are not supported in -source 8, followed by (use -source 16 or higher to enable records)

.NET Framework 4.8 is becoming part of history. Java 8 is not part of history. In 2026 a large amount of running enterprise Java is still on Java 8. Java 8 lacks almost everything in the Modern Java part of this book. It has no var, no records, no switch expressions and no text blocks.

Records need Java 16, and var needs Java 10. Without the record, a line such as var price = 950; fails on Java 8 with cannot find symbol. If you inherit a Java 8 codebase, check before you use a modern feature.

Note

Target Java 21 unless you control the whole deployment. As of September 2026, most production Java runs on Java 21. Java 21 has virtual threads and pattern matching, and every library supports it. Java 25 is the right choice for a new project. A release that is not LTS is for experiments.

Installing and switchingtwist#

SDKMAN installs several JDKs side by side, as you keep several .NET SDKs. It also switches between the JDKs:

# install SDKMAN once
curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash

sdk list java                        # every version and vendor, with its identifier
sdk install java 25.0.4-tem          # Temurin 25
sdk install java 21.0.12+1.1-tem     # Temurin 21 alongside it
sdk use java 21.0.12+1.1-tem         # this shell only
sdk default java 25.0.4-tem          # new shells

java -version                        # what am I actually running
Reading the code
sdk list java

This command lists every JDK that SDKMAN can install, with the identifier to use. It marks the JDKs that you already have.

sdk use java 21.0.12+1.1-tem

This command switches only the current terminal to that JDK. This is useful when you want to try one project on an older version.

sdk default java 25.0.4-tem

This command sets the JDK that every new terminal starts with.

java -version

This command prints the version of the java command on your path, so you can check which JDK is really in use.

Gotcha

SDKMAN identifiers are exact. sdk install java 25-tem fails, because the identifier includes the patch release, as in 25.0.4-tem. The identifier changes with every quarterly update. Copy the identifier from sdk list java. The identifiers above were current in September 2026.

Which JDK a project usestrap#

In .NET, a global.json file pins the SDK a folder uses.

.NET refresherglobal.json: pinning the .NET SDK for a folder

A global.json file names one SDK version. Every dotnet command uses that version in the folder of the file, and in the folders below it.

{
  "sdk": { "version": "10.0.100", "rollForward": "latestFeature" }
}

With SDKMAN, a .sdkmanrc file in the project folder does the same for the JDK:

sdk env init      # writes .sdkmanrc naming the current JDK, such as java=25.0.4-tem
sdk env           # switches this shell to the JDK that .sdkmanrc names

sdk env init writes the file once. Commit the file. Then anyone who runs sdk env in the folder gets the same JDK.

Gotcha

JAVA_HOME matters, but not everywhere, and this difference causes the confusion. The mvn and gradle launcher scripts first check the variable JAVA_HOME. If it is set, they run $JAVA_HOME/bin/java. If it is not set, they run the first java on PATH. An IDE compiles against the JDK set in its project settings. That JDK can be a different JDK from the one that the scripts use.

That is why a project can build in the IDE and fail on the command line. When the versions disagree, check both settings. Check JAVA_HOME for the terminal, and check the project SDK for the IDE.

Adding a librarytwist#

Your service needs input validation. In .NET you would run dotnet add package. The Java build tools have no such command.

Gotcha

There is no mvn add. You edit pom.xml in your editor and paste the library's name. Every Java developer does this, and nobody finds it strange. IntelliJ autocompletes the name. See Maven vs csproj.

Adding the validation library looks like this:

<!-- pom.xml: the whole of "adding a package" -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
    <!-- no version: the Spring Boot parent chooses it -->
</dependency>

The groupId and artifactId together name the library, like a NuGet package id. There is no version, because the Spring Boot parent file chooses a compatible version. The next ./mvnw command downloads the library.

Which distribution#

Several vendors build and ship the JDK, each from the same OpenJDK source code:

DistributionVendorPick it when
Eclipse TemurinEclipse Adoptiumby default, because it is free and TCK-certified, with no conditions
Amazon CorrettoAmazonyou deploy on AWS
Azul ZuluAzulyou want commercial support options
Oracle JDKOracleyour employer has a contract
GraalVMOracleyou want native-image ahead-of-time compilation
Microsoft Build of OpenJDKMicrosoftfamiliar vendor, Azure shops

Each of these distributions passes the Technology Compatibility Kit (TCK). The TCK is the test suite that proves that a JDK behaves like Java. The differences between the distributions are support, licensing and a few extras. So do not spend a week choosing. Take Temurin.

Running source directly#

Since Java 11, you can run a single .java file with no separate compile step. Since Java 22, such a program can have several files. Java 25 finalised compact source files and instance main methods Java 25. This feature removes the extra code that made the Java hello world program a joke:

C# top-level statements
// Program.cs
Console.WriteLine("Hello");

// dotnet run
Java 25 compact source file
// Hello.java
void main() {
    IO.println("Hello");
}

// java Hello.java

The whole program is the method void main(). The program has no class around the method, no String[] args and no static. IO.println writes a line, like Console.WriteLine. The feature is final in Java 25, as JEP 512, so it is safe in scripts and teaching. Most real code is still in an ordinary class with a public static void main(String[] args) method.

LegacyThe full main method

You will see this form in almost every existing codebase, and a build tool still expects it as an entry point:

public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello");
    }
}

System.out.println does the same as Console.WriteLine in C#, and it is the form that you will see in real code. IO.println is new in Java 25.

Check yourself
1
You have three JDKs installed, and a Maven build compiles against the wrong one. Where do you look first?
JAVA_HOME. The mvn and gradle scripts use it when it is set. An IDE compiles against the JDK set in its project settings. That is why the terminal and the IDE can disagree.
2
An expert asksWhich Java version should a new production service target, and why not the newest?
It should target a long-term support (LTS) release, which is Java 21 or Java 25. The releases in between get six months of updates, and no updates after that. So those releases are for trying features, not for shipping.
3
What are the JDK, the JRE and the JVM?
The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is the program that runs compiled Java code, as the CLR runs IL. A Java Runtime Environment (JRE) is a JVM with its libraries and no compiler. The Java Development Kit (JDK) adds the compiler and the tools. So a developer installs the JDK, like the .NET SDK.

Quick reference#

Task.NETJava

Rundotnet runjava Foo, or mvn spring-boot:run
Run one filedotnet run Foo.cs, from .NET 10java Foo.java
REPLdotnet-script / C# Interactivejshell
Testdotnet testmvn test
Packagedotnet publishmvn package
Add dependencydotnet add package Xedit pom.xml by hand
Cleandotnet cleanmvn clean

Here are three more items, which you look up by their .NET name:

.NETJavaNote
dotnet --list-sdkssdk list javamarks each JDK that SDKMAN has installed on this machine
dotnet --versionjava -versionprints to stderr, but java --version, with two dashes, prints to stdout

IntelliJ for Visual Studio users#

Day one · Chapter 04· 6 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

Most Java developers use IntelliJ IDEA. It is made by JetBrains, the company that also makes ReSharper and Rider. What you know from Visual Studio works in IntelliJ IDEA too, but under other names and with other keys.

KindC#JavaNote
twistVisual StudioIntelliJ IDEA, one download since version 2025.3free for core Java and Kotlin, but an Ultimate subscription adds the full Spring and database tooling Why
twistVS CodeVS Code with the Red Hat Java and Spring Boot extension packsa lighter option than IntelliJ, and you will also meet Eclipse in older organisations Why
twista solution that holds projectsa project that holds modulesThe names moved. An IntelliJ project is what Visual Studio calls a solution, and an IntelliJ module is what Visual Studio calls a project. Why
twistBilling.slna parent pom.xml that lists its moduleseach module is a folder with its own pom.xml, and builds one JAR Why
trapVisual Studio's Build menu, with MSBuild hidden behind itthe build tool owns the project, and the IDE reads its fileswhen the IDE and mvn clean package disagree, trust the command line Why
twistCtrl+.Alt+Enterthe key to learn first, because it fixes errors, adds imports and offers language upgrades Why
twistVisual Studio's keysSettings, Keymap, Visual StudioIntelliJ has a Visual Studio keymap, but most people adapt to its own keys Why
twistauto-properties, written by the compilergetters and setters, generated with Cmd+NJava has no properties, so the IDE writes the methods. A record removes most of these methods. Why
twistthe Immediate windowEvaluate Expression, Alt+F8debugging works in much the same way as in Visual Studio, but under different names Why
trapEdit and Continue while debuggingHotSwapreplaces method bodies only, so you must restart if you add a field or change a signature Why
twistRoslyn analyzers and StyleCopError Prone, Checkstyle and SpotBugsseparate tools that you add to the build, and that your build server should run Why

Which IDE, and what is freetwist#

IntelliJ IDEA is one download since version 2025.3. It is free for core Java and Kotlin development. The free download now also includes a Spring Boot project wizard, basic Spring highlighting and a database schema viewer. An Ultimate subscription adds the full Spring and database tooling (as of October 2026).

VS Code with the Red Hat Java and Spring Boot extension packs is a lighter option. You will also meet Eclipse in older organisations. Whichever IDE you choose, the build tool builds and runs the service. The build tool here is Maven. So these commands work, whichever IDE you use:

./mvnw spring-boot:run     # start the service
./mvnw test                # run its tests

./mvnw is the Maven wrapper. These commands do not need an IDE. For more about the Maven wrapper, see the section Five minutes to a running service in the previous chapter.

The project model is differenttrap#

The names moved, and the owner moved too. In Java, the build tool decides how the code is organised, and the IDE reads the files of the build tool.

Visual StudioIntelliJ IDEANote
Solution (.sln)Projectthe top-level thing you open, and it holds every module in the build
Project (.csproj)Moduleeach module has its own pom.xml and produces one JAR
Assembly outputJARbuilt by Maven or Gradle, and the IDE asks the build tool to build it
Solution ExplorerProject tool windowshows the file tree, and it opens with Cmd+1 on macOS, or Alt+1 on Windows and Linux
Package ManagerMaven or Gradle tool windowshows the tree, but you add dependencies by editing pom.xml
Build menuBuild, or the Maven panelthe IDE delegates to the build tool

In Java, a parent pom.xml that lists its modules does the same as a solution file:

<!-- billing/pom.xml: the parent, doing the job of Billing.sln -->
<packaging>pom</packaging>
<modules>
    <module>billing-core</module>   <!-- a folder with its own pom.xml -->
    <module>billing-api</module>    <!-- each module builds one JAR -->
</modules>

<packaging>pom</packaging> says that this file builds nothing itself. The file only lists its modules. Each <module> names a folder with its own pom.xml, and each module builds one Java archive (JAR).

Gotcha

The build tool is the source of truth, not the IDE. When you add a dependency to pom.xml, IntelliJ re-imports the project before it can use the dependency. The re-import is usually automatic. To start it yourself, use the refresh button in the Maven panel. Sometimes a build works in the IDE but fails on mvn clean package. This almost always means that the IDE's view of the project is no longer the same as the build tool's view. Trust the command line.

The key to learn firsttwist#

IntelliJ has a Visual Studio keymap, under Settings, then Keymap. But most people adapt to IntelliJ's own keys. The quick reference lists those keys.

Note

Alt+Enter is like Ctrl+. in Visual Studio, but it does more. It fixes errors, adds imports, adds a missing dependency and generates a missing method. It also offers language upgrades. For example, it can turn an anonymous class into a lambda, or a chain of if statements into a switch expression.

Here is the first of those upgrades, in code that sorts a list of names by length:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Grace", "Ada", "Linus"));

// Before: put the cursor on new Comparator, press Alt+Enter, and choose Replace with lambda.
names.sort(new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.length() - b.length(); }
});

// After the fix:
names.sort((a, b) -> a.length() - b.length());
Reading the code
new Comparator<String>() {

This is called an anonymous class. It is a class with no name, and it is defined and created in one expression. Comparator does the same as IComparer<T> in C#.

(a, b) -> a.length() - b.length()

This is the same comparison, written as a lambda. C# writes =>. Java writes ->. For more about lambdas, see the section Lambdas and method references.

Generating the boilerplate Java expects#

Java has no properties, so getters and setters are real methods that someone has to write. But nobody types these methods. Cmd+N generates constructors, getters, setters, equals, hashCode, toString and delegating methods. Here is a customer class in both languages:

C#: the compiler generates it
public class Customer
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public string Email { get; set; }
}
Java: the IDE generates it
public class Customer {
    private String name;
    private String email;

    // Generated with Cmd+N, then Getter and Setter.
    public String getName()          { return name; }
    public void   setName(String n)  { this.name = n; }
    public String getEmail()         { return email; }
    public void   setEmail(String e) { this.email = e; }
}

getName and setName are ordinary methods that read and write a private field. IntelliJ writes them for you, but they are still code that you read and maintain. Most of that extra code disappears when the type can be a record Java 16. See Records.

Debugging#

Debugging works in much the same way as in Visual Studio, but under different names:

FeatureVisual StudioIntelliJ
Conditional breakpointright-click breakpointright-click breakpoint
Immediate windowImmediateEvaluate Expression, Alt+F8
WatchWatch windowVariables panel, or Add to Watches
Data tipshoverhover
Edit and ContinuesupportedHotSwap, method bodies only
Exception breakpointException SettingsBreakpoints, Java Exception Breakpoints
Attach to processDebug, AttachRun, Attach to Process

The condition of a conditional breakpoint is a Java expression. It is evaluated at the line of the breakpoint, so it can use any variable in scope:

// Right-click the breakpoint, then type the condition:
order.customer().id() == 1042 && order.lines().size() > 10

The condition is ordinary Java. == compares the customer's numeric id, and && joins the two tests. The debugger stops only when both tests are true.

Gotcha

Hot reload is weaker than Edit and Continue. Standard HotSwap replaces method bodies only. If you add a field or change a signature, you must restart. Spring Boot DevTools does a fast restart. The JetBrains Runtime and the paid JRebel do more than standard HotSwap. But do not expect hot reload to work as smoothly as it does in C#.

Static analysis#

In Java, a set of separate, mature tools does the same as Roslyn analyzers. You add these tools to the build. IntelliJ's own inspections are strong by default, and they do roughly the same as ReSharper. But your build server should run these tools:

.NETJavaCatches
Roslyn analyzersError Pronereal bug patterns at compile time
StyleCopCheckstyleformatting and naming
FxCop / analyzersSpotBugsbytecode-level bug patterns
EditorConfigEditorConfigsupported by IntelliJ directly
dotnet formatSpotlessapplies formatting in the build

Error Prone runs inside the compiler, so a bug like this one fails the build instead of reaching code review:

if (amount < 0) {
    // Error Prone reports DeadException: the exception is created but never thrown.
    new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount");
}

The line new IllegalArgumentException(...) creates an exception and then discards it, because the throw is missing. The compiler accepts the line, but Error Prone stops the build.

Check yourself
1
What is the Java equivalent of the solution file, and who owns it?
It is a parent pom.xml that lists the modules. The build tool is the source of truth, not the IDE. So if a build works only in IntelliJ, the IDE's view of the project is no longer the same as the build tool's view.

RunCtrl+F5Ctrl+R
DebugF5Ctrl+D
