Classes, constructors and initialisation#

Language core · Chapter 05· 8 min read

A Java class works almost exactly like a C# class. It has one superclass, it can implement many interfaces, and its constructors can call each other. Most of the differences are only in how the code is written.

KindC#JavaNote
twistclass A : Base, IFooclass A extends Base implements Fooextends names the one superclass, and implements lists the interfaces Why
trapsealed class Invoicefinal class InvoiceJava has a sealed keyword too, and it means something else Why
sameabstract class Discountabstract class DiscountThe keyword and its meaning are the same. No code can create an object of the class directly.
twiststatic class MoneyMatha final class with a private constructorJava has no static classes, so a class that only holds static methods is written this way Why
twiststructrecordJava has no structs. A record compares by value, but it is still an object. Why
twist: this(...)this(...) as the first statementcalls another constructor of the same class Why
twist: base(...)super(...) as the first statementsuper(...) calls the superclass constructor. Since Java 25, checks may come before the call. Why
twiststatic Foo() { }static { }a static initialiser block, which runs once, the first time the class is used Why
twistfield initialiserfield initialiserC# runs a field initialiser before the base constructor. Java runs it after super() returns. Why
twistno equivalentinstance initialiser { }a bare block in the class body, which runs after super() and before each constructor body Why
twistoverride@Override@Override is an annotation that the compiler checks. It is optional, but Java developers always write it. Why
twistToString()toString()called by string concatenation and by loggers to print the object Why
twistEquals(object)equals(Object)equals compares values, but == on two objects compares references Why
twistGetHashCode()hashCode()must return the same value for two objects that are equal according to equals Why
twistGetType()getClass()returns a Class object, which is like a System.Type object in C# Why
twistMemberwiseClone()clone()a shallow copy that skips constructors, so use a copy constructor instead Why
twist~Money()finalize()deprecated for removal since Java 18, so release resources with try-with-resources Why
twistMonitor.Wait / Monitor.Pulsewait() / notify()Every Java object has these methods. They are a 1990s API, so use java.util.concurrent. Why

Declarationtwist#

ServiceBase is a base class that the team wrote.

C#
public class OrderService : ServiceBase, IDisposable
{
    public void Dispose() { }
}

public sealed class Invoice { }
public abstract class Discount { }
public static class MoneyMath { }
Java 25
public class OrderService extends ServiceBase
        implements AutoCloseable {
    @Override public void close() { }
}

public final class Invoice { }
public abstract class Discount { }
// Java has no static classes; see below.
Reading the code
extends ServiceBase

extends names the superclass. C# writes a colon there. A class has only one superclass, as in C#.

implements AutoCloseable

implements lists the interfaces. AutoCloseable does the same as IDisposable in C#. It has one method, close(). The Java form of using is called try-with-resources. It calls close() at the end of the block.

@Override public void close() { }

@Override does the same as the override keyword in C#. Java also writes @Override on a method that implements an interface method.

public final class Invoice

final means that no class may extend Invoice, like sealed in C#.

The other declaration rules are in this table:

C#JavaNote
: Baseextends Basea class has only one superclass, as in C#
: IFooimplements Fooa class may implement many interfaces, as in C#
sealed classfinal classno class can extend a final class, and the Java keyword sealed means something else
abstract classabstract classThe keyword and its meaning are the same. The class cannot be instantiated.
static classfinal class + private constructorJava has no static classes, so this form is the usual replacement
partial classno equivalentone class cannot be split across files, so use composition or generated code
internal classpackage-private (no keyword)visible only to the same package, not to the whole JAR
nested classstatic nested classa non-static nested class also holds a hidden reference to its outer object

The row about nested classes is a trap. See Inner classes capture the outer instance.

C# refresherPartial classes: one class split across filesC# 2

A C# partial class is declared in several files and compiled as one class. The usual reason is to keep generated code and hand-written code in separate files.

// Customer.g.cs, generated
public partial class Customer { public string Name { get; set; } = ""; }

// Customer.cs, written by hand
public partial class Customer { public bool IsVip => Name.StartsWith("VIP"); }

sealed in C# is final in Javatrap#

PredictA class marked sealed, as in C##
Does this compile?
public sealed class Invoice { }
Show the answer
No: sealed class must have subclasses

In Java, a sealed class says which types may extend it. No other type may extend the class. Invoice names no types, so it does not compile. To learn what sealed is used for, see the section Sealed types.

Write public final class Invoice { }.

No static classestwist#

static class

Java has no static classes. A class that only holds static helper methods is usually written as a final class with a private constructor. java.util.Objects and java.util.Collections are written this way, and so is this class:

public final class MoneyMath {
    private MoneyMath() { throw new AssertionError("no instances"); }

    public static BigDecimal round(BigDecimal v) {
        return v.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    }
}

The private constructor stops other code from creating a MoneyMath. The AssertionError stops the class itself from creating a MoneyMath by mistake. Some code uses an interface with only static methods instead. But an interface shows less clearly what you mean, because an interface exists to be implemented.

No structstwist#

struct

Java has no structs either. Every type that you declare is a class, and a variable holds a reference to an object. When you want a small value that compares by its contents, the closest type is a record. Here is a discount percentage in both languages:

C#
public readonly record struct Percentage(decimal Value);
Java 25
public record Percentage(BigDecimal value) { }

Both types compare by value. You cannot change a Percentage after it is created, in C# or in Java. But the Java record is still an object. It is on the heap, and a variable holds a reference to it. When you pass a Java record, the reference is copied, not the object. When you pass a C# struct, the struct itself is copied. For more about records, see the chapter Records.

Constructors and chainingtwist#

C#
public class ExpressOrder : Order
{
    public ExpressOrder(Customer customer)
        : this(customer, []) { }

    public ExpressOrder(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines)
        : base(customer, lines) { }
}
Java 25
public class ExpressOrder extends Order {

    public ExpressOrder(Customer customer) {
        this(customer, List.of());
    }

    public ExpressOrder(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        super(customer, lines);
    }
}
Reading the code
this(customer, List.of());

This line calls the other constructor of the same class, like : this(...) in C#. List.of() makes an empty list, like the [] on the C# side.

super(customer, lines);

This line calls the constructor of the superclass Order, like : base(...) in C#.

Gotcha

For most of Java's history, this(...) or super(...) had to be the first statement of a constructor. So a constructor could not check an argument before the call. Java 25 finalised flexible constructor bodies Java 25. Now statements may come before the call, as long as they do not use the object being built:

public ExpressOrder(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines) {
    if (lines.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no lines");  // legal since Java 25
    super(customer, lines);
}

On Java 21 and earlier, the if line does not compile. The workaround on those versions is a private static helper method that is called inside the argument, as in super(customer, requireLines(lines)). A lot of existing code has this workaround.

Initialiser blocks#

Java has two kinds of initialiser block. Both kinds run at predictable points. Both kinds appear in real code, particularly in older code and in static registries. In this example, a registry maps a file format to the object that handles the format. Handler is an interface that the team wrote, and JsonHandler is one implementation of Handler.

public class Registry {

    private static final Map<String, Handler> HANDLERS;

    static {
        HANDLERS = new HashMap<>();
        HANDLERS.put("json", new JsonHandler());
    }

    private final long created;

    {
        created = System.nanoTime();
    }

    public Registry() { }
}
Reading the code
private static final Map<String, Handler> HANDLERS;

This line declares a class-level constant. The constant is static because it belongs to the class. It is final because it is assigned once, in the block below.

static {

This block is called a static initialiser. It runs once, the first time the class is used, like a static constructor in C#. A class can have several static initialisers, and they run from top to bottom.

created = System.nanoTime();

This line is inside the bare { } block, which is called an instance initialiser. The block runs before every constructor body, just after super(). An instance initialiser is rare, because a constructor is usually clearer.

A field initialiser runs at the same point as an instance initialiser, after super() returns. An example of a field initialiser is private String season = "winter sale";. C# runs the field initialisers of a subclass before the base constructor. So when a Java superclass constructor calls an overridden method, the method sees the fields of the subclass before they are set. For an example, see this prediction.

Note

Class initialisation is lazy and thread-safe, as it is in C#. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) guarantees that the static initialiser of a class runs exactly once, before any static member is read. So a static field that is set in a static initialiser is a safe way to create one shared object. It is safe even when many threads start at the same time.

Every class extends Object#

As in C#, every class inherits from a root class, and a class overrides a few methods of the root class. In Java, the root class is Object. The method names start with a lower-case letter. The rules about these methods are kept by convention, and the compiler does not check them. Here is Money, which is an amount in a currency. It overrides the three methods that you will write most often:

C#
public class Money(decimal amount, string currency)
{
    public decimal Amount { get; } = amount;
    public string Currency { get; } = currency;

    public override string ToString() => $"{Amount} {Currency}";
    public override bool Equals(object? o) =>
        o is Money m && Amount == m.Amount && Currency == m.Currency;
    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Amount, Currency);
}

string kind = money.GetType().Name;  // "Money"
Java 25
public class Money {
    private final BigDecimal amount;
    private final String currency;

    public Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
        this.amount = amount;
        this.currency = currency;
    }

    @Override public String toString() { return amount + " " + currency; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Money m
            && amount.equals(m.amount) && currency.equals(m.currency);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(amount, currency); }
}

String kind = money.getClass().getSimpleName();  // "Money"
Reading the code
@Override public String toString()

@Override is an annotation. It marks a method as a replacement for an inherited method, and the compiler checks that the method really replaces one. @Override does the same as the override keyword in C#, but Java does not require it.

o instanceof Money m

This expression tests the type and names the result in one step, like o is Money m in C#. It is called a type pattern.

amount.equals(m.amount)

equals compares values. In Java, == on two objects compares references, even for BigDecimal. equals on a BigDecimal also compares the number of decimal places. To learn why that matters for money, see Equality, hashing and comparison.

Objects.hash(amount, currency)

This call combines the fields into one hash code, like HashCode.Combine in C#.

money.getClass().getSimpleName()

getClass() returns the class of the object. The result is like a System.Type in C#. getSimpleName() gives the name of the class without the package.

In practice, you rarely write these three methods yourself. A record generates all three methods from its fields. See Records.

Object has three more methods that you should recognise and not call. finalize() has been deprecated for removal since Java 18. To release resources, use try-with-resources. wait() and notify() exist on every object. The closest matches in C# are Monitor.Wait and Monitor.Pulse. wait() and notify() are a 1990s API, so use java.util.concurrent. See wait, notify and notifyAll.

Legacyclone() and Cloneable

Java's cloning mechanism is widely considered a design mistake. Cloneable is a marker interface, and it has no clone method. The default implementation of clone makes a shallow copy of the fields and skips constructors. You will see cloning in existing code. Prefer a copy constructor, a static factory, or a record with a with-style method.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
public static class OrderRules
{
    public static bool IsSmall(List<OrderLine> lines) => lines.Count <= 3;
}
public final class OrderRules {
    private OrderRules() { }

    public static boolean isSmall(List<OrderLine> lines) {
        return lines.size() <= 3;
    }
}

Java has no static classes. final stops subclasses. The private constructor is the part that is most often forgotten. Without the private constructor, any code can write new OrderRules().

2
An expert asksOlder Java code often calls a private static helper inside super(...), as in super(customer, requireLines(lines)). Why, and what changed in Java 25?
On Java 21 and earlier, super(...) must be the first statement of a constructor, so the only place for a check is inside the argument. Java 25 allows statements before the call, as long as they do not use the object being built.
Next · Language core06Access modifiers and packages6 min

Access modifiers and packages#

Language core · Chapter 06· 6 min read

The access keywords of Java look like the access keywords of C#. A package is like a namespace in C#. It is a named group of classes, and it is tied to a folder. In C#, the assembly decides who has access. In Java, the package decides it.

KindC#JavaNote
sameprivate Money total;private Money total;the same, but in Java you must write private to get it
trapdecimal fee; with no keywordBigDecimal fee; with no keywordprivate in C#, but package-private in Java, so the whole package can change it Why
trapprotected, for subclasses onlyprotected, which also opens the packageJava cannot say subclasses only. With protected, the whole package gets access too. Why
twistnamespace Acme.Orders;package com.acme.orders;a package name is lower-case, is a reversed domain, and matches the folders Why
trapAcme.Orders.Internal, inside Acme.Orderscom.acme.orders.internal, a package of its ownpackages do not nest, so it sees no package-private member of com.acme.orders Why
twistusing System.Text;import java.util.List;Java imports types, not namespaces, and has no aliases Why
twistusing static System.Math;import static java.lang.Math.*;names one member, or all of a type's static members with .* Why
twistinternal, for the whole assemblyno keyword, for one packageJava has no internal, and package-private is the nearest level Why
twist[InternalsVisibleTo]tests in the same packagetests under src/test/java declare the package they test Why
twistAcme.Billing.Apicom.acme.billing.apithe reversed domain stops classes from different vendors colliding Why

The mappingtrap#

One class can show all four of Java's access levels:

package com.acme.billing;

public class Invoice {
    private Money total;                      // this class only
    void attach(Payment payment) { }          // no keyword: this package only
    protected void recalculate() { }          // this package, and subclasses anywhere
    public Money total() { return total; }    // everyone
}

attach has no keyword, so it is package-private. This means that every class in the same package can use it, and no other class can. C# has no such level. To make a field private, you must write private, as the code does for total.

Gotcha

Forgetting a modifier is not the same as writing private. Your C# habit gives exactly the wrong result. See No modifier means package-private.

The table lists the four access levels of Java, from widest to narrowest, with the nearest C# keyword for each level:

Java modifierVisible toClosest C#
publiceveryonepublic
protectedpackage + subclasses anywhereno exact equal
(none)the same package onlyno equal, package-private
privatethe declaring classprivate
Gotcha

protected is not a narrowing of public in Java the way you expect. protected also gives access to the whole package. For an example, see this prediction. Java cannot express “subclasses only”, for a field or for a method. The package is the boundary, so keep unrelated classes out of the package.

Packages are not namespacestwist#

A C# namespace is a logical grouping. It does not have to match the folder layout, and one file can declare several namespaces. A Java package is tied to folders. Every build tool and IDE expects the package to match the folder that the file is in. The compiled class files must be in matching folders, because the Java runtime uses the folders to find the class files. See the chapter How Java runs your code.

C#
// Anywhere/AtAll/OrderService.cs
namespace Acme.Orders;

public class OrderService { }
Java 25
// src/main/java/com/acme/orders/OrderService.java
package com.acme.orders;

public class OrderService { }

The Java file declares package com.acme.orders;. The file is in the folders com/acme/orders/, under src/main/java. Maven looks for source code in src/main/java.

A package inside a packagetrap#

PredictA package-private field, read from a sub-package#
Does this compile?
// com/acme/orders/Order.java
package com.acme.orders;

public class Order { long id; }

// com/acme/orders/internal/Audit.java
package com.acme.orders.internal;

import com.acme.orders.Order;

class Audit {
    long idOf(Order order) { return order.id; }
}
Show the answer
No: id is not public in Order; cannot be accessed from outside package

Packages do not nest. com.acme.orders and com.acme.orders.internal look nested in the IDE's tree. But to the compiler they are two unrelated packages. A package-private member of com.acme.orders is not visible to com.acme.orders.internal.

In C#, Acme.Orders.Internal can see internal members of Acme.Orders, because the two namespaces share an assembly. The two Java packages share nothing. Code that needs a package-private member must be in the same package as that member.

Imports#

Imports work almost like using directives in C#, with three differences. Java imports types, not namespaces. Java has no import aliases. And Java imports nothing for the whole project.

C#JavaNote
using System;import java.util.List;Java imports types, not namespaces
using System.Collections.Generic;import java.util.*;A C# using always takes a whole namespace. Java writes .* to take a whole package.
using RX = System.Text.RegularExpressions;no alias importswhen two types clash, write one of them with its full package name instead
global usingno equivalenteach file lists its own imports, but the IDE adds them for you
implicit usingsjava.lang is always importedjava.lang is imported everywhere. It contains types such as String, Object and Integer.

Here are the common forms side by side:

C#
global using System.Linq;  // every file in the project
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;  // a namespace
using static System.Math;  // a type's static members
using Rx = System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex;

var r = new Rx("a+");
var m = Max(1, 2);
Java 25
import java.util.*;  // every type in java.util
import java.util.regex.Pattern;  // one type
import static java.lang.Math.max;  // one static member

var p = Pattern.compile("a+");
int m = max(1, 2);
java.sql.Date d = null;  // no alias: a clashing name is written in full
Reading the code
import java.util.*;

This line imports every type in java.util. It does not import the types in the packages below java.util, such as java.util.regex, because packages do not nest.

import static java.lang.Math.max;

This is a static import, like using static in C#. It imports one static method, so max(1, 2) needs no class name. import static java.lang.Math.*; imports every static member of Math.

java.sql.Date d = null;

Java has no import aliases. Sometimes two types share a name, such as java.util.Date and java.sql.Date. Then you write one of them with its full package name every time.

Note

Java 25 added module import declarations Java 25. An example is import module java.base;. A module import declaration imports every exported package of a module at once. This is useful for scripts, but it is usually too broad for production code.

There is no internal#

The missing internal is a real gap, and it affects how Java libraries are designed. C# gives you an access level for the whole assembly, and InternalsVisibleTo for tests. The options in Java are weaker. The strongest option is the Java Platform Module System (JPMS). It hides whole packages, not single classes. The table lists the options:

GoalJava approachCost
Hide from other packageskeep it package-privatetests must share the package
Hide from other JARsJPMS module, do not exportall-or-nothing per package
Signal do not usename the package .internalconvention only, not enforced
Grant test accessput tests in the same packagestandard practice

Remember the last row. Java tests are normally in the same package as the code they test. The tests are under src/test/java, not under src/main/java. So the tests get package-private access, and they need nothing like InternalsVisibleTo. For the module system, see the chapter Modules, JPMS and the missing internal.

C# refresherInternalsVisibleTo: letting a test project see internal membersC# 2
// in the production project
[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("Billing.Tests")]

internal static class InvoiceNumbers { ... }   // Billing.Tests may now call it
// src/main/java/com/acme/billing/InvoiceNumbers.java
package com.acme.billing;
class InvoiceNumbers {                       // no modifier: package-private
    static String next() { ... }
}

// src/test/java/com/acme/billing/InvoiceNumbersTest.java
package com.acme.billing;                    // same package, so the test can see it
class InvoiceNumbersTest {
    @Test void startsWithInv() { assertTrue(InvoiceNumbers.next().startsWith("INV")); }
}

InvoiceNumbers has no access keyword, so only code in com.acme.billing can use it. The test is under src/test/java, but it declares the same package. So the test can call InvoiceNumbers.next() directly.

Here is the whole mapping, starting from the C# keywords that you know:

C# modifierVisible toClosest Java
publiceveryonepublic
protectedsubclasses onlyno exact equal (Java's is wider)
internalthe assemblypackage-private, roughly
protected internalassembly or subclassesprotected, roughly
private protectedsubclasses in the assemblyno equal
privatethe declaring typeprivate
C# refresherC# access modifiers: internal, protected internal and private protectedC# 7

internal opens a member to the whole assembly. The combined modifiers use the assembly boundary to change protected. protected internal makes protected wider. private protected makes protected narrower.

public class Account
{
    internal decimal Limit;           // any code in this assembly
    protected internal decimal Fee;   // subclasses anywhere, or any code in this assembly
    private protected decimal Rate;   // subclasses, but only those in this assembly
}

Package naming#

A package name is a reversed domain name, all lower-case, with no underscores. An example is com.acme.billing.api. The convention is universal, and the tools assume it. Unlike in C#, the company prefix is not decoration. It exists so that Java archive (JAR) files from different vendors never collide on the classpath.

// src/main/java/com/acme/billing/api/InvoiceController.java
package com.acme.billing.api;    // reverse domain, lowercase, and it matches the folders

The folders under src/main/java follow the package name. The folders are com/acme/billing/api, with one folder for each part of the name.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this file in Java: 
namespace Acme.Billing;

internal class InvoiceNumbers
{
    int counter;

    public string Next() => "INV-" + ++counter;
}
package com.acme.billing;

class InvoiceNumbers {
    private int counter;

    public String next() { return "INV-" + ++counter; }
}

You must write private on the field. With no keyword, every class in com.acme.billing could change the field. The class has no keyword on purpose. Package-private is the nearest level that Java has to internal.

2
An expert asksWhy are Java tests in the same package as the code they test?
Java has no internal and nothing like InternalsVisibleTo. A test under src/test/java can declare the same package as the code that it tests. Then the test gets package-private access. So the code can stay hidden from every other package.
Next · Language core07Interfaces, abstract classes and sealing8 min

Interfaces, abstract classes and sealing#

Language core · Chapter 07· 8 min read

Java interfaces and abstract classes work almost like interfaces and abstract classes in C#. Java adds sealed types. A sealed type is an interface or a class that names every type that may extend it. So the compiler can check that a switch covers all of these types.

KindC#JavaNote
twistinterface IPriceLookupinterface PriceLookupJava interface names have no I prefix Why
twistdefault interface methoddefault boolean has(...) { ... }an interface method with a body, and every implementing class inherits it Why
twistIEnumerable<out T>List<? extends T>Java has no in or out, so you write a wildcard where the type is used Why
twistconst int MaxLines = 50; in an interfaceint MAX_LINES = 50;no keyword is needed, because every interface field is public, static and final Why
samea method that implements an interfacepublic Money find(String productId)the method needs public in both languages, and C# reports CS0737 without it Why
twistvoid ILogger.Log(string m)no equivalentone public method serves every interface that declares that signature Why
twistevent Action<Order> PlacedList<Consumer<Order>> plus onPlaced(...)Java has no events, so keep a list of listeners instead Why
twistabstract record Payment plus derived recordssealed interface Payment permits Card, BankTransfer, Vouchera closed set of types, so the compiler knows every kind Why
twista switch ending in a discard arma switch with no defaultover a sealed type, Java checks that every kind is handled, but C# only warns (CS8509) Why
newno equivalentfinal, sealed or non-sealedeach permitted type says whether its own branch stays closed Why
twistno equivalentpermits left outwhen every subtype is in the same file, the compiler finds them without a permits list Why
sameabstract class with abstract methodsabstract class with abstract methodsthe same keywords and the same meaning as in C# Why
trapvirtualno keyword, because every method is virtualwrite final to stop a method being overridden Why
twistoverride@Override@Override is an annotation that the compiler checks. It is optional, but always write it. Why

Interfacestwist#

Both versions use a class called EmptyLookup. This class finds nothing, and its code is not shown.

C#
public interface IPriceLookup
{
    Money? Find(string productId);

    // This is a default interface method.
    // Its default method body is used unless a class overrides it.
    bool Has(string productId) => Find(productId) is not null;

    // Interfaces may have static members.
    static IPriceLookup Empty => new EmptyLookup();

    // And private helpers.
    private static void Log(string m) { }
}
Java 25
public interface PriceLookup {
    Money find(String productId);

    // This method has a default body.
    default boolean has(String productId) {
        return find(productId) != null;
    }

    // Interfaces may have static methods.
    static PriceLookup empty() {
        return new EmptyLookup();
    }

    // And private helpers.
    private void log(String m) { }
}
Reading the code
Money find(String productId);

The return type has no ?. Java has no nullable reference types, so any reference may be null. For what to do about null, see the chapter Nullability: Optional and JSpecify.

default boolean has(String productId)

default gives an interface method a body, like a default interface method in C#. Every class that implements PriceLookup gets this method, and may override it.

static PriceLookup empty()

This is a static method on the interface. You call it as PriceLookup.empty().

private void log(String m)

This is a private helper. Only the methods of the interface itself can call it.

The table shows when each feature arrived, and what C# has that Java does not have:

FeatureC#Java
Default method bodyC# 8Java 8
Static methodC# 8Java 8
Private methodC# 8Java 9
Constant fieldyes, since C# 8yes, implicitly public static final
Fieldsstatic fields only, since C# 8no (constants only)
Explicit implementationyesno
Generic variance on the interfaceyes, in/outno, use-site only

Variance, and constants in an interface#

C# refresherGeneric variance on the interface: in and outC# 4

A C# interface can promise that it only produces T. It says this with out. Or it can promise that it only consumes T, with in. Because of out, the compiler accepts an IEnumerable<string> where an IEnumerable<object> is expected.

interface IProducer<out T> { T Next(); }
interface IConsumer<in T>  { void Take(T item); }

IEnumerable<object> items = new List<string>();   // allowed by IEnumerable<out T>

Action<object> print = o => Console.WriteLine(o);
Action<string> printText = print;                 // allowed by Action<in T>

Java has no variance on the declaration. Java says the same thing in the place where the type is used, with a wildcard. For example, a parameter of type List<? extends Number> accepts a List<Integer>. See Variance is at the use site.

C# refresherConstant fields and static fields in an interfaceC# 8

Since C# 8, an interface can have a constant and a static field. An instance field is still an error.

interface ILimits
{
    const int MaxLines = 50;     // a constant
    static int Counter = 1;      // a static field, which code can reassign
}

ILimits.Counter++;               // compiles
Gotcha

Every field in an interface is implicitly public static final. You cannot declare instance state, and you cannot declare a field that can be reassigned:

public interface Limits {
    int MAX_LINES = 50;      // a constant, read as Limits.MAX_LINES
}

Older code sometimes uses a “constant interface”. Classes implement this interface only to inherit constants such as MAX_LINES. That is a known mistake. Put constants in a final class or an enum instead.

Implementing an interface methodtwist#

An implementing method with no access modifier

This does not compile in C# or in Java. A method that implements an interface method must be public. C# reports CS0737. The Java compiler reports the same problem in other words.

find(String) in EmptyLookup cannot implement find(String) in PriceLookup attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public#
Means
A method declared in an interface is public, although it has no keyword. In a class, no keyword means package-private. An implementing method may not be less visible than the method that it implements.
Fix
Write public Money find(String productId).
What triggers it
interface PriceLookup {
    Money find(String productId);
}

class EmptyLookup implements PriceLookup {
    Money find(String productId) { return null; }     // no public
}

No explicit interface implementationtwist#

C# refresherExplicit interface implementationC# 1

An explicit implementation is a member that is implemented for one interface only. You can call it through that interface. You cannot call it through the class.

interface ILogger { void Log(string m); }

class FileLog : ILogger
{
    void ILogger.Log(string m) { }       // no access modifier
}

new FileLog().Log("x");                  // does not compile
((ILogger)new FileLog()).Log("x");       // compiles
Explicit interface implementation

In C#, you can implement the same method signature separately for two interfaces. You can also hide a member, so that it is not among the public members of the class. You cannot do these things in Java. If two interfaces declare the same signature, one method implements the signature for both interfaces, and that method is always public:

interface Printer { void close(); }
interface Channel { void close(); }

class Device implements Printer, Channel {
    public void close() { }              // one method serves both, and it must be public
}

One close() method serves both interfaces. Now suppose that two interfaces, A and B, both give the same method a default body. Then the class must override the method and choose one default body explicitly:

public class Both implements A, B {
    @Override public String name() {
        return A.super.name();     // pick a specific default
    }
}

A.super.name() calls the default version of name() in interface A. In C#, base.Name() calls the version of a base class in a similar way.

No eventstwist#

event

Java has no event keyword. The usual replacement is a list of listeners. Each listener is an object with one method to call. In both versions below, service is an OrderService:

C#
public class OrderService
{
    public event Action<Order>? Placed;

    public void Place(Order order)
    {
        Placed?.Invoke(order);
    }
}

service.Placed += order => Console.WriteLine(order.Id);
Java 25
public class OrderService {
    private final List<Consumer<Order>> placedListeners = new ArrayList<>();

    public void onPlaced(Consumer<Order> listener) { placedListeners.add(listener); }

    public void place(Order order) {
        placedListeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(order));
    }
}

service.onPlaced(order -> System.out.println(order.id()));
Reading the code
private final List<Consumer<Order>> placedListeners

A list of listeners replaces the event. Consumer<Order> is a built-in functional interface. This is an interface with one method. Here the method is accept, which takes an Order and returns nothing. Consumer<Order> does the same as Action<Order> in C#.

placedListeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(order));

This line calls every listener, one after another, as Placed?.Invoke(order) does in C#.

service.onPlaced(order -> System.out.println(order.id()));

This line subscribes with a lambda. C# writes += to subscribe. Spring applications often use application events for this instead. See Application events.

Sealed types: Java's discriminated unionstwist#

sealed means a different thing in each language. For an example, see this prediction. The table shows what each language writes:

IntentC#Java
Cannot be extended at allsealed classfinal class
Only named types may extendno equivalentsealed interface / sealed class

From Java 17, an interface can be sealed. A sealed interface lists its complete set of subtypes. Here are three kinds of payment:

public sealed interface Payment
        permits Card, BankTransfer, Voucher {
}

public record Card(String last4) implements Payment { }
public record BankTransfer(String iban) implements Payment { }
public record Voucher(String code) implements Payment { }
Reading the code
permits Card, BankTransfer, Voucher

The complete list comes after permits. The compiler rejects any other class that implements Payment. Each permitted type must itself choose one of three keywords. final ends the branch. sealed names a closed set of its own. non-sealed opens the branch again. See The rules for permits.

public record Card(String last4) implements Payment { }

Each kind is a record. A record is a short class that only holds data. A record is final already, so it needs no keyword.

Because the set is closed, a switch over a Payment needs no default arm. For an example, see No default over a sealed type.

Overriding needs no keywordtrap#

PredictA subclass declares a method its superclass already has#
What does this print?
class Discount {
    String describe() { return "discount"; }
    String label() { return "10% " + describe(); }
}

class SeasonalDiscount extends Discount {
    String describe() { return "winter sale"; }
}

System.out.println(new SeasonalDiscount().label());
Show the answer
10% winter sale

Every Java method can be overridden unless it is marked final. A method in a subclass with the same name and parameters overrides the method of the superclass. Java needs no keyword for this, and it gives no warning.

The same classes in C#, with the methods made public, print 10% discount. In C#, the new method only hides the old method, and the compiler warns with CS0108.

Mark a method final when overriding it would break the class. Write @Override on every method that is meant to override another method.

Gotcha

Java methods are virtual by default. So a subclass can override a method that you did not plan as an extension point, unless you mark the method final. See An overridable method called from a constructor.

Abstract classestwist#

In everything important, abstract classes in Java are the same as abstract classes in C#. You need an abstract class when the type has state or constructors. Otherwise, prefer an interface with default methods.

C#Java
abstract class Cabstract class C
abstract void M();abstract void m();
override void M()@Override void m()
virtual by opt-invirtual by default, use final to opt out
new (member hiding)no equivalent for methods

Here is a discount with one method of each kind:

C#
public abstract class Discount
{
    public abstract decimal Amount(decimal total);  // must be overridden
    public virtual string Describe() => "discount";  // may be overridden
    public string Code() => "D";  // cannot be overridden
}

public class TenPercent : Discount
{
    public override decimal Amount(decimal total) => total * 0.10m;
}
Java 25
public abstract class Discount {
    public abstract BigDecimal amount(BigDecimal total);  // must be overridden
    public String describe() { return "discount"; }  // may be: no keyword needed
    public final String code() { return "D"; }  // final: cannot be overridden
}

public class TenPercent extends Discount {
    @Override public BigDecimal amount(BigDecimal total) {
        return total.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.10"));
    }
}
Reading the code
public String describe() { return "discount"; }

This method has no keyword, and yet any subclass may override it. In C#, you must write virtual to allow that.

public final String code()

final on a method forbids overriding. The method is then like a C# method without virtual.

@Override public BigDecimal amount

The @Override annotation is optional, but always write it. If you mistype the method signature, the compiler then reports an error. Without @Override, the mistyped method becomes a new method, and nothing warns you.

The rules for permits#

The permitted subtypes of a sealed type follow four rules:

RuleDetail
Same module or packagepermitted subtypes must be in the same module, or same package if unnamed
Every subtype must chooseit must be final, sealed, or non-sealed
permits may be omittedif all subtypes are in the same file
non-sealedreopens the hierarchy for that branch

Here a sealed interface keeps one branch closed and leaves another open:

public sealed interface Event permits UserEvent, SystemEvent { }

public final class UserEvent implements Event { }        // closed
public non-sealed class SystemEvent implements Event { } // anyone may extend this branch

UserEvent is final, so nothing may extend it. SystemEvent is non-sealed, so any class may extend it. A switch case for SystemEvent also covers those subclasses.

Note

This is one of the few places where Java is ahead of C#. Sealed interfaces are available from Java 17. Pattern matching in switch is available from Java 21. Together they give you a closed set of types that the compiler checks. To get the same safety, C# developers usually need a library such as OneOf, or a visitor pattern. See Sealed types and pattern matching.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
public interface IPriceLookup
{
    Money? Find(string productId);

    bool Has(string productId) => Find(productId) is not null;
}

public class EmptyLookup : IPriceLookup
{
    public Money? Find(string productId) => null;
}
public interface PriceLookup {
    Money find(String productId);

    default boolean has(String productId) {
        return find(productId) != null;
    }
}

public class EmptyLookup implements PriceLookup {
    @Override public Money find(String productId) { return null; }
}

The word that is easiest to forget is default. Without default, the compiler rejects the body with the message interface abstract methods cannot have body.

2
An expert asksA sealed interface permits a class, and the compiler demands that the class be final, sealed or non-sealed. Why?
The set of types under a sealed interface stays closed only if every branch says how it continues. final ends the branch. sealed names the next closed set. non-sealed opens the branch again on purpose. A record needs no keyword, because a record is final already.

Methods and parameters#

Language core · Chapter 08· 9 min read· Quick reference

A Java method looks like a C# method, but most of the parameter features of C# are missing. For a job that C# does with a keyword, Java uses an overload, a return value or a helper class. Java has lambdas too, but it uses interfaces in place of delegates.

KindC#JavaNote
twistint limit = 100an overload for each shorter callJava has no optional parameters, so a shorter overload calls the full one Why
twistCountOrders("paid", limit: 50)a builder: .timeout(...).build()Java has no named arguments, so a builder sets one value per call Why
twista parameter name, seen by reflectionarg0, unless compiled with -parametersFrameworks match values by parameter name. Spring Boot's parent POM and its Gradle plugin set the flag. Why
twistint.TryParse(s, out var value)OptionalInt parsed = parseQuantity(s)everything is passed by value, even an object reference, so a method gives a result as its return value Why
twistref parameters, or a tuplerecord Pair(int a, int b) { }a method returns several results together in one record Why
twistparams object[] argsObject... argsvarargs are the same idea as params, and they must also be the last parameter Why
twistname.IsBlank()Strings.isBlank(name)Java has no extension methods, so a static helper takes the value Why
twistcalls chained left to rightcalls nested inside-outa static helper wraps its argument, but streams are the exception Why
twistprice * quantity + shippingprice.multiply(quantity).add(shipping)Java has no operator overloading, so BigDecimal uses methods Why
twistdelegate decimal PriceRule(Order o);interface PriceRule { BigDecimal apply(Order o); }a functional interface has one method, and a lambda can implement that method Why
twistx => x + 1x -> x + 1the lambda is the same, but Java writes the arrow as -> instead of => Why
twist(x, y) => x + y(x, y) -> x + yseveral parameters go in brackets, exactly as in C# Why
twist() => Foo()() -> foo()Empty brackets mean that there are no parameters. Supplier<T> does the same as Func<T> in C#. Why
twistFoo.Bar (method group)Foo::barpasses the method itself as a lambda Why
twist() => new Foo()Foo::newpasses the constructor as a factory function Why
twistFunc<int, string>Function<Integer, String>primitives must be boxed in a generic Why
twistAction<T>Consumer<T>a function that takes a T and returns nothing Why
twistshow(42)show.apply(42)Call the one method of the interface. The method is apply on a Function and accept on a Consumer. Why
samePredicate<T>Predicate<T>The name and the meaning are the same. A Predicate takes a T and returns a boolean. Why
trapa lambda that changes a locala lambda that only reads localsa captured local must never be reassigned, so count with an AtomicInteger Why

Signaturestwist#

countOrders has an optional flag and an optional limit. Java writes one overload for each shorter call. This set of overloads is called an overload ladder.

C#
public int CountOrders(
    string filter,
    bool caseSensitive = false,
    int limit = 100)
{
    ...
}

var n = CountOrders("paid", limit: 50);
Java 25
public int countOrders(String filter) {
    return countOrders(filter, false, 100);
}
public int countOrders(String filter, boolean caseSensitive) {
    return countOrders(filter, caseSensitive, 100);
}
public int countOrders(String filter, boolean caseSensitive, int limit) {
    ...
}

int n = countOrders("paid", false, 50);  // no named arguments
Reading the code
return countOrders(filter, false, 100);

Each shorter overload adds the missing values and calls the full version. The full version does the real work.

int n = countOrders("paid", false, 50);

Java has no named arguments. So you pass every value in order, up to the value that you want to set. Here you must write false only because the limit comes after it.

Builders stand in for named argumentstwist#

Optional and named parameters

Java has no optional parameters and no named parameters. These are the three replacements, in order of preference:

  • Overload ladder. Each shorter overload calls the overload with every parameter. This is fine for two or three parameters.
  • Builder. This is the standard answer when there are more parameters. A builder takes more code to write, but it is pleasant to call. Most libraries offer builders.
  • A parameter object. Use one object for all the arguments when the arguments belong together. The object is usually a record.
// A builder is the usual replacement for named and optional arguments.
var req = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .uri(URI.create("https://example.com"))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .header("Accept", "application/json")
        .GET()
        .build();
Reading the code
HttpRequest.newBuilder()

This call starts a builder. A builder is an object that you set up one value at a time. At the end, the builder creates the real object. HttpRequest belongs to the HTTP client that is built into the Java Development Kit (JDK).

.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))

Each method sets one named value. A value that you do not set keeps its default.

.build();

This call creates the finished HttpRequest from all the values that were set.

Parameter names and the -parameters flag#

Gotcha

Parameter names are not in the compiled output by default. Reflection sees arg0, arg1, unless the class was compiled with the -parameters flag:

javac -parameters OrderService.java

That matters when a framework matches values to parameters by name. Spring does this for some constructor injection and request binding.

Spring Boot sets the -parameters flag for you. With Maven, the parent Project Object Model (POM) file of Spring Boot sets the flag. With Gradle, the Spring Boot plugin sets the flag. A build that you set up yourself may not set the flag. The same is true for a build that does not use the parent POM.

No ref, no outtwist#

Java passes every argument by value. An object reference is passed by value too. This means that a method can change the object that the reference points at. But the method cannot make the caller's variable point at another object. So a method gives its result to the caller as the return value:

C#
if (int.TryParse(s, out var value))
{
    Use(value);
}
Java 25
// Return a value that can be empty, instead of an out parameter.
OptionalInt parsed = parseQuantity(s);
if (parsed.isPresent()) {
    use(parsed.getAsInt());
}
Reading the code
OptionalInt parsed = parseQuantity(s);

parseQuantity is a small helper that you would write yourself. It returns an empty OptionalInt when the text is not a number. Java's own method Integer.parseInt throws a NumberFormatException in that case. OptionalInt is the int version of Optional. An OptionalInt is a box that holds a value or nothing.

parsed.getAsInt()

This call takes the number out, after isPresent() has confirmed that there is a number. Use and use represent the code that you would write next.

Several results come back in a recordtwist#

C#
void Swap(ref int a, ref int b) { ... }
void Print(in BigStruct s) { ... }  // read-only, by reference
Java 25
// Return a record when there are several results.
record Pair(int a, int b) { }
Pair swapped = swap(a, b);
Reading the code
record Pair(int a, int b) { }

A record is a short class that only holds data. Here one record returns several results to the caller. C# would use ref parameters or a tuple for this.

Pair swapped = swap(a, b);

swap returns a new Pair with the two values in the opposite order. The caller's own variables are not changed.

C# refresherTuples: multiple return valuesC# 7

A C# method can return several values at once as a tuple. The caller can then assign the parts of the tuple to separate variables.

(int Min, int Max) Range(int[] xs) => (xs.Min(), xs.Max());

var (lo, hi) = Range([3, 1, 4]);     // lo is 1, hi is 4

Varargs#

Varargs are the same idea as params in C#. The same rule applies, so a varargs parameter must be the last parameter:

C#
void Log(string fmt, params object[] args) { }
Log("a {0}", 1);
Java 25
void log(String fmt, Object... args) { }
log("a %s", 1);

Object... args does the same as params object[] args in C#. The caller passes any number of values, and the method receives an array. In the format string, C# writes {0}. Java writes %s.

Gotcha

Passing an array to a varargs parameter of type Object... is ambiguous. The call log("x", myArray) passes each element of the array as a separate argument. It does not pass the array as one argument. To pass the array as one argument, write a cast, as in log("x", (Object) myArray). Compilers warn about this, and you should read the warning.

No extension methodstwist#

name is a string that may be null.

C#: an extension method
public static class StringExtensions
{
    public static bool IsBlank(this string? s) =>
        string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s);
}

if (name.IsBlank()) { ... }  // reads as if String had it
Java: a static utility method
public final class Strings {
    private Strings() { }

    public static boolean isBlank(String s) {
        return s == null || s.isBlank();
    }
}

if (Strings.isBlank(name)) { ... }  // the helper's class comes first
Reading the code
public final class Strings

This is a utility class. It is final, it has a private constructor, and it holds only static methods. For more about utility classes, see the chapter Classes, constructors and initialisation.

s == null || s.isBlank()

String has had its own isBlank() method since Java 11. But a call to isBlank() on null throws, so the helper checks for null first.

Extension methods

These are the replacements for an extension method:

  • A static utility class. You write StringUtils.isBlank(s) in place of s.IsBlank(). This is why Apache Commons and Guava exist.
  • A default method. Use one if you own the interface.
  • A class that wraps the original object. Use one when the extension is large.

Why Java code reads inside-out#

Java has no extension methods, so a helper wraps its argument. C# code reads from left to right. Java code often reads from the inside to the outside:

var readOnly = Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(xs));

Collections.unmodifiableList is written first and runs last. C# would write a chain of calls here. Streams are the important exception. This is one reason why streams feel so different from the rest of the language.

No operator overloading#

C# refresherOperator overloading: defining + for your own typeC# 1
public readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount)
{
    public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b) => new(a.Amount + b.Amount);
}

var total = price + shipping;     // calls the operator above

Java overloads exactly one operator, which is + for strings. Java does not let you overload any other operator. That matters most in money code. In the example below, every variable is a decimal in C# and a BigDecimal in Java:

C#
decimal total = price * quantity + shipping;
if (total > limit) { ... }
Java 25
BigDecimal total = price.multiply(quantity).add(shipping);
if (total.compareTo(limit) > 0) { ... }

BigDecimal cannot define operators, so it uses methods. The method multiply replaces *. The method add replaces +. The test compareTo(limit) > 0 replaces >. When a C# developer first writes money code in Java, this is the most common source of mistakes that produce no error. See Numbers, money and time.

Lambdas and method referencestwist#

Java has no delegates. In Java, a delegate type becomes an interface with exactly one method to implement. This kind of interface is called a functional interface. It is also called a single abstract method (SAM) type. You can use any lambda with the right parameters and return type as a value of this interface.

C#
delegate decimal PriceRule(Order o);  // a named delegate type

Func<int, string> show = n => n.ToString();
Action<string> print = Console.WriteLine;  // method group
Predicate<string> empty = string.IsNullOrEmpty;
Func<List<int>> make = () => new List<int>();
Java 25
interface PriceRule { BigDecimal apply(Order o); } // a functional interface

Function<Integer, String> show = n -> n.toString();
Consumer<String> print = System.out::println;  // method reference
Predicate<String> empty = String::isEmpty;
Supplier<List<Integer>> make = ArrayList::new;  // constructor reference
Reading the code
interface PriceRule { BigDecimal apply(Order o); }

The delegate type becomes an interface with one method. A lambda such as o -> BigDecimal.TEN matches this interface.

Function<Integer, String> show = n -> n.toString();

Function<Integer, String> does the same as Func<int, string> in C#. A Java generic type cannot hold a plain int, so the code uses the wrapper type Integer.

Consumer<String> print = System.out::println;

This is called a method reference. The form Type::method passes an existing method as a lambda, like a method group in C#. Consumer<String> does the same as Action<string> in C#.

Supplier<List<Integer>> make = ArrayList::new;

This is called a constructor reference. It is a function that creates a new list. Supplier<T> does the same as Func<T> in C#.

Calling a lambdatwist#

names is a list of strings.

C#
Func<int, string> show = n => n.ToString();
Action<string> print = Console.WriteLine;

print(show(42));          // prints 42
names.ForEach(print);
Java 25
Function<Integer, String> show = n -> n.toString();
Consumer<String> print = System.out::println;

print.accept(show.apply(42));   // prints 42
names.forEach(print);
Reading the code
print.accept(show.apply(42));

C# runs a delegate with brackets. A Java lambda is an object, so you call the one method of its interface. On a Function, that method is apply. On a Consumer, that method is accept.

names.forEach(print);

forEach calls print once for each element.

A lambda and the variables around ittrap#

PredictA lambda that counts in a local variable#
These lines are inside a method. Do they compile?
var lines = List.of("mug", "pen", "cup");
int count = 0;
lines.forEach(line -> count++);
System.out.println(count);
Show the answer
No: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final

Captured variables must be effectively final. A Java lambda may use a local variable only if that variable is never reassigned after it is set. C# captures the variable itself and lets you change it. If you type the same lines at the jshell prompt, they compile and print 3. The rule applies when the lines are inside a method.

The usual workaround is the class AtomicInteger from java.util.concurrent.atomic:

var counter = new AtomicInteger();
lines.forEach(line -> counter.incrementAndGet());
System.out.println(counter.get());     // prints 3

An AtomicInteger is an object whose value can change. So the lambda only reads the variable that points to the object. The rule is awkward, but it prevents a whole group of surprises. The rule also makes it safe to pass a lambda to another thread.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
Func<string, int> length = s => s.Length;
Action<int> print = Console.WriteLine;

print(length("mug"));     // prints 3
Function<String, Integer> length = s -> s.length();
Consumer<Integer> print = System.out::println;

print.accept(length.apply("mug"));     // prints 3

A Java lambda is an object, so you call the one method of its interface. On a Function, that method is apply. On a Consumer, that method is accept. The type arguments are Integer, never int.

2
An expert asksDoes Java pass objects by reference?
No. Java passes every argument by value. An object reference is passed by value too. A method can change the object that the reference points at. But the method cannot make the caller's variable point at another object. So Java has no ref and no out.

Quick reference#

This table lists every C# parameter pattern and its replacement in Java:

C# patternJava replacement
out parameterreturn Optional, or a record
TryParseOptional-returning method, or catch NumberFormatException
ref parameterreturn the new value and reassign
Multiple return valuesa record, or a small value class
ref struct / SpanByteBuffer, MemorySegment, or an array plus offsets
in parameternothing needed, because everything is already by value

High-performance C# code also passes Span<T>. A Span<T> is a view over memory that avoids copying. The nearest tools in Java are ByteBuffer and MemorySegment. You will rarely need them in a web service.

C# refresherSpan and stackalloc: a view over memory, with no copyC# 7
Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[256];        // on the stack: no heap allocation
ReadOnlySpan<char> head = text.AsSpan(0, 3);     // a view of text, not a copy

Fields, properties and immutability#

Language core · Chapter 09· 6 min read

Java has no properties. In Java, a property is a naming convention. You write a private field, a getX() method that reads the field, and a setX() method that changes the field. For data that never changes, a record writes all of this code for you.

KindC#JavaNote
twist{ get; set; }getX() / setX()frameworks find the getter and the setter by this exact naming rule Why
twist{ get; }final field + getX()the field is read-only after construction, so assign it in the constructor Why
twist{ get; init; }final field + constructorThe field is set once in the constructor. A record does this for every field. Why
twist=> expressiona plain methodthe method computes the value on each call, and there is no backing field Why
twistrequiredno equivalentmake the field final and require its value in the constructor Why
twistfield keywordno equivalentdeclare the backing field yourself, and the getter and the setter use that field Why
trapa property, whatever its namegetName(), isActive(), setName(v)a method without the prefix is no property, so Jackson silently skips it Why
twistrecord Customer(long Id, string Name)record Customer(long id, String name) { }one line replaces the fields, constructor and accessors Why
twistcustomer.Namecustomer.name()record accessors have no get prefix, but current Jackson and Spring read them Why
twistreadonlyfinala final field is assignable once, but final fixes the reference, not the object it points to Why
twistconst, or static readonlystatic finalone form for both, with a name in capitals such as MAX_RETRIES Why
samea const is copied into the code that uses ita static final constant is copied toocallers keep the old value of a changed constant until they recompile Why
twistno equivalent@Getter @Setter @Builder, from LombokLombok writes the accessors while the class compiles, and it is common in older code Why

The property gaptwist#

C#
public class Customer
{
    public long Id { get; init; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public string Label => $"{Name} ({Id})";
}
Java 25
public class Customer {
    private final long id;
    private String name;

    public Customer(long id) { this.id = id; }

    public long   getId()           { return id; }
    public String getName()         { return name; }
    public void   setName(String v) { this.name = v; }
    public String getLabel() {
        return name + " (" + id + ")";
    }
}
Reading the code
private final long id;

final means that the field is set once, in the constructor. This does the same as { get; init; } in C#.

public String getName()

This is a getter. Its name is get plus the property name, and the property name starts with a capital letter.

public void setName(String v)

This is a setter. Its name is set plus the property name.

public String getLabel()

A computed value is an ordinary method. The get prefix lets frameworks treat the method as a read-only property.

This class has private fields, getters and setters, and it has no framework base class. A class like this is often called a plain old Java object (POJO). When a POJO follows the naming rules exactly, it is also called a JavaBean.

C# also has required and init. Since C# 14, it also has the field keyword. Java has none of these three keywords. In their place, Java uses a final field that the constructor sets.

C# refresherrequired, init-only and the field keywordC# 14

required forces the caller to set a property when the caller creates the object. init allows the caller to set the property only at that moment. The field keyword of C# 14 names the hidden backing field inside an accessor.

public class Customer
{
    public required string Id { get; init; }   // must be set at creation, then fixed

    public string Name
    {
        get;
        set => field = value.Trim();           // field: the compiler's backing field
    }
}

var c = new Customer { Id = "C1", Name = " Ada " };   // leave out Id: compile error

The names are the contracttrap#

PredictA getter without the get prefix#
Jackson turns a Customer into JSON. What does this print?
public class Customer {
    private final String name = "Ada";
    private final boolean active = true;

    public String name() { return name; }
    public boolean isActive() { return active; }
}

// ObjectMapper is Jackson's class for writing JSON.
System.out.println(new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(new Customer()));
Show the answer
{"active":true}

The naming rule is exact, and tools depend on it. The getter for a name property is getName(). The getter for a boolean is isActive(). The setter is setName(v). If the prefix is wrong, the JSON library Jackson will not write the field. There is no error. The value is just missing.

Name the method getName(), or make Customer a record. Jackson reads the name() accessor of a record, although the accessor has no get prefix.

The last line of the example is written for Jackson 3. On Jackson 2, writeValueAsString declares a checked exception. So the call also needs a try or a throws clause.

Records make most of this disappeartwist#

A record is a good choice for immutable data, such as a data transfer object (DTO), a value object or a query result. In the code below, customer is an existing Customer:

C# record
public record Customer(long Id, string Name, string Email)
{
    public string Label => $"{Name} ({Id})";
}

var renamed = customer with { Name = "Ada" };
Java 16+ record
public record Customer(long id, String name, String email) {
    public String label() {
        return name + " (" + id + ")";
    }
}

// No with expression: build a new one. See the Records chapter.
var renamed = new Customer(customer.id(), "Ada", customer.email());
Reading the code
public record Customer(long id, String name, String email)

This one line declares the fields, a constructor and the accessors. It also declares equals, hashCode and toString.

public String label()

A record can have methods too.

new Customer(customer.id(), "Ada", customer.email())

Java records have no with expression. So you create a changed copy yourself, with a call to the constructor.

Gotcha

Record accessors have no get prefix. You read a record component name with c.name(), not with c.getName(). This breaks the JavaBean naming rule on purpose. Older framework versions expected getX(), so they could not read records. Modern Jackson and Spring support records. But a library that has not been updated since about 2021 may not support them.

final is not readonly, quite#

C# has the keywords readonly and const. Java has one keyword, final:

C#JavaMeaning
readonly fieldfinal fieldassignable once, in constructor or initialiser
conststatic finala compile-time constant, which is copied into the code that uses it
static readonlystatic finalassigned in a static initialiser
readonly structno equivalentas of Java 25 there are no user-defined value types, so use a record
init-onlyfinal + constructorassign once in the constructor, and a record does this automatically
Gotcha

final makes the reference unchangeable, not the object. This is identical to readonly in C#. It surprises people equally in both languages:

private final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

names.add("ada");             // fine, mutating the list
names = new ArrayList<>();    // does not compile, rebinding the reference

names.add changes the list that the field points to, and final allows this. names = new ArrayList<>() makes the field point at a new list, and final forbids this. For a list that truly cannot change, use List.of(...) Java 9, which returns a list that throws on any change.

static final constants#

Constants look like this in each language:

C#
public const int MaxRetries = 3;
public static readonly TimeSpan Timeout =
    TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
Java 25
public static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;
public static final Duration TIMEOUT = Duration.ofSeconds(30);

Java uses static final for both const and static readonly. MAX_RETRIES is written in capitals with underscores. Constants are the one place where Java does not use camelCase. All Java code follows this rule.

Gotcha

Some static final fields hold a primitive or a String that is a compile-time constant. The value of such a field is copied into the code that uses it, exactly like a const in C#. Suppose that you publish a library and later change such a constant. A user of the library who does not recompile keeps the old value. For anything that might change, use a static method or a value that is computed at run time.

A word on Lombok#

LegacyProject Lombok

Lombok is a tool that reads annotations such as @Getter while your code compiles. It writes getters, setters, constructors, equals, hashCode and builders for you. A tool of this kind is called an annotation processor. You will see Lombok in very many Java codebases. Lombok saved developers a lot of work before records existed.

@Getter @Setter @Builder
public class Customer {
    private String name;
    private String email;
}

@Getter and @Setter generate the accessors for every field. @Builder generates a builder. All of this happens while the class compiles.

Lombok is not deprecated, and it is still widely used. But it has a disadvantage. Lombok depends on the internal parts of the compiler. This has caused failures on several Java Development Kit (JDK) upgrades. For immutable data, a record is now the better answer, and a record needs no dependency. For mutable entities, many teams still use Lombok. Entities are the classes that Hibernate stores in the database.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
public class Customer
{
    public long Id { get; init; }
    public bool Active { get; set; }
}
public class Customer {
    private final long id;
    private boolean active;

    public Customer(long id) { this.id = id; }

    public long getId() { return id; }
    public boolean isActive() { return active; }
    public void setActive(boolean active) { this.active = active; }
}

init becomes a final field that the constructor sets. The getter of a boolean starts with is, not get. Frameworks find all three methods by their names.

2
An expert asksA class declares private final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();. Can its code still add a name to the list? What does final promise?
Yes. names.add("ada") compiles, and the list grows. final fixes the reference, not the object. The field can never point at another list, but the list itself can change. readonly in C# has the same rule. For a list that cannot change, use List.of(...), which returns a list that throws on any change.
