Records#

Modern Java · Chapter 10· 6 min read

A record is a short class that holds data and compares by value. C# and Java records look almost the same. Java records are stricter. You can never reassign a field of a Java record. Java 16

KindC#JavaNote
twistrecord OrderLine(string ProductId, ...)record OrderLine(String productId, ...) { }the braces are required, even when the body is empty Why
twistline.Quantityline.quantity()an accessor method, with brackets and no get prefix Why
samevalue equalityvalue equalitytwo records with equal components are equal, with no code to write
twistrecord structno equivalenta Java record is always a reference type, never a struct Why
newno equivalentpublic Money { ... }a compact constructor, which checks values before they are stored Why
twistline with { Quantity = 3 }line.withQuantity(3)Java has no with expression, so you write a wither method yourself Why
twista record that holds a List<T>lines = List.copyOf(lines)the list inside can still change, as in C#, so copy it in the compact constructor Why
twista record as a DTO or a value objectthe same, but never a JPA entityHibernate needs a no-argument constructor and fields it can change Why
twistpositional pattern on a recordcase Card(String last4)a record pattern takes a record apart by position, inside a switch Why

The basicstwist#

OrderLine is one product on an order. Money is a small record too. It holds an amount and a currency.

C#
public record OrderLine(string ProductId, int Quantity, Money UnitPrice);

var line = new OrderLine("mug", 2, new Money(9.50m, "EUR"));
Console.WriteLine(line);
Console.WriteLine(line.Quantity);
var more = line with { Quantity = 3 };
Java 25
public record OrderLine(String productId, int quantity, Money unitPrice) { }

var line = new OrderLine("mug", 2, new Money(new BigDecimal("9.50"), "EUR"));
System.out.println(line);
System.out.println(line.quantity());  // note the ()
// no with expression: see below
Reading the code
public record OrderLine(String productId, int quantity, Money unitPrice) { }

From this header, Java generates a private final field for each component. Java also generates an accessor method for each component, one constructor, and the methods equals, hashCode and toString. The braces are required, even when the body is empty.

line.quantity()

The accessor is a method. You call it with brackets, and its name has no get prefix. In C#, Quantity is a property.

System.out.println(line);

This line prints OrderLine[productId=mug, quantity=2, unitPrice=Money[amount=9.50, currency=EUR]]. The Java output uses square brackets. In C#, the output of ToString uses braces.

This table compares the other features of C# records and Java records:

FeatureC# recordJava record
Immutable by defaultinit-only, but can add settersalways, no exceptions
Positional syntaxyesyes
Nominal (body) propertiesyesno, only components
with expressionyesno
Value equalityyesyes
Inheritancerecords can inherit recordsno inheritance at all
Can implement interfacesyesyes
struct variantrecord structno
Custom constructoryesyes, plus compact form
C# refresherC# records: positional, nominal, inheritance, record struct and withC# 10

You can declare a C# record by its parameters or by a body of properties. A C# record can inherit another record, and it can be a value type. It compares by value.

public record Point(int X, int Y);                              // positional
public record Customer { public string Name { get; init; } = ""; }  // nominal: a body
public record Shape(string Name);
public record Circle(string Name, double R) : Shape(Name);      // inherits a record
public readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount);            // a value-type record

var p = new Point(1, 2);
Console.WriteLine(p == new Point(1, 2));                        // True: value equality
var q = p with { Y = 5 };                                       // a copy with one change

Checking values: the compact constructornew#

An amount of money must never be negative. It should also always have two decimal places, so that 9.5 and 9.50 compare as equal. For rules like these, Java records have a form of constructor that C# does not have. It is called the compact constructor. A compact constructor checks or adjusts the values, and it does not repeat the parameter list or the assignments:

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {

    // A compact constructor: no parameter list, and no assignments to fields.
    public Money {
        if (amount.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount");
        amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    }

    // Any extra constructor must call the main one.
    public Money(String amount) {
        this(new BigDecimal(amount), "EUR");
    }
}
Reading the code
public Money {

This is the compact constructor. It has no parameter list, because its parameters are the components of the record. It runs before the fields are set.

amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);

This line assigns to the parameter, not to the field. When the body ends, Java copies each parameter into its field. So you are not allowed to write this.amount = amount here. setScale rounds the amount to two decimal places, and it uses banker's rounding.

this(new BigDecimal(amount), "EUR");

An extra constructor must call the main constructor. It does that with this(...). So the checks run for every record.

The missing with expressiontwist#

with expressions

As of Java 25, Java has no with expression and nothing that replaces it. Here are the options. In this code, line is an order line of two mugs:

var line = new OrderLine("mug", 2, new Money(new BigDecimal("9.50"), "EUR"));

// 1. Just construct it: fine for small records.
var more = new OrderLine(line.productId(), 3, line.unitPrice());

// 2. A hand-written "wither": common in domain code.
public record OrderLine(String productId, int quantity, Money unitPrice) {
    public OrderLine withQuantity(int q) { return new OrderLine(productId, q, unitPrice); }
}

// 3. A builder, for records with many components.
Reading the code
new OrderLine(line.productId(), 3, line.unitPrice())

This line repeats every component and changes one of them. That is fine for three components, but it is a lot to write for eight components.

public OrderLine withQuantity(int q)

This method writes that construction once, inside the record. So callers can write line.withQuantity(3). A method like this is called a wither.

A feature like with has been discussed for a future release. It is called derived record creation, and it is not in Java 25. For a record with more than about four components, the practical answer is a builder. For an example of a builder, see the chapter Methods and parameters.

A record that holds a listtwist#

PredictA record that holds a list#
What does this print?
public record Order(long id, List<OrderLine> lines) { }

var price = new Money(new BigDecimal("9.50"), "EUR");
var lines = new ArrayList<OrderLine>();
var order = new Order(1, lines);              // an order with no lines
lines.add(new OrderLine("mug", 2, price));
System.out.println(order.lines().size());
Show the answer
1

Records are shallowly immutable. The field lines can never point to another list. But the list that it points to can still change, and the caller kept a reference to that list. C# has the same problem with a record that holds a List<T>.

Copy the list in the compact constructor:

public record Order(long id, List<OrderLine> lines) {
    public Order {
        lines = List.copyOf(lines);   // an unmodifiable copy
    }
}

List.copyOf makes a copy that nobody can change. A later change to the caller's list does not change the order. And the list inside the order throws UnsupportedOperationException if anyone tries to add to it.

Where records fittwist#

Records are a good choice for data that is created once and then only read. The usual example is a data transfer object (DTO). The usual exception is a Jakarta Persistence (JPA) entity:

// Data sent out of the service: created once, then only read. A record.
public record OrderSummary(long id, String customerName, Money total) { }

// A database entity: Hibernate creates it empty, then sets its fields. A class.
// It is a different Order from the record in the prediction.
@Entity
public class Order {
    @Id private long id;
    protected Order() { }
}

OrderSummary only carries values, so it is a record. This Order is not the record from the section A record that holds a list. It is the entity that Hibernate loads and saves. Hibernate needs the no-argument constructor protected Order() { }. Hibernate also needs fields that it can change. So the entity stays a class. For more about entities, see the chapter Data access.

UseSuitableWhy
DTO / API request or responseyesJackson reads and writes records with no extra setup
Value object (Money, Range)yesa value that never changes is safe to share and to use as a map key
Query result / projectionyesSpring Data supports record projections
Pattern-matching payloadyesa switch can take a record apart into its components
JPA entitynoHibernate needs a no-argument constructor and fields it can change
Mutable domain objectnoevery field is final, so an object that changes state cannot be a record
Needs inheritancenoa record is final and cannot extend another class, so use an interface instead

Records and pattern matching#

Record patterns depend on records. The components of a record are part of its type, so a switch can take a record apart by position. This example uses the sealed type Payment from the chapter Interfaces, abstract classes and sealing:

String describe(Payment p) {
    return switch (p) {
        case Card(String last4) when last4.equals("0000") -> "a test card";
        case Card(String last4)                           -> "card ending " + last4;
        case BankTransfer(String iban)                    -> "transfer from " + iban;
        case Voucher(String code)                         -> "voucher " + code;
    };
}
Reading the code
case Card(String last4)

This is a record pattern. If p is a Card, the pattern puts the component of the card into the variable last4. Components are matched by position.

when last4.equals("0000")

This is a guard, like when in C#. The arm matches only if the condition is also true.

C# can also match patterns on positional records. But C# has no equivalent of a Java sealed type. So the C# compiler cannot know that the set of cases is complete, and it warns unless you add a discard arm.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java, where line is an OrderLine: 
public record OrderLine(string ProductId, int Quantity, Money UnitPrice);

var more = line with { Quantity = 3 };
public record OrderLine(String productId, int quantity, Money unitPrice) {
    public OrderLine withQuantity(int quantity) {
        return new OrderLine(productId, quantity, unitPrice);
    }
}

var more = line.withQuantity(3);

Java has no with expression, so you write the wither yourself. The braces after the record header are required, even on a record with no body.

2
An expert asksWhy can a JPA entity not be a record?
JPA creates an entity through a no-argument constructor and then sets its fields. A record has no such constructor, because its constructor takes every component. And the fields of a record are final, so they cannot be set later. Use a record for the data that you send out, and use a class for the entity.

Sealed types and pattern matching#

Modern Java · Chapter 11· 9 min read

Pattern matching tests what kind of object you have, and gives you a typed variable for it in one step. Java patterns work like C# patterns. Over a sealed type Java 17, the Java compiler checks that a switch handles every case.

KindC#JavaNote
twistis T xinstanceof T xthe same type test with a binding, spelled instanceof in Java Why
twistis not T x!(o instanceof T x)Java has no is not, so put the test in brackets and negate it Why
twisto is int io instanceof Integer itest against the wrapper type, because a boxed int is an Integer Why
twistswitch expression armscase T x ->each arm is written case pattern -> result, not pattern => result Why
samewhen clausewhen clausethe same keyword for an extra condition, added in Java 21 Why
twist_ discarddefaultJava uses default, or _ for unnamed variables Why
twista _ arm, even when every kind has an armno default over a sealed typeJava checks that every permitted type has an arm. Without the _ arm, C# only warns (CS8509). Why
trapnull =>case nulldefault does not catch null, so without case null the switch throws NullPointerException Why
twistproperty pattern { X: 1 }no equivalenttest the property in a when clause instead Why
twistlist pattern [1, .., 2]no equivalentJava has no form for this, so check the size and the elements in ordinary code Why
twistrelational pattern > 5only inside whenwrite case Integer i when i > 5 instead of a bare > 5 Why
twistpositional patternrecord patternJava 21 added the record pattern. It works on records and takes them apart by component. Why
twist_ inside a positional pattern_ inside a record patternan unnamed pattern skips a component you do not need, and it was added in Java 22 Why
samea nested positional pattern over a null componentMoney(_, var currency) never matches nullAs in C#, the whole pattern then fails. But var matches null in both languages.
trapOrder(_, Customer c) skips a null customerOrder(_, Customer c) matches it, and c is nulla type pattern that covers the component's whole type also matches null in Java Why
twistno equivalentquantity instanceof int wholeThe test is true only when the double holds a whole number that fits an int. It is a preview in Java 25, so do not ship it. Why

Type patterns Java 16twist#

C#
void Refund(Payment payment, decimal amount)
{
    if (payment is Card card)
    {
        RefundToCard(card.Last4, amount);
    }
}
Java 25
void refund(Payment payment, BigDecimal amount) {
    if (payment instanceof Card card) {
        refundToCard(card.last4(), amount);
    }
}
Reading the code
payment instanceof Card card

If payment is a Card, the test creates a new variable, card. The variable has the type Card and is already cast. This is called a type pattern. It is the same idea as is Card card in C#.

C# writes o is int i. Java writes o instanceof Integer i, because a boxed number is tested against its wrapper type.

Sometimes an if leaves the method when the test fails. Then the variable is also in scope after that if, as in C#:

C#
void RefundCardOnly(Payment payment, decimal amount)
{
    if (payment is not Card card)
    {
        throw new ArgumentException("only card payments can be refunded");
    }
    RefundToCard(card.Last4, amount);  // card can be used here
}
Java 25
void refundCardOnly(Payment payment, BigDecimal amount) {
    if (!(payment instanceof Card card)) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("only card payments can be refunded");
    }
    refundToCard(card.last4(), amount);  // card can be used here
}
Reading the code
!(payment instanceof Card card)

Java has no is not. So put the whole test in brackets and negate it with !.

LegacyCast after instanceof

Before Java 16, a type test and a cast were two separate steps. Every Java codebase older than about 2021 has this code in many places:

if (payment instanceof Card) {
    Card card = (Card) payment;
    refundToCard(card.last4(), amount);
}

(Card) payment is the cast. It still compiles, but do not write it now.

Pattern matching in switch Java 21twist#

Payment is a sealed interface with three kinds. For its declaration, see the chapter Interfaces, abstract classes and sealing. A payment is null until the order is paid. A test card ends in 0000.

C#
string Describe(Payment? payment) => payment switch
{
    null => "not paid yet",
    Card c when c.Last4 == "0000" => "a test card",
    Card c => $"card ending {c.Last4}",
    BankTransfer t => $"transfer from {t.Iban}",
    Voucher v => $"voucher {v.Code}",
    _ => throw new ArgumentException("unknown payment")
};
Java 25
String describe(Payment payment) {
    return switch (payment) {
        case null -> "not paid yet";
        case Card c when c.last4().equals("0000") -> "a test card";
        case Card c -> "card ending " + c.last4();
        case BankTransfer t -> "transfer from " + t.iban();
        case Voucher v -> "voucher " + v.code();
    };
}
Reading the code
case null

This arm handles a missing payment, as the null => arm does in C#.

case Card c when c.last4().equals("0000")

This is a type pattern with a condition after when. The condition is called a when guard. The arm matches only if payment is a Card and the condition is true, as in C#. Strings are compared with equals, because == in Java only checks whether two variables point to the same object.

case Card c -> "card ending " + c.last4();

Arms are tried from top to bottom, so the guarded Card arm must come first. If you put the guarded arm after this arm, the compiler reports that the guarded arm can never match. C# reports the same error.

No default over a sealed typetwist#

The two versions of describe differ at the end. Without the _ arm, the C# compiler only warns (CS8509). The C# switch then throws at run time for a payment that no arm handles. Java needs no default, because Payment is sealed and lists exactly three kinds. Then a colleague adds a fourth kind:

PredictA fourth kind of payment#
Does this compile?
sealed interface Payment permits Card, BankTransfer, Voucher, GiftCard { }
record Card(String last4) implements Payment { }
record BankTransfer(String iban) implements Payment { }
record Voucher(String code) implements Payment { }
record GiftCard(String number) implements Payment { }   // added this week

String describe(Payment payment) {
    return switch (payment) {
        case Card c -> "card ending " + c.last4();
        case BankTransfer t -> "transfer from " + t.iban();
        case Voucher v -> "voucher " + v.code();
    };
}
Show the answer
No: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

A switch over a sealed type must have an arm for every permitted type. Payment is sealed, so the compiler knows its four kinds. This switch handles only three kinds. C# cannot check this, because nothing stops another assembly from adding a kind. So without the _ arm, the C# compiler only warns (CS8509).

Add case GiftCard g. Do not add default. With default, the switch would compile again, and the compiler would not report the next new kind.

A switch on nulltrap#

Gotcha

A switch on a reference type throws NullPointerException unless you write case null. Java kept this old behaviour so that existing code would not change meaning. For an example, see the prediction a switch on a null string. In a C# switch expression, a null arm or the _ arm handles null. In Java, default does not handle null. If null can arrive, write case null. To send null to the fallback arm, write case null, default ->.

This version of describe names one kind of payment. It sends every other kind, and also a missing payment, to one arm:

String describe(Payment payment) {
    return switch (payment) {
        case Card c -> "card ending " + c.last4();
        case null, default -> "not a card";
    };
}

Suppose you write a plain default in place of case null, default. Then describe(null) throws NullPointerException.

Patterns Java does not havetwist#

C#
string Size(Order order) => order switch
{
    { Lines.Count: 0 } => "empty",  // a property pattern
    { Lines: [_] } => "one line",  // a list pattern: exactly one element
    { Lines.Count: > 10 } => "large",  // a relational pattern (> 10)
    _ => "normal"
};
Java 25
String size(Order order) {
    return switch (order) {
        case Order o when o.lines().isEmpty() -> "empty";
        case Order o when o.lines().size() == 1 -> "one line";
        case Order o when o.lines().size() > 10 -> "large";
        case Order o -> "normal";
    };
}
Reading the code
case Order o when o.lines().isEmpty()

Java has no property, list or relational patterns. The type pattern Order o matches every order, so the when guard does all the testing.

case Order o -> "normal";

This arm has no guard, so it matches every order that no earlier arm matched. That makes the switch complete, so the switch needs no default.

When every arm is a guard like this, plain if statements work equally well. Many Java developers would write if statements here.

C# refresherC# positional, property, list and relational patternsC# 11

A C# pattern can take a record apart by position. It can test properties by name, and it can match the shape of a list. It can also compare with < or > directly.

var where = point switch
{
    (0, 0)   => "origin",               // positional pattern
    { X: 0 } => "on the y axis",        // property pattern
    _        => "elsewhere"
};

bool framed = numbers is [1, .., 9];    // list pattern: starts with 1, ends with 9

var feel = celsius switch { > 30 => "hot", < 0 => "freezing", _ => "mild" };  // relational

Record patterns#

A type pattern gives you the whole object, and you then call its accessors. A record pattern Java 21 takes the record apart as it matches. It puts each component into its own variable. Here is the receipt description again, written with record patterns:

C#
string Describe(Payment payment) => payment switch
{
    Card(var last4) => $"card ending {last4}",  // a positional pattern
    BankTransfer(var iban) => $"transfer from {iban}",
    Voucher(var code) => $"voucher {code}",
    _ => throw new ArgumentException("unknown payment")
};
Java 25
String describe(Payment payment) {
    return switch (payment) {
        case Card(var last4) -> "card ending " + last4;
        case BankTransfer(var iban) -> "transfer from " + iban;
        case Voucher(var code) -> "voucher " + code;
    };
}
Reading the code
case Card(var last4)

This pattern matches a Card and puts its one component into a new variable, last4. With var, the compiler infers the type, which is String here. You may write String last4 instead.

case Voucher(var code) -> "voucher " + code;

Components are matched by position, in the order in which the record declares them. A positional pattern in C# works the same way. The switch still needs no default, because Payment is still sealed.

Nested patterns and unnamed variables#

A record pattern can hold other record patterns. The shop sells in euros, and a price check warns about any order line that is priced in another currency. An order line holds a Money, and Money is itself a record. So one pattern can take both records apart:

if (line instanceof OrderLine(var productId, _, Money(_, var currency))
        && !currency.equals("EUR")) {
    System.out.println(productId + " is priced in " + currency);
}
Reading the code
OrderLine(var productId, _, Money(_, var currency))

This pattern matches an OrderLine and puts its productId into a variable. It skips the quantity. Then it takes the unit price apart. There it skips the amount and puts the currency into a variable.

_

This is called an unnamed pattern Java 22. It matches any value and gives the value no name, like the discard in C#. Use it for a component that you do not need.

C# nests positional patterns in the same way. The same test in C# is line is OrderLine(var productId, _, Money(_, var currency)).

Note

A nested record pattern never matches null, in Java and in C#. Suppose the unitPrice of an order line is null. That line does not match Money(_, var currency), so the whole pattern fails. The check then skips that line and reports nothing. A var component accepts null in both languages, so productId can be null. If a null matters, test for it separately. The two languages differ for a nested type pattern. See A null component inside a record pattern.

A null component inside a record patterntrap#

A record pattern names a record and gives one pattern for each of its components. A C# positional pattern does the same. Here _ skips the id, and Customer c is a type pattern for the customer:

PredictAn order with no customer#
What does this print?
record Customer(String name) { }
record Order(long id, Customer customer) { }

var order = new Order(2, null);               // a guest order: no customer
if (order instanceof Order(_, Customer c)) {
    System.out.println("placed by " + c);
} else {
    System.out.println("no customer");
}
Show the answer
placed by null

A type pattern inside a record pattern also matches null. Customer c covers the component's whole type, so Java matches it without a test. That is why c is null. In C#, order is Order(_, Customer c) is false for this order, and the else branch runs.

Take the component apart instead. The pattern Order(_, Customer(var name)) never matches a null customer, in Java or in C#. Or keep the type pattern and add && c != null.

What is still preview#

One more kind of pattern exists, but only as a preview feature. A preview feature is finished but not yet final, and it is disabled unless you ask for it. The feature here is called Primitive types in patterns, instanceof and switch Java 25 preview. It lets a pattern test the value of a number. For example, instanceof int on a double is true only if the value converts to an int and nothing is lost.

Imagine quantities that are imported from a spreadsheet. Every number arrives as a double:

// Preview in Java 25: compile and run with --enable-preview.
double quantity = 3.0;                 // for example, read from a spreadsheet
if (quantity instanceof int whole) {   // matches: 3.0 converts to an int with no loss
    System.out.println(whole + " items");
}
boolean exact = 2.5 instanceof int;    // false: the conversion would lose the .5
Reading the code
quantity instanceof int whole

This test is true, because 3.0 fits in an int exactly. So whole becomes 3.

2.5 instanceof int

This test is false, because converting 2.5 to an int would lose the .5.

This is the feature's third preview in Java 25. Do not use it in code you ship. C# has no counterpart. In C#, quantity is int whole on a double does not compile.

Gotcha

Anything marked preview in this book needs --enable-preview when you compile and again when you run. Preview features are not covered by the usual compatibility promises. They can change or disappear in the next release. Class files that were compiled with preview features do not load on any other Java Development Kit (JDK) version.

Check yourself
1
TranslateA C# switch over an Order has this arm. Write the arm in Java: { Lines.Count: > 10 } => "large"
case Order o when o.lines().size() > 10 -> "large"; Java has no property or relational patterns, so a type pattern matches the order and a when guard does the test.
2
An expert asksIn a switch over a Payment, why does Java reject the arm case Card c when c.last4().equals("0000") when it is written after a plain case Card c arm?
Arms are tried from top to bottom. The plain case Card c already matches every card, so the guarded arm could never run. The compiler reports this case label is dominated by a preceding case label. Write the guarded arm first.
Next · Modern Java12Switch expressions and statements6 min

Switch expressions and statements#

Modern Java · Chapter 12· 6 min read

Java has two kinds of switch. The arrow form Java 14 works like the switch expression in C#. It is the form to write. The old colon form works like the switch statement in C#. You only need to read the colon form.

KindC#JavaNote
twistvalue switch { ... }switch (value) { ... }the value goes in brackets after the keyword Why
twistpattern => resultcase pattern -> resultthe word case, and an arrow instead of => Why
twistor between patternscomma between labelslabels that share an arm are separated by a comma, as in case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> Why
twist_defaultthe fallback arm, used when no other arm matches Why
samethrow in an armthrow in an armin both languages, an arm can throw instead of giving a value
twista missing case is a warning (CS8509), and an exception at run timea missing case is a compile errorover an enum or a sealed type, Java checks every case and needs no default Why
twistCard => CardFee(total)case Card c -> { ...; yield fee; }C# arms cannot hold statements. A Java block arm ends with yield, because the compiler rejects return there. Why
twistyield returnno equivalentyield in Java only gives the value of a block to its switch, and it produces no sequence Why
trapa case with no break is a compile errora case with no break falls throughin the old colon form the next case runs too, and Java compiles it with no warning Why
twistgoto done;break scan;leaves the labelled loop and every loop inside it Why
twistswitch on a longno equivalenta switch takes int, String, enums and patterns, but not long, so use if and else Why

The arrow formtwist#

Here day is a DayOfWeek. DayOfWeek is an enum that both .NET and Java provide:

C#
DayOfWeek day = DayOfWeek.Friday;
var packing = day switch
{
    DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday => "packed on Monday",
    DayOfWeek.Friday => "packed today, delivered next week",
    _ => "packed today"
};
Java 25
import java.time.DayOfWeek;

DayOfWeek day = DayOfWeek.FRIDAY;
var packing = switch (day) {
    case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> "packed on Monday";
    case FRIDAY -> "packed today, delivered next week";
    default -> "packed today";
};
Reading the code
switch (day) {

The value that is tested goes in brackets after switch. C# puts the value before the keyword and writes day switch.

case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> "packed on Monday";

Each arm starts with case. An arrow -> separates the labels from the result. C# writes => there. Two labels share this arm, and a comma separates them. C# writes or between two labels. Enum constants are usually written without the type name. So you write SATURDAY, not DayOfWeek.SATURDAY.

default -> "packed today";

This is the fallback arm, like _ in C#.

In Java, this arrow form is called a switch expression. The whole switch produces a value, so the statement ends with a semicolon after the closing brace, as in C#.

Multi-statement arms#

In the chapter Interfaces, abstract classes and sealing, a card payment cost a flat fee of 0.30. Suppose the fee changes to 1.4 percent of the order total, but never less than 0.30. The card arm now needs two steps. An arm of a C# switch expression cannot hold statements, so C# moves the steps into a method. Java puts the steps in a block that ends with yield:

C#
decimal Fee(Payment payment, decimal total) => payment switch
{
    Card => CardFee(total),
    BankTransfer or Voucher => 0m,
    _ => throw new ArgumentException("unknown payment")
};

decimal CardFee(decimal total) => Math.Max(total * 0.014m, 0.30m);
Java 25
BigDecimal fee(Payment payment, BigDecimal total) {
    return switch (payment) {
        case Card c -> {
            BigDecimal percentFee = total.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.014"));
            yield percentFee.max(new BigDecimal("0.30"));
        }
        case BankTransfer t -> BigDecimal.ZERO;
        case Voucher v -> BigDecimal.ZERO;
    };
}
Reading the code
case Card c -> {

The arm's result is a block in braces instead of a single expression.

yield percentFee.max(new BigDecimal("0.30"));

yield ends the block and gives the arm its value. Here the value is the larger of the two fees. A return here would try to leave the whole method, and the compiler rejects it.

Gotcha

In Java, yield only gives the value of a block to its switch. It is not related to yield return in C#, which produces a sequence one value at a time. Java has no yield return at all. For what Java uses in its place, see the chapter Streams vs LINQ.

C# refresheryield return: C# iteratorsC# 2

A C# method with yield return produces a sequence lazily. The method produces each value only when the caller asks for it. Then the method pauses until the next request.

IEnumerable<int> Evens(int max)
{
    for (var i = 0; i <= max; i += 2)
        yield return i;       // hand back one value, then pause here
}

foreach (var n in Evens(6)) Console.Write(n);   // 0246

Exhaustivenesstwist#

A switch that returns a value must handle every possible value. The compiler checks that for a sealed type. See No default over a sealed type. The compiler checks an enum in the same way:

enum OrderStatus { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED }

// No default: all four constants are covered.
// Add a fifth constant and this method stops compiling.
String label(OrderStatus status) {
    return switch (status) {
        case NEW       -> "waiting for payment";
        case PAID      -> "being packed";
        case SHIPPED   -> "on its way";
        case CANCELLED -> "cancelled";
    };
}

OrderStatus is an enum with four constants. For how a Java enum differs from a C# enum, see the chapter Enums. The switch covers all four constants, so it needs no default. In C#, a missing case is only a warning, and the switch throws SwitchExpressionException at run time.

The old colon formtrap#

Existing code often uses the older colon form. In the colon form, a label ends in a colon, such as case NEW:, and statements follow the label. Learn to recognise the colon form, but do not write it.

PredictA colon switch with one break#
What does this print?
enum OrderStatus { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED }

OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.NEW;
switch (status) {
    case NEW:
        System.out.println("send a payment reminder");
    case PAID:
        System.out.println("reserve stock");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("nothing to do");
}
Show the answer
send a payment reminder reserve stock

In the colon form, a case with no break runs on into the next case. This is called fall-through. A colon label starts a series of statements that continues until a break. There is no break after the first println, so a new order also reserves stock. C# reports an error for this, but Java compiles it and reports nothing.

The arrow form cannot fall through at all, so this bug cannot happen in the arrow form. When several labels need the same action, list the labels in one arm, as in case NEW, PAID ->.

The old statement form#

LegacyColon switch with fall-through

The colon form is still legal and still common. It causes a well-known bug, which is a missing break. For an example, see the section The old colon form. Write the arrow form instead.

Java has no goto. C# code mostly uses goto to leave nested loops. Java leaves nested loops with a labelled break. Here, orders is a List<Order>, and the scan stops at the first order line with a quantity of zero:

C#
foreach (var order in orders)
    foreach (var line in order.Lines)
        if (line.Quantity == 0)
            goto done;
done:
Console.WriteLine("scan finished");
Java 25
scan:
for (var order : orders)
    for (var line : order.lines())
        if (line.quantity() == 0)
            break scan;          // leaves both loops
System.out.println("scan finished");
Reading the code
scan:

This is a label. A label is a name followed by a colon, and it is placed just before the outer loop.

for (var order : orders)

This loop does the same as foreach in C#. Java writes the keyword for, and a colon between the variable and the collection. C# writes in there.

break scan;

This statement leaves the loop labelled scan, and it leaves the inner loop too. A plain break would leave only the inner loop. continue scan; also works, and it continues with the next order.

What you can switch on#

The arrow form works on more types than the old switch did, but not on every type. Here is what a switch accepts:

TypeJavaNote
int, short, char, byteyesthe original switch types, allowed since Java 1.0
Stringyesallowed since Java 7, and labels are compared with equals, not with ==
enumyesallowed since enums arrived in Java 5, and you write the constant name without its type
sealed interface / classyessince Java 21, with a type pattern for each permitted subtype
any Objectyessince Java 21, with type patterns and usually a default arm
long, float, double, booleannouse if/else, or preview primitive patterns

Strings work as labels. The shop sorts uploaded product files by their extension. Here extension holds text such as "png":

String kind = switch (extension) {
    case "jpg", "png" -> "image";       // strings are compared with equals()
    case "pdf"        -> "document";
    default           -> "other";
};

Each label is compared with equals, so "png" matches any string with those three letters. It does not matter whether the two strings are the same object. With ==, it would matter.

Gotcha

You cannot switch on long. This gap is strange, and it exists for historical reasons. It surprises developers who switch on a timestamp or an ID. Use if/else if, or a Map<Long, ...> lookup.

1
TranslateWrite this in Java, where status is an OrderStatus: 
var canCancel = status switch
{
    OrderStatus.New or OrderStatus.Paid => true,
    _ => false
};
var canCancel = switch (status) {
    case NEW, PAID -> true;
    default -> false;
};

The value goes in brackets after switch. Labels that share an arm are separated by commas. Enum constants are written without the type name.

2
An expert asksAn arm of a Java switch expression can be a block of statements. Why does the block end with yield, and not with return?
A switch expression must produce a value, and yield gives the block's value to the switch. return would leave the whole method, so the compiler rejects it there. In Java, yield is not related to yield return in C#. The Java yield produces no sequence.

var, strings and text blocks#

Modern Java · Chapter 13· 10 min read

This chapter covers local variables declared with var Java 10, and everyday work with strings. It also covers text blocks Java 15, which are like raw string literals in C#. var works as it does in C#. The differences are in strings.

KindC#JavaNote
samevar count = 0;var count = 0;the compiler infers the type of a local variable from its value, as in C# Why
twist(a, b) => a + b(var a, var b) -> a + bJava also accepts var on the parameters of a lambda, but C# allows var on local variables only Why
trapvar names = new List<string>();var names = new ArrayList<>();with var, the empty diamond has no declared type to use, so the list holds Object Why
twist$"{a} and {b}"a + " and " + bJava has no string interpolation. For many values, use "%s and %s".formatted(a, b). Why
twist$"{x:F2}""%.2f".formatted(x)Java uses printf-style specifiers such as %.2f, %d and %s Why
twiststring.FormatString.formatJava fills the %s placeholders in order, so they have no numbers like {0} and {1} Why
sameStringBuilderStringBuilderJava has the same class with the same methods, and you use it in the same way Why
twiststring.Join(",", xs)String.join(",", xs)Pass a separator and then the items. The items must be text, so a list of numbers does not compile. Why
twiststring.IsNullOrEmpty(s)s == null || s.isEmpty()you write the null check yourself, because isEmpty() alone throws on null Why
twiststring.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s)s == null || s.isBlank()isBlank() arrived in Java 11 and ignores whitespace, like the C# method Why
sames.Contains(t)s.contains(t)the name and the meaning are the same, and both methods throw if t is null Why
traps == ts.equals(t)== compares references, so it fails on strings built at run time and reports no error Why
twist""" raw string literal""" text blockthe same three quotes, but Java needs a line break after the opening quotes Why
twist\d in a raw string\\d in a text blocka text block still processes escapes, so a regular expression keeps doubled backslashes Why

vartwist#

C#
var lines = new List<OrderLine>();
var count = 0;
foreach (var line in lines) { count += line.Quantity; }
Java 25
var lines = new ArrayList<OrderLine>();
var count = 0;
for (var line : lines) { count += line.quantity(); }
Reading the code
var lines = new ArrayList<OrderLine>();

The compiler reads the value on the right and gives lines the type ArrayList<OrderLine>. After that the type cannot change, exactly as in C#. ArrayList does the same as List<T> in C#.

for (var line : lines)

var works in loops too. For a for-each loop, C# writes foreach and in. Java writes for and a colon.

Java allows var in the same places as C#, with one small difference. In Java, a lambda may declare its parameters with var, as in (var a, var b) -> a + b.

ContextC# varJava var
Local variableyesyes
for / foreach variableyesyes
Fieldnono
Method parameternono
Return typenono
Lambda parameterimplicityes, explicit var allowed
Without an initialisernono
With nullnono

var and the diamondtrap#

Predictvar with an empty diamond#
Does this compile?
import java.util.ArrayList;

var names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("mug");
String first = names.get(0);
Show the answer
No: incompatible types: Object cannot be converted to String

var with an empty diamond gives you a list of Object. The empty brackets <> are called the diamond. The diamond asks the compiler to take the type argument from the variable's declared type. With var there is no declared type, so the compiler uses Object. The first two lines compile, and the list accepts any value.

When you use var, write the type argument: var names = new ArrayList<String>();. Or declare the type and keep the diamond: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();.

No string interpolationtwist#

The next example uses three values. name is a String. orderId is a long. total is a BigDecimal.

C#
var greeting = $"Hello {name}, your order {orderId} comes to {total:F2} EUR";
Java 25
var greeting = "Hello " + name + ", your order " + orderId + " comes to " + total + " EUR";
var formatted = "Hello %s, your order %d comes to %.2f EUR".formatted(name, orderId, total);
Reading the code
"Hello " + name + ", your order "

Joining with + turns orderId and total into text for you.

.formatted(name, orderId, total)

formatted fills in a template, like string.Format in C#. %s takes any value as text. %d takes a whole number. %.2f takes a decimal number and shows it with two decimal places. The values fill the placeholders in order.

String interpolation

Java has no $"...", and this is still true in Java 25. String templates were previewed in Java 21 and 22 and then withdrawn. They are not in Java 23, 24 or 25, and the design is being reconsidered. Code from tutorials that used string templates no longer compiles.

To learn when to use each replacement, see the section Choosing a replacement.

Formatting and everyday string methodstwist#

Here productId, note and total are single values. productIds is a list of strings.

C#
var label = string.Format("{0} x {1}", productId, quantity);
var csv = string.Join(", ", productIds);
var noNote = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(note);
var isGift = note.Contains("gift");
var shown = $"{total:F2}";
Java 25
var label = String.format("%s x %s", productId, quantity);
var csv = String.join(", ", productIds);
var noNote = note == null || note.isBlank();
var isGift = note.contains("gift");
var shown = "%.2f".formatted(total);
Reading the code
String.format("%s x %s", productId, quantity)

Java fills the placeholders in order. C# numbers its placeholders {0} and {1}.

note == null || note.isBlank()

Java has no IsNullOrWhiteSpace. isBlank() is true for text that is empty or holds only whitespace. But calling isBlank() on null throws, so the null check comes first. To do the same as IsNullOrEmpty, call isEmpty() in the same way.

Choosing a replacementtwist#

The code below shows the replacements for interpolation, and when to use each replacement. name, orderId and total are the values from the section No string interpolation. lines holds the lines of the order.

// Joining with +: fine for a few pieces, and the compiler makes it efficient.
String opening = "Hello " + name + ", your order " + orderId;

// formatted or String.format: when you need a fixed number of decimal places.
String totalLine = "Total: %.2f EUR".formatted(total);
String amount = String.format("%,.2f", total);   // 1,234.50 with an English locale

// StringBuilder: in a loop, or when building something large.
var sb = new StringBuilder();
for (var line : lines) sb.append(line.productId()).append(',');

// A text block plus formatted: for text that spans several lines.
String email = """
    Hello %s,

    Your order %d has shipped.
    """.formatted(name, orderId);
Reading the code
String.format("%,.2f", total)

String.format is the older form of the same template method. Every Java version has it. The comma in %,.2f adds thousands separators.

sb.append(line.productId()).append(',');

append returns the builder, so you can chain the calls. A StringBuilder in C# works the same way.

""".formatted(name, orderId);

A text block is an ordinary String, so formatted works on it too.

Comparing stringstrap#

Gotcha

== on strings compares references, not contents. The comparison often appears to work, because the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) reuses one object for identical string literals. So "abc" == "abc" is true. C# has an operator overload that makes == compare the text of two strings. Java has no such overload. To predict the result yourself, see == on two strings.

Compare the text with equals. Here typed is a voucher code that a customer typed:

import java.util.Objects;

boolean equal = typed.equals("SPRING");           // what C#'s == does for strings
boolean safe = Objects.equals(typed, "SPRING");   // the same, and no exception if typed is null

typed.equals throws when typed is null. Objects.equals returns false instead.

C# refresherString == in C#: an operator overload that compares contentsC# 1
string a = "abc";
string b = new string("abc".ToCharArray());   // a different object, same characters
Console.WriteLine(a == b);                    // True: string overloads == to compare text

Text blockstwist#

C# raw string literal
var json = """
    {
      "orderId": 1042,
      "status": "PAID"
    }
    """;
Java 15+ text block
String json = """
    {
      "orderId": 1042,
      "status": "PAID"
    }
    """;
Reading the code
String json = """

Three quotes and a line break open the text block. Java requires the line break, so the text starts on the next line.

""";

Java removes the indentation that every line shares. Here that is four spaces, so the text starts at the brace. The closing quotes count as a line too. If you move the closing quotes further left, the indentation is kept.

The differences are in the details:

BehaviourC# raw stringJava text block
Opening delimiter""" on its own line""" must be followed by a newline
Indentation strippingrelative to closing """relative to the least-indented line and closing """
Escapes processednoyes, so \n, \t and \" still work
Interpolation$""" ... """none
Line continuationno\ at end of line joins lines
Trailing spacepreservedstripped, unless \s is used
Gotcha

A Java text block still processes escape sequences such as \n. So \d is an invalid escape and does not compile. You still write \\d. A raw string in C# does no escape processing at all. Use a text block for SQL, JSON and HTML, and accept the doubled backslashes in a regular expression.

IsMatch in Javatrap#

A customer's note may mention a product code such as sku-1042. In C#, sku.IsMatch(note) tells you whether the note contains a product code. In Java, the classes Pattern and Matcher replace the Regex class of .NET. Matcher has a method with a name similar to IsMatch:

PredictA product code inside a note#
What does this print?
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

Pattern sku = Pattern.compile("sku-\\d+");   // in a Java string, \\d is the regex \d
String note = "please wrap sku-1042 as a gift";
System.out.println(sku.matcher(note).matches());
Show the answer
false

matches() is not IsMatch. Matcher.matches() requires the entire text to match the pattern. The note holds more than the product code. So the call returns false, and nothing reports an error.

Write sku.matcher(note).find(), which searches for the pattern anywhere in the text. For the rest of Regex, see the section Regular expressions.

Regular expressions#

In Java, the classes Pattern and Matcher replace the Regex class of .NET. The pattern syntax is almost the same. But Java splits the work between two objects, and every backslash is doubled. Here the shop splits a phone number such as 555-0199 into its first three digits and its last four digits. phone holds one number, and notes holds text that may contain several numbers:

C#
var re = new Regex(@"(?<area>\d{3})-(?<num>\d{4})");

var m = re.Match(phone);
if (m.Success)
{
    var area = m.Groups["area"].Value;
}

var all = re.Matches(notes);
var hidden = re.Replace(phone, "$1-XXXX");
Java 25
import java.util.regex.*;

Pattern re = Pattern.compile("(?<area>\\d{3})-(?<num>\\d{4})");

Matcher m = re.matcher(phone);
if (m.find()) {
    String area = m.group("area");
}

List<MatchResult> all = re.matcher(notes).results().toList();
String hidden = re.matcher(phone).replaceAll("$1-XXXX");
Reading the code
Pattern.compile("(?<area>\\d{3})-(?<num>\\d{4})")

This line compiles the pattern once. Every backslash is written twice, because in a Java string \\ means one backslash. Named groups use the same (?<name>...) syntax as .NET.

re.matcher(phone)

A Matcher applies the pattern to one piece of text. It remembers its position in that text, so you make a new Matcher for each input.

m.find()

find() searches for the pattern anywhere in the text, like Match followed by Success in C#.

m.group("area")

This call reads a named group, like Groups["area"].Value in C#.

results().toList()

This line gets every match, like Matches in C#. results() returns a stream, which is like a LINQ sequence in C#. toList() collects the stream into a list. For more about streams, see the chapter Streams vs LINQ.

The next example shows options and the other everyday methods. A customer's note may mention product codes such as SKU-1042, typed in any mix of upper and lower case:

C#
var sku = new Regex(@"sku-\d+",
    RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.Compiled);

bool mentionsProduct = sku.IsMatch(note);
string[] pieces = sku.Split(note);  // the text between the codes
Java 25
Pattern sku = Pattern.compile("sku-\\d+",
    Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);  // Java has no Compiled option

boolean mentionsProduct = sku.matcher(note).find();  // not matches()
String[] pieces = sku.split(note);  // the same, but no empty last piece
Reading the code
Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE

Options are constants on Pattern. You pass them as the second argument. Java has no option like RegexOptions.Compiled, so leave it out.

sku.matcher(note).find()

This call does the same as IsMatch in C#. Use find(), because the similar-looking matches() succeeds only if the whole text matches.

sku.split(note)

This call returns the text between the codes. When the note ends with a code, Split in .NET also returns an empty last piece. split in Java does not return that empty piece.

Here is the full mapping from Regex in .NET:

.NETJavaNote
new Regex(p)Pattern.compile(p)compile the pattern once and store it in a static final field
re.Match(s)p.matcher(s).find()matcher is stateful and NOT thread-safe
re.IsMatch(s)p.matcher(s).find()matches() requires the WHOLE string to match
re.Matches(s)p.matcher(s).results()added in Java 9, and it returns a Stream of MatchResult, one per match
m.Groups["name"]m.group("name")named groups use the same (?<name>...) syntax in both languages
m.Groups[1]m.group(1)group(0) is the whole match in both languages
re.Replace(s, r)m.replaceAll(r)the replacement refers to a group as $1 in both languages
re.Split(s)p.split(s)Java drops an empty last piece, which .NET keeps. String.split compiles the pattern on each call.
RegexOptions.IgnoreCasePattern.CASE_INSENSITIVEpass it as the second argument to Pattern.compile
RegexOptions.Compiledno equivalentJava has no such option, so leave it out when you translate
@"verbatim"no equivalentevery backslash must be doubled
Gotcha

Java has no verbatim string, and that causes two traps.

Every backslash is doubled. \d in a .NET verbatim string is "\\d" in Java. A text block does not help, because it still processes escapes. In this one place, C# raw strings are clearly better, and Java has no workaround.

matches() is not IsMatch. Matcher.matches() requires the entire text to match. find() searches for the first occurrence. Using the method with the familiar-looking name is a common bug, and nothing reports an error. For an example, see the prediction a product code inside a note.

Note

A Pattern never changes and is safe to share between threads. So compile it once into a private static final field. A Matcher does change, and it is not safe to share between threads. So create a new Matcher each time. String.matches, String.split and String.replaceAll compile the pattern again on every call. That is fine for an occasional call, but it is slow in a loop.

Concatenation performance#

Note

Do not use StringBuilder out of habit. Since Java 9, the compiler turns a + b + c into a single call. That call calculates the final length and builds the string once. StringBuilder is still the right tool inside a loop, because there the compiler cannot join the pieces for you. For a fixed number of pieces, plain + is both clearer and faster.

Here are the two cases together, using the order's lines:

// A fixed number of pieces: plain + builds the string once.
String summary = "Order " + orderId + " has " + count + " lines";

// A loop: use a StringBuilder, because += would build a whole new string each time round.
var sb = new StringBuilder();
for (var line : lines) sb.append(line.productId()).append('\n');

In the loop, text += line.productId() would copy all the text built so far on every pass. So the work grows much faster than the number of lines. sb.append adds the text to the same builder, as it does in C#.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java. quantity is an int. productId is a string. unitPrice is a BigDecimal. 
var label = $"{quantity} x {productId} at {unitPrice:F2} EUR";
var label = "%d x %s at %.2f EUR".formatted(quantity, productId, unitPrice);

Java has no string interpolation. Each placeholder names the kind of value. %d takes a whole number, and %s takes any text. %.2f does the same as :F2. The values fill the placeholders in order.

2
An expert asksA colleague shows that "abc" == "abc" is true in Java, and concludes that == compares strings by their text. Why is it true, and why is the conclusion wrong?
The JVM reuses one object for identical string literals, so both sides are the same object. A string built while the program runs is a different object, even when it has the same text. A string read from a request is one example. For such a string, == is false. Compare strings with equals.

Enums#

Modern Java · Chapter 14· 6 min read

A C# enum is a named number. A Java enum is a class with a fixed set of objects, one for each constant. So a constant can have fields and methods of its own.

KindC#JavaNote
twistenum OrderStatus { New = 1, Paid = 2 }enum OrderStatus { NEW, PAID }each constant is an object, not a named number Why
twist(Status) 2no equivalentJava has no cast from int, so index into values() only if you must Why
trap(int) ee.ordinal()ordinal() is the position in the declaration. Never store it, because a new constant shifts it. Why
new[Description] attributea field on the enumgive the enum a constructor argument, such as a label Why
newa switch, or a class for each optiona method body on each constanteach constant can supply its own version of a method Why
twistEnum.Parse<T>(s)Status.valueOf(s)matches the exact name, and throws IllegalArgumentException if unknown Why
twistEnum.TryParseno equivalentvalueOf throws IllegalArgumentException for an unknown name and NullPointerException for null, so catch both Why
twistEnum.GetValues<T>()Status.values()returns a new copy of the array on every call, so keep the array in a field if you need it often Why
twiste.ToString()e.name()name() is always the constant as declared, but toString() can be overridden Why
twistDictionary keyed by enumEnumMapa map backed by an array indexed by ordinal, so lookups are fast Why
twist[Flags]EnumSetJava has no bitwise enums, but an EnumSet is a bit vector inside Why
twistOrderStatus.New =>case NEW ->a case label is the bare constant, without the type name Why
twista singleton classenum ExchangeRates { INSTANCE; }a one-constant enum has exactly one object, but in a Spring application, use a bean Why

The shape of the differencetwist#

C#
public enum OrderStatus
{
    New = 1,
    Paid = 2,
    Shipped = 3,
    Cancelled = 4
}

var status = (OrderStatus) 2;          // Paid
int number = (int) OrderStatus.Paid;   // 2
Java 25
public enum OrderStatus {
    NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED
}

OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.valueOf("PAID");
int position = OrderStatus.PAID.ordinal();  // 1, but see the next section
Reading the code
NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED

These are the constants, written in capitals by convention. There are no numbers to choose. Each constant is a single object of type OrderStatus, and it is created when the enum is first used.

OrderStatus.valueOf("PAID")

This call finds a constant by its name, like Enum.Parse in C#. Java has no cast from a number to an enum.

OrderStatus.PAID.ordinal()

This call returns the position of the constant in the list, counting from 0. The position is not a value that you chose.

Storing an enum as a numbertrap#

PredictAn order status stored as a number#
What does this print?
enum OrderStatus { NEW, ON_HOLD, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED }   // ON_HOLD was added this week

int stored = 1;   // saved last month with PAID.ordinal(), when PAID came second
System.out.println(OrderStatus.values()[stored]);
Show the answer
ON_HOLD

Never persist ordinal(). ordinal() is the position in the declaration. So when you add a constant, every constant after it gets a new number, and nothing warns you. Every order that was stored as 1 changes from paid to on hold.

Store name() instead. A code field that you control is even better. For an example, see the section Enums with state and behaviour.

Enums with state and behaviournew#

The order page shows a label for each status, and the database stores a one-letter code. In C#, you would keep the labels in a separate switch or dictionary, or attach the labels with a [Description] attribute. A Java enum holds this data itself:

public enum OrderStatus {
    NEW("N", "waiting for payment"),
    PAID("P", "being packed"),
    SHIPPED("S", "on its way"),
    CANCELLED("C", "cancelled");

    private final String code;
    private final String label;

    OrderStatus(String code, String label) {   // an enum constructor is always private
        this.code = code;
        this.label = label;
    }

    public String code()  { return code; }
    public String label() { return label; }
}

String shown = OrderStatus.SHIPPED.label();   // "on its way"
Reading the code
NEW("N", "waiting for payment"),

Each constant passes arguments to the constructor. The list of constants ends with a semicolon, because more code follows.

private final String code;

This is an ordinary field. It is a final field, which is set once in the constructor. So the code of a constant never changes.

OrderStatus(String code, String label)

This is the constructor. It is always private, even without the keyword. So no code outside the enum can create a fifth status.

OrderStatus.SHIPPED.label()

This line calls a method on a constant, as on any object.

Storing code() in the database fixes the ordinal() problem. A new constant gets a new code, and the existing codes do not change.

Constants with their own behaviournew#

A constant can also supply its own version of a method. The shop offers two delivery options. Standard delivery costs 4.95, but it is free for orders of 50 or more. Express delivery always costs 9.95:

public enum Delivery {
    STANDARD {
        public BigDecimal price(BigDecimal total) {
            return total.compareTo(new BigDecimal("50")) >= 0 ? BigDecimal.ZERO : new BigDecimal("4.95");
        }
    },
    EXPRESS {
        public BigDecimal price(BigDecimal total) {
            return new BigDecimal("9.95");
        }
    };

    public abstract BigDecimal price(BigDecimal total);
}

BigDecimal cost = Delivery.STANDARD.price(new BigDecimal("62.00"));   // 0: free from 50
Reading the code
public abstract BigDecimal price(BigDecimal total);

This line declares a method with no body, so every constant must supply a body.

STANDARD {

This is a constant with a body of its own. The body supplies price for standard delivery.

total.compareTo(new BigDecimal("50")) >= 0

BigDecimal has no >= operator. compareTo returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. So >= 0 means that the total is at least 50.

C# enums cannot hold methods. So in C#, this usually becomes a switch, or a small class for each option. A Java enum keeps the whole closed set of options in one place, together with the rule of each option.

Everyday enum operationstwist#

Here text holds a status that arrived in a request, such as "PAID". The variable counts will count orders by status:

C#
var status = Enum.Parse<OrderStatus>("Paid");
bool ok = Enum.TryParse<OrderStatus>(text, out var parsed);
OrderStatus[] all = Enum.GetValues<OrderStatus>();
string name = OrderStatus.Paid.ToString();  // "Paid"
var counts = new Dictionary<OrderStatus, int>();
Java 25
import java.util.EnumMap;

var status = OrderStatus.valueOf("PAID");  // throws if unknown
OrderStatus parsed;
try {
    parsed = OrderStatus.valueOf(text);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException | NullPointerException e) {
    parsed = null;  // not a known status
}
OrderStatus[] all = OrderStatus.values();  // a new array each call
String name = OrderStatus.PAID.name();  // "PAID"
var counts = new EnumMap<OrderStatus, Integer>(OrderStatus.class);
Reading the code
OrderStatus.valueOf("PAID")

This call finds the constant by its exact name. There is no option to ignore case.

catch (IllegalArgumentException | NullPointerException e)

Java has no TryParse. So you catch the exceptions that valueOf throws for an unknown name and for null. The | catches either type.

OrderStatus.values()

This call returns every constant in declaration order, like Enum.GetValues in C#. It returns a new array on every call, so keep the array in a field if you need it often.

new EnumMap<OrderStatus, Integer>(OrderStatus.class)

This is a map whose keys are enum constants. The map is kept in an array indexed by position, so it is faster than an ordinary map. OrderStatus.class is the type itself as a value, like typeof(OrderStatus) in C#.

Flags become an EnumSettwist#

[Flags] enums

Java has no flags enums and no bitwise arithmetic on enums. An order can need gift wrapping, express handling and careful packing, in any combination. In C#, that is a [Flags] enum. In Java, it is an EnumSet. An EnumSet stores one bit for each constant inside, so it is as fast as a flags enum, and it is easier to read:

C#
[Flags]
enum Handling { None = 0, GiftWrap = 1, Express = 2, Fragile = 4 }

var handling = Handling.GiftWrap | Handling.Fragile;
if (handling.HasFlag(Handling.Fragile)) { }
Java 25
import java.util.EnumSet;

enum Handling { GIFT_WRAP, EXPRESS, FRAGILE }

var handling = EnumSet.of(Handling.GIFT_WRAP, Handling.FRAGILE);
if (handling.contains(Handling.FRAGILE)) { }
Reading the code
EnumSet.of(Handling.GIFT_WRAP, Handling.FRAGILE)

This is a set that holds two constants. C# combines two flags with |. The empty set is EnumSet.noneOf(Handling.class). It does the same as None in C#.

handling.contains(Handling.FRAGILE)

This call does the same as HasFlag in C#.

Enums and switch#

You saw a switch over OrderStatus in the chapter Switch expressions. That switch needs no default, because it covers every constant. Here is the switch again, to show how the labels are written:

String label = switch (status) {
    case NEW       -> "waiting for payment";
    case PAID      -> "being packed";
    case SHIPPED   -> "on its way";
    case CANCELLED -> "cancelled";
};

The switch has four labels, from NEW to CANCELLED. The four labels cover every constant, so the switch needs no default.

Note

Inside a case label, you write the constant without the type name. So you write NEW, not OrderStatus.NEW. Before Java 21, the form with the type name was a compile error. Since Java 21, both forms compile, but the name without the type is still the convention that you will see.

The enum singleton#

An enum with one constant has exactly one object. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) guarantees that, even when objects are saved and loaded again or created through reflection. That makes a one-constant enum the most reliable way to write a singleton in Java. Here the shop keeps one shared table of exchange rates:

public enum ExchangeRates {
    INSTANCE;

    private final Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void put(String currency, BigDecimal rate) { rates.put(currency, rate); }
    public BigDecimal get(String currency)             { return rates.get(currency); }
}

ExchangeRates.INSTANCE.put("USD", new BigDecimal("1.08"));
Reading the code
INSTANCE;

This is the only constant, so there is exactly one ExchangeRates object in the program.

new ConcurrentHashMap<>()

This is a map that several threads can use at the same time, like ConcurrentDictionary in C#.

In an application that uses Spring, you would make this a bean instead. A bean is an object that Spring creates once and gives to every class that needs it. It is still useful to recognise the enum singleton in library code.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this C# line in Java: bool ok = Enum.TryParse<OrderStatus>(text, out var parsed);
OrderStatus parsed;
try {
    parsed = OrderStatus.valueOf(text);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException | NullPointerException e) {
    parsed = null;  // not a known status
}

Java has no TryParse. Call OrderStatus.valueOf(text), and catch the two exceptions that it can throw. It throws IllegalArgumentException for an unknown name. It throws NullPointerException when text is null.

2
An expert asksWhy can a Java enum constant hold a code and a label, when a C# enum member cannot?
A C# enum member is a name for a number. A Java enum is a class, and each constant is one object of that class. So the enum can have final fields, a private constructor and methods.
