Generics and type erasure#

Modern Java · Chapter 15· 9 min read

Java generics look like C# generics. A class or a method takes a type parameter, with an optional constraint. The most important difference is called type erasure. Java checks type arguments when it compiles, and then removes them.

KindC#JavaNote
twistwhere T : Base<T extends Base>classes and interfaces both use extends Why
twistwhere T : IFoo, IBar<T extends Foo & Bar>Join bounds with &. If one bound is a class, it must come first. Why
twistwhere T : classno equivalentevery type argument is a reference type, so Java needs no such constraint Why
twistwhere T : structno equivalentJava has no user-defined value types to constrain to Why
twistwhere T : unmanagedno equivalentJava has no unmanaged or pointer types Why
trapList<string> and List<int> are two typesone class at run timeJava erases type arguments when it compiles, so a running program cannot see them Why
twistwhere T : new()no equivalentJava has no new T(), so pass a Supplier<T> such as Customer::new instead Why
twistx is List<string>x instanceof List<?>a list does not know its element type at run time, so only List<?> can be tested Why
twistdefault(T)nulla type parameter is always a reference type, so null is its only default Why
twisttypeof(T)a Class<T> parameterthe caller passes Customer.class, because T is erased Why
twistIEnumerable<out T>List<? extends T>variance is written at each use, with a wildcard Why
twistIComparer<in T>Comparator<? super T>for the consumer side, C# declares in and Java writes ? super Why
twistList<int>List<Integer> or int[]A type argument cannot be a primitive, so each int is boxed into an Integer. An int[] holds plain ints. Why
twistDictionary<int,V>Map<Integer,V>every int key is boxed into an Integer object Why
twistIEnumerable<int>IntStreama stream of plain ints, so nothing is boxed Why
twistNullable<int> / int?Integeran Integer can be null, so it does the same as int? in C# Why
twistJsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<Customer>>(json)new TypeReference<List<Customer>>() { }an anonymous subclass keeps the full generic type, so Jackson can read it back Why
twistthe non-generic ArrayList of System.CollectionsList raw = new ArrayList();A raw type disables type checking. You will see it in old code, but never write it. Why

Declarationtwist#

C#
public interface IHasId { long Id { get; } }

public class InMemoryRepository<T> where T : IHasId
{
    private readonly Dictionary<long, T> items = new();

    public void Save(T item) => items[item.Id] = item;
    public T? Find(long id) => items.GetValueOrDefault(id);
}
Java 25
public interface HasId { long id(); }

public class InMemoryRepository<T extends HasId> {
    private final Map<Long, T> items = new HashMap<>();

    public void save(T item) { items.put(item.id(), item); }
    public T find(long id) { return items.get(id); }
}
Reading the code
public class InMemoryRepository<T extends HasId>

The type parameter follows the class name, as in C#. Java writes the constraint inside the angle brackets, with extends. C# writes where T : IHasId after the class. Java uses extends for interfaces too.

Map<Long, T>

The key type is Long, not long, because a type argument cannot be a primitive type. See No primitive type arguments.

items.put(item.id(), item);

Because T extends HasId, the compiler lets you call id() on any T.

return items.get(id);

get returns null when the id is missing, like GetValueOrDefault in C#.

Several constraints are joined with &, as in <T extends HasId & Comparable<T>>. The C# constraints class, struct and unmanaged have no Java form, because every type argument in Java is a reference type.

What erasure takes awaynew#

Java checks type arguments when it compiles, and then removes them. This is called type erasure. In C#, the runtime knows every type argument.

PredictA list of strings and a list of numbers#
What does this print?
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> quantities = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(names.getClass() == quantities.getClass());
Show the answer
true

While the program runs, List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. Java removed both type arguments when it compiled, so each object is a plain ArrayList. In C# the two lists have different types, because the runtime knows every type argument.

While the program runs, no code can ask a list which type it holds. Code that needs the type takes the type as a value. See Passing the type yourself.

In the same way, the class InMemoryRepository<T extends HasId> from the section Declaration is a plain InMemoryRepository while the program runs. This is true for every T. Inside the class, Java treats T as its constraint, HasId. So any code that needs to know T at run time does not compile. Here Box<T> is any generic class, and x is any object:

Gotcha

The four lines marked no do not compile in Java, and all four lines work in C#:

class Box<T> {
    void tryThings(Object x) {
        T t = new T();                           // no: T is unknown at run time
        T[] a = new T[10];                       // no: nor can an array of T be created
        boolean b = x instanceof List<String>;   // no: a list does not know its element type
        Class<T> c = T.class;                    // no: T has no class literal
    }
    static int count;                            // one count shared by every Box, whatever T is
}
Reading the code
T t = new T();

C# allows this with a new() constraint. Java has no T at run time, so it has nothing to create.

x instanceof List<String>

At run time a List<String> is only a List, so Java cannot make this test. x instanceof List<?> compiles, because it only asks whether x is a list.

static int count;

A static field belongs to the class, and after erasure there is only one class. In C#, Box<int> and Box<string> each have their own count.

The workaround is to pass the type yourself. See Passing the type yourself. That is why Java APIs have many Class<T> parameters. C# would use typeof(T) there.

C# refresherdefault(T) and dynamicC# 4

default gives the zero value of a type parameter. dynamic delays member lookup until run time.

T FirstOrZero<T>(List<T> xs) => xs.Count > 0 ? xs[0] : default;   // null, 0 or false

dynamic x = "hello";
int n = x.Length;              // resolved at run time, with no compile-time check

Java has no default(T) and no dynamic. A type parameter is always a reference type, so its only default is null. For late binding, Java uses reflection, or a Map<String, Object>.

Passing the type yourselftwist#

Here mapper is the ObjectMapper of Jackson. Jackson is the JSON library that most Java services use. json holds one customer:

C#
// typeof(T) is available here: T exists at run time
T Read<T>(string json) =>
    JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json)!;

var customer = Read<Customer>(json);
Java 25
<T> T read(String json, Class<T> type) {
    return mapper.readValue(json, type);
}

var customer = read(json, Customer.class);
Reading the code
Class<T> type

The caller passes the type as a value. Class<T> is like Type in C#, but Class<T> has a type argument. So the compiler knows that the method returns a T.

read(json, Customer.class)

Customer.class is the type as a value, like typeof(Customer) in C#.

mapper.readValue(json, type)

Spring Boot 3 uses Jackson 2. With Jackson 2, readValue also declares a checked exception, so this method must add throws JsonProcessingException. Spring Boot 4 uses Jackson 3. With Jackson 3, readValue does not declare a checked exception.

Note

This is why these methods all take a .class value:

  • getBean(OrderService.class) in Spring
  • readValue(json, Customer.class) in Jackson
  • mock(OrderRepository.class) in Mockito

Variance is at the use sitetwist#

C#
// Declared once, on the interface: IEnumerable<out T>.
// Contravariance is declared the same way: IComparer<in T>.
void PrintAll(IEnumerable<Payment> payments)
{
    foreach (var p in payments) Console.WriteLine(p);
}

List<Card> cards = new() { new Card("4242") };
PrintAll(cards);  // fine: IEnumerable<Card> converts to IEnumerable<Payment>
Java 25
// Written where the type is used: List<? extends Payment>.
void printAll(List<? extends Payment> payments) {
    for (var p : payments) System.out.println(p);
}

List<Card> cards = List.of(new Card("4242"));
printAll(cards);  // fine: a List<Card> is a List<? extends Payment>
Reading the code
List<? extends Payment> payments

? extends Payment is called a wildcard. With the wildcard, the parameter accepts a list of Payment, or a list of any type that implements Payment. Reading from the list gives you a Payment. Adding to the list is not allowed, because the list might really be a List<Card>. A Voucher does not belong in a List<Card>.

printAll(cards);

Without the wildcard, printAll(List<Payment>) would reject a List<Card>. A Java List is not converted automatically. The same is true for a List<T> in C#.

Note

Java developers remember this rule as PECS. PECS means Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter produces values for you to read, use ? extends. If a parameter consumes values that you supply, use ? super.

? extends does the same as the out keyword in C#. ? super does the same as the in keyword in C#. C# writes the keyword once, on the interface. Java writes the wildcard where the type is used.

? super, and the four wildcard forms#

The other direction is ? super, which does the same as the in keyword in C#. This method adds test cards to any list that can hold cards:

void addTestCards(List<? super Card> target) {
    target.add(new Card("0000"));
}

List<Payment> payments = new ArrayList<>();
addTestCards(payments);   // fine: a List<Payment> can hold cards
Reading the code
List<? super Card> target

This parameter accepts a list of Card, or a list of any type above Card. Two such types are Payment and Object. You can add a Card. But reading gives you only an Object, because the list might hold other payments too.

Here are the four forms that a list type can have:

WildcardMeansYou canMnemonic
List<String>exactly String, so a List<Object> is not acceptedread and write Stringinvariant
List<? extends Number>a list of Number or of any subtype, such as Integerread as Number, cannot addproducer
List<? super Integer>a list of Integer or of any supertype, such as Numberadd Integer, read as Objectconsumer
List<?>a list of something, so you only know that each element is an Objectread as Object, cannot addany

No primitive type arguments#

A type argument must be a class, so List<int> is not legal Java. You write List<Integer>. Each int is then wrapped in an Integer object. This wrapping is called boxing.

List<Integer> quantities = new ArrayList<>();
quantities.add(42);                        // boxed: stored as an Integer object

int[] raw = new int[1_000_000];            // one block of ints, no objects
int total = IntStream.of(raw).sum();       // a stream of plain ints: nothing is boxed
Reading the code
quantities.add(42);

42 is an int, so Java wraps it in an Integer before storing it. C# boxes a value in the same way when it stores the value as an object.

IntStream.of(raw).sum()

IntStream is a stream built for int, so the numbers are not boxed. For more about streams, see the chapter Streams vs LINQ.

A map key is boxed in the same way. C# writes Dictionary<int, V>. Java writes Map<Integer, V>. An Integer can also be null, so it does the same as int? in C#.

Gotcha

Boxing uses more memory and makes code slower. A List<Integer> of a million entries holds a million separate objects on the heap, plus an array that points to them. In C#, a List<int> is one block of ints.

There are two workarounds. For storage, use int[]. For processing, use the streams built for numbers, which are IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream. Project Valhalla aims to fix this problem properly, but it is not part of Java 25.

Getting type information back#

Erasure removes the type argument from an object. But a compiled class still keeps the type arguments that are written in its field types, its method signatures and its superclass. Libraries such as Jackson and Spring read these type arguments to recover a full generic type. Here json holds a JSON array of customers:

// The { } creates a subclass whose superclass keeps List<Customer>.
List<Customer> customers = mapper.readValue(json, new TypeReference<List<Customer>>() { });

// Spring's version of the same trick, when calling another service.
List<Customer> body = restClient.get().uri("/customers").retrieve()
        .body(new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<Customer>>() { });
Reading the code
new TypeReference<List<Customer>>() { }

This expression creates an object of an anonymous subclass. An anonymous subclass is a class with no name. The braces declare the class at this place in the code. Its superclass is TypeReference<List<Customer>>. The compiled class keeps this superclass, so Jackson can read the type argument from it.

new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<Customer>>() { }

This is the same idea, in the RestClient of Spring. Customer.class alone would lose the List around Customer.

Gotcha

This trick is a subclass that exists only to keep a type argument. It looks strange until you know why it exists. When you see new TypeReference<...>() { } with the trailing braces, the code is using this trick. Without the braces, the code does not compile, because TypeReference is abstract.

Raw types#

LegacyRaw types

Generics arrived in Java 5, in 2004. Older code had to keep compiling, so you can still write List with no type argument. That is called a raw type. Everything in a raw type is an Object, type checking is off, and the compiler only warns you. A raw type does the same as the non-generic ArrayList of System.Collections in C#.

List raw = new ArrayList();          // legal, but the compiler warns
raw.add("mug");
raw.add(1);
String s = (String) raw.get(1);      // compiles, then throws ClassCastException when it runs
Reading the code
List raw = new ArrayList();

This line has no type argument, so the list accepts any value. Here the list accepts a string, and then a number.

(String) raw.get(1)

The cast compiles, because the compiler no longer knows what the list holds. When the code runs, the element is an Integer, and the cast throws ClassCastException.

Treat every unchecked warning as an error. If you must silence a warning, put @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") on the smallest declaration you can. Add a comment that says why the code is safe.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java, with a List as the parameter. Card is one kind of Payment: 
void PrintAll(IEnumerable<Payment> payments)
{
    foreach (var p in payments) Console.WriteLine(p);
}

PrintAll(new List<Card> { new("4242") });
void printAll(List<? extends Payment> payments) {
    for (var p : payments) System.out.println(p);
}

List<Card> cards = List.of(new Card("4242"));
printAll(cards);

A plain List<Payment> parameter rejects a List<Card>. Java writes variance where the type is used. ? extends does the same as the out keyword in C#. Java developers remember the rule as PECS, which means producer extends, consumer super.

2
An expert asksWhy does new T() not compile in Java, when C# allows it with a new() constraint?
Java checks type arguments when it compiles and then removes them. This is called type erasure. While the program runs there is no T, so there is nothing to create. Pass a Class<T>, or a Supplier<T> such as Customer::new.
3
A colleague new to Java declares List<int> quantities. Why does it not compile, and what do you write?
A type argument cannot be a primitive type. The compiler reports unexpected type, and asks for a reference type. Write List<Integer>. In that list, each int is boxed into an Integer object. For many numbers, an int[] holds plain ints.

Annotations and attributes#

Modern Java · Chapter 16· 8 min read

An annotation in Java does the same as an attribute in C#. C# writes [Obsolete]. Java writes @Deprecated. You use an annotation in the same way as an attribute. It attaches information that the compiler, a framework or a tool reads.

KindC#JavaNote
twist[Attr]@Attran @ prefix instead of square brackets Why
same[Attr] on its own line@Attr on its own linestacked one per line above the declaration, as in C#
twist[Attr(1, Name = "x")]@Attr(value = 1, name = "x")named arguments work the same, but a member called value may be set without its name Why
twist[Obsolete]@Deprecatedpair it with a @deprecated javadoc tag that names the replacement Why
twistnameof(x)no equivalentwrite the name as a string, and use IntelliJ's rename or a test to keep it correct Why
newno equivalent@Retentionit says how long the annotation survives, and only RUNTIME is visible to reflection Why
trapan attribute is always readable by reflection@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)without it your own annotation is invisible at run time, because the default is CLASS Why
twistclass AuditedAttribute : Attributepublic @interface Auditedan annotation type is declared with @interface, and its members look like methods Why
twistAttributeUsage@Targetit says which declarations the annotation may be attached to Why
twistAllowMultiple = true@Repeatableadded in Java 8, and it needs a second annotation that is the container Why
twisteveryday attributes, such as [Obsolete]@Override, @Deprecated, @SuppressWarningsa few annotations appear in almost every Java codebase Why
twist[Conditional]no equivalentJava has no way to remove calls at compile time Why
trapa misspelt override is a compile error (CS0115)a misspelt method without @Override compilesIt is a new method that overrides nothing, and no error says so. Always write @Override. Why
twista C# source generatoran annotation processora javac plugin that reads annotations and writes new source files as you compile Why
twistGetCustomAttribute<T>()getAnnotation(T.class)returns null when the annotation is missing or not kept at run time Why

Syntaxtwist#

Here orders is the controller's OrderRepository:

C#
[Route("/orders")]
public class OrderController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("{id}")]
    public Order Get(long id, [FromQuery] bool withLines) => orders.Find(id);
}
Java 25
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Order get(@PathVariable long id, @RequestParam boolean withLines) {
        return orders.find(id);
    }
}
Reading the code
@RestController

This is an annotation. It is an @ followed by a name. C# puts the name in square brackets. This annotation tells Spring that the class answers web requests.

@RequestMapping("/orders")

This annotation has an argument. The argument is written in brackets like a method call, as in C#.

@RequestParam boolean withLines

Annotations go on parameters too. This annotation reads withLines from the query string, like [FromQuery] in C#.

Named argumentstwist#

C#
[Obsolete("Use FindById instead", DiagnosticId = "SHOP001")]
public Order Find(long id) => FindById(id);
Java 25
/** @deprecated Use {@link #findById(long)} instead. */
@Deprecated(since = "2.0", forRemoval = true)
public Order find(long id) { return findById(id); }
Reading the code
@Deprecated(since = "2.0", forRemoval = true)

Named arguments are written name = value, as in C#. Java annotations take no positional arguments, except for a member called value. For that member, see the section Declaring one.

/** @deprecated Use {@link #findById(long)} instead. */

This is a Javadoc comment. A Javadoc comment does the same as an XML doc comment in C#. Its @deprecated tag is written in lower case, and it tells readers what to use instead. The annotation is written with a capital letter, and it tells the compiler.

C# refreshernameof: a member's name as a checked stringC# 6
throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(order));   // "order", and a rename updates it

Java has no nameof. Names inside annotations and messages are plain strings, so a rename can leave them out of date. The rename in IntelliJ updates most of these strings. But only a test really guarantees that the names are still correct.

Retention: the concept C# lacksnew#

The shop wants a log entry every time an order changes. You write your own annotation, @Audited. You put it on the methods that change orders. Then your code looks for the annotation while the program runs. Frameworks such as Spring, Jackson, JUnit and Jakarta Persistence (JPA) find annotations the same way. C# attributes are always kept in the compiled assembly, and reflection can always read them.

PredictAn annotation of your own, read while the program runs#
What does this print?
import java.lang.reflect.Method;

@interface Audited { }

class OrderService {
    @Audited
    public void cancel(long orderId) { }
}

Method cancel = OrderService.class.getMethod("cancel", long.class);
System.out.println(cancel.getAnnotation(Audited.class));
Show the answer
null

If you write your own annotation and forget @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME), it silently disappears before your framework can see it. The default is CLASS, not RUNTIME. That default is the opposite of what you want almost every time. Here cancel is a Method object. Method does the same as MethodInfo in C#. The Method object finds no annotation to return.

Add the line that people forget. It keeps the annotation in the compiled class, and reflection can find the annotation there:

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Audited { }

How long an annotation survives is called its retention. Whether code can see the annotation depends on the retention:

RetentionSurvives toUsed for
SOURCEcompiler only@Override, @SuppressWarnings, Lombok
CLASSthe .class file, not reflectionbytecode tools, and it is the default
RUNTIMEreflectionSpring, Jackson, JUnit, JPA

Declaring one#

Here is @Audited in full. It holds the action being audited and who performs it. In C# an attribute is a class that derives from Attribute. In Java, an annotation is declared with @interface:

C#
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method)]
public class AuditedAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Action { get; }
    public AuditedAttribute(string action) => Action = action;
}
Java 25
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Audited {
    String action();
    String actor() default "system";
}
Reading the code
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)

@Target is like AttributeUsage in C#. Here it says that the annotation may only go on methods.

public @interface Audited {

@interface declares an annotation type, not a class.

String action();

A member is declared like a method with no body. You set the member when you use the annotation, as in @Audited(action = "cancel").

String actor() default "system";

default gives a member a value. The annotation uses this value when you do not set the member.

Note

A member named value is special. It can be set without its name. @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") is a short form of @SuppressWarnings(value = "unchecked"). The @Tag("billing") below works the same way. That is why so many annotations call their main member value.

To allow the same attribute twice on one declaration, C# needs one flag. Java needs a second annotation to hold the repeats. This second annotation is called the container. Here a test method gets two tags:

C#
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method, AllowMultiple = true)]
public class TagAttribute(string name) : Attribute { }

[Tag("billing"), Tag("slow")]
void Run() { }
Java 25
@Repeatable(Tags.class)
public @interface Tag { String value(); }

public @interface Tags { Tag[] value(); }  // the container

@Tag("billing") @Tag("slow")
void run() { }
Reading the code
@Repeatable(Tags.class)

This line allows @Tag more than once on a declaration. It also names the container that holds the repeats.

public @interface Tags { Tag[] value(); }

This is the container. It is an annotation whose value is an array of Tag. You never write the container on a method yourself. The compiler wraps repeated tags in the container.

Ones you will see constantlytwist#

The first five annotations in the table are part of Java itself. The other annotations come from libraries that later chapters cover. The [Conditional] attribute in C# has no counterpart in Java. No annotation removes calls at compile time.

AnnotationMeaning
@Overrideasserts that the method overrides a supertype method, so the compiler catches typos
@Deprecateddoes the same as [Obsolete], and you pair it with a @deprecated tag in the Javadoc
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")silences a specific compiler warning
@FunctionalInterfaceasserts that the interface has exactly one abstract method
@SafeVarargsasserts that a generic varargs method does not leak the array
@Nullable / @NonNullthey say whether a value may be null, as the chapter on Optional and JSpecify explains
@Entity, @Columnthese JPA annotations map a class to a table, and a field to a column
@Test, @ParameterizedTestthese JUnit annotations mark a test method, or a test that runs once per set of inputs
@Service, @Component, @Beanthese Spring annotations mark a class that is a bean, or a method that makes a bean
@JsonProperty, @JsonIgnorethese Jackson annotations rename a JSON property, or leave a field out of the JSON

Here are three of these annotations in code:

@FunctionalInterface
interface Pricing { BigDecimal price(Order order); }   // a second abstract method will not compile

class Cart {
    private final Map<String, Object> cache = new HashMap<>();

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")                     // silence one known warning
    List<String> names() { return (List<String>) cache.get("names"); }

    @Override
    public String toString() { return "Cart"; }        // checked: it must override something
}
Reading the code
@FunctionalInterface

This annotation promises that the interface has exactly one abstract method, so that it can be written as a lambda. If you add a second abstract method, the compiler reports an error.

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")

Because of erasure, the cast from Object to List<String> cannot be checked while the program runs, so the compiler warns. This annotation silences that one warning, for this one method.

@Override

This annotation asks the compiler to check that toString really overrides a method from a supertype. Here the supertype is Object.

Always write @Overridetrap#

Gotcha

Always write @Override. The annotation is optional. But without @Override, a small mistake in the signature makes a new method when you intended an override. The compiler reports no error. The mistake might be a capital letter, a boxed parameter or an extra argument. Here the mistake is the lower-case s:

class Cart {
    public String tostring() { return "Cart"; }     // compiles, and overrides nothing
}

class Basket {
    @Override
    public String tostring() { return "Basket"; }   // rejected by the compiler
}

In Basket, the compiler reports that tostring() does not override or implement a method from a supertype. The override keyword in C# is required, so this bug cannot happen in C#.

Annotation processing vs source generators#

An annotation processor is a plugin for javac that runs while your code compiles. It reads annotations and can write new source files. These files are compiled in the same run. Annotation processing is a mature pipeline. It is older than C# source generators by well over a decade, and a lot of the ecosystem depends on it.

C# refresherSource generators: C# code written at compile timeC# 9

A source generator reads your code during compilation and adds more C# to it. The best-known source generator writes the serialisation code for System.Text.Json, so no reflection runs.

[JsonSerializable(typeof(Order))]
internal partial class AppJson : JsonSerializerContext { }   // the generator fills it in

string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, AppJson.Default.Order);

MapStruct is a processor that writes mapping code. You declare an interface, and MapStruct writes the class that implements it. Here OrderDto is a record that holds the fields that the API returns:

@Mapper(componentModel = "spring")
public interface OrderMapper {
    OrderDto toDto(Order order);     // MapStruct writes the implementation at compile time
}
Reading the code
@Mapper(componentModel = "spring")

This annotation marks the interface for MapStruct. componentModel = "spring" makes the generated class a Spring bean, so it can be injected into other classes.

OrderDto toDto(Order order);

This is a method with no body. MapStruct writes the body. The body copies each field of Order to the field of OrderDto that has the same name.

Each .NET way of producing code has a Java counterpart:

.NETJavaDoes
Source generatorsAnnotation processors (APT)generate code at compile time
Roslyn analyzersError Prone, annotation processorsreport errors at compile time
IL weaving (Fody)bytecode manipulation (ByteBuddy)rewrite after compilation
Reflection at startupreflection, or APTframeworks increasingly prefer APT

These are the processors that you are most likely to meet. Some of them generate what a record now gives you with no extra code:

ToolGeneratesReplaces in .NET
Lombokgetters, setters, builders, equalsboilerplate, or a source generator
MapStructtype-to-type mappersAutoMapper, but at compile time
Micronaut / QuarkusDI wiring, no runtime reflectioncompile-time DI
JPA metamodeltyped criteria query classesEF Core's typed queries
Immutablesimmutable value classesrecords
Note

Look more closely at the comparison of MapStruct with AutoMapper. AutoMapper decides its mappings by reflection while the program runs. So a missing property fails only at that time. MapStruct writes a plain Java class when you compile, so mapping problems appear in the build. A field that MapStruct cannot convert is an error. A field with no match is a warning, or an error if you ask for one. The generated mapper is as fast as code that you write yourself.

Reading annotations at runtime#

Reading an annotation while the program runs works the same way in both languages. You find the method through reflection, and then you ask the method for the annotation. Here the audit code checks cancel on OrderService:

C#
var attr = typeof(OrderService)
    .GetMethod("Cancel")!
    .GetCustomAttribute<AuditedAttribute>();
if (attr is not null) Log(attr.Action);
Java 25
Method cancel = OrderService.class.getMethod("cancel", long.class);
Audited a = cancel.getAnnotation(Audited.class);
if (a != null) log(a.action());
Reading the code
OrderService.class.getMethod("cancel", long.class)

This call finds the public method cancel that takes a long. Java needs the parameter types, because several methods can share a name.

cancel.getAnnotation(Audited.class)

This call is like GetCustomAttribute in C#. It returns null when the method has no @Audited. It also returns null when the retention of the annotation is not RUNTIME.

This only works for RUNTIME retention. Spring, Jackson and JUnit all rely on RUNTIME retention. That is why Java frameworks have long spent time at startup scanning the classpath. That is also why Quarkus and Micronaut moved that work to compile time.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
[Obsolete("Use FindById instead")]
public Order Find(long id) => FindById(id);
/** @deprecated Use {@link #findById(long)} instead. */
@Deprecated
public Order find(long id) { return findById(id); }

@Deprecated takes no message. The replacement is named in the Javadoc comment, with the lower-case @deprecated tag.

2
An expert asksWhat does @Override actually do, given it is only an annotation?
It makes the compiler check that the method really does override something. Without @Override, a method with a slightly wrong signature becomes a new method, and the compiler reports no error.

Nullability: Optional and JSpecify#

Nullability · Chapter 17· 6 min read

Java has no string?. The language cannot say that a value may be null, so the compiler never warns you before you use a null value. Optional<T> closes part of that gap. JSpecify annotations close another part.

KindC#JavaNote
twiststring? nameString namethe Java language has no way to say that a value may be null Why
twiststring name (non-null)String namethe same declaration, but nothing enforces non-null in Java Why
twistname!.Lengthname.length()Java has no ! operator, so the call simply throws if name is null Why
twistname?.Lengthname == null ? null : name.length()Java has no ?. operator, so chain with Optional.map instead Why
twista ?? ba != null ? a : bObjects.requireNonNullElse(a, b) also works, but it throws when a and b are both null Why
twista ??= bif (a == null) a = b;Java has no ??= operator, so write the if statement in full Why
newcustomer?.Name ?? "unknown"find(id).map(Customer::name).orElse("unknown")return Optional from a method that may find nothing Why
trapa nullable field or parametera plain type, never OptionalOptional is for return values only, so do not use it for fields, parameters or collections Why
trapfound ?? LoadGuest()found.orElseGet(() -> loadGuest())orElse(loadGuest()) calls loadGuest even when a value is present Why
new<Nullable>enable</Nullable>@NullMarked on the packageeverything in the package is non-null unless it is marked @Nullable Why
newNullable reference types warningsJSpecify + NullAway or IntelliJyou opt in with annotations, but only a checker tool turns them into errors Why
twistArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(x)Objects.requireNonNull(x)throws NullPointerException if x is null, and otherwise returns x so that you can assign it Why

The gap, stated plainlytwist#

Some customers never set a nickname, so the lookup can find nothing. Here id is the customer's id:

C#
string? name = FindNickname(id);  // may be null
int a = name!.Length;             // "trust me"
int? b = name?.Length;            // null if name is null
string shown = name ?? "none";    // a fallback
name ??= "none";                  // assign only if null
Java 25
String name = findNickname(id);   // nothing says it may be null
int a = name.length();            // throws if name is null
Integer b = name == null ? null : name.length();
String shown = Objects.requireNonNullElse(name, "none");
if (name == null) name = "none";
Reading the code
String name = findNickname(id);

Nothing in the type says that the value may be null. You learn it from the documentation of the method, or when the program fails.

int a = name.length();

Java has no ! operator, because there is no warning to silence. If name is null, this line throws NullPointerException.

name == null ? null : name.length()

Java has no ?. operator, so you write the null check yourself. The result is an Integer, not an int, because an int cannot be null.

Objects.requireNonNullElse(name, "none")

This method is like ?? in C#. It returns the first argument if that argument is not null. Otherwise it returns the second argument. But unlike ??, the method throws NullPointerException when both arguments are null. The method arrived in Java 9.

C# refresherNullable reference types: string? and the compiler's warningsC# 8

When nullable reference types are on, a plain string promises that the value is not null. A string? may be null. The compiler warns when you use a value that may be null without checking it first.

// MyApp.csproj: <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
string? name = Find();
Console.WriteLine(name.Length);       // warning CS8602: possibly null
if (name is not null)
    Console.WriteLine(name.Length);   // fine: the compiler saw the check

Optional is for return valuesnew#

A search for a customer by id may find nobody. Instead of returning null, the Java repository method can return an Optional<Customer>. An Optional<Customer> is a box that holds one customer or is empty. The caller has to open the box, so the caller cannot forget the empty case. Java 8

C#
Customer? Find(long id);

var customer = Find(7);
var name = customer?.Name ?? "unknown";
Java 25
Optional<Customer> find(long id);

String name = find(7)
        .map(Customer::name)
        .orElse("unknown");
Reading the code
.map(Customer::name)

If a customer was found, map applies a function to the customer and keeps the result. Here the result is the name. If no customer was found, or if the function returns null, the result is empty. Customer::name is a method reference. It is a short way of writing the lambda c -> c.name().

.orElse("unknown")

This call opens the box. It returns the name if there is one, and otherwise "unknown". orElse is like ?? in C#, but Java always calculates the argument of orElse. See the section Where Optional goes wrong.

Here are the other methods of Optional, each with the nearest C# form:

Optional methodDoesC# analogy
Optional.of(x)wraps, throws if x is nulln/a
Optional.ofNullable(x)wraps, empty if nulln/a
Optional.empty()absentnull
.map(f)transform if present?.
.flatMap(f)transform returning Optional?. returning nullable
.filter(p)keep if it matchesn/a
.orElse(v)value or default??
.orElseGet(sup)value or lazily computed default?? with a factory
.orElseThrow()value or NoSuchElementException?? throw
.ifPresent(c)run if presentif (x is not null)
.isPresent() / .isEmpty()testis not null / is null
.stream()0 or 1 element streamn/a, and Java 9 added this method

Where Optional goes wrongtrap#

Gotcha

Optional is not a general-purpose nullable wrapper. Its designers meant Optional for return values, when finding nothing is a normal outcome. Do not use Optional for these three things:

  • Fields. An Optional cannot be serialised, and it adds an extra object to every instance.
  • Method parameters. Callers have to wrap their argument, and they can still pass null anyway. Offer two overloads instead.
  • Collections. An empty list already means that nothing was found, so never return Optional<List<T>>.

And a variable of type Optional can itself be null. Never return null from a method whose return type is Optional.

PredictorElse with a method call as its default#
What does this print?
static String loadGuestName() {
    System.out.println("reading the database");
    return "guest";
}

Optional<String> found = Optional.of("Ada");
String name = found.orElse(loadGuestName());
System.out.println(name);
Show the answer
reading the database Ada

Java calculates the argument of orElse first, even when a value is present. So Java runs loadGuestName() before it calls orElse, and the database is read although a name was found.

If the default is slow to compute or has side effects, use orElseGet. orElseGet takes a lambda, and it runs the lambda only when the Optional is empty:

String name = found.orElseGet(() -> loadGuestName());   // nothing is read: a name was found

JSpecify: the annotation standardnew#

Java has had a dozen competing @Nullable annotations. JSpecify is the industry's effort to agree on one set. Spring Framework 7 and Spring Boot 4 use JSpecify throughout, and this is making it the standard. JSpecify is a small library that you add to the build. For the dependency, see the section Adding JSpecify to the build.

The default goes in a special file called package-info.java. This file is in the folder of a package:

// src/main/java/com/acme/billing/package-info.java
@NullMarked                       // everything in this package is non-null by default
package com.acme.billing;

import org.jspecify.annotations.NullMarked;

@NullMarked makes every type in the package non-null unless the type is marked @Nullable. It works like <Nullable>enable</Nullable> in a C# project file. The file package-info.java holds only the package declaration, so the annotation applies to the whole package.

Inside the package, you mark only the exceptions. Here is the Invoices class, which keeps invoices by id:

// src/main/java/com/acme/billing/Invoices.java, in the same package
import org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable;

public class Invoices {
    private final Map<String, Invoice> byId = new HashMap<>();

    public Invoice load(String id) {             // id and the result are never null
        return Objects.requireNonNull(byId.get(id), "no invoice " + id);
    }

    public @Nullable Invoice find(String id) {   // the result may be null
        return byId.get(id);
    }
}

load has no annotation, so its parameter and its result are non-null. A checker reports any caller that passes null. @Nullable on find makes callers test the result before they use it.

Nothing in the Java Development Kit (JDK) enforces these annotations, so you need a tool that checks them:

CheckerRunsStrength
IntelliJ inspectionsin the IDEgood, but IDE-only
NullAwaybuild, via Error Pronefast, practical, catches most real bugs
Checker Frameworkbuildrigorous and sound, but slower and harder to learn
Gotcha

Without one of those tools in your build, JSpecify annotations are documentation. The annotations will not fail a build and will not warn at compile time. If your team adopts JSpecify annotations, add a checker to the build at the same time. Without a checker, the annotations will stop being true within months.

Adding JSpecify to the build, and the annotations it replaces#

The competing annotations came from javax.annotation, JetBrains, Spring, the Checker Framework and Android. To use the JSpecify annotations instead, add the library to your Maven pom.xml:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.jspecify</groupId>
  <artifactId>jspecify</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0</version>          <!-- stable since 2024 -->
</dependency>

This Maven dependency does the same as a PackageReference in .NET. The groupId, the artifactId and the version together name the library.

Defensive checks#

Public constructors and methods often check their arguments first. Then a null argument causes a clear failure at the start of the call, and not a failure later, deep inside the code. Here an order cannot be created without a customer:

C#
public Order(Customer customer)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(customer);
    _customer = customer;
}
Java 25
public Order(Customer customer) {
    this.customer =
        Objects.requireNonNull(customer, "customer");
}
Reading the code
Objects.requireNonNull(customer, "customer")

This call throws NullPointerException with the message customer if customer is null. Otherwise it returns customer, so the check and the assignment fit in one statement. The second argument names the parameter. In C#, ThrowIfNull adds the name of the parameter for you.

Note

Java 14 added helpful NullPointerException messages, which you turned on with a flag. They have been on by default since Java 15. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) tells you which expression was null. An example is Cannot invoke "Customer.name()" because "order.customer" is null. That removes most of the difficulty of finding the null in a chain of calls. Developers who left Java before 2020 often do not know about these messages.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java. FindOrder may find no order, an order may have no customer, and a customer may have no email: 
Order? FindOrder(long id);

var email = FindOrder(42)?.Customer?.Email ?? "no email";
Optional<Order> findOrder(long id);

String email = findOrder(42)
        .map(Order::customer)
        .map(Customer::email)
        .orElse("no email");

A method that may find nothing returns an Optional. Each ?. becomes a map. If the function of a map returns null, the map gives an empty Optional. So a missing customer or a missing email also ends at orElse.

2
An expert asksWhy is Optional the wrong type for a field, a method parameter or a list?
The designers of Optional meant it for return values. In a field, an Optional cannot be serialised, and it adds an object to every instance. A caller can still pass null for an Optional parameter. An empty list already means that nothing was found.

Collections#

Collections and streams · Chapter 18· 8 min read· Quick reference

Java has the same data structures as .NET, under different names. ArrayList does the same as List<T> in C#. HashMap does the same as Dictionary in C#. Java code declares the interface and creates the class. For example, it declares a List and creates an ArrayList.

KindC#JavaNote
twistIEnumerable<T>Iterable<E>an Iterable can be iterated more than once Why
twistIEnumerator<T>Iterator<E>an Iterator is a one-pass cursor like IEnumerator, but it can also remove() Why
twistList<T>ArrayList<E>ArrayList is the everyday list, and it is backed by an array, like List<T> Why
twistDictionary<K,V>HashMap<K,V>no guaranteed iteration order, so use LinkedHashMap to keep insertion order Why
twistIDictionary<K,V>Map<K,V>A Map is not a Collection. Iterate entrySet(), keySet() or values(). Why
twistQueue<T>ArrayDeque<E>Use offer() and poll(). ArrayDeque is the fast general-purpose queue. Why
twistStack<T>ArrayDeque<E>use push() and pop(), and avoid the legacy java.util.Stack class Why
twistSortedDictionary<K,V>TreeMap<K,V>it is kept sorted by key, like SortedDictionary, so firstKey() is the smallest key Why
twistConcurrentDictionary<K,V>ConcurrentHashMap<K,V>it is a thread-safe map, and its computeIfAbsent does the same as GetOrAdd Why
twistKeyValuePair<K,V>Map.Entry<K,V>An entry is one key and its value, read with getKey() and getValue(). The method entrySet() returns entries. Why
twistList<string> a = ["mug", "cup"]new ArrayList<>(List.of("mug", "cup"))Java has no collection expression, so copy a fixed list into a list you can add to Why
twistImmutableList<T>List.of(...)it makes an unmodifiable list that rejects nulls, and it was added in Java 9 Why
trapnew List<string> { "mug" }, then AddList.of("mug"), then addList.of and Map.of return collections that throw on any change Why
twisttags.RemoveAll(...)tags.removeIf(String::isBlank)removing inside a for loop over the list fails in both languages Why
twistList<string> ids = new List<string>()List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>()declare the interface and create the class, so another implementation is a one-line change Why
twistlist[0]list.getFirst()available from Java 21, and before that you write list.get(0) Why
twistlist[^1]list.getLast()available from Java 21, and before that you write list.get(list.size() - 1) Why
traplist.Reverse()list.reversed()it returns a reversed view, but Collections.reverse reverses the list itself Why
traplist[1..3]list.subList(1, 3)it returns a view of the same list, but the C# range makes a copy Why
twistthe non-generic System.Collections types, such as HashtableVector, Hashtable, Stack, Enumerationthese legacy collections lock on every call, so write ArrayList, HashMap and ArrayDeque Why

The interface hierarchytwist#

Collection<String> ids = new ArrayList<>();      // a List, a Set and a Queue are Collections
Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();    // a Map is not a Collection
for (var entry : stock.entrySet()) { }           // so loop over its entries, keys or values

A Map is not a Collection. So you loop over its entrySet(), its keySet() or its values(). Each entry gives its key with getKey() and its value with getValue(). The picture shows every interface. The classes that you create are beneath each interface:

Iterable or Iteratortwist#

Gotcha

IEnumerable<T> is Iterable<E>, not Iterator<E>. The match is exact. You can loop over an Iterable again and again. An Iterable is also the type that for (var x : xs) accepts. An Iterator is a cursor that makes one pass, like IEnumerator<T> in C#. If you confuse Iterable with Iterator, you write methods whose results can be read only once.

The code below reads the product ids of an order through each of the two types:

C#
IEnumerable<string> ids = ["mug", "cup"];
foreach (var id in ids) { }       // as often as you like

IEnumerator<string> e = ids.GetEnumerator(); // one pass
while (e.MoveNext()) Console.WriteLine(e.Current);
Java 25
Iterable<String> ids = List.of("mug", "cup");
for (var id : ids) { }            // as often as you like

Iterator<String> it = ids.iterator();  // one pass
while (it.hasNext()) System.out.println(it.next());

ids.iterator() returns the cursor. hasNext() asks whether another element is left. next() moves to that element and returns it. C# divides the same work between MoveNext() and Current.

Everyday collectionstwist#

The code below has a queue of order numbers, an undo stack, a sorted price list and a stock cache:

C#
var queue = new Queue<long>();
queue.Enqueue(1042); var next = queue.Dequeue();

var stack = new Stack<string>();
stack.Push("add mug"); var undo = stack.Pop();

var prices = new SortedDictionary<string, decimal>
    { ["mug"] = 9.50m, ["cup"] = 4.00m };
KeyValuePair<string, decimal> first = prices.First();

var cache = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, int>();
cache.GetOrAdd("mug", _ => 12);
Java 25
Deque<Long> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer(1042L); var next = queue.poll();

Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push("add mug"); var undo = stack.pop();

var prices = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(
    "mug", new BigDecimal("9.50"), "cup", new BigDecimal("4.00")));
Map.Entry<String, BigDecimal> first = prices.firstEntry();

var cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>();
cache.computeIfAbsent("mug", k -> 12);
Reading the code
Deque<Long> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

Queue and Deque are interfaces. The class that you create is ArrayDeque. It is a double-ended queue. In Java it replaces both Queue<T> and Stack<T> from .NET.

queue.offer(1042L); var next = queue.poll();

offer adds to the back, like Enqueue in C#. poll takes from the front, like Dequeue in C#. On an empty queue, Dequeue throws, but poll returns null.

prices.firstEntry()

A TreeMap keeps its keys sorted, like SortedDictionary in C#. So its first entry has the smallest key, which is cup. Map.Entry does the same as KeyValuePair in C#.

cache.computeIfAbsent("mug", k -> 12);

computeIfAbsent does the same as GetOrAdd in C#. It runs the lambda only when the key is missing, and it stores the result. A plain get returns null for a missing key. See reading a missing key.

C# refresherOrderedDictionary (.NET 9): the insertion-ordered dictionary.NET 9

This is a generic dictionary that is new in .NET 9. It keeps keys in the order in which they were added. It can also be read by position.

var od = new OrderedDictionary<string, int> { ["b"] = 2, ["a"] = 1 };
foreach (var (key, value) in od) Console.Write(key);   // "ba": insertion order
int second = od.GetAt(1).Value;                         // 1: read by position

Creating collectionstrap#

PredictAdding to a list made with List.of#
What happens on the second line?
var ids = List.of("mug", "cup");
ids.add("pot");
System.out.println(ids.size());
Show the answer
It throws UnsupportedOperationException.

List.of(...) and Map.of(...) Java 9 return immutable collections. These collections throw UnsupportedOperationException on any change, and they reject null elements. These methods are not a replacement for new ArrayList<>().

If you need to add to the list later, copy it with new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)). Arrays.asList is different again. It returns a fixed-size view of an array.

C# has collection expressions and initialisers. Java has factory methods such as List.of. Here are an order's product ids, its quantities and its tags:

C#
// collection expression
List<string> a = ["mug", "cup"];
var b = new List<string> { "mug", "cup" };
var c = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["mug"] = 2 };
IReadOnlyList<string> d = ["mug"];
var tags = new HashSet<string> { "gift" };
var frozen = ImmutableList.Create("mug", "cup");
Java 25
var a = new ArrayList<>(List.of("mug", "cup"));
var b = List.of("mug", "cup");       // fixed
var c = Map.of("mug", 2);            // fixed
List<String> d = List.of("mug");
var tags = new HashSet<>(Set.of("gift"));
var frozen = List.of("mug", "cup");  // fixed
Reading the code
new ArrayList<>(List.of("mug", "cup"))

List.of makes a fixed list. new ArrayList<>(...) copies the fixed list into a list that you can add to. In Java, this is the closest match to new List<string> { ... } in C#.

var b = List.of("mug", "cup");

This is a fixed list. Adding, removing or replacing an element throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Map.of("mug", 2)

The arguments are keys and values, and each key is followed by its value. Here they make a fixed map with one entry.

Map.of takes at most 10 key-value pairs. For more pairs, use Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(k, v), ...).

Modifying while iteratingtwist#

If you remove from a list while a for loop iterates over it, the code fails in both languages. C# has RemoveAll on a List<T> for this. Java has the same idea, and calls it removeIf. A Java Iterator can also remove an element:

Gotcha

Here tags is a List<String> that can change:

// usually throws ConcurrentModificationException
for (var tag : tags) if (tag.isBlank()) tags.remove(tag);

// correct: removeIf is the usual answer
tags.removeIf(String::isBlank);

// correct: remove through the iterator itself
var it = tags.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) if (it.next().isBlank()) it.remove();
Reading the code
tags.remove(tag)

This call changes the list while the hidden iterator of the loop is still using it. The loop usually fails on its next step with ConcurrentModificationException. C# throws InvalidOperationException for the same mistake.

tags.removeIf(String::isBlank);

This one call removes every element for which the test is true. String::isBlank is a method reference. It is short for tag -> tag.isBlank().

it.remove();

This call removes the element that next() just returned. That is safe, because the iterator itself makes the change.

subList and reversedtrap#

In C#, the range operator takes part of a list, as in ids[1..3]. In Java, subList(1, 3) takes the same two elements:

PredictClearing part of a list#
What does this print?
var ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("mug", "cup", "pot", "tray"));
var middle = ids.subList(1, 3);
middle.clear();
System.out.println(ids);
Show the answer
[mug, tray]

subList returns a view, not a copy. Changing the sublist changes the list behind it. In C#, ids[1..3] makes a copy. So clearing the copy leaves all four ids in the list.

If you want a copy, make one with new ArrayList<>(ids.subList(1, 3)).

Gotcha

reversed() does not turn the list around. It returns a reversed view Java 21 and leaves the list as it was. In C#, List<T>.Reverse() reverses the list itself:

var names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("mug", "cup", "pot"));
names.reversed();             // names is still [mug, cup, pot]: the view is thrown away
Collections.reverse(names);   // names is now [pot, cup, mug]

Use the view that reversed() returns, or call Collections.reverse to change the list itself.

Declare the interface, instantiate the class#

Note

Here the Java convention is stricter than the C# convention. Follow the Java convention from the start. Declare variables, fields, parameters and return types with the interface. Name the class only where you create the object:

List<String> productIds = new ArrayList<>();            // yes
Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();           // yes

ArrayList<String> overSpecified = new ArrayList<>();    // avoid

When you declare List, you can change to another implementation later by changing one line. The empty <> is called the diamond. It takes the type argument from the declared type, so nothing is repeated.

Sequenced collections#

Java 21 added sequenced collections Java 21. With this feature, any collection with a defined order has methods for its first and last elements. Before Java 21, each type had its own way to reach these elements, or no way. The code below has the product ids of an order, and a stock list that remembers the order of insertion:

var ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("mug", "cup", "pot"));

ids.getFirst();        // "mug", was ids.get(0)
ids.getLast();         // "pot", was ids.get(ids.size() - 1)
ids.addFirst("tray");
ids.reversed();        // a reversed view, not a copy

var stock = new LinkedHashMap<String, Integer>();
stock.put("mug", 12);
stock.put("cup", 3);
stock.firstEntry();    // mug=12, the first one added
Reading the code
ids.getFirst();

This call returns the first element. It works on any ordered collection. It is like ids[0] in C#.

ids.reversed();

This call returns a reversed view. The view shows the same list back to front. A change to the list shows in the view, and a change to the view shows in the list. In C#, List<T>.Reverse() reverses the list itself.

stock.firstEntry();

A LinkedHashMap remembers the order in which keys were added. So its first entry is the entry that was added first.

Note

subList also returns a view. For an example, see clearing part of a list. If you add to or remove from the list behind the sublist, the sublist throws ConcurrentModificationException the next time you use it.

Legacy collections#

LegacyVector, Hashtable, Stack, Enumeration

These collections are from Java 1.0. Later they were changed to implement the modern interfaces, but every method takes a lock. So every call is slowed by locking that you almost never need. And these collections are still not safe for operations that take several calls. You will see them in old code:

LegacyUse instead
VectorArrayList, or CopyOnWriteArrayList if concurrent
HashtableHashMap, or ConcurrentHashMap if concurrent
java.util.StackArrayDeque
EnumerationIterator
Collections.synchronizedListConcurrentHashMap-backed types, or a proper concurrent collection

Replacing them is usually a one-line change:

Vector<String> old = new Vector<>();          // locks on every call
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();        // write this instead

Stack<Integer> oldStack = new Stack<>();      // extends Vector, and iterates bottom first
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();    // push, pop and peek, with no locking
Reading the code
Vector<String> old = new Vector<>();

Every call locks the vector, even when only one thread ever uses it.

Stack<Integer> oldStack = new Stack<>();

Stack extends Vector, so it locks too. A loop over a Stack visits the bottom of the stack first.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
var stock = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["mug"] = 12, ["cup"] = 3 };
foreach (var (id, count) in stock)
    Console.WriteLine($"{id}: {count}");
Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("mug", 12, "cup", 3));
for (var entry : stock.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(entry.getKey() + ": " + entry.getValue());
}

A Map is not a Collection, so the loop iterates over its entrySet(). The map that Map.of returns is fixed. So new HashMap<> copies it into a map that you can change.

2
An expert asksWhy does Java code declare a List<String> and not an ArrayList<String>?
The convention is to declare variables, fields, parameters and return types with the interface. The class is named only where the object is created. You can then change to another implementation by changing one line.

Quick reference#

.NETJavaNote
ICollection<T>Collection<E>it has iteration, and it adds size, add, remove and contains
IList<T>List<E>an ordered collection that you can index by position with get(i)
LinkedList<T>LinkedList<E>it is almost always slower than ArrayList, so avoid it

Equality, hashing and comparison#

Collections and streams · Chapter 19· 7 min read

In Java, == on two objects asks whether they are the same object. It never compares values, and no operator overloading can change that. Values are compared with equals. And equals must always agree with hashCode.

KindC#JavaNote
trapa == b on stringsa.equals(b)in Java, == compares objects, so strings, dates and every other object need equals Why
trapa == b, either may be nullObjects.equals(a, b)two nulls count as equal, and nothing throws Why
twistReferenceEquals(a, b)a == bthis is the only meaning that == has for objects in Java Why
trapa == b on two int or int? valuesa.equals(b) on two Integer valuesan Integer from -128 to 127 is a shared object, so == seems to work on small values Why
twistGetHashCode()hashCode()Override it together with equals, as in C#. By default javac does not warn when you forget. Why
samechanging a key while it is in a HashSetthe set can no longer find itThe bucket came from the old hash code, as in C#. So keep the fields that hashCode uses final.
twistHashCode.Combine(x, y)Objects.hash(x, y)hash the same fields that equals compares Why
twistIEquatable<T>equals(Object)there is no typed version, so check the type with instanceof Why
trapAmount == o.Amountamount.compareTo(m.amount) == 0BigDecimal.equals also compares the number of decimal places Why
twistIComparable<T>Comparable<T>it gives a type its natural order, through the method compareTo Why
twistOrderBy(o => o.Status)Comparator.comparing(Order::status)ThenBy becomes thenComparing, and OrderByDescending adds reversed() Why

== versus equalstrap#

Java reverses the C# habit. In Java, == means identity, and equals means value. For the effect on a string comparison, see == on two strings. In the code below, a and b are any two objects:

boolean same = a == b;                 // are they the same object?
boolean equal = a.equals(b);           // do they have the same value? Throws if a is null.
boolean safe = Objects.equals(a, b);   // the same, and safe when either side is null

Objects.equals counts two nulls as equal. Objects is in the package java.util.

CompareC#Java
Value equalitya == b, a.Equals(b)a.equals(b)
Value equality, null-safea == bObjects.equals(a, b)
Reference identityReferenceEquals(a, b)a == b
Primitivesa == ba == b
Orderinga.CompareTo(b)a.compareTo(b)
Custom orderingIComparer<T>Comparator<T>
Gotcha

The boxed-integer cache. Integer is the object form of int. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) keeps one shared Integer object for each value from −128 to 127. So == appears to work on small numbers. Above 127, == stops working, and nothing warns you. See two Integers with the same value.

The same trap exists for Long, Short and Byte. It also exists for Character.

The equals and hashCode contracttwist#

PredictA map key that overrides equals only#
What does this print?
class ProductKey {
    final String id;
    ProductKey(String id) { this.id = id; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof ProductKey k && id.equals(k.id); }
}

var stock = new HashMap<ProductKey, Integer>();
stock.put(new ProductKey("mug"), 12);
System.out.println(stock.get(new ProductKey("mug")));
Show the answer
null

ProductKey does not override hashCode, so the method comes from Object. That hashCode is different for every object. So the two equal keys go into different buckets. The lookup finds nothing in its bucket and returns null, although an equal key is in the map.

C# fails in the same way, but the C# compiler warns you. By default, javac does not warn you.

Override hashCode whenever you override equals, and use the same fields in both methods. Or make the key a record. A record writes both methods for you.

HashMap does the same as Dictionary in C#. The Java HashSet does the same as the HashSet in C#. Both Java classes find an object in two steps. First hashCode picks a bucket. Then equals checks the objects in that bucket. So equals and hashCode must agree, and nothing enforces this. These are the rules:

RuleMeaning
Reflexivean object always equals itself, so a.equals(a) is true
Symmetricif a.equals(b) is true, then b.equals(a) is true
Transitiveif a equals b and b equals c, then a equals c
Consistentrepeated calls give the same result
Nulla.equals(null) is false, and it never throws
hashCode agreementif a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()

The last rule is the one that breaks systems. Suppose two objects are equal but have different hash codes. Then a HashSet can store both of them. Now suppose the hash code of an object changes while the object is in a set. The object stays in its old bucket, and no lookup finds it there.

Writing themtwist#

Two amounts of money are equal when the amount and the currency match. The classes below implement that equality with methods that you write yourself:

C#
public sealed class Money : IEquatable<Money>
{
    public decimal Amount { get; init; }
    public string Currency { get; init; }

    public bool Equals(Money? o) =>
        o is not null && Amount == o.Amount
                      && Currency == o.Currency;

    public override bool Equals(object? o) =>
        Equals(o as Money);
    public override int GetHashCode() =>
        HashCode.Combine(Amount, Currency);
}
Java 25
public final class Money {
    private final BigDecimal amount;
    private final String currency;

    public Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
        this.amount = amount;
        this.currency = currency;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Money m)) return false;
        return amount.compareTo(m.amount) == 0
            && currency.equals(m.currency);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(amount.stripTrailingZeros(), currency);
    }
}
Reading the code
if (!(o instanceof Money m)) return false;

equals takes an Object. So this line first checks that o is a Money, and gives it the name m. The line also returns false when o is null.

amount.compareTo(m.amount) == 0

This line compares the amounts by value. On a BigDecimal, equals also compares the number of decimal places. This is a trap.

Objects.hash(amount.stripTrailingZeros(), currency)

Objects.hash does the same as HashCode.Combine in C#. stripTrailingZeros() gives 1.0 and 1.00 the same hash code, because equal objects must have equal hash codes.

Or write none of this code. A record builds both methods from its components. As a record, the map key from the prediction needs one line:

public record ProductKey(String id) { }

ProductKey now has both methods. Money as a record needs one more step. For that step, see BigDecimal inside equals.

The cost of Objects.hashdeep dive
Note

Objects.hash(...) takes varargs, so it creates an array for its arguments on every call. For a type that is hashed very often, the classic form 31 * result + field.hashCode() is faster. But measure first.

BigDecimal inside equalstrap#

Gotcha

BigDecimal.equals compares scale as well as value. The scale is the number of decimal places. So for equals, 1.0 and 1.00 are not equal. In C#, 1.0m == 1.00m is true:

var a = new BigDecimal("1.0");
var b = new BigDecimal("1.00");
a.equals(b);            // false: the scales differ
a.compareTo(b) == 0;    // true: the values match

That is why the Money.equals method in the previous section calls compareTo. A record compares each component with equals. So when Money is a plain record, 1.0 EUR and 1.00 EUR are not equal. To make them equal, give every amount the same scale in the compact constructor. The compact constructor was shown in the chapter Records. Here it sets the scale:

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
    public Money {
        amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);   // 1.0 becomes 1.00
    }
}

setScale stores every amount with two decimal places. So the generated equals and hashCode agree for 1.0 and 1.00. For the rest, see the section Money is BigDecimal.

Ordering#

Sorting works the same way in both languages. You supply the comparison. C# code usually passes a lambda or uses OrderBy from LINQ. Java code builds a Comparator. In the code below, orders is a List<Order>. Each order has an id, a status and the time when it was placed:

C#
orders.Sort((a, b) => a.Id.CompareTo(b.Id));

var sorted = orders
    .OrderBy(o => o.Status)
    .ThenByDescending(o => o.PlacedAt)
    .ToList();
Java 25
import static java.util.Comparator.reverseOrder;

orders.sort(Comparator.comparingLong(Order::id));

var sorted = orders.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::status)
            .thenComparing(Order::placedAt, reverseOrder()))
    .toList();
Reading the code
Comparator.comparingLong(Order::id)

This call builds a comparison from a key. Here the key is the id, so orders are compared by their id. comparingLong avoids boxing each long. comparingInt does the same for an int.

orders.stream()

This call makes a stream. A stream is like a LINQ query in C#. For more about streams, see the next chapter, Streams vs LINQ.

Comparator.comparing(Order::status)

This call compares by status, in the order in which the enum declares its constants.

.thenComparing(Order::placedAt, reverseOrder())

When two orders have the same status, this call compares the time when each order was placed, newest first. It is like ThenByDescending in C#.

The rest of the LINQ ordering methods map to Java like this:

LINQJava Comparator
OrderBy(f)Comparator.comparing(f)
OrderByDescending(f)Comparator.comparing(f).reversed()
ThenBy(f).thenComparing(f)
ThenByDescending(f).thenComparing(f, Comparator.reverseOrder())
key is intComparator.comparingInt(f), avoids boxing
nullsComparator.nullsFirst(cmp) / nullsLast(cmp)

A type gets its own natural order by implementing Comparable. Comparable does the same as IComparable in C#. In the example below, versions of the shop's API are ordered by major number, and then by minor number:

C#
public record Version(int Major, int Minor) : IComparable<Version>
{
    public int CompareTo(Version? o) =>
        (Major, Minor).CompareTo((o!.Major, o.Minor));
}
Java 25
public record Version(int major, int minor)
        implements Comparable<Version> {
    private static final Comparator<Version> ORDER =
        Comparator.comparingInt(Version::major)
                  .thenComparingInt(Version::minor);

    public int compareTo(Version o) {
        return ORDER.compare(this, o);
    }
}
Reading the code
implements Comparable<Version>

This line gives Version a natural order. Collections.sort, TreeSet and TreeMap use the natural order when you pass them no comparator.

private static final Comparator<Version> ORDER =

The comparison is built once and kept in a constant. It is not rebuilt on every call.

Gotcha

Comparable.compareTo should be consistent with equals. This means that when a.compareTo(b) == 0, a.equals(b) should be true. When it is not true, the sorted collections behave differently from the hashed collections. The sorted collections are TreeSet and TreeMap, and they use compareTo. The hashed collections are HashSet and HashMap, and they use equals.

BigDecimal is the standard example. The values 1.0 and 1.00 are equal by compareTo but not by equals. So a TreeSet keeps one of them, and a HashSet keeps both.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite these two members of a Customer class in Java. The id is a long and the email a string: 
public override bool Equals(object? o) =>
    o is Customer c && Id == c.Id && Email == c.Email;

public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Id, Email);
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Customer c && id == c.id && Objects.equals(email, c.email);
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(id, email);
}

The email needs Objects.equals, for two reasons. == on two objects only asks whether they are the same object. And email.equals would throw on a null email. The id is a primitive long, so == is right for the id.

2
An expert asksA Customer is in a HashSet, and its hashCode uses the email. The code then changes that customer's email. Why does customers.contains(customer) now return false?
The set chose the customer's bucket from the hash code that the customer had when it was added. The new email gives a new hash code. So the lookup searches in the wrong bucket, although the customer is still in the set. Keep the fields that equals and hashCode use final, or use a record.
