Streams vs LINQ#

Collections and streams · Chapter 20· 9 min read· Quick reference

Java streams do the same as LINQ to Objects in C#. The idea is the same, but the names are different. Java has no LINQ to SQL. The reason is that a Java lambda compiles to ordinary code, and no library can read that code and turn it into SQL.

KindC#JavaNote
twistcustomers.Where(...).Select(...).ToList()customers.stream().filter(...).map(...).toList()a list is not a stream, so you ask it for one first with stream() Why
trapnames.OrderBy(n => n)names.stream().sorted(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)sorted() alone puts every capital before every lower-case letter, but C# uses the culture's order Why
twistorders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines)orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())most operators only change their name, but the lambda of flatMap must return a stream Why
trapenumerating one query twicecollect once, then reuse the lista stream can be used only once, and a second use throws IllegalStateException Why
twistorders.GroupBy(o => o.Status)orders.stream().collect(groupingBy(Order::status))collect finishes a stream, and the Collectors class holds grouping, joining and counting Why
twistorders.GroupBy(o => o.Status).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count())orders.stream().collect(groupingBy(Order::status, counting()))a second collector, such as counting() or summingInt(f), says what to keep for each group Why
traporders.ToDictionary(o => o.Id)orders.stream().collect(toMap(Order::id, o -> o))toMap throws on a duplicate key, as ToDictionary does, and also on a null value Why
traporders.AsParallel()orders.parallelStream()every parallel stream shares one pool of threads, so never use it for I/O Why
twistproductIds.Chunk(100)productIds.stream().gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(100))a gatherer is an intermediate operation of your own, from Java 24 Why
twistlines.Sum(l => l.Quantity)lines.stream().mapToInt(OrderLine::quantity).sum()IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream hold primitives without boxing them Why
trapEnumerable.Range(0, 10)IntStream.range(0, 10)the second argument is where to stop, not how many to produce Why
twistdb.Customers.Where(c => c.Age > 18)a JPQL string, the Criteria API or jOOQJava has no expression trees, so no library can turn a lambda into SQL Why
twistyield return nStream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2).limit(10)Java has no generators, but Stream.iterate and Stream.generate build a lazy sequence Why

The shapetwist#

Here customers is a List<Customer>:

C#
var names = customers
    .Where(c => c.Name.EndsWith("Doe"))
    .Select(c => c.Name)
    .OrderBy(n => n)
    .ToList();
Java 25
var names = customers.stream()
    .filter(c -> c.name().endsWith("Doe"))
    .map(Customer::name)
    .sorted()
    .toList();
Reading the code
customers.stream()

A list is not a stream, so you first ask the list for a stream. C# lets you call Where on the list itself.

.filter(c -> c.name().endsWith("Doe"))

Where becomes filter. C# writes the lambda with =>. Java writes it with ->.

.map(Customer::name)

Select becomes map. Customer::name is called a method reference. It is short for c -> c.name().

.sorted()

This is OrderBy with the natural order. For strings, the natural order in Java is not the order that C# uses. See Sorting strings. Pass a Comparator to sort another way.

.toList();

This step runs the pipeline and collects the result. Nothing runs until this last step. In the same way, a LINQ query does nothing until you enumerate it.

That is the whole pattern. You start a stream, chain operations, and finish with one step that produces a result.

Sorting stringstrap#

Gotcha

sorted() does not order strings as OrderBy does. sorted() puts every capital letter before every lower-case letter. C# uses the order of the culture:

import java.text.Collator;

var names = List.of("bob Doe", "Zed Doe", "amy Doe", "Ann Doe");

names.stream().sorted().toList();
// [Ann Doe, Zed Doe, amy Doe, bob Doe]

names.stream().sorted(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER).toList();
// [amy Doe, Ann Doe, bob Doe, Zed Doe], as C#'s OrderBy(n => n) gives

names.stream().sorted(Collator.getInstance(Locale.ENGLISH)).toList();
// [amy Doe, Ann Doe, bob Doe, Zed Doe]

String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER ignores case. A Collator orders text for the locale that you pass to it. Collator is in the package java.text.

Operator translationtwist#

Each order has a list of lines, and each line has a product id:

C#
var productIds = orders
    .Where(o => o.Lines.Count > 2)
    .SelectMany(o => o.Lines)
    .Select(l => l.ProductId)
    .Distinct()
    .Skip(10).Take(5)
    .ToList();

bool anyEmpty = orders.Any(o => o.Lines.Count == 0);
var first = orders.FirstOrDefault();
int lineCount = orders.Sum(o => o.Lines.Count);
Java 25
var productIds = orders.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.lines().size() > 2)
    .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())
    .map(OrderLine::productId)
    .distinct()
    .skip(10).limit(5)
    .toList();

boolean anyEmpty = orders.stream()
    .anyMatch(o -> o.lines().isEmpty());
var first = orders.stream().findFirst().orElse(null);
int lineCount = orders.stream()
    .mapToInt(o -> o.lines().size()).sum();
Reading the code
.flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())

SelectMany becomes flatMap. The lambda of flatMap must return a stream. So the lambda turns each order's list of lines into a stream.

.skip(10).limit(5)

Skip becomes skip. Take becomes limit.

.anyMatch(o -> o.lines().isEmpty());

Any with a test becomes anyMatch.

findFirst().orElse(null)

findFirst returns an Optional. Adding orElse(null) gives the behaviour of FirstOrDefault.

.mapToInt(o -> o.lines().size()).sum();

sum is a method of IntStream, which is a stream of plain int values. So you map to int first.

For every LINQ operator with its stream counterpart, see the quick reference.

C# refresherLINQ operators: TakeWhile, SkipWhile, Concat, All, Single, Aggregate, Zip, Chunk and moreC# 3

This code shows the rest of the LINQ column of the table. Each operator has one line, with what it returns.

IEnumerable<int> xs = [1, 2, 3, 12], ys = [4, 5];
xs.TakeWhile(x => x < 10);           // 1, 2, 3: stops at the first failure
xs.SkipWhile(x => x < 10);           // 12: drops items while the test holds
xs.Concat(ys);                       // xs followed by ys
xs.Reverse();                        // last to first
xs.All(x => x > 0);                  // true if every item matches
xs.Single(x => x == 12);             // the only match; throws on none or several
xs.Average(); xs.Min(); xs.Max();    // aggregates
xs.Aggregate(1, (acc, x) => acc * x);    // a fold with a starting value: 72
xs.Zip(ys);                          // (1, 4), (2, 5): pairs, up to the shorter
xs.Chunk(2);                         // [1, 2], [3, 12]
xs.DefaultIfEmpty(0);                // xs, or a single 0 if xs is empty
xs.AsParallel().Select(Score);       // PLINQ: the query runs on several threads

Reading a stream twicetrap#

PredictOne stream, read twice#
What happens on the last two lines?
var names = List.of("Ann Doe", "Bob Ray", "Cy Doe");
var does = names.stream().filter(n -> n.endsWith("Doe"));

var a = does.toList();
var b = does.toList();
System.out.println(b);
Show the answer
The second toList() throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed

A stream can be used exactly once. A stream is a pipeline over a source. The first finishing step runs the pipeline, and the stream cannot be used after that. In C#, the same IEnumerable would simply run the query again. This difference causes bugs when you translate LINQ.

Either create the stream again, or collect it once into a List and reuse the list.

Collectorstwist#

collect is the general way to finish a stream. The Collectors class has the convenient operations that LINQ has, such as grouping, joining and counting:

C#
var byStatus = orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.Status)
    .ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count());

var csv = string.Join(", ", names);
Java 25
import static java.util.stream.Collectors.*;

var byStatus = orders.stream()
    .collect(groupingBy(Order::status, counting()));

var csv = names.stream().collect(joining(", "));
// or simply: String.join(", ", names)
Reading the code
import static java.util.stream.Collectors.*;

This line imports the static methods of Collectors, so groupingBy and counting need no class name.

groupingBy(Order::status, counting())

This call groups the orders by status. It counts the orders of each group and does not list them. The result is a Map<OrderStatus, Long>.

joining(", ")

This collector joins strings with a separator, like string.Join in C#.

These are the collectors you will use most:

CollectorProduces
toList() / toSet()a List or Set
toMap(k, v)a Map, and it throws on duplicate keys
toMap(k, v, merge)a Map with a merge function for duplicates
groupingBy(f)Map<K, List<T>>
groupingBy(f, downstream)Map<K, R>, e.g. counting(), summingInt()
partitioningBy(p)Map<Boolean, List<T>>
joining(sep, prefix, suffix)a String
counting(), summingInt(f), averagingDouble(f)aggregates
teeing(c1, c2, merge)two collectors combined, added in Java 12

toMap and null valuestrap#

Gotcha

Collectors.toMap throws on a null value. toMap throws IllegalStateException on a duplicate key. ToDictionary in LINQ also throws on a duplicate key. But toMap also throws NullPointerException when a value is null. ToDictionary accepts a null value. Here one order without a customer stops the whole stream:

import static java.util.stream.Collectors.toMap;

Map<Long, Customer> customerByOrder = orders.stream()
        .collect(toMap(Order::id, Order::customer));   // throws if any customer is null

Remove the null values first with a filter, or fill a HashMap in a loop. If duplicate keys are possible, use the form of toMap with three arguments. The third argument says how to merge two values.

Parallel streamstrap#

Gotcha

parallelStream() looks like AsParallel(), but it is more dangerous. A parallel stream runs on a pool of threads that the whole program shares. This pool is called the common ForkJoinPool. So one slow parallel stream can delay every other parallel stream in the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), including parallel streams inside libraries. A parallel stream is also useful only for large amounts of pure calculation that split evenly.

Follow these simple rules. Do not use a parallel stream for I/O. Use virtual threads for I/O instead. See the chapter Threads are cheap now. Do not use a parallel stream on a LinkedList, or on a source backed by an Iterator. Measure before and after. For any work with a deadline, run the work on your own pool.

// I/O on the shared pool: one slow call holds up every parallel stream in the JVM
long up = urls.parallelStream().filter(this::isReachable).count();   // do not do this

// large, CPU-bound and easy to split: the case where it can pay off
double total = IntStream.range(0, 50_000_000).parallel().mapToDouble(Math::sqrt).sum();
Reading the code
urls.parallelStream().filter(this::isReachable)

Each isReachable call waits for the network. While the call waits, it holds one of the few threads of the shared pool.

IntStream.range(0, 50_000_000).parallel()

This line calculates fifty million square roots. The work is pure calculation, and it splits evenly across the cores of the processor.

A range of numberstrap#

Gotcha

The second argument of IntStream.range is where to stop, not how many to produce. In C#, Enumerable.Range(5, 8) takes a count, and gives the eight numbers from 5 to 12. In Java, range(5, 8) stops before the 8:

import java.util.stream.IntStream;

int[] numbers = IntStream.range(5, 8).toArray();         // 5, 6, 7
int[] closed = IntStream.rangeClosed(5, 8).toArray();    // 5, 6, 7, 8

For Enumerable.Range(start, count), write IntStream.range(start, start + count). IntStream is a stream of plain int values. See Primitive streams.

Gatherers#

For a long time, streams had no way to add your own intermediate operation. Stream gatherers Java 24 fixed that. The feature also includes built-in gatherers for operations that LINQ has and streams did not have. Here productIds is a list of strings, and prices is a list of BigDecimal. quantities is a list of Integer:

// Fixed-size batches, like LINQ's Chunk(n).
var batches = productIds.stream()
        .gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(100))
        .toList();                       // List<List<String>>

// A sliding window of three neighbours.
var windows = prices.stream().gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(3)).toList();

// A running total, like a fold that keeps every step.
var running = quantities.stream().gather(Gatherers.scan(() -> 0, Integer::sum)).toList();
Reading the code
Gatherers.windowFixed(100)

This gatherer groups the elements into lists of 100, like Chunk(100) in LINQ. The last list can be shorter.

Gatherers.windowSliding(3)

This gatherer makes lists of three neighbours. The first list holds the first three elements. The next list holds the second to the fourth element, and so on.

Gatherers.scan(() -> 0, Integer::sum)

This gatherer makes a running total. It starts from 0 and adds each element in turn. After each element, it sends the total so far to the next step.

Note

Before Java 24 there was no clean way to batch a stream. Every codebase had its own partitioning helper, or used Lists.partition from Guava. If you are on Java 21, that is still the situation. Gatherers were a preview in Java 22 and 23.

Primitive streams#

Generics cannot hold primitives. So Java has IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream. These three stream types avoid boxing every element. Here each order line has a quantity:

int total = lines.stream()
        .mapToInt(OrderLine::quantity)   // Stream<OrderLine> to IntStream
        .sum();

IntStream.range(0, 10).forEach(System.out::println);

// boxing back when you need a collection
List<Integer> xs = IntStream.range(0, 10).boxed().toList();
Reading the code
.mapToInt(OrderLine::quantity)

This step turns a stream of order lines into a stream of plain int values.

IntStream.range(0, 10)

This call gives the numbers 0 to 9. In Enumerable.Range, the second argument is how many numbers to produce. Here the second argument is where to stop. rangeClosed(0, 10) would include 10.

.boxed()

This step wraps each int in an Integer, so that the numbers can go into a List<Integer>.

NeedMethod
Stream to IntStreammapToInt / mapToLong / mapToDouble
IntStream to Streamboxed(), or mapToObj(f)
A rangeIntStream.range(a, b) or rangeClosed(a, b)
StatisticssummaryStatistics() gives count, sum, min, max and average

No expression trees#

C# refresherExpression trees and IQueryable: a lambda as dataC# 3

When a C# lambda is assigned to an Expression<...>, it becomes a data structure that a library can read. That is how EF Core turns a Where into SQL.

Expression<Func<Customer, bool>> adult = c => c.Age > 18;   // data, not code
Console.WriteLine(adult.Body);                              // (c.Age > 18)

IQueryable<Customer> q = db.Customers.Where(c => c.Age > 18);
string sql = q.ToQueryString();                             // ... WHERE [c].[Age] > 18
Expression trees / IQueryable

C# can inspect a lambda as data and translate it. That is how EF Core turns Where(c => c.Age > 18) into SQL. Java lambdas compile directly to bytecode and cannot be inspected. So no Java object-relational mapper (ORM) can do this. The standard ORM in Java is Jakarta Persistence (JPA). With JPA, you write queries as strings in the Jakarta Persistence Query Language (JPQL), or you build them with an API:

ApproachLooks likeType-safe
JPQL string"select c from Customer c where c.age > :age"no
Criteria APIcb.greaterThan(root.get("age"), 18)partly
JPA metamodelcb.greaterThan(root.get(Customer_.age), 18)yes, generated at compile time
jOOQdsl.selectFrom(CUSTOMER).where(CUSTOMER.AGE.gt(18))yes, generated from the schema

jOOQ is the most similar to LINQ to SQL. It generates a typed domain-specific language (DSL) from your actual database schema, so a renamed column breaks the build. See Data access.

C# refresheryield return: a lazy sequence in C#C# 2
IEnumerable<int> Powers()
{
    for (var n = 1; ; n *= 2) yield return n;   // endless, computed on demand
}

var first10 = Powers().Take(10).ToList();       // 1, 2, 4 ... 512
yield return

Java has no generators. To produce a lazy sequence, use Stream.iterate or Stream.generate with a limit. Or write an Iterator yourself. The code below produces the powers of two, and a run of order numbers:

List<Integer> powers = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2).limit(10).toList();   // 1, 2, 4 ... 512
List<Integer> ids = Stream.iterate(1000, n -> n < 1010, n -> n + 1).toList();   // 1000 ... 1009
Reading the code
Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2).limit(10)

This is an endless stream that starts at 1 and doubles each time. limit(10) takes the first ten values, like Take(10) on an endless yield return.

Stream.iterate(1000, n -> n < 1010, n -> n + 1)

This form has three arguments, and it exists from Java 9. It stops by itself when the test fails, like a for loop.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java. lines is a list of order lines, and the result gives the number of units sold of each product: 
var unitsByProduct = lines
    .GroupBy(l => l.ProductId)
    .ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Sum(l => l.Quantity));
import static java.util.stream.Collectors.*;

Map<String, Integer> unitsByProduct = lines.stream()
    .collect(groupingBy(OrderLine::productId, summingInt(OrderLine::quantity)));

groupingBy alone gives a map of lists. Its second argument is a collector that says what to keep for each group. Here the collector is summingInt. The collector counting() would count the lines instead.

2
An expert asksWhy can no Java library turn a lambda into SQL, as EF Core does?
C# can give a lambda to a library as an expression tree, which is data that the library can read. A Java lambda compiles directly to bytecode and cannot be inspected. So queries are written as JPQL strings, with the Criteria API, or with jOOQ.
3
An expert asksWhy should a parallel stream never call another service or a database?
Every parallel stream runs on one pool of threads that the whole program shares. This pool is called the common ForkJoinPool. A call that waits for the network holds one of the few threads of that pool. So one slow parallel stream can delay every other parallel stream in the JVM. Use virtual threads for I/O, and keep parallel streams for large, pure calculations.

Quick reference#

LINQStreamNote
Wherefilter
Selectmap
SelectManyflatMap
OrderBysorted(comparator)sorted() alone puts capitals first in strings, so pass String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER or a Collator

Aggregatereducereduce(seed, (acc, x) -> ...) is the form with a starting value

Files and I/O#

Collections and streams · Chapter 21· 7 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

The Files class in Java does the same as System.IO.File in .NET. Path is the type for a path. Almost everything you need is a static method of Files.

KindC#JavaNote
twistFile.ReadAllTextFiles.readString(p)added in Java 11, and it reads UTF-8 unless you pass a charset Why
twistFile.ReadAllLinesFiles.readAllLines(p)reads the whole file into memory, so use Files.lines for big files Why
twistFile.WriteAllTextFiles.writeString(p, s)added in Java 11, and it writes UTF-8 and replaces the file Why
twistFile.AppendAllTextFiles.writeString(p, s, APPEND)pass StandardOpenOption.APPEND to add to the end Why
sameFile.ExistsFiles.exists(p)the same check, on a Path in place of a string
trapFile.DeleteFiles.delete(p) / deleteIfExists(p)delete throws NoSuchFileException if the file is missing Why
twistFile.Copy / MoveFiles.copy / Files.movepass REPLACE_EXISTING to overwrite Why
twistDirectory.CreateDirectoryFiles.createDirectories(p)creates any missing parent folders too, like CreateDirectory Why
twistPath.Combine("a","b")Path.of("a","b")or dir.resolve("b") to add one part to an existing Path Why
twistPath.GetFileNamep.getFileName()returns a Path, so call toString() for the name as text Why
twistPath.GetExtensionno equivalentJava has no method for this, so take the text after the last dot yourself Why
twistPath.GetTempFileNameFiles.createTempFile(prefix, suffix)creates an empty temporary file and returns its Path Why
trapFile.ReadLines (lazy)Files.lines(p)returns a Stream, so it must be closed Why
trapDirectory.GetFilesFiles.list(dir).filter(Files::isRegularFile)Files.list returns the sub-folders of the folder too, in a Stream that must be closed Why
trapDirectory.EnumerateFiles(recursive)Files.walk(dir).filter(Files::isRegularFile)Files.walk returns the folders of the tree too, in a Stream that must be closed Why
trapturning bytes into textnew String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)always pass a charset, because before Java 18 the default was the charset of the machine Why
twistFileStreamFiles.newInputStream / newOutputStreamthese are byte streams, so wrap them in a Buffered stream for speed Why
twistStreamReaderFiles.newBufferedReader(p)a buffered text reader, UTF-8 unless you say otherwise Why
trapasm.GetManifestResourceStream("MyApp.config.json")getClass().getResourceAsStream("/config.json")a file under src/main/resources is inside the JAR, not on disk Why

The everyday operationstwist#

The shop exports each day's orders to data/orders.csv, and an import job reads them back. Here src, dst and dir are more paths. The variable more is extra text to add:

C#
string path = Path.Combine("data", "orders.csv");

string text = File.ReadAllText(path);
string[] lines = File.ReadAllLines(path);
File.WriteAllText(path, text);
File.AppendAllText(path, more);

bool there = File.Exists(path);
File.Delete(path);
File.Copy(src, dst, overwrite: true);
Directory.CreateDirectory(dir);
Java 25
Path p = Path.of("data", "orders.csv");

String text = Files.readString(p);
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(p);
Files.writeString(p, text);
Files.writeString(p, more, StandardOpenOption.APPEND);

boolean there = Files.exists(p);
Files.deleteIfExists(p);
Files.copy(src, dst, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
Files.createDirectories(dir);
Reading the code
Path p = Path.of("data", "orders.csv");

A Path joins its parts with the right separator for the operating system, like Path.Combine in .NET. A Path is an object, not a string.

Files.readString(p)

This call reads the whole file as UTF-8 text. It exists from Java 11. readAllLines gives a list of lines instead.

StandardOpenOption.APPEND

writeString replaces the file unless you pass this option. With this option, writeString adds to the end of the file, like AppendAllText.

Files.deleteIfExists(p);

Files.delete throws NoSuchFileException if the file is missing. In C#, File.Delete does nothing if the file is missing, and reports no error. deleteIfExists behaves like the C# method.

StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING

Without this option, copy throws if the target already exists.

Names, lazy reading and folder listingstwist#

C#
string name = Path.GetFileName(path);   // "orders.csv"
string ext = Path.GetExtension(path);   // ".csv"

foreach (var line in File.ReadLines(path)) { }   // lazy
string[] files = Directory.GetFiles("data");
var all = Directory.EnumerateFiles(
    "data", "*", SearchOption.AllDirectories);

string tmp = Path.GetTempFileName();
using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
Java 25
String name = p.getFileName().toString();
int dot = name.lastIndexOf('.');
String ext = dot < 0 ? "" : name.substring(dot);

try (var lines = Files.lines(p)) { }         // lazy
try (var entries = Files.list(Path.of("data"))) { }
try (var all = Files.walk(Path.of("data"))) { }

Path tmp = Files.createTempFile("orders", ".csv");
try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(p)) { }
Reading the code
p.getFileName().toString()

getFileName returns a Path. toString turns that Path into text, here orders.csv.

dot < 0 ? "" : name.substring(dot)

Java has no method like GetExtension. So the code takes the text from the last dot, which is .csv here. When the name has no dot, the code takes an empty string.

try (var lines = Files.lines(p)) { }

This is a try-with-resources block. It does the same as using in C#. Whatever is declared in the brackets is closed when the block ends. Files.lines reads lazily, like File.ReadLines, but it holds the file open until the stream is closed.

Files.list(Path.of("data"))

This call gives the entries of one folder, and the entries include sub-folders. Directory.GetFiles returns only files. Add .filter(Files::isRegularFile) to get the same result as Directory.GetFiles.

Files.walk(Path.of("data"))

This call gives every file and folder below data, and data itself. EnumerateFiles returns only files, so add the same filter here.

Files.createTempFile("orders", ".csv")

This call creates an empty temporary file with that prefix and suffix, and returns its path.

Close every stream of lines or filestrap#

Gotcha

Files.lines, Files.walk and Files.list return a stream that holds an open file handle. In .NET, File.ReadLines releases the file when it reaches the end. The Java stream does not release the file when it reaches the end, and on Windows the file stays locked. So each of these streams must be opened in a try-with-resources block. Here the import job of the shop counts the lines of data/orders.csv that are not blank:

// leaks a file handle
long leaky = Files.lines(p).filter(l -> !l.isBlank()).count();

// correct
try (var lines = Files.lines(p)) {
    long count = lines.filter(l -> !l.isBlank()).count();
}
Reading the code
long leaky = Files.lines(p).filter(l -> !l.isBlank()).count();

count() finishes the stream, but nothing closes the stream. So the file can stay open for as long as the program runs.

try (var lines = Files.lines(p)) {

The stream is closed when the block ends, even if an exception is thrown inside the block.

This is the most common Java file-handling bug. It usually appears as “too many open files” under load, and not as an obvious failure.

Charsets, and why to always pass one#

Java's older I/O classes use the machine's default character set when you do not pass one. A character set is also called a charset. So the same code can produce different text on a developer's Mac and in a Linux container. This is the classic cause of wrong characters in place of accented letters in Java systems. Here bytes holds text received from another system, and file is a File:

// depends on the machine; avoid
new String(bytes);
new FileReader(file);
new PrintWriter(file);

// explicit; always do this
new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
Files.newBufferedReader(p, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
Files.readString(p);          // UTF-8 by contract, safe
Reading the code
new String(bytes);

This line turns the bytes into text with the default charset of the machine, whichever charset that is.

new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

This line names the charset, so the result is the same on every machine.

Note

Java 18 changed the default charset to UTF-8 for most APIs. This removes most of the problem on a modern Java Development Kit (JDK). On Java 17 and earlier, the problem is still real. Some APIs still follow the encoding of the console, and System.out is one of them. Passing the charset has no disadvantage, and it works on every version.

Streams, readers and buffering#

Java splits I/O into byte streams and character streams. In .NET, one Stream and a StreamReader mostly hide this split.

KindJava typeFor
Bytes inInputStreambinary reading
Bytes outOutputStreambinary writing
Characters inReadertext reading
Characters outWritertext writing
BufferingBufferedInputStream / BufferedReaderthese wrap the types above, and they always help
BridgingInputStreamReader(in, charset)bytes to characters

The code below reads the first line of a file through these layers. Then it copies one file to another:

import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8;

try (var in = Files.newInputStream(p);
     var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in, UTF_8))) {
    String first = reader.readLine();
}

// copy a stream, the Java equivalent of CopyTo
try (var in = Files.newInputStream(src); var out = Files.newOutputStream(dst)) {
    in.transferTo(out);          // Java 9
}
Reading the code
new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in, UTF_8))

This line has three layers. The first layer is the bytes of the file. The second layer is an InputStreamReader, which turns bytes into characters with UTF-8. The third layer is a BufferedReader, which reads ahead in large blocks. In .NET, a StreamReader does all three jobs.

try (var in = Files.newInputStream(p);

A try-with-resources can open several things, separated by semicolons. They are closed in reverse order when the block ends.

in.transferTo(out);

This call copies everything from one stream to the other, like CopyTo in C#. It was added in Java 9.

Gotcha

Reading one byte or character at a time without a buffer is very much slower in Java than the same .NET code. In .NET, FileStream buffers by default. Java streams do not buffer by default. Wrap a Java stream in a Buffered* class unless you have a reason not to.

Walking a directory tree#

The shop's import job looks for export files in a folder tree. Files.walk visits every entry below a folder. newDirectoryStream matches the names in one folder against a pattern. Here dir is the folder that holds the exports:

// every .csv file under data, as a list
try (var paths = Files.walk(Path.of("data"))) {
    List<Path> exports = paths
            .filter(Files::isRegularFile)
            .filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".csv"))
            .toList();
}

// at most two levels deep, following symbolic links
try (var paths = Files.walk(dir, 2, FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS)) {
    paths.forEach(System.out::println);
}

// names that match a pattern, in one folder
try (var found = Files.newDirectoryStream(dir, "*.{csv,tsv}")) {
    for (Path p : found) System.out.println(p.getFileName());
}
Reading the code
.filter(Files::isRegularFile)

This filter keeps the files and removes the folders.

Files.walk(dir, 2, FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS)

This call goes at most two levels down, and it follows symbolic links. Without this option, walk does not follow symbolic links.

Files.newDirectoryStream(dir, "*.{csv,tsv}")

This call lists one folder and keeps the names that match the pattern. Here the pattern matches files that end in .csv or .tsv.

.NETJava
Directory.EnumerateFiles(dir, "*.csv")Files.newDirectoryStream(dir, "*.csv")
Directory.EnumerateFiles(dir, "*", AllDirectories)Files.walk(dir).filter(Files::isRegularFile)
Directory.EnumerateDirectoriesFiles.list(dir).filter(Files::isDirectory)
new DirectoryInfo(d).GetFiles()Files.list(d).filter(Files::isRegularFile)

Reading a file from inside the JAR#

Anything under src/main/resources is packaged into the Java archive (JAR) and read through the classpath. When the program runs, such a file is not a file on disk. Opening it with Files.readString(Path.of("config.json")) works in the IDE and fails after packaging. This failure is confusing, and it is very common on a first deployment. Read the file as a resource instead, as you would read an embedded resource in .NET:

C#
// embedded resource
var asm = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
using var s = asm.GetManifestResourceStream(
    "MyApp.config.json");
Java 25
try (var in = getClass()
        .getResourceAsStream("/config.json")) {
    String json = new String(
        in.readAllBytes(), UTF_8);
}
Reading the code
.getResourceAsStream("/config.json")

This call finds the resource on the classpath and opens it as a stream of bytes. It returns null if there is no such resource.

in.readAllBytes()

This call reads every byte. Then new String(..., UTF_8) turns the bytes into text.

Note

In Spring, a cleaner form is ClassPathResource. Another cleaner form is to inject @Value("classpath:config.json") Resource r. A leading slash in the name that you pass to getResourceAsStream means “from the classpath root”. Without the leading slash, the lookup is relative to the package of the class.

Threads are cheap now#

Concurrency · Chapter 22· 13 min read

Java has no await, and you do not need one. C# made waiting on I/O cheap by making methods asynchronous. Java made threads cheap instead. Since Java 21, ordinary blocking code can run on a virtual thread. A virtual thread uses almost no resources while it waits.

KindC#JavaNote
newasync Task<T> BuildAsync()T build()Java has no async or await, so write a blocking method and run it on a virtual thread Why
newawait SomeIoAsync()someIo()just call the method, because blocking is fine on a virtual thread Why
newBuildAsync(7).Result, blocking on an async methodbuild(7)Blocking is the normal style. Java has no Task<T> in signatures, no ConfigureAwait and no context to deadlock on. Why
newno equivalenta virtual threada Thread whose stack is on the heap, so it starts at a few hundred bytes, not at about 1 MB Why

twistTask.WhenAll(a, b)a.get(); b.get();This is for two plain calls on virtual threads. StructuredTaskScope does the same in a scope, but it is still a preview feature in Java 25. Why

twistCancellationTokenThread.interrupt()cooperative in both languages, so the target must check, or be blocked in a call that checks Why

The colour problem, and how Java sidestepped itnew#

An order report needs the customer and the customer's orders. Each of them is fetched from another service. In C#, a method that awaits becomes async Task. Then every caller must become async Task too, up to the top of the call chain. This is called function colouring. Java never introduced the colour:

C#
// every caller of this must also become async
async Task<Report> BuildAsync(int id)
{
    Customer c = await _api.GetCustomerAsync(id);
    Orders   o = await _api.GetOrdersAsync(id);
    return Merge(c, o);
}

// calling it from sync code blocks the calling thread
var r = BuildAsync(7).Result;
Java 21+
// no colour. Callers are unaffected.
Report build(int id) {
    Customer c = api.getCustomer(id);   // blocks
    Orders   o = api.getOrders(id);     // blocks
    return merge(c, o);
}

// run it on a virtual thread and it scales anyway
Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> build(7));

Thread.startVirtualThread runs build on a new virtual thread. The ordinary kind of thread is called a platform thread. On a platform thread, each blocking call would hold a whole operating-system thread while it waits. On a virtual thread, a blocking call uses almost no resources.

A virtual thread runs on a real thread. This real thread is called the carrier of the virtual thread. When getCustomer waits for the network, the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) takes the virtual thread off its carrier. The JVM keeps the state of the virtual thread on the heap. The carrier then runs something else. await does the same in .NET. But in Java no compiler rewrote your method, and the signature of the method never changed.

In C#, .Result blocks the calling thread until the task finishes. Under a single-threaded synchronisation context, this causes a deadlock. The rest of the method waits for the calling thread, and the calling thread waits for the method to finish. ASP.NET Core has no synchronisation context. In ASP.NET Core, .Result holds a thread-pool thread for the whole wait.

A platform thread reserves about 1 MB for its stack. A virtual thread is a Thread whose stack is on the heap. The stack starts at a few hundred bytes, so a program can run millions of virtual threads. For the mechanism, see What a virtual thread actually is.

C# refresherConfigureAwait(false): not resuming on the caller's contextC# 5

By default, await resumes on the context it started on, such as a UI thread. Library code adds ConfigureAwait(false) to resume on any pool thread. This avoids one kind of deadlock.

var json = await http.GetStringAsync(url).ConfigureAwait(false);
// continues on a thread-pool thread, not the caller's synchronisation context
async / await

Java has no async or await keywords, and it will not get them. In place of the keywords, you choose where you run the code, not how you write it.

Creating and running themtwist#

Here handle(id) processes one order.

C#
async Task RunAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    var a = Task.Run(() => Handle(7));
    var b = Task.Run(() => Handle(8));
    await Task.WhenAll(a, b);

    await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), ct);

    using var gate = new SemaphoreSlim(20);
    await gate.WaitAsync(ct);
    try { await CallDbAsync(ct); } finally { gate.Release(); }
}
Java 25
void run() throws Exception {
    try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        var a = exec.submit(() -> handle(7));
        var b = exec.submit(() -> handle(8));
        a.get(); b.get();  // wait for both
    }
    Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1));  // interrupt() cancels it

    var gate = new Semaphore(20);
    gate.acquire();
    try { callDb(); } finally { gate.release(); }
}
Reading the code
void run() throws Exception {

Three calls in this method throw the checked exception InterruptedException. The calls are get, sleep and acquire. get also throws ExecutionException. So the method declares throws or catches these exceptions.

try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

This is a try-with-resources block. It does the same as a using block in C#. The executor starts a new virtual thread for every task, and pools nothing. The block closes the executor at the end. Closing the executor waits for every submitted task.

var a = exec.submit(() -> handle(7));

This line submits one task, like Task.Run. submit returns a Future, which is like a Task in C#.

a.get(); b.get();

Each get waits for the result of one task, like await. The two get calls together do the same as Task.WhenAll.

Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1));

This line blocks only the virtual thread. Calling interrupt() on the thread ends the sleep early. Java cancels by interrupting a thread.

var gate = new Semaphore(20);

The semaphore lets at most 20 threads pass acquire at the same time, like SemaphoreSlim in C#.

Async streamsdeep dive
C# refresherIAsyncEnumerable and await foreach: an async streamC# 8

An async iterator returns each value when the value is ready. The caller reads the values with await foreach.

async IAsyncEnumerable<int> TicksAsync()
{
    for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
    {
        await Task.Delay(1000);
        yield return i;
    }
}

await foreach (var t in TicksAsync()) Console.WriteLine(t);

Java has no async streams. In Java, a producer thread puts the values into a BlockingQueue, and the consumer takes the values from the queue.

What a virtual thread actually is#

A virtual thread is a Thread whose stack is on the Java heap. Its stack is not a fixed stack that the operating system reserves. Two numbers explain the whole design:

  • A platform thread is the ordinary kind of thread. It reserves around 1 MB of stack when it is created. Tens of thousands of platform threads are already a problem.
  • A virtual thread starts at a few hundred bytes, and its stack grows as needed. Millions of virtual threads are normal.

Virtual threads run on a small pool of carrier threads. By default, the pool has as many carrier threads as the machine has processors. So a million virtual threads that multiply matrices run exactly as fast as the carrier threads allow, plus a little overhead.

Most blocking operations in the Java Development Kit (JDK) know about virtual threads. Examples are network calls, Thread.sleep and most locks. When a virtual thread blocks in one of these operations, the runtime copies the stack of the thread to the heap. The runtime then frees the carrier. When the operation completes, the virtual thread continues on any carrier that is free.

You can set the size of the carrier pool when the JVM starts:

java -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=8 -jar billing.jar

-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=8 gives the scheduler eight carriers. But the default is nearly always right. The .NET thread pool adds threads slowly when all of its threads are blocked. The carrier pool rarely needs to grow, because a blocked virtual thread releases its carrier.

Three ways to start a virtual thread#

There are three ways to start a virtual thread. The code shows them roughly in order, with the way that you will use most often first. Here ids is a list of order ids, and handle(id) processes one order:

// 1. An executor; the one you'll use in real code.
//    Not a pool: it creates a fresh virtual thread per task.
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int id : ids) {
        exec.submit(() -> handle(id));
    }
}   // close() waits for every task to finish

// 2. Fire one off.
Thread t = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> handle(7));
t.join();

// 3. Build one without starting it; when you need a name or an
//    uncaught-exception handler.
Thread t2 = Thread.ofVirtual()
                  .name("import-", 0)
                  .unstarted(() -> handle(7));
t2.start();
Reading the code
} // close() waits for every task to finish

The try-with-resources block closes the executor at the end. Closing the executor waits for every submitted task.

Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> handle(7));

This line starts one virtual thread immediately. join() waits for the thread to finish, like Wait() on a task in C#.

.name("import-", 0)

This call names the threads import-0, import-1 and so on. The names help when you read logs or thread dumps.

Note

ExecutorService has been AutoCloseable since Java 19. That is why try (var exec = ...) works in the code above. The block does not end until every submitted task has finished. So the block waits for all the tasks, and you write no extra code for the wait.

Is your Spring Boot service on virtual threads?new#

A controller method blocks its thread while it waits for the database or for another service. The wait is cheap or expensive, depending on the kind of thread that the request runs on. This controller reports the kind of thread:

PredictThe thread behind a Spring Boot request#
Nothing in the service's configuration mentions threads. A client sends GET /thread. What comes back?
@RestController
class ThreadController {

    @GetMapping("/thread")
    String thread() {
        return "virtual=" + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual();
    }
}
Show the answer
virtual=false

Spring Boot does not use virtual threads unless you ask. The property spring.threads.virtual.enabled is false by default, on Boot 3.2 and later and on Boot 4. So the request ran on a platform thread from the fixed pool of the web server. On a platform thread, each blocking call holds an operating-system thread while it waits.

If you set spring.threads.virtual.enabled to true, the same request returns virtual=true.

A single property makes Spring Boot run your whole web tier on virtual threads. The property works from Boot 3.2 onward, on Java 21 or later:

spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true

With enabled: true, Tomcat runs each request on a new virtual thread, not on a thread from a fixed pool. So each controller method also runs on a new virtual thread. A blocking controller is then no longer a scalability problem. The settings that set the size of the thread pool no longer have an effect. In a test run without the property, the thread of the request was named http-nio-auto-1-exec-1. With the property, the thread was named tomcat-handler-0.

Blocking becomes the normal style again#

Once blocking is cheap, patterns that felt expensive in .NET become ordinary. Retrying a blocking call is the clearest example. Retry is also one of the places where Spring Boot 4 changed. Retry support moved from an add-on library into Spring Framework itself. In the code below, a client fetches an exchange rate from another service. restClient is a Spring RestClient that is set up to call that service:

// Boot 3.5: needs the Spring Retry dependency,
// or Resilience4j, as an explicit add-on.
import org.springframework.retry.annotation.EnableRetry;
import org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable;

@EnableRetry
@Configuration
class RetryConfig { }

@Service
class RatesClient {

    @Retryable(maxAttempts = 3)
    public Rate fetch(String pair) {
        return restClient.get()          // blocks, fine on a
                .uri("/rates/{p}", pair) // virtual thread
                .retrieve()
                .body(Rate.class);
    }
}
// Boot 4.0: @Retryable is part of Spring Framework 7 itself.
// No extra dependency.
import org.springframework.resilience.annotation.EnableResilientMethods;
import org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable;

@EnableResilientMethods
@Configuration
class RetryConfig { }

@Service
class RatesClient {

    @Retryable(maxRetries = 3)
    public Rate fetch(String pair) {
        return restClient.get()          // blocks, fine on a
                .uri("/rates/{p}", pair) // virtual thread
                .retrieve()
                .body(Rate.class);
    }
}

In both versions, @Retryable wraps fetch, so that a failed call is tried again. fetch itself stays a plain blocking method. But check the number. In Boot 3, maxAttempts = 3 means three calls in total. In Boot 4, maxRetries = 3 means three retries after the first call, so up to four calls. @EnableRetry and @EnableResilientMethods enable the feature.

In Boot 4, import the annotation from org.springframework.resilience.annotation, as the imports show. Spring Framework 7 also has an interface called Retryable. This interface is in org.springframework.core.retry, and an IDE may offer the interface first.

When virtual threads are the wrong tooltrap#

Gotcha

Virtual threads do nothing for CPU-bound work. They make waiting cheap, not calculating. For work that keeps the processor busy, keep a pool of ordinary threads. Make the size of the pool close to the number of processor cores. Executors.newFixedThreadPool creates such a pool. Use the pool for the work that you would give to Parallel.For in C#.

Gotcha

Never pool virtual threads. A pool exists so that the cost of creating a thread is shared among many tasks. But a virtual thread has almost no cost to create. To limit concurrency, limit the resource, not the number of threads. Here ids is a list of order ids, and load(id) reads one order. The database allows 20 connections:

var gate = new Semaphore(20);
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int id : ids) {
        exec.submit(() -> {
            gate.acquire();
            try { return load(id); } finally { gate.release(); }
        });
    }
}

exec.submit starts a virtual thread for every order. gate.acquire() lets only 20 of these threads reach the database at the same time.

Sometimes a virtual thread cannot leave its carrier while it is blocked. Such a virtual thread is called pinned. Since Java 24, only native code that is called through the Java Native Interface (JNI) pins a virtual thread. For the history, see the section Pinning.

Pinning: the one performance trap#

Sometimes a blocked virtual thread cannot be taken off its carrier. Such a virtual thread is called pinned. A pinned virtual thread keeps its carrier, so the carrier cannot run anything else. On Java 21 to 23 there were two causes. One cause was blocking inside a synchronized block. A synchronized block does the same as a lock statement in C#. The other cause was blocking inside native code that is called through JNI.

JDK Enhancement Proposal (JEP) 491 fixed the synchronized case in Java 24 Java 24. A virtual thread now leaves its carrier correctly while it is blocked inside a synchronized block. The old advice was to rewrite every synchronized block as a ReentrantLock. So that advice no longer applies. On Java 24 and later, only native code pins.

If you are on Java 21, the old workaround still matters. In the code below, monitor is any object that is used as a lock. lock is a ReentrantLock, and db.query waits for the database:

// pinned the carrier on Java 21-23 while waiting on I/O
synchronized (monitor) {
    var row = db.query(sql);
}

// comes off the carrier correctly on every version
lock.lock();
try {
    var row = db.query(sql);
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}
Reading the code
synchronized (monitor) {

This line holds monitor as a lock, like lock (monitor) in C#. On Java 21 to 23, waiting on I/O inside the block pinned the carrier. For more about synchronized, see Mutual exclusion.

lock.lock();

This line takes a ReentrantLock explicitly. The unlock call in the finally block releases the lock. Waiting while the thread holds a ReentrantLock never pinned.

To find pinning on Java 21 to 23, run with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full. This option prints a stack trace whenever a virtual thread blocks while it is pinned. Current Java versions no longer have that option. Use the JDK Flight Recorder event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned instead.

ThreadLocal on virtual threadstrap#

C# refresherAsyncLocal: a value that flows with the async callC# 9
static readonly AsyncLocal<string?> User = new();

User.Value = "ada";
await Task.Run(() => Console.WriteLine(User.Value));   // "ada": it flows into the task
Gotcha

ThreadLocal still works, but scales badly. One ThreadLocal value per thread was fine with 200 threads. With 500,000 threads, it is a memory problem. Use ScopedValue Java 25 instead. ScopedValue is also the closer match to AsyncLocal<T>. A ScopedValue cannot be changed. It lasts only for a block of code, not until the thread ends. In the code below, the current user is kept while handle processes one order:

// before: one value for each thread, kept until remove() or the end of the thread
static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>();

// after: one value for one block of code
static final ScopedValue<String> CURRENT_USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

ScopedValue.where(CURRENT_USER, "ada").run(() -> handle(order));

While run executes, CURRENT_USER.get() returns "ada". When run returns, the value is gone. For a full comparison of ScopedValue and AsyncLocal, see ScopedValue replaces AsyncLocal.

What you'll still meet in existing code#

LegacyExecutors.newFixedThreadPool(n)

Before Java 21, this was the default for I/O work. The size of the pool was guessed, and then tuned after each incident. You will see this call everywhere, and it still works. For I/O work on Java 21 and later, replace it with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() and delete the size. Keep a fixed pool only for work that keeps the processor busy.

LegacyCompletableFuture chains as the async style

Before virtual threads, non-blocking Java meant chaining thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine. Such a chain is the closest match in Java to a Task continuation chain in C#. It is about as readable as ContinueWith was before await:

// still compiles, still works, rarely the right choice now
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> api.getCustomer(id))
    .thenCombine(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> api.getOrders(id)),
                 this::merge)
    .join();

The two supplyAsync calls start the fetches. thenCombine merges the results when both results arrive, and join waits for the merged value.

CompletableFuture is still the right tool when you need a value that completes later, as the next chapters show. It is no longer the right tool if you only want to run two blocking calls at the same time.

LegacyThread.stop() and Thread.suspend()

Both methods have been unsafe since Java 1.2. suspend() was removed in Java 23. stop() still compiles against Java 25, but it throws and does not stop anything. Java 26 removes stop(). There has never been a safe way to kill a thread from outside, in Java or in .NET. Cancellation is cooperative. You interrupt the thread, and then the thread must notice the interrupt itself.

Migration checklist#

If your .NET instinct isDo this in JavaBecause
Make the method asyncLeave it blockingvirtual threads unmount for you
Add Task<T> to the signatureReturn Tno colouring to propagate
Tune the thread pool sizeDelete the poolone virtual thread per task
Worry about sync-over-asyncDon'tthere is no async to be over
Use AsyncLocal for contextScopedValueimmutable, scope-bounded
Fire-and-forget with Task.Runexec.submit on a scoped executorkeeps the join

Put together, the report from the start of this chapter runs like this:

// no async signature, no tuned pool, and nothing left running unwatched
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<Report> report = exec.submit(() -> build(7));   // build() stays blocking
    publish(report.get());
}   // close() waits for anything still running

build is the same blocking method as before. submit runs it on a virtual thread, and report.get() waits for the result.

Check yourself
1
An expert asksWhy does Java have no async and await?
Java made threads cheap instead. When a virtual thread blocks, the JVM takes the thread off its carrier and keeps the state of the thread on the heap. await does the same in .NET. No compiler rewrites the method, so there is no function colouring.
2
TranslateWrite this in Java, where both calls wait on the database: 
async Task<Report> BuildAsync(long id)
{
    var customer = Task.Run(() => LoadCustomer(id));
    var orders = Task.Run(() => LoadOrders(id));
    await Task.WhenAll(customer, orders);
    return new Report(customer.Result, orders.Result);
}
Report build(long id) throws Exception {
    try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        Future<Customer> customer = exec.submit(() -> loadCustomer(id));
        Future<List<Order>> orders = exec.submit(() -> loadOrders(id));
        return new Report(customer.get(), orders.get());
    }
}

The executor is not a pool. It starts a new virtual thread for every task, so there is no size to choose. Never pool virtual threads. get throws checked exceptions, so the method declares throws.

3
An expert asksWhat is pinning, and is it still a problem?
A pinned virtual thread cannot leave its carrier while it is blocked. On Java 21 to 23, blocking inside a synchronized block pinned the virtual thread. Java 24 fixed that, so now only native code pins.

Structured concurrency and cancellation#

Concurrency · Chapter 23· 7 min read

Structured concurrency is like Task.WhenAll plus a CancellationToken in C#. Subtasks start inside a scope, and no subtask outlives the scope. Structured concurrency is still a preview feature in Java 25 Java 25 preview. So production code on Java 21 or 25 uses an ExecutorService instead.

KindC#JavaNote
twistTask.WhenAll(a, b)fork twice, then joinStructured concurrency is a preview feature in Java 25. With it, join waits for every subtask, and fails as soon as one fails. Why
twistCancellationTokenSourcethe scope itselfleaving the try block cancels every subtask still running, so no token is passed down Why
twisttry/finally to clean upthe try-with-resources blockno subtask can outlive the block that opened the scope Why
trapTask.WhenAll, a finished APIStructuredTaskScope, behind --enable-previewJava 25 has the fifth preview of StructuredTaskScope. The flag is needed to compile and to run, and the API still changes. Why
twistTask.WhenAny(a, b)a scope configured to complete on the first successJoiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow() returns the first result and cancels the rest Why
twistCancelAfter(timeout)a timeout configured on the scopeC# sets the timeout on the token source, but Java sets the timeout on the scope Why
twista token passed down by handa scope around the subtasksA token cancels but does not contain. A scope ties each subtask to the block that started it. Why
twistTask.WhenAll(a, b), on final APIsexec.submit twice, then get()This is the pattern to ship on Java 25, for two plain calls on virtual threads. A failure does not cancel the other task. Why
twistct.IsCancellationRequestedThread.currentThread().isInterrupted()Cancellation is cooperative in both languages. In Java, interrupt() sets a flag, which the thread must check. Why
twistct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()Thread.interrupted() checks, mostly implicitblocking JDK calls see the flag and throw InterruptedException for you Why
trapOperationCanceledExceptionInterruptedExceptionthe call that throws it clears the interrupt flag, so restore the flag or let the exception propagate Why
twistAsyncLocal<T>ScopedValue.where(USER, "ada").run(...)ScopedValue is final in Java 25. It is immutable, bound for one block, and inherited by forked subtasks. Why

The problem it solvestwist#

C#
async Task<Report> BuildAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var a = FetchCustomerAsync(id, ct);
    var b = FetchOrdersAsync(id, ct);
    await Task.WhenAll(a, b);
    return Merge(a.Result, b.Result);
}
Java 25 (preview)
Report build(int id) throws Exception {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
        var a = scope.fork(() -> fetchCustomer(id));
        var b = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrders(id));

        // waits; propagates the first failure
        scope.join();

        return merge(a.get(), b.get());
    }
}
Reading the code
StructuredTaskScope.open()

This call opens a scope. By default, the scope waits for every subtask, and it fails as soon as one subtask fails.

scope.fork(() -> fetchCustomer(id));

This line starts a subtask on its own virtual thread. fork returns a handle to the future result of the subtask.

scope.join();

This line waits for the subtasks. If one subtask failed, join throws, and the other subtask is cancelled.

merge(a.get(), b.get())

This line reads the result of each subtask. The results are ready after join has returned.

When the code leaves the try block, every subtask that is still running is cancelled. This happens when the block ends normally, by an exception or by an interrupt. No token is passed down, because the scope is the token.

Gotcha

Structured concurrency needs --enable-preview when you compile and again when you run. Class files built with preview features will not load on any other Java Development Kit (JDK) version.

C# refresherCancellationTokenSource, CancelAfter and Task.WhenAnyC# 8

A token source cancels every task that holds its token. It cancels when you call Cancel(), or after a timeout. WhenAny finishes as soon as the first task finishes.

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));        // cancel automatically after 2 s

try
{
    var first = await Task.WhenAny(PrimaryAsync(cts.Token), BackupAsync(cts.Token));
    cts.Cancel();                                // stop the one still running
    Use(await first);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) { }          // the 2 s ran out

void Work(CancellationToken ct) => ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();

Completion policies#

open() with no argument waits for every subtask, and it fails as soon as one subtask fails. To choose a different policy, pass a Joiner. The choice of policy is like the choice between WhenAll and WhenAny in C#. In the code below, the shop asks two exchange-rate services for the same rate. The shop takes the answer that arrives first:

// first one home wins, the rest are cancelled
try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(
        StructuredTaskScope.Joiner.<Rate>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow())) {
    scope.fork(() -> primary.fetch(pair));
    scope.fork(() -> secondary.fetch(pair));
    return scope.join();          // the winning value
}
Reading the code
StructuredTaskScope.Joiner.<Rate>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow()

This is a policy that finishes with the first successful result and cancels the other subtasks. It is like Task.WhenAny, followed by code that cancels the tasks that did not finish first. <Rate> names the result type, because Java cannot infer the type here.

return scope.join();

With this policy, join returns the first successful result.

A timeout is also set on the scope. In C#, you call CancelAfter on the token source instead. Here joiner is any of the policies in the table below:

StructuredTaskScope.open(joiner, config -> config.withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)))

The second argument configures the scope. withTimeout gives the scope two seconds to finish.

These are the policies that Java 25 offers:

JoinerBehaviour.NET analogue
anySuccessfulResultOrThrow()returns the first successful result and cancels the restTask.WhenAny
allSuccessfulOrThrow()a stream of all subtasks, all succeededTask.WhenAll
awaitAll()waits for all, success or failureWhenAll then inspect
awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow()waits for all, and throws on any failureWhenAll with fail-fast
allUntil(Predicate)cancels when the predicate is satisfiedno direct equivalent
Note

Blog posts from 2023 or 2024 use an older form of the API, with new StructuredTaskScope<>() and ShutdownOnFailure. The older form no longer matches Java 25. Java 26 has the sixth preview, and it changes the API again. For example, anySuccessfulResultOrThrow() is renamed to anySuccessfulOrThrow().

Why a scope rather than a token#

Note

The idea is the same as the idea behind structured programming. A task started with executor.submit() is like a goto. The lifetime of the task has nothing to do with the code that started it. So a task can leak, or it can keep running after its caller has returned. A scope ties the lifetime of each subtask to the block of code that started it. A subtask cannot outlive that block, and thread dumps show which task started which subtask.

A CancellationToken in C# gives you cancellation, but not containment. Nothing stops you from forgetting to await a task. And nothing makes the task stop when its caller returns.

In code, the difference looks like this. refreshCache reloads the shop's product cache:

// unstructured: the task can outlive the method that started it
void start() { executor.submit(this::refreshCache); }   // who waits for it? nobody

// structured (preview): the subtask cannot outlive the block
void refresh() throws InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
        scope.fork(this::refreshCache);
        scope.join();                                    // finished before the block ends
    }
}
Reading the code
void start() { executor.submit(this::refreshCache); }

This method starts the refresh and returns immediately. Nothing waits for the refresh, and nothing stops the refresh if the caller is cancelled.

scope.fork(this::refreshCache);

The refresh runs inside the scope, so the block cannot end until the refresh has finished.

What to write on Java 25twist#

Until structured concurrency is final, write the order report like this for production. The code uses only final APIs, and it needs no preview flag. It reports a failure and guarantees cleanup:

Report build(int id) throws Exception {
    try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        Future<Customer> a = exec.submit(() -> fetchCustomer(id));
        Future<Orders>   b = exec.submit(() -> fetchOrders(id));

        // get() rethrows a task's failure as ExecutionException, a first and then b
        return merge(a.get(), b.get());
    }
    // close() waits for all tasks; on exception the block still exits cleanly
}
Reading the code
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()

This is the executor from the chapter Threads are cheap now. It starts one virtual thread per task.

merge(a.get(), b.get())

get waits for each result, one after the other. If a task failed, get throws ExecutionException, which wraps the task's own exception.

Gotcha

This pattern does not fail fast, and it does not cancel the other task. A failure in b appears only after a.get() has returned. close() waits for the other task and does not interrupt it. If cancelling matters, call b.cancel(true) in a catch block. Or use invokeAny or invokeAll, which follow their own rules. Structured concurrency exists to solve this problem.

Cancellation is interruptiontrap#

Java cancels a thread by interrupting it with Thread.interrupt(). An interrupt is cooperative, like a CancellationToken in C#. interrupt() sets a flag on the thread. Blocking calls in the JDK throw InterruptedException when they see the flag.

PredictThe interrupt flag inside the catch block#
What does this print?
Thread t = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted());
    }
});
t.interrupt();
t.join();
Show the answer
false

A blocking call clears the interrupt flag when it throws InterruptedException. In the catch block, the flag is already false. Suppose you catch the exception, ignore it, and do not call Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Then every caller loses the cancellation signal, and the thread keeps working. This mistake is like catching OperationCanceledException in C# and ignoring it. But the Java mistake is much easier to make by accident.

Either restore the flag and return, or let the exception propagate. It is never enough to log the exception.

Here a long import processes the order file in chunks. The import must stop when it is cancelled:

public void work() {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        try {
            doChunk();
            Thread.sleep(100);          // throws InterruptedException if interrupted
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();  // restore the flag!
            return;
        }
    }
}
Reading the code
while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted())

This line checks the interrupt flag between chunks, like a check of ct.IsCancellationRequested in C#.

Thread.sleep(100);

When the thread is interrupted, a blocking call such as sleep throws InterruptedException. It does not wait until its time has passed.

Thread.currentThread().interrupt();

This line sets the flag again for the callers, because sleep cleared the flag when it threw.

A loop with no blocking call in it must check the flag itself. The statement if (Thread.interrupted()) throw new InterruptedException(); does the same as ThrowIfCancellationRequested in C#. Thread.interrupted() reads the flag and clears it.

ScopedValue replaces AsyncLocal#

Scoped values Java 25 are final in Java 25. So scoped values are ready for production, unlike structured concurrency. A scoped value carries context, such as the current user, down a chain of calls. You do not pass the context as a parameter. Forked subtasks inherit the scoped values:

C#
static readonly AsyncLocal<string> User = new();

User.Value = "ada";
await DoWorkAsync();     // sees "ada"
Java 25
static final ScopedValue<String> USER =
        ScopedValue.newInstance();

ScopedValue.where(USER, "ada").run(() -> {
    // USER.get() is "ada" here, and in forked subtasks
    doWork();
});                      // rebound to nothing after the block
Reading the code
ScopedValue.newInstance()

This call creates the key. The key is usually in a static final field, like the static AsyncLocal in C#.

ScopedValue.where(USER, "ada").run(() -> {

This line binds USER to "ada" while the lambda runs. Code that is called from inside the lambda reads the value with USER.get().

When run returns, USER is unbound again, so the value cannot leak into later work. This table compares AsyncLocal and ScopedValue:

AsyncLocal<T>ScopedValue<T>
Mutable, assign any timeImmutable, bound for a block
Lifetime is ambientLifetime is the block
Flows to async continuationsInherited by forked subtasks
Can leak if never clearedCannot leak, because it unbinds on block exit
Note

ScopedValue is also the recommended replacement for ThreadLocal on virtual threads. A ThreadLocal holds one value per thread, so a million virtual threads means a million values. For ThreadLocal and ScopedValue side by side, see the chapter Threads are cheap now.

Check yourself
1
Structured concurrency looks perfect for your fan-out. Can you ship it?
No, you cannot ship it on Java 25. Structured concurrency is still a preview. Java 25 has the fifth preview, and the API has changed between previews. The code needs --enable-preview to compile and again to run. Its class files will not load on any other JDK version.
2
An expert asksWhy does Java tie subtasks to a scope instead of passing a cancellation token?
A CancellationToken gives you cancellation, but not containment. Nothing stops you from forgetting to await a task, and nothing makes the task stop when its caller returns. A scope ties the lifetime of each subtask to the block that started it, so no subtask can outlive the block.
3
TranslateWrite this in Java, for code that runs on virtual threads: 
static readonly AsyncLocal<string> User = new();

User.Value = "ada";
DoWork();     // reads User.Value
static final ScopedValue<String> USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

ScopedValue.where(USER, "ada").run(() -> doWork());   // doWork reads USER.get()

Do not use a ThreadLocal. A ThreadLocal keeps one value for each thread, and a million virtual threads means a million values. A ScopedValue has no setter. It is bound while run executes. It is final in Java 25, so it needs no preview flag.
