CompletableFuture and Task#

Concurrency · Chapter 24· 6 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens

CompletableFuture<T> does the same as Task<T> in C#. It is a value that arrives later, and it has methods that chain more work onto that value. Now that Java has virtual threads, you need CompletableFuture far less, because most concurrent code can simply block.

KindC#JavaNote
twistTask<T>CompletableFuture<T>a value that arrives later, with methods to chain more work onto it Why
twistTask (void)CompletableFuture<Void>a future that carries no result, such as the one thenAccept returns Why
twistTask.FromResult(v)CompletableFuture.completedFuture(v)a future that is already complete when you create it Why
twistTask.Run(f)CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(f)runs f on another thread, and completes the future with its result Why
twistTask.Run(action)CompletableFuture.runAsync(action)the form for work that returns no value Why
twistTaskCompletionSource<T>new CompletableFuture<>()create it empty, then call complete(value) when the result arrives Why
twistawait task.join(), or just block on a virtual threadJava has no await, so chained code reads like C# before await Why
twist.Result / .GetAwaiter().GetResult().join()join() throws an unchecked CompletionException that wraps the cause Why
twist.ContinueWith(t => f(t.Result)).thenApply(f)runs f on the result when it arrives Why
twist.ContinueWith returning Task.thenCompose(f)flattens a future of a future into one Why
twistcombine two results.thenCombine(other, fn)waits for both futures, then merges their two results with fn Why
twistTask.WhenAll(a, b)CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b)Use it for futures in older code. It completes when every future completes, but it carries no results, so read each future. Why
twistTask.WhenAny(a, b)CompletableFuture.anyOf(a, b)the result is typed Object, so you must cast it back Why
twisttry/catch around await.exceptionally(fn) or .handle(fn)exceptionally returns a replacement value when the future fails Why
trapblocking inside Task.RunsupplyAsync(f, exec)with no executor argument, the work shares the common pool, and blocking there starves it Why
twistTask.DelayCompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(...)it returns an executor that runs a task after a delay, and it was added in Java 9 Why
twistIProgress<T>no equivalentpass a Consumer<Integer> and call it as the work progresses Why
twistTask, for all concurrent workCompletableFuture, for a value that completes laterto run two blocking calls at once, use virtual threads and an executor instead Why
twista Task you only wait forFuture, from ExecutorService.submitthe Java 5 interface has no chaining, so you can only call get(), cancel() and isDone() Why

Translationtwist#

A CompletableFuture is a value that arrives later. In the code below, compute() is some calculation. client is a payment client that reports each reply through a callback. a and b are two tasks that are already running.

C#
Task<int> ready = Task.FromResult(42);
Task<int> work = Task.Run(() => Compute());

var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<string>();
client.OnReply += r => tcs.SetResult(r);   // completed by hand
string reply = await tcs.Task;

await Task.WhenAll(a, b);
var first = await Task.WhenAny(a, b);
Java 25
var ready = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(42);
var work = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> compute());

var reply = new CompletableFuture<String>();
client.onReply(reply::complete);  // completed by hand
String text = reply.join();

CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join();
Object first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(a, b).join();
Reading the code
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> compute())

This call runs the lambda on another thread, like Task.Run in C#. It completes the future with the result of the lambda.

new CompletableFuture<String>()

This is an empty future, like a TaskCompletionSource in C#. Nothing completes the future until some code calls complete.

client.onReply(reply::complete);

When the reply arrives, the client calls complete. That call gives the future its value.

reply.join()

join waits for the value, like .Result in C#. On a virtual thread, waiting uses almost no resources.

Object first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(a, b).join();

anyOf returns an Object, so you must cast the result to the type that you expect.

Reporting progress#

C# refresherIProgress: reporting progress from async workC# 5
var progress = new Progress<int>(pct => bar.Value = pct);   // runs on the caller's context
await ImportAsync(file, progress);

async Task ImportAsync(string file, IProgress<int> progress)
{
    progress.Report(50);                                     // half way
}

Java has no IProgress. The method that does the work takes a Consumer<Integer> as a parameter. Consumer is in the package java.util.function. The method calls the Consumer as the work progresses:

void importFile(String file, Consumer<Integer> progress) {
    progress.accept(50);    // half way
}

importFile("orders.csv", pct -> System.out.println(pct + "%"));

accept does the same as Report in C#. The lambda runs on the thread that calls accept.

Chaining#

C# hid the chaining behind await. Java never hid it. So code that uses CompletableFuture reads like C# code from before await, which was full of ContinueWith calls.

Suppose the work has three steps. Fetching a customer returns a future. Decorating the customer is a plain calculation. Enriching the customer returns another future. In C# you would await each step. With CompletableFuture you chain the steps:

C#
var report = await FetchCustomerAsync(id)
    .ContinueWith(t => Enrich(t.Result))
    .Unwrap();

// or, idiomatically
var c = await FetchCustomerAsync(id);
var report = await EnrichAsync(c);
Java 25
CompletableFuture<Report> f =
    fetchCustomerAsync(id)
        .thenApply(this::decorate)        // sync transform
        // enrichAsync returns another future
        .thenCompose(this::enrichAsync);

Report report = f.join();
Reading the code
.thenApply(this::decorate)

thenApply runs decorate on the result when the result arrives. It is like ContinueWith with a plain function.

.thenCompose(this::enrichAsync);

Use thenCompose when the next step itself returns a future. It flattens the future of a future into one future, like Unwrap after ContinueWith.

Report report = f.join();

This line waits for the whole chain to finish.

An executor is an object that supplies the threads. These are the chaining methods, and where each method runs:

MethodRunsReturns
thenApply(fn)on the completing threadCompletableFuture<R>
thenApplyAsync(fn)on the common pool, or a supplied executorCompletableFuture<R>
thenCompose(fn)fn returns a future, and thenCompose flattens itCompletableFuture<R>
thenCombine(other, fn)when both completeCompletableFuture<R>
thenAccept(consumer)side effectCompletableFuture<Void>
exceptionally(fn)only on failureCompletableFuture<T>
handle(fn)on success or failureCompletableFuture<R>
whenComplete(action)on success or failure, but does not change the valueCompletableFuture<T>
Gotcha

allOf returns CompletableFuture<Void>, not a future of the results. Task.WhenAll gives you a Task<T[]>. But after allOf you must read each future yourself. Here ids is a list of order ids, and load(id) fetches one order:

import static java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture.supplyAsync;

List<CompletableFuture<Order>> futures = ids.stream()
        .map(id -> supplyAsync(() -> load(id)))
        .toList();

CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();

List<Order> orders = futures.stream()
        .map(CompletableFuture::join)   // safe: all are already complete
        .toList();
Reading the code
.map(id -> supplyAsync(() -> load(id)))

This line starts one future for each id.

CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();

allOf takes an array, so the list is converted to an array first. Then join waits for every future.

.map(CompletableFuture::join)

This line collects each result. Here join returns at once, because every future has already completed.

Which thread does the work#

Gotcha

The *Async methods without an executor argument run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). That pool has one thread fewer than your processor has cores. Parallel streams share the pool, and so does everything else in the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Blocking on that pool starves everything that shares it.

Always pass an executor for anything that blocks. Here httpCall waits for another service:

var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpCall(), exec)   // blocking, but on a virtual thread
        .thenApplyAsync(this::transform, exec);
Reading the code
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()

This is the executor from the chapter Threads are cheap now. It gives each task its own virtual thread.

.thenApplyAsync(this::transform, exec);

Every *Async step takes the executor as its last argument. Without that argument, the step runs on the common pool again.

An executor can also start its work after a delay. This is the nearest thing in Java to Task.Delay followed by more work:

var later = CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS, exec);
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpCall(), later);   // starts after two seconds

delayedExecutor wraps exec. Each task that you pass to later waits two seconds, and then runs on exec.

Exceptions#

A failed future wraps the cause in another exception. join throws the cause inside a CompletionException. get throws the cause inside an ExecutionException. This is the same wrapping that AggregateException does in .NET, and it is just as annoying.

C# refresherAggregateException: several failures wrapped in oneC# 3
try { Task.WaitAll(a, b); }
catch (AggregateException ex)
{
    foreach (var inner in ex.InnerExceptions) Log(inner);   // the real exceptions
}

Here future is a CompletableFuture<Report>, and log is the logger of the class:

try {
    var r = future.join();
} catch (CompletionException e) {
    Throwable cause = e.getCause();     // the real exception
}

// or handle it in the pipeline
future.exceptionally(ex -> {
        log.warn("failed", ex);
        return Report.empty();
    })
    .thenAccept(this::publish);
Reading the code
} catch (CompletionException e) {

join wraps the task's exception in a CompletionException.

Throwable cause = e.getCause();

getCause returns the exception that the task actually threw.

future.exceptionally(ex -> {

exceptionally handles a failure inside the chain. The lambda receives the exception and returns a replacement value. Here the replacement value is an empty report, so publish still runs.

Note

get() throws two checked exceptions, ExecutionException and InterruptedException. join() throws the unchecked CompletionException. Inside a lambda, join() is almost always the right choice, because checked exceptions do not work well in lambdas. See Exceptions and resources.

When to still use ittwist#

These are the cases where CompletableFuture is still the right tool:

SituationUse
Two blocking calls concurrentlyvirtual threads + an executor, not CompletableFuture
Adapting a callback API to a valueCompletableFuture, completed manually
Caffeine or another async cacheCompletableFuture, because the API requires it
Spring WebFlux / reactive codeMono/Flux, which are a different model again
Fire-and-forget with a completion hookCompletableFuture.runAsync(...).thenRun(...)

Here client is a messaging client that reports each reply, or each error, through a callback:

// adapting a callback API: the future is completed by hand
CompletableFuture<Reply> send(Request request) {
    var done = new CompletableFuture<Reply>();
    client.send(request, done::complete, done::completeExceptionally);
    return done;
}
Reading the code
client.send(request, done::complete, done::completeExceptionally);

The client calls complete with the reply, or completeExceptionally with an error. Either call finishes the future.

return done;

The caller gets a future, like the Task of a TaskCompletionSource in C#. The caller can wait for the future, or chain more work onto it.

LegacyFuture, the Java 5 interface

The original Future from Java 5 has no chaining methods at all. You can only call get(), cancel() and isDone(). The call to get() blocks. ExecutorService.submit returns a Future. A Future is good enough when you intend to block on a virtual thread anyway. CompletableFuture implements Future, so it does everything that Future does, and more.

Check yourself
1
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpCall()) waits on another service. Which threads run it, and what is the risk?
With no executor argument, the work runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). That pool has one thread fewer than the processor has cores, and parallel streams share it. Blocking there starves everything that shares the pool. So pass an executor as the second argument for anything that blocks.

Locks, atomics and the memory model#

Concurrency · Chapter 25· 8 min read

Each basic tool has a close match in C#. synchronized does the same as lock. AtomicInteger does the same as Interlocked. ConcurrentHashMap does the same as ConcurrentDictionary. Both languages also have volatile, and the Java keyword gives stronger guarantees than the C# keyword.

KindC#JavaNote
twistlock (_gate) { ... }synchronized (gate) { ... }the same mutual exclusion, and any object can be the lock Why
twistlock (this)a synchronized methodthe method modifier locks on this, so prefer a private final lock object Why
twistMonitor.TryEnter(o, ts)lock.tryLock(t, unit)ReentrantLock adds timeouts, interruption and fairness. Unlock it in a finally block. Why
twistInterlocked.Increment(ref x)atomicInt.incrementAndGet()Java has no ref parameters, so the operations are methods of an object that holds the number Why
trapInterlocked.CompareExchange(ref x, v, c)atomicRef.compareAndSet(c, v)the expected value comes first, but CompareExchange puts the new value first Why
twistInterlocked for high contentionLongAdder, far better under contentionfor a counter that many threads write constantly and that is read now and then Why
twistvolatilevolatileIt is the same for a stop flag or double-checked locking. Java also keeps all volatile reads and writes in one order. Why
twistVolatile.Read / Writevolatile field, or VarHandlemark the field volatile, so that another thread sees the latest value Why
twistLazy<T>a static holder classIt is lazy and thread-safe with no locking. Stable values are like Lazy<T>, and they are a preview feature in Java 25. Why
twistConcurrentDictionary<K,V>ConcurrentHashMap<K,V>the thread-safe HashMap, and its reads never lock Why
twistGetOrAdd(k, factory)computeIfAbsent(k, fn)it is atomic, so the function runs at most once per key, unlike GetOrAdd Why
trapa GetOrAdd factory that calls GetOrAdda computeIfAbsent function that calls the map againJava holds a lock while the function runs, so it can throw IllegalStateException with the message Recursive update Why
twistAddOrUpdatecompute(k, fn) / merge(k, v, fn)compute and merge update a value atomically Why
twistBlockingCollection with capArrayBlockingQueue<E>a bounded queue with a fixed capacity set when it is created Why
twistChannel<T>BlockingQueue, or SubmissionPublisherJava has no async channel, so a BlockingQueue on virtual threads is the usual answer Why

Mutual exclusiontwist#

C#
private readonly object _gate = new();
private long _total;

public void Add(int x)
{
    lock (_gate)
    {
        _total += x;
    }
}
Java 25
private final Object gate = new Object();
private long total;

public void add(int x) {
    synchronized (gate) {
        total += x;
    }
}
Reading the code
private final Object gate = new Object();

This is a private object that is used only as the lock, like _gate in the C# code. Any object can be a lock in Java.

synchronized (gate) {

Only one thread at a time can be inside a block that is synchronized on gate. lock (_gate) in C# works the same way.

synchronized is also a method modifier. On an instance method, it locks on this. On a static method, it locks on the class itself:

public synchronized void add(int x) { total += x; }   // locks on this

Every call to add now locks the object itself.

Gotcha

Never synchronized on this or on a public field. Any other code that holds a reference to your object can lock on it too. Use a private final lock object. The same advice applies to lock (this) in C#. But the method modifier in Java makes the mistake much easier to make by accident.

ReentrantLock#

When you need a timeout, a wait that can be interrupted, fairness, or several conditions to wait on, synchronized is not enough:

NeedC#Java
Basic mutual exclusionlocksynchronized, or ReentrantLock
Try with timeoutMonitor.TryEnter(o, ts)lock.tryLock(t, unit)
Interruptible acquireThread.Interrupt() ends the wait for any locklock.lockInterruptibly()
Read/write splitReaderWriterLockSlimReentrantReadWriteLock
Condition variableMonitor.Wait / PulseCondition.await / signal
Fair queueingnonew ReentrantLock(true)
Non-reentrantSemaphoreSlim(1)Semaphore(1)

In the interruptible row, Java is the reverse of C#. In C#, Thread.Interrupt() ends a wait for any lock, and the waiting thread gets a ThreadInterruptedException. In Java, a thread that waits to enter a synchronized block ignores interrupt() until it gets the lock. So a wait that must be cancellable needs lockInterruptibly().

Here a stock update stops waiting after 200 milliseconds, instead of waiting for the lock forever:

private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

if (lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try {
        mutate();
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();          // ALWAYS in a finally
    }
} else {
    throw new TimeoutException();
}
Reading the code
lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)

tryLock waits at most 200 milliseconds for the lock, like Monitor.TryEnter with a timeout in C#. It returns false if the lock was still busy after that time.

lock.unlock();

A ReentrantLock is not released automatically. So always put the call to unlock in a finally block.

throw new TimeoutException();

You decide what the code does when the lock did not become free in time.

Note

On Java 21 to 23, ReentrantLock was the better choice on virtual threads, because waiting inside synchronized pinned the thread to its carrier. Since Java 24, both ReentrantLock and synchronized are fine on virtual threads. See Threads are cheap now.

Atomicstrap#

Without a lock, two threads can read the same old count, and then one of the additions is lost. Marking the field volatile does not help, because count++ is still a read followed by a write. For one number, a lock is more than you need. Both languages have atomic operations. An atomic operation updates a value in one step that no other thread can interrupt:

C#
private int _count;
Interlocked.Increment(ref _count);
Interlocked.Add(ref _count, 10);
Interlocked.Exchange(ref _count, 0);            // set, returning the old value
Java 25
private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();
count.incrementAndGet();
count.addAndGet(10);
count.getAndSet(0);                             // set, returning the old value
Reading the code
new AtomicInteger()

Java has no ref parameters. So the atomic operations are methods of an object that holds the number.

count.incrementAndGet();

This call adds one and returns the new value, like Interlocked.Increment in C#.

PredictcompareAndSet with the arguments in C# order#
What does this print?
var count = new AtomicInteger(4);
// C#: Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref count, 5, 4) sets the value to 5 if it is 4
boolean changed = count.compareAndSet(5, 4);
System.out.println(changed + " " + count.get());
Show the answer
false 4

compareAndSet takes the expected value first. CompareExchange puts the new value first. So the C# order asks Java to set 4 if the value is 5. The value is 4, so nothing changes, and nothing warns you.

Write count.compareAndSet(4, 5), and check the boolean that it returns.

The other operations map as follows:

.NETJava
Interlocked.Add(ref x, n)atomicInt.addAndGet(n)
Interlocked.Exchange(ref x, v)atomicRef.getAndSet(v)
n/aatomicInt.updateAndGet(fn)
n/aatomicRef.accumulateAndGet(v, fn)
Note

LongAdder is for a counter that many threads update at the same time. It spreads the count over several cells, and it sums the cells when you read the count. Under that load, LongAdder performs far better than AtomicLong. Use LongAdder for metrics and counters that are written constantly and read only now and then.

volatile means more in Java#

C# refresherVolatile.Read and Volatile.WriteC# 6

Volatile.Read and Volatile.Write are explicit reads and writes. They are not cached or reordered, so another thread sees the latest value.

private bool _stop;

void Run()  { while (!Volatile.Read(ref _stop)) Work(); }
void Stop() => Volatile.Write(ref _stop, true);   // Run sees it on its next check
Gotcha

Both languages have the keyword volatile, but its guarantees differ:

C# volatileJava volatile
Reorderingacquire on read, release on writesequentially consistent, so every thread agrees on one order
Visibilitythe field, plus writes made before a volatile writethe field, plus writes made before a volatile write
Atomicity of 64-bitnot allowed, because volatile cannot be applied to long or doubleguaranteed for volatile long and double
Use for a flagyesyes
Use for double-checked lockingsufficientsufficient

In practice, both keywords are enough for the two everyday uses. These uses are a stop flag and double-checked locking.

The rule in the Visibility row is called happens-before in Java. It says that a thread that sees a volatile write also sees every write made before that volatile write.

The difference between the two keywords appears only in one case. A thread writes one volatile field and then reads a different volatile field. Java keeps these two steps in order, and C# may not.

Java 5 repaired the Java memory model in 2004. So an older article that calls double-checked locking broken in Java describes a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) that no longer exists.

For a plain field, a VarHandle does the same as Volatile.Read and Volatile.Write in C#. VarHandle is in the package java.lang.invoke. Here STOP is a VarHandle for the field stop. The field is a plain boolean:

void run()  { while (!(boolean) STOP.getVolatile(this)) work(); }
void stop() { STOP.setVolatile(this, true); }   // run sees it on its next check

getVolatile and setVolatile read and write the field as if it were declared volatile. You will rarely need these two methods, because marking the field volatile is the usual answer.

Here the shop's configuration is loaded once, on first use. The first thread that needs the configuration loads it:

// correct in Java 5+ with volatile
private volatile Config config;

public Config get() {
    var c = config;
    if (c == null) {
        synchronized (this) {
            c = config;
            if (c == null) config = c = load();
        }
    }
    return c;
}
Reading the code
private volatile Config config;

volatile guarantees that a thread that sees the new Config also sees it fully built.

var c = config;

This line reads the field once into a local variable. So the usual path needs only a single read of the field.

if (c == null) config = c = load();

The second check is inside the lock. It stops two threads that both saw null from loading the configuration twice.

Note

It is better still to avoid double-checked locking. A static holder class gives you lazy, thread-safe initialisation with no locking at all:

private static class Holder {
    static final Config INSTANCE = load();
}
public static Config get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }

Holder is not initialised until get first reads Holder.INSTANCE. The JVM runs that initialisation exactly once, no matter how many threads arrive at the same time.

Java 25 also previews stable values Java 25 preview. A stable value is essentially the same as Lazy<T> in C#. After initialisation, the just-in-time (JIT) compiler can treat a stable value as a constant.

C# refresherLazy: create a value on first useC# 9
private static readonly Lazy<Config> _config = new(() => Load());   // thread-safe by default
public static Config Config => _config.Value;                     // Load() runs on first read

Concurrent collectionstwist#

Here pair is a currency pair, and job is a job to process:

C#
var rates = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, Rate>();
Rate r = rates.GetOrAdd(pair, p => Fetch(p));   // may call Fetch twice

var hits = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, int>();
hits.AddOrUpdate("home", 1, (_, n) => n + 1);

var jobs = new BlockingCollection<Job>(boundedCapacity: 100);
jobs.Add(job);                 // waits while full
Job next = jobs.Take();        // waits while empty
Java 25
var rates = new ConcurrentHashMap<String, Rate>();
Rate r = rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, p -> fetch(p));   // at most once

var hits = new ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>();
hits.merge("home", 1, Integer::sum);

BlockingQueue<Job> jobs = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);
jobs.put(job);                 // waits while full
Job next = jobs.take();        // waits while empty
Reading the code
rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, p -> fetch(p))

This call returns the cached rate. If the map has no rate for the key, the call runs fetch and stores the result. It runs fetch at most once per key. In C#, GetOrAdd may call Fetch twice when two threads race.

hits.merge("home", 1, Integer::sum);

merge stores 1 if the key is new. Otherwise it combines the old value with 1 by calling Integer::sum. This is like AddOrUpdate in C#.

new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100)

This is a queue that holds at most 100 jobs, like a bounded BlockingCollection in C#.

C# refresherChannel, CountdownEvent, ManualResetEventSlim and BarrierC# 8
var ch = Channel.CreateBounded<Job>(100);        // an async producer-consumer queue
await ch.Writer.WriteAsync(job);
Job next = await ch.Reader.ReadAsync();

using var done = new CountdownEvent(3);          // three Signal() calls release Wait()
using var gate = new ManualResetEventSlim();     // Set() opens it for every waiter
using var round = new Barrier(4);                // four threads meet, then all continue

Java has no async channel. In its place, use a BlockingQueue and read it from a virtual thread. The class SubmissionPublisher pushes each item to its subscribers instead. It is in the package java.util.concurrent.

These are the other concurrent types:

.NETJavaNote
ConcurrentQueue<T>ConcurrentLinkedQueue<E>an unbounded queue whose operations never wait
BlockingCollection<T>LinkedBlockingQueue<E>optionally bounded, and take() waits for an item while put() waits for space
ConcurrentBag<T>no direct equalJava has no unordered bag, but a ConcurrentLinkedQueue is usually good enough
ImmutableList + swapCopyOnWriteArrayList<E>every write copies the array, so use it only when writes are rare
CountdownEventCountDownLatchcounts down to zero once, and cannot be reset
BarrierCyclicBarrierreleases all waiters, then resets for the next round
ManualResetEventSlimCountDownLatch, or a Conditiona one-shot gate is a CountDownLatch(1), but a gate that can be reset needs a Condition
SemaphoreSlimSemaphoreIt is a counting semaphore. Call acquire() to take a permit, and release() to return it.

A function that calls back into the maptrap#

computeIfAbsent(key, fn) is like GetOrAdd in C#. It returns the stored value. If the map has no value for the key, it runs the function and stores the result. A cache that fills itself often has a function that reads the same cache. Here a Fibonacci function remembers its results. The same code with GetOrAdd prints 102334155 in C#:

PredictA function that calls computeIfAbsent on its own map#
What does this print?
static final Map<Integer, Long> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

static long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return n;
    return cache.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2));
}

System.out.println(fib(40));
Show the answer
It throws java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update.

computeIfAbsent holds a lock on part of the map while the function runs. A function that calls the same map again, even indirectly, can meet that lock, and then the map throws. This does not happen for every key, so a test can pass.

In C#, GetOrAdd runs its factory outside any lock. That is why the factory can run twice for one key. It is also why GetOrAdd does not have this problem.

Keep the function short and self-contained. Here, read with get, calculate the value outside the map, and store the value with putIfAbsent.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
var views = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, int>();

void Viewed(string productId) =>
    views.AddOrUpdate(productId, 1, (_, n) => n + 1);
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> views = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

void viewed(String productId) {
    views.merge(productId, 1, Integer::sum);
}

merge stores 1 for a new key. For an existing key, it adds 1 to the old value. It does this in one atomic step. A get followed by a put loses updates when two threads race.

2
An expert asksWhy is volatile not enough for count++?
volatile makes every write visible to other threads, but count++ is a read followed by a write. Two threads can read the same old value, and one of the additions is lost. incrementAndGet updates the value in one step that no other thread can interrupt.

Legacy concurrency you will still meet#

Concurrency · Chapter 26· 7 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

Everything in this chapter still works and is common in production code. But you should not write any of it on Java 21 or later. It is here so that you can read existing code and know what to replace it with.

KindC#JavaNote
twistTask.Run(() => Handle(id))pool.submit(() -> handle(id)).NET has always pooled threads for you, but in Java before 21 you created and sized the pool yourself Why
twistThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItempool.submit(task), on a pool you createboth queue work to a pool, but in Java before 21 you made the pool, sized it and shut it down Why
twistnew Thread(DoWork)new Thread(this::doWork)This is the Java 1.0 API. Write Thread.ofVirtual().start(...) or use an executor instead. Why
twista thread pool you never sizeExecutors.newFixedThreadPool(50)the size is a guess, so for work that waits, use a virtual-thread executor instead Why
trapa pool with nothing to shut downpool.shutdown() in a finally blockif code from before Java 19 forgets this call, the pool's threads keep the program running Why
twistMonitor.Wait / Pulsequeue.wait() / queue.notify()You must hold the lock and wait in a loop. A BlockingQueue does this correctly. Why
twista lock around every callCollections.synchronizedMap(...)a check followed by an update is still a race, so use ConcurrentHashMap Why
trapa timer that runs many tasksjava.util.Timerone task that throws kills its only thread, so use ScheduledExecutorService Why
trapThreadLocal<T>ThreadLocalcall remove() in a pool, and prefer ScopedValue on virtual threads Why
twistno pool to managetry (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor())This is the most common change. There is no size to guess, and closing the block waits for every task. Why

What older code looks liketwist#

The order service's older code handles each incoming order on a thread pool:

What .NET taught you
// .NET has always pooled for you
ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(_ => Handle(id));

var t = Task.Run(() => Handle(id));
await t;
What older Java code does
// pre-21 Java: you sized the pool yourself
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);
Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> handle(id));
f.get();
pool.shutdown();
Reading the code
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50)

This call creates a pool of exactly 50 platform threads. A platform thread is the ordinary kind of thread. Each platform thread is backed by an operating-system thread. The number 50 is a guess that you had to make.

Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> handle(id));

This line submits a task, like Task.Run in .NET. It returns a Future, which is like a Task in .NET. Then f.get() waits for the task to finish.

pool.shutdown();

You must shut down a pool when you have finished with it. If you do not, the threads of the pool keep the program running.

Raw threads#

Legacynew Thread(...).start()

This is the Java 1.0 API. Each platform thread reserves about 1 MB of memory for its stack. Creating a platform thread also needs a call into the operating system. That is why thread pools exist. Here doWork is the job to run:

Thread t = new Thread(() -> doWork());
t.setName("worker-1");
t.setDaemon(true);
t.start();
t.join();
Reading the code
t.setDaemon(true);

A daemon thread does not keep the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) running. When only daemon threads are left, the program ends. setDaemon(true) does the same as IsBackground = true in .NET.

t.join();

This line waits for the thread to finish, like Join() in .NET.

Replace it with Thread.ofVirtual().start(...) for work that waits, or with an executor. The Thread class itself is not deprecated. Virtual threads are Thread objects too.

Here is the same worker thread in both languages:

C#
var t = new Thread(DoWork) { IsBackground = true, Name = "worker-1" };
t.Start();
t.Join();

// t.Abort() cannot kill it: it throws PlatformNotSupportedException on .NET Core and later
Java 25
Thread t = new Thread(this::doWork, "worker-1");
t.setDaemon(true);          // the JVM will not wait for it
t.start();
t.join();

// t.stop() cannot kill it either: interrupt() and let it notice
Reading the code
new Thread(this::doWork, "worker-1")

The second argument names the thread, as Name does in C#.

interrupt() and let it notice

You cannot kill a thread safely from outside, in .NET or in Java. Ask the thread to stop with interrupt(). For how a thread notices the request, see the section Cancellation is interruption.

Concept.NETJavaNote
Background threadIsBackground = truesetDaemon(true)the JVM exits without waiting for it to finish
Foreground threaddefaultdefaultthe JVM will not exit until this thread finishes
NameThread.NamesetName()the name appears in thread dumps and logs, so name your threads
PriorityThread.PrioritysetPriority()only a hint that the OS may ignore, so do not rely on it
Wait for completionJoin()join()blocks until the thread ends, exactly like Join()
Kill itAbort(), which only throwsstop(), which only throwscannot be done safely on either platform, so ask the thread to stop instead

Fixed thread pools#

LegacyExecutors.newFixedThreadPool(n)

Before Java 21, this was the standard way to run work that waits. A larger pool gives more throughput, but it uses more memory. A wrong size causes the classic production incident. If the pool is too small, requests queue. If the pool is too large, memory runs out. Here tasks is a list of jobs that each load one order:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);
try {
    List<Future<Order>> fs = pool.invokeAll(tasks);
    for (var f : fs) use(f.get());
} finally {
    pool.shutdown();
    pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
}
Reading the code
pool.invokeAll(tasks)

This call runs every task and waits for all of them. It returns one Future for each task.

pool.shutdown();

This line stops the pool from accepting new work. Then awaitTermination waits up to 30 seconds for the running tasks to finish.

Replace it with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() for work that waits, and delete the size. Keep a fixed pool of platform threads only for work that keeps the processor busy.

The Executors class has several factories. Virtual threads replace some of the factories, and other factories are still the right tool:

FactoryGives youModern replacement
newFixedThreadPool(n)n platform threadsvirtual threads, for I/O
newCachedThreadPool()unbounded, reusedvirtual threads
newSingleThreadExecutor()serial executionstill fine for serialising work
newScheduledThreadPool(n)timer-like schedulingstill the right tool
newWorkStealingPool()ForkJoinPoolstill right for CPU-bound divide and conquer
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()one virtual thread per taskJava 21+
Gotcha

ExecutorService has been AutoCloseable only since Java 19. Older code shuts the pool down in a finally block instead. There you will see shutdown(), awaitTermination() and shutdownNow(). If the code forgets these calls, the pool's threads keep running, so the JVM never exits. That is a common cause of a build or a command-line tool that hangs after it finishes its work.

wait, notify and notifyAll#

LegacyObject.wait() / notify()

This is the original way to wait for a condition, and it is built into every object. You must hold the lock of the object when you call these methods. They are well known for being easy to use wrongly. A missed notify leaves a thread waiting forever. A call to notify in place of notifyAll can wake the wrong waiter. And a waiting thread can wake up for no reason, so the call to wait must always be in a loop. Here a worker takes the next order from a shared queue, and waits while the queue is empty:

synchronized (queue) {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) {    // while, never if, spurious wakeups are real
        queue.wait();
    }
    return queue.poll();
}
Reading the code
synchronized (queue) {

wait and notify work only while you hold the lock of the object that you wait on.

while (queue.isEmpty()) {

This is a loop, never an if. When the thread wakes, the queue may still be empty.

queue.wait();

This line releases the lock and sleeps until another thread calls queue.notify() or notifyAll(). Then the thread takes the lock again.

Replace it with a BlockingQueue, which does exactly this and does it correctly. Or use a ReentrantLock with a Condition.

Synchronized wrappers#

LegacyCollections.synchronizedMap and friends

These wrappers put a lock around every method. The lock makes each single call safe. But the lock does not protect a check that is followed by an update, so the code below is still a race. Here stock counts items per product, and productId names one product:

Map<String, Integer> stock = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());

if (!stock.containsKey(productId)) {   // another thread can insert here
    stock.put(productId, 0);
}
Reading the code
Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())

Every single call, such as containsKey or put, takes the map's lock.

if (!stock.containsKey(productId)) {

The check and the put are two separate calls. Between the two calls, another thread can insert the same key. Then the value from one thread overwrites the value from the other thread.

Replace it with ConcurrentHashMap and its atomic compound operations. The operations are putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent and merge.

java.util.Timer#

LegacyTimer and TimerTask

A Timer runs all its tasks on one thread. A single task that throws an unchecked exception kills that thread. Every other scheduled task is then cancelled, and nothing reports it. Replace it with ScheduledExecutorService, or with Spring's @Scheduled. Here poll checks the payment provider for updates every 30 seconds:

var sched = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1);
sched.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::poll, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
Reading the code
Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1)

This call creates a scheduler with one thread. Unlike a Timer, the scheduler survives a task that throws.

sched.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::poll, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

This line runs poll immediately, and then every 30 seconds.

Even with ScheduledExecutorService, an uncaught exception cancels that one repeating task. Wrap the body of the task in a try/catch if the task must keep running.

ThreadLocal#

LegacyThreadLocal

ThreadLocal in Java does the same as ThreadLocal<T> in .NET. It holds one value for each thread. It is still correct for platform threads, but it has two problems on modern Java. With virtual threads you may have a million threads, and so a million values. And in a pool, a value that you forget to remove is still there for the next task that reuses the thread. Here the current user is kept while one request is handled:

private static final ThreadLocal<User> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();

CURRENT.set(user);
try {
    doWork();
} finally {
    CURRENT.remove();      // essential in a pooled thread
}
Reading the code
CURRENT.set(user);

This line stores the user for this thread only. Code that is called later on the same thread reads the user with CURRENT.get().

CURRENT.remove();

This line clears the value. In a pool, the thread then serves another request. Without this line, that request would see this user.

Replace it with ScopedValue Java 25. A ScopedValue cannot be changed, lasts for one block, and cannot leak. It is the closer match to AsyncLocal in C#. See Structured concurrency. For ThreadLocal and ScopedValue side by side, see the chapter Threads are cheap now.

Before and aftertwist#

Most of these changes are small. The most common change replaces a fixed pool with virtual threads. It looks like this:

// before: a pool sized by guesswork, shut down by hand
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);

// after: one virtual thread per task, closed and joined by try-with-resources
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    exec.submit(task);
}
Reading the code
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);

This is the old pool. It has a guessed size, and a shutdown that you must remember.

try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

This is the new executor. It has no size to guess. Closing the executor at the end of the block waits for every task.

Check yourself
1
A command-line tool written before Java 19 finishes its work, but the process never exits. What is the likely cause, and the fix?
The likely cause is a thread pool that nobody shut down. Its threads keep the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) running. Older code must call pool.shutdown() in a finally block. Since Java 19 an ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so a try-with-resources block closes the pool for you.

Quick reference#

If you seeReplace with
new Thread(...)Thread.ofVirtual(), or an executor
newFixedThreadPool for I/OnewVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor
wait / notifyBlockingQueue, or Condition
Collections.synchronizedMapConcurrentHashMap
java.util.TimerScheduledExecutorService
ThreadLocalScopedValue
Thread.stop / suspendnothing, because suspend is gone and stop only throws
CompletableFuture merely to parallelise blocking callsvirtual threads

Reactive: WebFlux and Reactor#

Concurrency · Chapter 27· 9 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens

Reactor does the same as Rx.NET. WebFlux is a Spring web stack that never blocks. You probably do not need it. The main argument for reactive Java was that threads were too expensive to give one to each request. Virtual threads Java 21 removed that argument.

KindC#JavaNote
twistTask<T>Mono<T>zero or one value that arrives later, like a Task Why
twistIAsyncEnumerable<T>Flux<T>a stream of any number of values that arrive over time Why
twistIObservable<T>Flux<T>one type covers both the pull and the push styles Why
twistTask.FromResult(v)Mono.just(v)a Mono that already holds its value Why
twistTask.CompletedTaskMono.empty()a Mono that completes with no value Why
twist.Select.maptransform each value as it arrives Why
twist.Where.filterkeep only the values that match Why
twist.SelectMany.flatMapeach value becomes a publisher, and the results merge Why
twisttwo awaits, then Merge(c, o)Mono.zip(a, b).map(...)C# awaits each call, one after the other, but in Reactor a combinator pairs the two results Why
trapasync code, for throughputSpring MVC on virtual threadsdo not adopt WebFlux for throughput, because blocking code scales to the same numbers on Java 21 Why
twistIAsyncEnumerable + ChannelFlux + backpressureReactor lets a slow consumer tell the producer to send less Why
twistresults that arrive over timeFlux, as server-sent eventsreactive code still fits streams, backpressure and very large fan-out Why
trapawait.block(), almost always wrongblock() waits for the value, but on one of Reactor's non-blocking threads it throws IllegalStateException instead Why
trapa blocking call in async codea blocking call on an event-loop threadit stalls unrelated requests, so one blocking library undoes the whole model Why
trapan ORM behind async codeR2DBC, with no ORM at allthere is no reactive JPA, so WebFlux means giving up Spring Data JPA Why
trapcalling a method that returns a Taskbuilding a Mono or Fluxa Mono or Flux is a recipe, not a running computation, so nothing happens until something subscribes Why

The modeltwist#

Reactor is the library that WebFlux uses. Its two types match .NET types that you already know. Here order is an Order, and repo is a repository that can stream orders:

C#: Task, IAsyncEnumerable, Rx.NET
Task<Order> one = Task.FromResult(order);
Task none = Task.CompletedTask;
IAsyncEnumerable<Order> many = repo.StreamAsync();

IObservable<int> evens = Observable.Interval(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1))
    .Where(n => n % 2 == 0)
    .Select(n => (int)n);
Java: Reactor
Mono<Order> one = Mono.just(order);
Mono<Void> none = Mono.empty();
Flux<Order> many = repo.findAll();

Flux<Integer> evens = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .map(Long::intValue);
Reading the code
Mono<Order> one = Mono.just(order);

A Mono holds zero or one value that arrives later, like a Task<T> in .NET. The method just wraps a value that you already have, like Task.FromResult.

Flux<Order> many = repo.findAll();

A Flux is a stream of any number of values that arrive over time. It is like IAsyncEnumerable<T> or IObservable<T> in .NET.

Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1))

This call produces 0, 1, 2 and so on, one value each second, like Observable.Interval.

.map(Long::intValue);

map transforms each value, like Select in C#. interval counts in long values, so this line turns each value into an int.

Combining results: Mono.zip#

Combining two results shows the difference in style. C# awaits each call. Reactor combines two Mono objects into one:

C#: async/await
public async Task<Report> BuildAsync(int id)
{
    var c = await _api.GetCustomerAsync(id);
    var o = await _api.GetOrdersAsync(id);
    return Merge(c, o);
}
Java: Reactor
public Mono<Report> build(int id) {
    return Mono.zip(
            api.getCustomer(id),
            api.getOrders(id))
        .map(t -> merge(t.getT1(), t.getT2()));
}
Reading the code
Mono.zip(

This call waits for both Mono objects and pairs their values. The calls getCustomer and getOrders run at the same time.

.map(t -> merge(t.getT1(), t.getT2()));

zip pairs the two values into one object. getT1() and getT2() read the two values from that object.

Note

Java had Reactor instead of async/await. C# solved non-blocking I/O with a compiler transform. With that transform, you keep writing straight-line code. Java could not do the same, so the Java ecosystem built a library of combinators instead. That is why reactive Java reads like C# would read if await had never been added and everyone used ContinueWith.

Why the case for it collapsedtrap#

The argument for reactive code was never really about elegance. It was arithmetic:

QuantityBefore Java 21Java 21 and later
One requestone platform threadone virtual thread
One thread's stackabout 1 MBa few hundred bytes to start
10,000 concurrent requestsabout 10 GB of stacks, which is impossiblea few MB, which is not a problem
So the advice wasnever block, and restructure everything into callbacksblock, because it is fine

So on Java 21 and later, the same code can simply block:

What you'd write in C#
var c = await _api.GetCustomerAsync(id);
var o = await _api.GetOrdersAsync(id);
return Merge(c, o);
Java 21+: and it scales
var c = api.getCustomer(id);   // blocks
var o = api.getOrders(id);     // blocks
return merge(c, o);
Reading the code
var c = api.getCustomer(id);

This line blocks a virtual thread while it waits. A blocked virtual thread uses almost no resources.

The Java code in the second column needs no reactive types. You can debug it with a normal stack trace, and it scales to the same numbers. For more about blocking code on virtual threads, see the chapter Threads are cheap now.

Gotcha

Do not adopt WebFlux for throughput on a new Boot service. That decision made sense in 2018 and is usually wrong now. With WebFlux you lose readable stack traces, ordinary debugging and many of the libraries that block. Every future maintainer also has much more to learn. In return, you get a scalability property that the ordinary web framework of Spring already has on virtual threads. That framework is called Spring Model-View-Controller (MVC).

When it is still the right answertwist#

Reactive code still fits when the work really is a stream. It also fits when a library that you depend on is reactive. One example is the reactive database driver, which is called Reactive Relational Database Connectivity (R2DBC). These are the cases:

CaseWhy virtual threads do not solve it
Server-sent events, long-lived streamsthe value is many results over time, not one
Backpressure across a boundarya slow consumer must actually slow the producer
Very large fan-out (thousands of concurrent calls per request)a combinator graph expresses this better than thousands of scopes
Streaming a large result without buffering itFlux processes element by element
You are already on WebFluxmixing blocking code into it is worse than committing
R2DBC, RSocketthe library is reactive, and working against it is worse

Server-sent events are the clearest case. Here priceFeed publishes price changes, and every connected browser receives each new price as it happens:

// server-sent events: many values over one long-lived response
@GetMapping(value = "/prices", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public Flux<Price> prices() {
    return priceFeed.updates()
            .onBackpressureLatest();   // a slow client gets the latest price, not a backlog
}
Reading the code
produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE

This setting tells Spring to send server-sent events. With server-sent events, the response stays open and delivers many values over time.

.onBackpressureLatest();

If a client reads more slowly than prices change, the client gets the latest price. The client does not get a growing backlog of old prices.

Backpressure: what virtual threads do not give youdeep dive
Note

Backpressure is the concept with no equivalent in the virtual-thread model. Backpressure is the ability of a slow consumer to tell a fast producer to send less. A blocking pipeline has backpressure with no extra code, because if you stop reading, the producer blocks. But this works only within one process. Across a network or through a queue, Reactor makes backpressure an explicit part of the contract, and you can tune it. That is a real capability, and it is the strongest remaining argument for reactive code.

The blocking hazard#

Gotcha

A blocking call on an event-loop thread stalls unrelated requests. WebFlux runs on Netty. Netty is a network server with a small number of event-loop threads, roughly one for each processor core. Each event-loop thread serves many connections. It switches between the connections instead of waiting. If you block one event-loop thread, every request assigned to that thread stops. This includes requests that have nothing to do with your request:

@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
public Mono<Order> get(@PathVariable long id) {
    Order o = jdbcRepo.findById(id);     // blocking JDBC on an event loop
    return Mono.just(o);                 // catastrophic under load
}
Reading the code
Order o = jdbcRepo.findById(id);

This is a blocking database call. It holds the event-loop thread until the database answers.

This is why a WebFlux service must be non-blocking everywhere. One blocking library anywhere in the request path breaks the whole model. If you must block, move the call to a separate pool that is meant for blocking work:

return Mono.fromCallable(() -> jdbcRepo.findById(id))
           .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
Reading the code
Mono.fromCallable(() -> jdbcRepo.findById(id))

This line wraps the blocking call, so that the blocking call runs only when something subscribes.

.subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());

This line runs the blocking call on Reactor's pool for blocking work, so the event loop stays free.

Add the BlockHound agent to your tests. Then BlockHound reports an error for any blocking call that reaches an event loop.

.block() looks like await, because it waits for the value of a Mono. On an ordinary thread, .block() does wait. On one of Reactor's own non-blocking threads, Reactor refuses to wait and reports this error:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported in thread parallel-2#
Means
Code running on one of Reactor's non-blocking threads called block(). Waiting there would stall every request that the thread serves. The name of the thread is at the end of the message, and the name varies.
Fix
Return the Mono and let Spring subscribe to it, or chain the next step with map or flatMap.
What triggers it
Mono.just(2L)
    .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel())      // moves to one of Reactor's non-blocking threads
    .map(id -> findOrder(id).block())      // throws here
    .block();

WebFlux against MVC#

WebFlux never blocks. It is like an ASP.NET Core pipeline that is written entirely with callbacks. Spring MVC usually reads a database through Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) or Jakarta Persistence (JPA). WebFlux usually reads a database through R2DBC. Here is how the two web stacks of Spring compare:

Spring MVCSpring WebFlux
ServerTomcat (servlet)Netty (event loop)
Threadingone thread per requesta few event-loop threads
Return typesOrder, ResponseEntityMono, Flux
Data accessJDBC, JPAR2DBC, reactive Mongo
Blocking librariesfineforbidden in the request path
Stack tracesordinary and readableassembled from operators, and hard to read
Debuggingstep throughHooks.onOperatorDebug, and patience
Scales to 10k requestsyes, on virtual threadsyes

The same endpoint looks like this in each style:

// Spring MVC on virtual threads: plain types, and blocking is fine
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
Order get(@PathVariable long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }

// Spring WebFlux: reactive types all the way down
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
Mono<Order> get(@PathVariable long id) { return reactiveRepo.findById(id); }
Reading the code
Order get(@PathVariable long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }

This is Spring MVC, with a plain return type. The call blocks a virtual thread while the database answers.

Mono<Order> get(@PathVariable long id) { return reactiveRepo.findById(id); }

This is WebFlux. The method returns a Mono at once. Spring subscribes to the Mono and writes the order when the order arrives.

Gotcha

There is no reactive JPA. R2DBC is a different driver, with a different API. It has no object-relational mapper (ORM) at all. So there is no entity graph, no lazy loading, and no Hibernate. If you choose WebFlux for a service that mostly reads and writes a database, you give up Spring Data JPA. That loss is usually far larger than the thread cost that WebFlux removes.

Reading it#

Even if you never write reactive code, you will read it. Spring Cloud Gateway uses reactive code. So do some Kafka integrations and much existing service code. Here is a typical method, which streams the recent active orders of a customer. log is the logger of the class:

public Flux<OrderDto> recentOrders(String customerId) {
    return repo.findByCustomer(customerId)          // Flux<Order>
            .filter(Order::isActive)
            .take(20)
            .flatMap(this::enrich)                  // returns Mono<OrderDto> each
            .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.empty())       // swallow and continue
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
            .doOnNext(o -> log.debug("sending {}", o.id()));
}
Reading the code
repo.findByCustomer(customerId)

This call returns a Flux of the customer's orders. Each order is delivered as the database returns it.

.flatMap(this::enrich)

This line turns each order into a Mono<OrderDto>. It merges the results as they complete, so the results may arrive in a different order.

.onErrorResume(e -> Flux.empty())

If anything fails, this line sends nothing more. It does not send an error.

.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))

This line fails the stream if three seconds pass without a new element.

You will see these operators most often:

OperatorDoes
maptransform each element
flatMaptransform each into a publisher and merge, but order is not preserved
concatMapas flatMap, but preserves order
zipcombine several publishers element-wise
switchIfEmptyfall back when nothing was emitted
onErrorResumesubstitute a publisher on failure
retryWhenretry with a policy
timeoutfail if nothing arrives in time
subscribeOn / publishOnchoose which scheduler runs what
blockwait for the value, never in reactive code
Gotcha

Nothing happens until you subscribe. A Mono or Flux is a recipe, not a running computation. If you build one and then discard it, nothing happens at all. No request is sent, and no row is written. In Spring, the framework subscribes for you when you return a publisher from a controller. So if you forget to return the publisher, nothing runs, and nothing reports an error:

repo.save(order);            // does nothing, never subscribed
return repo.save(order);     // correct
Reading the code
repo.save(order); // does nothing, never subscribed

This line builds a Mono that would save the order, and then discards the Mono. Nothing subscribes, so nothing is saved.

return repo.save(order);

This line returns the Mono, so Spring can subscribe to it. Subscribing runs the save.

LegacyRxJava

Before Reactor, the reactive library in Java was RxJava. RxJava is a direct port of Rx.NET, and it is still common on Android. Spring standardised on Reactor. But Reactor and RxJava both implement the Reactive Streams specification, so their Publisher types work together. If you meet Observable and Single, the code uses RxJava. Reactor code has Flux and Mono instead.

Check yourself
1
Is WebFlux the right choice for a new database-backed service?
It is almost certainly not the right choice. Virtual threads removed the scalability argument. And with WebFlux you give up Spring Data JPA, readable stack traces and every blocking library.

Numbers, money and time#

Numbers and errors · Chapter 28· 8 min read

The number types are almost the same in Java as in C#. Money and dates are different. Money is the class BigDecimal. C# uses operators on a decimal. Java calls methods on a BigDecimal. Dates come from java.time.

KindC#JavaNote
sameint, long, short, float, double, charint, long, short, float, double, charthe same names and the same sizes in both languages Why
twistbyteno equivalentJava has no unsigned byte, so (byte) 200 is -56, and b & 0xFF gives 200 again Why
twistsbytebytea Java byte is signed, from -128 to 127, like sbyte in C# Why
twistushortcharchar is the only unsigned type in Java, and it is 16 bits wide Why
twistuintno equivalentJava has no uint, so use a long or the Integer.*Unsigned helpers Why
twistulongno equivalentJava has no ulong, but methods such as Long.toUnsignedString treat a long as unsigned Why
twistnint / nuintno equivalentJava has no native-sized integer types, so use int or long Why
twistboolbooleanthe same true or false, spelled boolean in Java Why
twistList<int>List<Integer>Java uses a wrapper type such as Integer wherever an object is needed Why
trapdecimalno equivalentJava has no decimal type, so money is a BigDecimal object, with a method for each operator Why
trap0.1mnew BigDecimal("0.1")always build it from a string, because new BigDecimal(0.1) keeps the error of the double Why
trapa == b on two decimalsa.compareTo(b) == 0equals also compares scale, so 1.0 and 1.00 are not equal Why
traptotal / 3total.divide(three, 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)divide with no scale throws when the result never ends, such as 1/3 Why
twistDateOnly, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpanLocalDate, Instant, Durationjava.time gives each kind of time its own immutable type Why
trapTimeSpanDuration, or Period for calendar daysone day as a Period and 24 hours as a Duration differ across a clock change Why
twistno equivalentDate, Calendar, SimpleDateFormatThese are the old date classes. Read them, never write them, and convert to java.time at the boundary. Why
twistx.ToString("N2")String.format("%,.2f", x)uses the server's default locale unless you pass one, such as Locale.ROOT Why
twistint.TryParse(s, out v)catch NumberFormatExceptionJava has no TryParse, so catch the exception that parseInt throws Why

Primitive typestwist#

C#
sbyte sb = -100;               // signed: -128 to 127
uint u = 3_000_000_000;
ulong max = ulong.MaxValue;
decimal price = 19.99m;
bool ok = true;
Java 25
byte sb = -100;                // Java's byte is C#'s sbyte
long u = 3_000_000_000L;       // no uint: use a wider type
String max = Long.toUnsignedString(-1L);   // "18446744073709551615"
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("19.99");
boolean ok = true;
Reading the code
byte sb = -100;

A Java byte holds −128 to 127, like sbyte in C#. To see what that range does to a value of 200, see the section A byte is signed.

long u = 3_000_000_000L;

Java has no uint, so a value above about two billion needs a long. The L marks a long literal.

Long.toUnsignedString(-1L)

This method reads the 64 bits of a long as an unsigned number. Java handles values the size of a ulong in this way.

These types are the same in both languages:

C#JavaSizeNote
shortshort16-bit
intint32-bit
longlong64-bit
floatfloat32-bit
doubledouble64-bit
charchar16-bita UTF-16 code unit in both, so an emoji takes two chars

Wrapper types#

Each primitive type has an object version. The object version is called a wrapper type. Java uses a wrapper type wherever an object is needed, such as in a List<Integer>.

Two wrappers have special names. The wrapper for int is Integer. The wrapper for char is Character. Every other wrapper has the name of its primitive type with a capital first letter, for example Long and Boolean. These are the common wrappers:

PrimitiveWrapperC# analogy
intIntegerint? (roughly)
longLonglong?
doubleDoubledouble?
booleanBooleanbool?
charCharacterchar?

Java converts between a primitive type and its wrapper type automatically. This conversion is called autoboxing. It is convenient, and it is also the source of two bugs. An earlier chapter already showed both bugs. See the Integer cache and the exception on unboxing a null.

Integer boxed = 42;          // autoboxing: Integer.valueOf(42)
int plain = boxed;           // unboxing: boxed.intValue()

Integer missing = null;
int oops = missing;          // NullPointerException: nothing to unbox
Reading the code
Integer boxed = 42;

This line is autoboxing. The compiler writes Integer.valueOf(42) for you.

int plain = boxed;

This line is unboxing. The compiler writes boxed.intValue() for you.

int oops = missing;

The variable missing is null, so there is no number to unbox. This line throws NullPointerException.

A byte is signedtwist#

Each language reads the same eight bits as a number:

C#
byte b = 200;                  // unsigned: 0 to 255
Console.WriteLine(b);          // prints 200
Java 25
byte b = (byte) 200;           // signed: -128 to 127
System.out.println(b);         // prints -56
System.out.println(b & 0xFF);  // prints 200
Reading the code
byte b = (byte) 200;

The number 200 does not fit in a signed Java byte, so the cast wraps the value to −56.

b & 0xFF

Masking with 0xFF reads the same eight bits as an unsigned number, so the result is 200 again.

Gotcha

Java's byte is signed, from −128 to 127. So when Java code reads binary data written by C# and prints a byte, it can show a negative number. Mask with b & 0xFF to get the unsigned value.

Money is BigDecimaltrap#

This example adds the price of three mugs at 19.99 each to a shipping amount. Then it checks the total against a limit amount:

C#
decimal price = 19.99m;
decimal total = price * 3 + shipping;

if (total > limit) { }
Console.WriteLine(total.ToString("C"));
Java 25
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("19.99");
BigDecimal total = price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(3))
                        .add(shipping);

if (total.compareTo(limit) > 0) { }
NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(total);
Reading the code
new BigDecimal("19.99")

The value is built from text, so it stays exact.

price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(3))

Java has no * for objects. The method multiply accepts only another BigDecimal. So BigDecimal.valueOf(3) makes a BigDecimal from the number 3.

.add(shipping)

This call returns a new value, because a BigDecimal never changes.

total.compareTo(limit) > 0

compareTo returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. So > 0 means that the total is larger than the limit.

NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(total)

This line formats money for the current locale, like ToString("C") in C#. NumberFormat is in java.text.

Each operator on a C# decimal has a method on a BigDecimal:

OperationBigDecimal
a + ba.add(b)
a - ba.subtract(b)
a * ba.multiply(b)
a / ba.divide(b, scale, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)
a > ba.compareTo(b) > 0
a == b (value)a.compareTo(b) == 0
roundinga.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)
from a literalnew BigDecimal("19.99"), always the String constructor
PredictA BigDecimal built from a double#
What does this print?
System.out.println(new BigDecimal(0.1));
System.out.println(new BigDecimal("0.1"));
Show the answer
0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625 0.1

new BigDecimal(0.1) is wrong. The double 0.1 is already imprecise, and the BigDecimal keeps that imprecise value. For the same error in a sum, see adding 0.1 and 0.2.

Always use the String constructor, or use BigDecimal.valueOf(double). The method valueOf converts the number with Double.toString first.

Gotcha

divide without a scale throws ArithmeticException when the result never ends, such as 1/3. Always give a scale and a RoundingMode.

equals compares scale. new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00")) is false. Use compareTo.

Note

Some teams store money as a long that counts the smallest unit, such as cents. They format the amount only for display. This avoids all three traps, and many payment systems do the same.

java.timetwist#

java.time Java 8 gives each kind of time its own type. In .NET, DateTime mixes the kinds of time together. If you know Noda Time, you already know this API. Noda Time was based on Joda-Time, and java.time is the successor of Joda-Time.

C# refresherNodaTime: separate types for instants and datesC# 1
Instant now = SystemClock.Instance.GetCurrentInstant();
LocalDate due = LocalDate.FromDateTime(DateTime.Today).PlusDays(30);
Conceptjava.time.NET
Date, no time, no zoneLocalDateDateOnly
Time, no date, no zoneLocalTimeTimeOnly
Date and time, no zoneLocalDateTimeDateTime (Unspecified)
Instant on the timelineInstantDateTimeOffset (UTC)
Date, time and zoneZonedDateTimeDateTimeOffset + TimeZoneInfo
Date, time and offsetOffsetDateTimeDateTimeOffset
Amount of timeDurationTimeSpan
Calendar amountPeriodno direct equal
Time zoneZoneIdTimeZoneInfo
FormattingDateTimeFormatterformat strings

These are the common operations:

C#
var now = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
var due = now.AddDays(30);
var d   = DateOnly.FromDateTime(DateTime.Today);
var span = due - now;
Java 25
var now = Instant.now();
var due = now.plus(30, ChronoUnit.DAYS);
var d   = LocalDate.now();
var span = Duration.between(now, due);
Reading the code
var now = Instant.now();

This is an exact point on the timeline, in UTC.

now.plus(30, ChronoUnit.DAYS)

An Instant has no calendar and no time zone, so it moves by an exact amount of time.

LocalDate.now()

This is today's date, with no time and no time zone.

Duration.between(now, due)

This is the time between two instants. In C#, you subtract two DateTimeOffset values and get a TimeSpan.

Note

All java.time types are immutable and thread-safe, including DateTimeFormatter. Every method that changes a value returns a new value, like the methods of DateTime in .NET. Examples are plusDays, withYear and truncatedTo.

A Period or a Durationtrap#

C# has TimeSpan for an amount of time. java.time has two types for an amount of time, Duration and Period. You can add a Duration or a Period to a date and time:

PredictOne day later, across a clock change#
What does this print?
// In London, the clocks go forward by one hour on 29 March 2026.
ZoneId london = ZoneId.of("Europe/London");
ZonedDateTime noon = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 28, 12, 0, 0, 0, london);

System.out.println(noon.plus(Period.ofDays(1)));
System.out.println(noon.plus(Duration.ofHours(24)));
Show the answer
2026-03-29T12:00+01:00[Europe/London] 2026-03-29T13:00+01:00[Europe/London]

Duration and Period are not interchangeable. Period is calendar time, in years, months and days. So the result is noon on the next day, even though that day is only 23 hours long. Duration is exact time, in seconds and nanoseconds. So 24 hours later is 1 pm.

Add a Period when you mean calendar days. Add a Duration when you mean exact time.

The old date API#

LegacyDate, Calendar and SimpleDateFormat

You will meet all three classes. Each class has a serious problem:

ClassProblem
java.util.Datemutable, and it is really an instant, despite the name
java.sql.Dateextends Date but forbids the time part
Calendarmonths are ZERO-based. January is 0
SimpleDateFormatNOT thread-safe, so a shared instance corrupts output silently
TimeZonesuperseded by ZoneId

A SimpleDateFormat that is shared across request threads is a common production bug. See Date and SimpleDateFormat are traps. DateTimeFormatter is immutable and safe to share.

Convert at the boundary, where your code meets an old library. Here oldDate is a java.util.Date from that library. The variable instant is an Instant:

Instant i = oldDate.toInstant();
Date d = Date.from(instant);
LocalDate ld = oldDate.toInstant().atZone(ZoneId.systemDefault()).toLocalDate();
Reading the code
oldDate.toInstant()

A Date is really an instant, so it converts directly.

Date.from(instant)

This is the other direction, for an old API that still needs a Date.

.atZone(ZoneId.systemDefault()).toLocalDate()

A date has a meaning only in a time zone. So you choose a time zone before you ask for the LocalDate.

Formatting numbers#

The next example formats and parses numbers. Here text holds a number typed by a customer:

C#
var s1 = 1234.5.ToString("N2");     // "1,234.50" in en-US
var s2 = 0.25.ToString("P0");       // "25%" in en-US
var s3 = 255.ToString("X");         // "FF"
int n = int.Parse("42");
double d = double.Parse("1.5", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
bool ok = int.TryParse(text, out var v);
Java 25
var s1 = String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%,.2f", 1234.5);            // "1,234.50"
var s2 = NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(Locale.UK).format(0.25); // "25%"
var s3 = Integer.toHexString(255).toUpperCase();                  // "FF"
int n = Integer.parseInt("42");
double d = Double.parseDouble("1.5");                             // the same in every locale
int v;
try { v = Integer.parseInt(text); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { v = 0; }
Reading the code
String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%,.2f", 1234.5)

Locale.ROOT fixes the format. The format has a comma between thousands and a dot before the decimals, and it does not depend on the settings of the server.

NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(Locale.UK).format(0.25)

This line formats a percentage, in British format.

try { v = Integer.parseInt(text); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { v = 0; }

Java has no TryParse, so you catch the exception that parseInt throws for bad input.

Gotcha

Integer.parseInt does not depend on the locale. But NumberFormat and String.format do depend on the locale. They use the default locale unless you pass a locale. Some locales use a comma as the decimal separator. A server that is set to such a locale formats 1.5 as 1,5. Pass Locale.ROOT explicitly for any text that another program will read.

These are the other format strings and parsers:

C#Java
x.ToString("C")NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(x)
x.ToString("P")NumberFormat.getPercentInstance().format(x)
x.ToString("X")Integer.toHexString(x)
int.Parse(s)Integer.parseInt(s)
double.Parse(s, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)Double.parseDouble(s), always invariant
Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
decimal unitPrice = 19.99m;
int quantity = 5;
decimal total = unitPrice * quantity;
decimal instalment = Math.Round(total / 3, 2, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero);
BigDecimal unitPrice = new BigDecimal("19.99");
int quantity = 5;
BigDecimal total = unitPrice.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(quantity));
BigDecimal instalment = total.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);

divide needs the scale and the rounding mode. Without them, 99.95 divided by 3 throws ArithmeticException, because the result never ends.

2
An expert asksWhich type does Java use for money, and why do you compare two amounts with compareTo and not with equals?
Java uses BigDecimal for money. The equals method of BigDecimal compares the scale as well as the value. So 1.0 and 1.00 are not equal. a.compareTo(b) == 0 compares the value only.

Exceptions and resources#

Numbers and errors · Chapter 29· 8 min read

Throwing and catching work as they do in C#, with one addition. An exception type that the compiler makes you declare or catch is called a checked exception. To release a resource, Java uses try-with-resources. The try-with-resources statement does the same as using in C#.

KindC#JavaNote
newno equivalentthrows IOExceptiona checked exception must be declared or caught, or the code does not compile Why
newno equivalentthrow new UncheckedIOException(e)application code usually wraps a checked exception, and passes it as the cause Why

trapa lambda that throws IOExceptiona lambda that catches it and rethrowsthe lambda types declare no checked exceptions, so wrap the exception inside the lambda Why
twistthrow new InvalidOperationException("...")throw new IllegalStateException("...")most .NET exceptions have a close Java match under another name Why
twistthrow new ArgumentException("...")throw new IllegalArgumentException("...")it covers every bad argument, and Java has no ArgumentOutOfRangeException Why

twistcatch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or SqlException)catch (IOException | SQLException e)since Java 7, one catch can name several types, but C# needs a when filter for this Why
twistthrow;throw e;Java rethrows the same object, so the trace is preserved Why
twistwhen (filter)no equivalentJava has no exception filters, so test inside the catch, and rethrow the rest Why
samefinallyfinallyidentical in both languages, and it runs whether or not the try block threw Why
twistusingtry-with-resourcesdoes the same as the block form of using, and it closes what its brackets declare Why
twistusing declarationno equivalent, always a blockJava has only the block form, so the block is the resource's scope Why

twistIAsyncDisposableno equivalentJava has no asynchronous form of close or of try-with-resources Why
twistDispose throws, and the first exception is loste.getSuppressed()Java throws the body's exception and keeps the close() failure in getSuppressed() Why
