Checked exceptionsnew#

Reading the day's order file can fail, because the file may be missing. In C#, nothing in the method's signature shows this. In Java, IOException is a checked exception, so the method must declare it with throws, or catch it:

C#
public string Read(string path)
{
    // may throw; nothing to declare
    return File.ReadAllText(path);
}
Java 25
public String read(String path) throws IOException {
    // must declare it, or catch it
    return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
}
Reading the code
throws IOException

This clause declares that read may throw IOException. Every caller must now catch the exception, or declare it too.

// may throw; nothing to declare

C# has no such clause. The designers of C# looked at the feature and chose not to copy it.

An exception type is checked unless it extends RuntimeException or Error. Those types are called unchecked, and they behave like every C# exception. For the whole tree, see the section The hierarchy.

The other option is to wrap the checked exception in an unchecked exception. Here p is the path to the order file:

public String read(Path p) {
    try {
        return Files.readString(p);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException(e);   // always keep the cause
    }
}
Reading the code
throw new UncheckedIOException(e);

The checked exception stops here, so callers have nothing to declare. The original exception is stored inside the new exception, as its cause.

Note

Most of the Java community now prefers wrapping for application code. Spring, Hibernate and the AWS SDK all convert checked exceptions to unchecked exceptions at their boundaries. Most callers cannot recover from an IOException. So a declaration in every layer adds nothing useful.

Keep checked exceptions for a library API, and only for expected conditions that a caller can really recover from. Propagate a checked exception through one or two layers at most.

Gotcha

Always pass the cause when wrapping. Write throw new RuntimeException(e), not throw new RuntimeException(e.getMessage()). If you leave out the cause, the original stack trace is lost. The same happens in C# when you leave out the inner exception in throw new X("...", inner).

The hierarchynew#

Every exception type is in one family tree. The place of a type in the tree decides whether the type is checked:

Throwable
  ├─ Error                    unchecked. JVM problems, do not catch
  │    ├─ OutOfMemoryError
  │    └─ StackOverflowError
  └─ Exception                CHECKED by default
       ├─ IOException         checked
       ├─ SQLException        checked
       └─ RuntimeException    unchecked
            ├─ NullPointerException
            ├─ IllegalArgumentException
            ├─ IllegalStateException
            └─ ...

IOException and SQLException are the checked exceptions that you will meet most often. This is the rule, in two lines:

RuleMeaning
Extends RuntimeException or Errorunchecked, so it behaves like every C# exception
Extends Exception, not RuntimeExceptionchecked, so it must be declared or caught

Your own exception type is checked or unchecked according to the class that it extends. The next type is unchecked, so no caller has to declare it:

public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public OrderNotFoundException(long orderId) {
        super("No order with id " + orderId);
    }
}

extends RuntimeException makes the type unchecked. With extends Exception, the type would be checked. super(...) passes the message to RuntimeException, like : base(...) in C#.

Checked exceptions and lambdastrap#

Gotcha

The functional interfaces in java.util.function declare no checked exceptions. So a lambda that you pass to map, forEach or Optional.map cannot throw a checked exception. Here paths is a list of files:

// does not compile
paths.stream().map(Files::readString).toList();

Files::readString can throw IOException. Catch the IOException inside the lambda, and rethrow it as an unchecked exception. For an example, see A lambda that reads a file. Teams often write a small Unchecked.wrap(...) helper, or use a library such as Vavr. Java 25 has no fix for this in the language itself.

Exception mappingtwist#

Here order is an order, and qty is a quantity. The variable closed says whether the order is already closed:

C#
ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(order);
if (qty <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(qty));
if (closed) throw new InvalidOperationException("already closed");
throw new NotSupportedException("read-only");

var v = dict[key];            // KeyNotFoundException if missing
Java 25
Objects.requireNonNull(order, "order");
if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive");
if (closed) throw new IllegalStateException("already closed");
throw new UnsupportedOperationException("read-only");

var v = map.get(key);         // null if missing: no exception
Reading the code
Objects.requireNonNull(order, "order");

This method is like ThrowIfNull in C#, but it throws NullPointerException, not an argument exception. That is the Java convention.

throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive");

Java has no ArgumentOutOfRangeException. IllegalArgumentException covers every bad argument.

var v = map.get(key);

A missing key does not cause an exception in Java. The method get returns null instead.

C#Java

InvalidOperationExceptionIllegalStateException

try, catch, finally#

Here is a try block that logs a failure, rethrows it, and always cleans up. The method doIt can throw an IOException or an SQLException:

C#
try
{
    Do();
}
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or SqlException)
{
    Log(ex);
    throw;              // rethrow, preserving the stack
}
finally
{
    Cleanup();
}
Java 25
try {
    doIt();
} catch (IOException | SQLException e) {   // multi-catch
    log(e);
    throw e;            // rethrow the same instance
} finally {
    cleanup();
}
Reading the code
catch (IOException | SQLException e)

This is one catch for two types, joined with |. C# needs a when filter for this.

throw e;

This line rethrows the same exception object, so the stack trace is kept. In C#, a throw with no exception after it does the same.

C# refresherException filters: catch ... whenC# 6

A filter decides whether a catch block applies at all. An exception that the filter rejects is never caught. So the exception keeps propagating, and its stack stays intact.

try { await CallAsync(); }
catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.NotFound)
{
    return null;              // only a 404 is caught; anything else propagates
}

Java has no exception filters. You catch the exception, test it, and rethrow it if you did not want it. Here insert saves an order, and duplicate handles an order number that already exists:

try { insert(order); }
catch (SQLException e) {
    if (!"23505".equals(e.getSQLState())) throw e;   // no filter: rethrow the rest
    return duplicate(order);                          // only a unique-key violation
}
Reading the code
if (!"23505".equals(e.getSQLState())) throw e;

23505 is the standard SQL code for a unique-key violation. Any other exception is rethrown unchanged.

Gotcha

Never return from a finally block. The return discards any exception that is leaving try or catch, and nothing is reported. In C#, a return in finally is a compile error. Java allows it. For an example, see A return inside finally.

try-with-resourcestwist#

Here dataSource provides database connections, and sql is an update statement:

C#
using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);
using var cmd = new SqlCommand(sql, conn);
conn.Open();
Java 25
try (var conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     var stmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    stmt.executeUpdate();
}   // closed in reverse order, even on exception
Reading the code
try (var conn = dataSource.getConnection();

Everything that is declared in the brackets is closed when the block ends, even if an exception is thrown.

var stmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {

This is a second resource, after a semicolon. Resources close in reverse order, so the statement closes first and then the connection.

C# refresherIDisposable and IAsyncDisposableC# 8
public sealed class Conn : IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable
{
    public void Dispose() { /* release now */ }
    public ValueTask DisposeAsync() => ValueTask.CompletedTask;
}

using var c = new Conn();          // Dispose() at the end of the scope
await using var d = new Conn();    // DisposeAsync() at the end of the scope

AutoCloseable does the same as IDisposable in C#. Your own class works in try-with-resources when it implements AutoCloseable:

public final class Conn implements AutoCloseable {
    @Override public void close() { /* release now */ }   // no throws: callers need no catch
}

try (var c = new Conn()) {
    use(c);
}                                  // close() runs here, even on an exception
Reading the code
public final class Conn implements AutoCloseable {

AutoCloseable has one method, close, like Dispose in C#.

try (var c = new Conn()) {

close() runs at the end of the block, even if use throws.

Note

AutoCloseable.close() declares throws Exception. Closeable narrows that to IOException. When your cleanup cannot fail, override close() without a throws clause. Then no caller needs a catch block.

PredictThe body throws, and then close throws#
What does this print?
class BrokenConn implements AutoCloseable {
    @Override public void close() { throw new IllegalStateException("close failed"); }
}

try (var c = new BrokenConn()) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("body failed");
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getMessage());
    System.out.println(e.getSuppressed()[0].getMessage());
}
Show the answer
body failed close failed

When the body throws and close() throws, Java keeps the exception from the body as the main exception. Java attaches the failure from close() to the main exception. The attached exception is called a suppressed exception, and getSuppressed() returns it. In the same situation, C# throws the exception from Dispose and loses the first exception.

You do not need to write anything differently. Catch the exception as usual. When a stack trace shows a "Suppressed:" section, that section is the failure from close().

Cleanup without a using block#

Legacyfinalize()

Object.finalize() has been deprecated for removal deprecated since Java 18. It is unpredictable, can make an unreachable object reachable again, delays garbage collection, and may never run at all. Do not override finalize(), and do not follow older guides that recommend it for releasing native resources.

The supported mechanism for cleaning up an object that nobody closed is Cleaner Java 9. It is roughly like a SafeHandle plus a finalizer queue in .NET. As in .NET, the normal path should still be to close the object explicitly. Here allocate and free represent native calls that reserve and release memory:

public class Buffer implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();

    // MUST be a static class holding no reference to the outer instance,
    // or the object can never become unreachable
    private record State(long handle) implements Runnable {
        @Override public void run() { free(handle); }
    }

    private final State state;
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

    public Buffer(long size) {
        this.state = new State(allocate(size));
        this.cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, state);
    }

    @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); }   // deterministic path
}
Reading the code
CLEANER.register(this, state)

This call asks the Cleaner to run state when this Buffer is no longer reachable, if nobody has closed the buffer by then.

private record State(long handle) implements Runnable {

This is the cleanup action. A nested record is never an inner class, so it holds no hidden reference to the Buffer. Such a reference would keep the Buffer reachable forever.

@Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); }

This is the normal path. close runs the cleanup now, and the cleanup will not run again later.

Note

The rule is the same as in .NET. The Cleaner is only for callers who forget to close, and it is not the main mechanism. Always give the type a close() method, and expect callers to use try-with-resources.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java: 
public string ReadOrderFile(string path)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(path);
    try
    {
        return File.ReadAllText(path);
    }
    catch (IOException ex)
    {
        throw new InvalidOperationException("cannot read " + path, ex);
    }
}
public String readOrderFile(String path) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(path, "path");
    try {
        return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("cannot read " + path, e);
    }
}

In Java, the method cannot ignore IOException, because it is checked. The method must catch it or declare throws IOException. Pass e to the new exception as the cause.

2
An expert asksJava application code usually turns a checked exception into an unchecked one. When should a method still declare a checked exception, and why only then?
Declare a checked exception in a library API, when the failure is an expected condition that the caller can really recover from. The compiler then makes that caller handle the failure. Propagate the exception through one or two layers at most. Most callers cannot recover, so for them a declared exception adds nothing useful.

How Java runs your code#

Build and tooling · Chapter 30· 17 min read· Quick reference

You know the language. This chapter shows how Java compiles, finds and starts your code. .NET finds your code for you. You must tell Java where to look. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) searches an ordered list of folders and Java archive (JAR) files. This list is called the classpath. The JVM uses the first match.

KindC#JavaNote
twistdotnet build writes MyApp.dlljavac writes .class files, and jar zips them into a JARJava shows the steps that dotnet build hides. The steps are compile, package and run. Why
twistthe .NET SDKa JDKa JRE is a runtime with no compiler, so install a JDK for development Why
twistan app built for a newer runtimeUnsupportedClassVersionErrorA runtime refuses bytecode newer than itself. The class file version is the release plus 44, so 69 is Java 25. Why
twistnamespace Acme, in any folderpackage com.acme, in the folder com/acmeclass files must be in folders that match the package name Why
trapdotnet MyApp.dll, a file pathjava -cp out com.acme.Appjava takes the package plus the class name, never a file path Why

trapone copy of each dependencytwo JARs with the same classthe JVM silently uses the first JAR, and a missing method fails later with NoSuchMethodError Why

trapno equivalentjava -cp lib -jar app.jarjava -jar ignores -cp and CLASSPATH, and reads only the JAR and its manifest Why

trapa file read from diskgetResourceAsStream("/rates.json")a path under src/main/resources works in the IDE and fails inside a JAR, so read the file from the classpath Why

From source to a running programtwist#

Java takes the same route as .NET, but more of the steps are visible. The Java compiler writes bytecode. Bytecode does the same as IL in .NET. The compiler writes the bytecode of each class into its own file. This file is called a class file.

These are the three commands in the diagram:

javac -d out src/com/acme/*.java
jar --create --file app.jar --main-class com.acme.App -C out .
java -jar app.jar

javac compiles, jar zips, and java starts the JVM.

.NET refresherWhat dotnet build writes: the .dll, deps.json and runtimeconfig.json

The C# compiler is Roslyn, and it runs as csc. It writes IL straight into an assembly. At startup, the runtime reads deps.json to find every dependency. You never build a search list yourself.

dotnet build
ls bin/Debug/net10.0/
# MyApp.dll                   the IL, compiled by Roslyn
# MyApp.deps.json             every dependency, and where to find it
# MyApp.runtimeconfig.json    which .NET runtime to start
.NETJavaMeaning
.cs file.java fileA .java file holds source code. A public class must be in a file named after the class.
Roslyn (csc)javacthe compiler, which writes bytecode and not machine code
ILbytecodethe portable instruction set, which the runtime compiles to machine code while the program runs
IL inside the .dllclass file (.class)A class file holds the bytecode of one class. The javac compiler writes one class file for each class, including nested classes.
assembly (.dll)JAR (.jar)a zip of class files plus a manifest, and it is the unit you ship and depend on
assembly manifestJAR manifesta text file inside a JAR that can name its main class and other JARs
CLRJVMthe runtime, which loads classes, checks them, and compiles hot code to machine code
.NET SDKJDKthe compiler, the tools and a runtime together, so install a JDK to write Java
.NET runtimeJREa runtime with no compiler, for running programs only, so install a JDK to develop

deps.json and assembly probingclasspaththe ordered list of folders and JARs the JVM searches for classes
no single equivalentclass loaderthe part of the JVM that finds a class on the classpath and loads it
dotnet MyApp.dlljava -jar myapp.jarruns a packaged application from the command line

JDK or JRE: which to install#

A Java Runtime Environment (JRE) and a Java Development Kit (JDK) both hold the runtime. Only a JDK holds the compiler:

java -version      # works with a JRE or a JDK: both have the runtime
javac -version     # works only with a JDK: a JRE has no compiler

javac is the compiler, so only a JDK includes it.

Note

For development, install a Java Development Kit (JDK). A JDK does everything that a JRE does, and it also has the compiler. Oracle stopped offering a separate JRE with Java 11. Oracle recommends jlink to build a small runtime instead. Some other vendors still ship a JRE for deployment.

Bytecode newer than the runtimetwist#

Every class file stores the Java release that it was compiled for. A runtime refuses bytecode that is newer than the runtime itself, with this error:

java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: com/acme/App has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0#
Means
The class was compiled for a newer Java than the Java that runs it. The class file version is the Java release plus 44, so 69 means Java 25 and 65 means Java 21.
Fix
Run the program on a Java that is at least as new as the target. Or compile for the older Java with javac --release 21. In Maven, set maven.compiler.release.
What triggers it

Compile for Java 25 and run on Java 21. The launcher prints Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class com.acme.App just before this line.

javac --release 25 -d out src/com/acme/*.java
/opt/java21/bin/java -cp out com.acme.App

One program, start to finishnew#

Maven and Gradle are the build tools for Java. They hide every step below, in the same way that dotnet build hides the compiler. Run the steps yourself once. After that, you can read every classpath error. Take two classes in the package com.acme. One rule matters here. The class files must be in folders that match the package name. For this rule, see the section Packages are not namespaces.

C#: the assembly knows where to start
// Program.cs, top-level statements
Console.WriteLine(new Greeter().Greet("java"));

// the entry point is recorded in the
// assembly, so this is all it takes:
//   dotnet run
Java: src/com/acme/App.java
package com.acme;

public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Greeter().greet("java"));
    }
}
// java is told where to look and what to start:
//   java -cp out com.acme.App
Reading the code
package com.acme;

This line puts App in the package com.acme, so the full name of the class is com.acme.App.

public static void main(String[] args)

This is the entry point. The java command starts the program in the main method of the class that you name.

java -cp out com.acme.App

This command runs the program. It gives the classpath after -cp, and then the full name of the class that has main.

App uses a second class, Greeter, which is in its own file:

// src/com/acme/Greeter.java
package com.acme;

public class Greeter {
    public String greet(String name) { return "hello " + name; }
}

Greeter is in the same package as App. So App can use Greeter without an import. Compile both classes. The -d option says where the class files go:

javac -d out src/com/acme/*.java

javac writes one class file for each class. It also turns the package name into folders, so com.acme becomes com/acme.

out/
└── com/
    └── acme/
        ├── App.class
        └── Greeter.class

The package plus the class name is called the fully qualified name of the class. The fully qualified name is also the path of the class file. So com.acme.App is the file App.class in the folder com/acme. Run the program:

java -cp out com.acme.App
# hello java

The only classpath entry is out. The java command looked under that folder for com/acme/App.class.

The name you pass to javatrap#

PredictStarting a class by its file path#
What happens?
ls out/com/acme
# App.class  Greeter.class

java out/com/acme/App.class
Show the answer
Error: Could not find or load main class out.com.acme.App.class, then Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: out.com.acme.App.class

The name you pass to java is the package plus the class, not a file path. Here java read the path as a class name, and no class has that name. java -cp out App fails too. The option -cp out/com/acme also fails, because the top folder of a package must be directly under a classpath entry.

Write java -cp out com.acme.App.

Could not find or load main class: every cause#

Error: Could not find or load main class com.acme.App#
Means
No classpath entry holds com/acme/App.class. The line after the message says why. ClassNotFoundException means that the file is on no classpath entry. NoClassDefFoundError ... (wrong name: com/acme/App) means that the classpath points inside the package folder.
Fix
Pass the fully qualified name. Point -cp at the folder or JAR that holds the top folder of the package. Here that is out, not out/com/acme.
What triggers it
java -cp target/classes com.acme.App   # the classes are in out, not target/classes
java -cp out App                       # the package is missing from the name
java -cp out/com/acme App              # the entry points inside the package

The classpath is a search listnew#

After an upgrade, your service has two copies of the billing library on its classpath. One copy is version 2.1. The other copy is an old version 1.9 that nobody removed. Which copy does Java use?

The first time your code uses a class, the JVM turns the fully qualified name of the class into a path. The fully qualified name is the package plus the class name. So com.acme.billing.Invoice becomes com/acme/billing/Invoice.class. The JVM then checks each classpath entry in the order listed. A classpath entry is a folder or a JAR. The JVM uses the first entry that has the file, and the search stops.

Think of a row of shelves that you search in order for a book. You take the first copy you find, even if a newer edition is on a later shelf. In one way, the comparison does not fit. A JAR is a zip file, not a folder, and the JVM looks inside the zip file.

On the command line, the list is one string:

java -cp "target/classes:lib/*" com.acme.App

target/classes:lib/* is a classpath with two entries. The first entry is the folder of compiled classes. The second entry is every JAR in the lib folder.

Note

Entries are separated by : on macOS and Linux, and by ; on Windows. An entry that ends in /* means every JAR in that folder. Put that entry in quotes, so that the shell does not change it. With no -cp and no CLASSPATH, the classpath is the current directory.

Two JARs, one classtrap#

Gotcha

Two JARs holding the same class do not conflict. One silently wins. In the diagram, billing-core-1.9.jar is never read. Suppose that code compiled against 1.9 calls a method that 2.1 removed. The result is a NoSuchMethodError at run time, far from its cause. This problem is called “JAR hell”. It is the reason that dependency resolution in Maven matters so much. For more about dependency resolution, see the chapter Maven vs csproj.

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'java.lang.String com.acme.Greeter.greet(java.lang.String)'#
Means
The class was found, but the method was not found. The class on the classpath is a different version from the version that your code was compiled against.
Fix
Find which JAR supplies the class. Change that JAR to the version that you compiled against. mvn dependency:tree shows which version of each library Maven chose.
What triggers it

Rename greet to hello in Greeter.java. Then recompile only that file, so the old App.class still calls greet:

javac -d out src/com/acme/Greeter.java
java -cp out com.acme.App

A class that is on no classpath entrytwist#

Two errors say that no classpath entry has a class:

java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: org.postgresql.Driver#
Means
Code asked for a class by name, as a string, and no classpath entry has the class. The name usually comes from configuration, for example the name of a database driver or of a plugin.
Fix
Add the dependency that contains the class. Give the dependency a dependency scope that is kept at run time. In Maven, that is the default scope compile, or the scope runtime.
What triggers it
Class.forName("org.postgresql.Driver");   // the driver's JAR is not on the classpath
java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: com/acme/Greeter#
Means
A class that was present when your code compiled is on no classpath entry now. The slashes show that the name comes from inside a compiled class file.
Fix
Put the class, or its JAR, back on the classpath. In Maven, provided and test dependencies are used to compile, but they are left out at run time.
What triggers it
rm out/com/acme/Greeter.class
java -cp out com.acme.App

Running with -cp or -jartwist#

To ship the program, zip the classes into a JAR. Also write the name of the main class into a small text file inside the JAR. This file is called the manifest. The jar command does both:

jar --create --file app.jar --main-class com.acme.App -C out .
java -jar app.jar
# hello java
Reading the code
jar --create --file app.jar

This part creates a JAR called app.jar. The jar command is the archiving tool of the JDK.

--main-class com.acme.App

This option writes Main-Class: com.acme.App into the manifest of the JAR, so that java -jar knows where to start.

-C out .

This part adds everything in the folder out, and it keeps the package folders.

A classpath with -jartrap#

PredictA classpath in front of -jar#
What happens?
# app.jar holds App.class, and its manifest names com.acme.App as the main class.
# Greeter.class is in the folder lib/com/acme, and not in the JAR.
java -cp lib -jar app.jar
Show the answer
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: com/acme/Greeter

java -jar ignores -cp. It ignores the CLASSPATH variable too. The JDK documentation says so. With -jar, classes come only from the JAR and from the JARs that its manifest names. So nothing looks in lib. An option written after the JAR name is not read by java at all. It is passed to your program as an argument.

There are three fixes. List the dependency in the manifest of the JAR. Or bundle the dependency inside the JAR, as Spring Boot does. Or remove -jar and write java -cp "app.jar:lib" com.acme.App.

Each way to start a program reads different things:

Questionjava -cp out com.acme.Appjava -jar app.jar
Where do classes come from?the entries listed after -cp, in orderthe JAR itself, plus any JARs its manifest names
Which class starts?the name typed after the classpaththe Main-Class line in the JAR's manifest
Are -cp and CLASSPATH used?yesno, both are silently ignored
Typical userunning from a build folder, or with a classpath you choosea packaged application, including a Spring Boot JAR
Note

A Spring Boot JAR is built for -jar. Its manifest names Spring Boot's own launcher as the Main-Class. The manifest names your class as Start-Class. The launcher then loads your dependencies from BOOT-INF/lib, which is inside the JAR. This is why a Boot JAR runs with no classpath at all.

Inside a JAR: the manifest#

A JAR is a zip file. Rename a JAR to .zip and you can open it. Next to the class files, a JAR holds the file META-INF/MANIFEST.MF. This file is the manifest. It is a short text file that java -jar reads to decide what to run.

Manifest-Version: 1.0
Main-Class: com.acme.App
Class-Path: lib/jackson-databind.jar lib/slf4j-api.jar

Main-Class names the class to start, and Class-Path lists two more JARs to put on the classpath. The table says what each line does:

AttributeDoesNote
Main-Classnames the class whose main method starts the programa fully qualified name, written without the .class suffix
Class-Pathadds more JARs to the classpaththe entries are separated by spaces, and each entry is resolved from the JAR's own folder, not from the directory you run from
no main manifest attribute, in app.jar#
Means
The JAR's manifest has no Main-Class line, so java -jar does not know which class to start.
Fix
Build the JAR with its main class set. You can do that with jar --main-class, with the Spring Boot plugin, or in the configuration of the Maven JAR plugin. Or run the JAR with java -cp app.jar com.acme.App.
What triggers it
jar --create --file app.jar -C out .     # no --main-class
java -jar app.jar
Gotcha

Class-Path entries resolve relative to the JAR's own location, not relative to the directory you run from. If you move the JAR without its lib folder, the JVM can no longer find any class that those entries named.

Class loading, at the level you need#

Classes are not all loaded at startup. Each class is loaded the first time your code uses it. The part of the JVM that finds a class and reads its bytecode is called a class loader. There are three class loaders. They are stacked so that the JDK's own classes always come first.

That is why putting your own java.lang.String on the classpath has no effect. The bootstrap loader finds the real java.lang.String first. Class loading also explains the two “not found” errors above. ClassNotFoundException is thrown when code asks a loader for a class by name and no loader finds the class. NoClassDefFoundError is thrown when your compiled code refers to a class and that class cannot be loaded at run time. A third error means that the class was found but could not be set up:

java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError#
Means
The class was found, but its static initialiser threw an exception. The static initialiser is the code that sets the static fields of the class. ExceptionInInitializerError does the same as TypeInitializationException in .NET. The Caused by line shows the real exception.
Fix
Fix the cause. Every later use of the class fails with NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class. So search the log for the first failure, not the last failure.
What triggers it
public class Rates {
    // NumberFormatException the first time Rates is used
    static final int DEFAULT = Integer.parseInt("12%");
}
Note

Application servers and some frameworks add their own loaders beneath these three loaders. Often there is one added loader for each application or plugin. The rarer failures happen in the added loaders. For further reading about class loaders, see the chapter Going deeper. You do not need that depth to run a Spring Boot service.

Resources live on the classpath tootrap#

Everything under src/main/resources is copied into the JAR, beside your classes. Those files are read through the classpath, not from disk. That is why application.yml is found wherever the JAR runs. Here the same file is read in two ways:

// works in the IDE, where resources are files on disk
String fromDisk = Files.readString(Path.of("src/main/resources/rates.json"));

// works everywhere: read it from the classpath
try (var in = getClass().getResourceAsStream("/rates.json")) {
    String cfg = new String(in.readAllBytes(), UTF_8);
}
Reading the code
Files.readString(Path.of("src/main/resources/rates.json"))

This call reads a file from disk, by its path in your project folder.

getClass().getResourceAsStream("/rates.json")

This call asks the classpath for the resource instead. That works inside a JAR too. The leading slash means “from the root of the classpath”.

new String(in.readAllBytes(), UTF_8)

This line reads every byte and turns the bytes into text. UTF_8 is StandardCharsets.UTF_8, imported with a static import.

Gotcha

A path under src/main/resources works in the IDE and fails inside a JAR. There is no such folder next to a packaged JAR. On a server or in a container, the first line throws NoSuchFileException. Nothing warns you while you develop.

For more about reading files and resources, see the chapter Files and I/O.

The two errors a misread resource gives#

java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: src/main/resources/rates.json#
Means
The code read a resource as a file on disk. That path exists in your project folder, but not next to a packaged JAR.
Fix
Read the resource through the classpath, with getClass().getResourceAsStream("/rates.json").
Cannot invoke "java.io.InputStream.readAllBytes()" because "in" is null#
Means
getResourceAsStream found nothing with that name. It returned null and did not throw. The null then causes this exception on the next line.
Fix
Check the name. A name with a leading slash, such as "/rates.json", is looked up from the root of the classpath. A name without a leading slash is looked up beside the calling class.
What triggers it

A typo in the name is enough. If the class was compiled without debug information, the message says "<local1>" instead of the variable's name.

try (var in = getClass().getResourceAsStream("/rates.jsn")) {
    String cfg = new String(in.readAllBytes(), UTF_8);
}

System properties and environment variables#

A .NET process takes settings mostly from one place. A JVM process takes settings from two separate places.

C#
// environment variable
var url = Environment
    .GetEnvironmentVariable("RATES_URL");

// the nearest thing to a system property:
// AppContext.GetData, fed by runtimeconfig.json
Java 25
// environment variable
String url = System.getenv("RATES_URL");

// system property, set with -Drates.url=...
String url2 = System.getProperty("rates.url");

System.getenv reads an environment variable, exactly as in .NET. System.getProperty reads a system property. You pass a system property to the JVM with -D when the JVM starts. Spring Boot reads environment variables, system properties and command-line arguments:

SettingPassed asRead withSpring key
Environment variableRATES_URL=...System.getenvrates.url, by relaxed binding
System propertyjava -Drates.url=... -jar app.jarSystem.getPropertyrates.url
Command-line argumentjava -jar app.jar --rates.url=...Spring onlyrates.url
Gotcha

When the same key is set more than one way, Spring Boot prefers the command-line argument, then the system property, then the environment variable. So a -D flag in a startup script overrides the environment variable that your container platform sets, and nothing reports it. For the full order, see the chapter Dependency injection and configuration.

Gotcha

-D must come before -jar. Everything after the JAR name is passed to your program as an argument. So java -jar app.jar -Dx=1 sets no property at all. Your program receives the text -Dx=1 in args.

LegacyThe CLASSPATH environment variable

Old instructions often tell you to set a CLASSPATH environment variable. The variable works, and it applies to every Java program started from that shell. That is almost never what you want. The variable mixes JAR versions across unrelated programs, and this is exactly how the NoSuchMethodError above happens. java -jar ignores the variable. Pass -cp explicitly, or let Maven build the classpath. If a machine behaves strangely, check that nothing has set CLASSPATH.

Where your dependencies actually live#

.NET refresherNuGet's cache: ~/.nuget/packages, nuget.config and project.assets.json

Restore downloads each package version once into a shared cache. It reads its feeds from nuget.config. It writes the resolved dependency graph into the obj folder.

dotnet restore
ls ~/.nuget/packages/newtonsoft.json/
# 13.0.3/                     one folder per version, shared by every project
cat nuget.config              # the package feeds, and their credentials
cat obj/project.assets.json   # the resolved graph, written by restore
.NETMavenNote
~/.nuget/packages~/.m2/repositorya shared cache on your machine, holding one copy of each version
nuget.config sources~/.m2/settings.xmlsays where packages are downloaded from, so it holds repositories, mirrors and credentials
obj/project.assets.jsonthe resolved dependency treecomputed on every build and not saved, but mvn dependency:tree prints it

When Maven builds, it downloads each dependency into the local repository. The dots of the group id become folders, for example ~/.m2/repository/org/slf4j/slf4j-api/2.0.16/. Maven then puts those JARs on the compile and test classpath. Your project never contains its dependencies. It contains only a description of the dependencies.

ls ~/.m2/repository/org/slf4j/slf4j-api/
# 2.0.16/

mvn dependency:build-classpath     # print the exact classpath Maven will use

mvn dependency:build-classpath prints every JAR that Maven will put on the classpath, in order. This is the list that this chapter is about.

error: error reading ~/.m2/repository/org/slf4j/slf4j-api/2.0.16/slf4j-api-2.0.16.jar; zip END header not found#
Means
A JAR in the local repository is incomplete or corrupt, usually because a download was interrupted. Two other messages mean the same thing. One message is invalid LOC header. The other message is Invalid or corrupt jarfile, which comes from java -jar.
Fix
Delete the folder of that artifact under ~/.m2/repository, and build again. mvn clean does not help, because it only empties target/. Deleting the folder is the Java version of clearing a stuck NuGet cache.

JVM flags at a glance#

FlagControlsExample
-Da system property your code or Spring reads-Dspring.profiles.active=prod
-Xan extra JVM option, mostly memory and diagnostics-Xmx512m, -Xss512k
-XX:an advanced or tuning option-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70
anything after the JARyour program's own arguments--server.port=9090

So the parts of a java command divide into three groups. -D is configuration. -X and -XX: tune the JVM itself. Everything after the JAR name belongs to your program. For more about tuning, see the chapter The JVM at runtime.

Unrecognized VM option 'MaxRAMPercentag=70'#
Means
The JVM does not know an -XX: option, usually because of a typo. The JVM refuses to start, and does not ignore the option. It may suggest the closest option that it knows.
Fix
Correct the spelling. java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version lists every option the JVM accepts.
What triggers it
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentag=70 -jar app.jar
Check yourself
1
What does UnsupportedClassVersionError: class file version 69.0 mean?
The class was compiled for a newer Java release than the release that runs it. The class file version is the release plus 44. So 69 is Java 25, 65 is Java 21, and 61 is Java 17. Check maven.compiler.release against the Java that runs the service.
2
An expert asksTwo JARs on the classpath hold different versions of the same class. Why is there no error at startup, and how does the problem show itself later?
The JVM takes the first copy of a class that it finds on the classpath, and then it stops searching. So the other JAR is never read. Code that was compiled against the other version then fails with NoSuchMethodError at run time, far from its cause.

Quick reference#

This table shows the commands that this chapter used:

TaskCommandNote
Compilejavac -d out src/com/acme/*.javawrites one class file per class, in folders that match each package
Run from classesjava -cp out com.acme.Appgive the classpath first, then the fully qualified name of the class with main
Packagejar --create --file app.jar --main-class com.acme.App -C out .zips the classes and records the main class in the manifest
Run a JARjava -jar app.jartakes everything from the manifest, and ignores -cp and CLASSPATH
Pass a settingjava -Drates.url=... -jar app.jarthis sets a system property, and the -D must come before -jar
Read a settingSystem.getProperty("rates.url")environment variables are read with System.getenv instead
Read a resourcegetClass().getResourceAsStream("/rates.json")goes through the classpath, so it also works inside a JAR
See the classpathmvn dependency:build-classpathprints every JAR Maven puts on the classpath, in order

Maven vs csproj#

Build and tooling · Chapter 31· 9 min read· Quick reference

Maven is a Java build tool, and pom.xml is its project file. MSBuild is a build engine that you script. Maven is a fixed sequence of build steps that you configure. You say what your project is. You do not say how to build it.

KindC#JavaNote
twistany folder layoutsrc/main/java and src/test/javaMaven expects every project to use the same folders Why
twistInternalsVisibleToa test in the same packagea test under src/test/java, in the package of the code it tests, sees package-private members Why
twistPackageIdgroupId + artifactIdan org prefix plus a name, so vendors never collide Why
twistVersionversionSNAPSHOT means "in development" Why
twistTargetFrameworkmaven.compiler.releasenames the Java release to compile for, as TargetFramework names the .NET release Why
twistPackageReferencedependencya dependency element, identified by group, artifact and version Why
twistProjectReferencedependency on a sibling modulewritten exactly like any other dependency, by coordinates Why
newno equivalent./mvnw packagerunning a phase runs every phase before it, so this command compiles, tests and then packages Why
twistdotnet add package Serilogno command, so edit pom.xmlthere is no mvn add command, so you add a dependency element to pom.xml yourself Why
twistdotnet restoreno separate stepMaven downloads what it needs during the build, into ~/.m2/repository Why
twistnuget.configsettings.xmlthis file is in ~/.m2, and it lists repositories, mirrors and credentials Why
twistglobal.jsonmvnw, the Maven wrappercommit it, because it fixes the Maven version and downloads that version on first use Why
twistDirectory.Build.propsa parent POMchildren inherit from the parent POM, but the parent POM is not textually included Why
twista Boot 3 tutorial on Boot 4spring-boot-starter-webmvcthe web starter was named spring-boot-starter-web until Boot 4.0 Why
twistDirectory.Packages.propsdependencyManagementsets versions centrally, so child modules can leave them out Why
twistno single equivalenta Maven profile, switched on with -Pa named block of configuration that varies the build, never the product Why
trapNuGet takes the higher versionMaven takes the nearest declarationadding a library can silently downgrade another one's dependency Why

The standard layouttwist#

Maven expects every project to use the same folders. If you use other folders, you must write extra configuration everywhere.

my-service/
├── pom.xml
├── mvnw                      ← wrapper script; commit it
├── mvnw.cmd
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/             ← production source
    │   │   └── com/acme/billing/BillingApp.java
    │   └── resources/        ← config, templates; goes into the JAR
    │       └── application.yml
    └── test/
        ├── java/             ← test source, SAME package names
        └── resources/

src/main/java holds the production code. src/test/java holds the tests. src/main/resources holds files such as application.yml. Maven puts these files into the Java archive (JAR), together with the compiled classes. mvnw is the Maven Wrapper.

Gotcha

Tests are under src/test/java, but they are in the same package as the code they test. That is how the tests get package-private access. C# uses InternalsVisibleTo for this. A test in a different package cannot see package-private members.

pom.xml against csprojtwist#

Maven's project file is called the Project Object Model (POM). Its file name is pom.xml. Both files below give the identity of a project, the platform version that it targets, and one logging library that it depends on:

csproj
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <PackageId>Acme.Billing</PackageId>
    <Version>1.0.0</Version>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Serilog"
                      Version="4.1.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
pom.xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>billing</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>
      UTF-8
    </project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
      <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
      <version>2.0.16</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
Reading the code
<groupId>com.acme</groupId>

This element says who publishes the project. It is written as a reversed domain name, like a package name.

<artifactId>billing</artifactId>

This is the project's own name. Together, groupId and artifactId do the same as PackageId in a csproj file.

<version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

SNAPSHOT marks a version that is still in development. Maven may fetch a newer build of a snapshot version. Maven never fetches a newer build of a released version.

<maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>

This property names the Java release to compile for, like TargetFramework in a csproj file.

<artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>

This is a dependency. It is named by its group, artifact and version, like a PackageReference in a csproj file.

Coordinates#

A NuGet package has one name, for example Serilog. A Maven artifact has two names and a version. Together, the two names and the version are called the coordinates of the artifact:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>      <!-- who publishes it -->
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>  <!-- which artifact -->
  <version>4.0.0</version>
  <scope>compile</scope>                            <!-- optional -->
</dependency>
Reading the code
<groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

This is the publisher. Here the publisher is the Spring Boot project.

<scope>compile</scope>

The scope says when the dependency is available. The default scope is compile, which means everywhere, like an ordinary PackageReference. The import scope is only for importing a bill of materials (BOM). For an example, see Profiles and BOMs.

ScopeAvailable at.NET analogy
compileeverywhere, and it is the defaultnormal PackageReference
providedcompile and test, not packageda framework reference
runtimerun and test, not compilea runtime-only dependency
testtest onlya test-project-only reference
importonly in dependencyManagementfor BOMs

The lifecyclenew#

Running a phase runs every phase before it. MSBuild has no equivalent for this idea. The idea explains the Maven command line.

Each command below does everything that the command above it does, and then more:

./mvnw test       # validate, compile, test
./mvnw package    # all of that, then builds the JAR in target/
./mvnw install    # all of that, then copies the JAR into ~/.m2/repository
Reading the code
./mvnw package

This command runs validate, compile and test. Then it builds the JAR in the target folder.

./mvnw install

This command does all of that. Then it copies the JAR into the local repository in ~/.m2. Other projects on the same machine can use the JAR from there. For more about that folder, see the section Where your dependencies actually live.

Note

mvn clean package is the command you will type a thousand times. It does a full rebuild. You run clean with Maven far more often than with dotnet build, because Maven does less incremental work.

Here are three .NET commands that you will use on day one, with their Maven versions:

dotnet test                                  # ./mvnw test
dotnet add package Serilog                   # no command: edit pom.xml by hand
dotnet list package --include-transitive     # ./mvnw dependency:tree

Maven has no command that adds a dependency. You add a dependency element to pom.xml yourself, and Maven downloads the dependency on the next build. For the other everyday commands, see the quick reference.

Maven also has no separate step like dotnet restore. A build downloads what it needs into the local repository. The build also puts those JARs on the classpath for you. The file ~/.m2/settings.xml says where Maven downloads from. This file does the same as nuget.config in .NET. It lists repositories, mirrors and credentials.

The wrapper#

Commit mvnw, mvnw.cmd and the .mvn/ folder to your repository. Together these files fix which Maven version the project uses. They download that version on first use. So the build server and every developer build with the same Maven version. The nearest .NET equivalent is a global.json file that fixes the SDK version.

./mvnw clean package        # always use the wrapper, not a system mvn
./mvnw -q test              # quiet
./mvnw -o package           # offline
./mvnw -pl billing-api -am package   # one module and what it depends on
Reading the code
./mvnw -o package

-o makes Maven work offline. Maven then uses only what is already in ~/.m2.

./mvnw -pl billing-api -am package

-pl selects one module of a multi-module build. -am also builds the modules that this module depends on.

A Spring Boot pomtwist#

Spring Boot supplies a parent POM that sets compatible versions for several hundred libraries. This parent POM is the biggest single convenience in the Java build world:

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.5.0</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.0.0</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
  <!-- RENAMED in Boot 4: web -> webmvc -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

In both versions, the parent element makes the POM of Spring Boot the parent of your POM. So the two starters need no version element. A dependency that brings a whole feature with it is called a starter. For example, one starter brings everything that a Spring web application needs.

Gotcha

spring-boot-starter-web became spring-boot-starter-webmvc in Boot 4.0. The change was part of a wider renaming to the pattern spring-boot-<technology>. This starter is the first line of your first pom.xml. So it is also the first thing that breaks when you follow a Boot 3 tutorial on Boot 4. See Migrating Boot 3 to 4.

Profiles and BOMs#

Two everyday Maven mechanisms have no single csproj equivalent.

In Maven, a named block of configuration is called a profile. You switch a profile on with a flag, a property or the environment. With profiles, one pom builds differently for the build server, for a GraalVM native image, or for a particular database. Here a profile runs the integration tests:

<profiles>
  <profile>
    <id>integration</id>
    <activation>
      <property><name>env.CI</name></property>   <!-- on when $CI is set -->
    </activation>
    <build><plugins>
      <plugin>
        <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
        <executions><execution><goals>
          <goal>integration-test</goal><goal>verify</goal>
        </goals></execution></executions>
      </plugin>
    </plugins></build>
  </profile>
</profiles>
Reading the code
<id>integration</id>

This is the profile's name. You use the name with -P on the command line.

<property><name>env.CI</name></property>

This element switches the profile on automatically when the CI environment variable is set. Most build servers set this variable.

<artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>

This is the plugin that runs integration tests. It runs them as part of the verify phase.

You can also switch a profile on yourself, and check which profiles are on:

./mvnw -Pintegration verify      # activate explicitly
./mvnw help:active-profiles      # which are actually on
Reading the code
./mvnw -Pintegration verify

-P switches a profile on by name.

./mvnw help:active-profiles

This command lists the profiles that are really on. Check this list first when a profile seems to be ignored.

Gotcha

Do not use profiles to build a different artifact for each environment. The purpose of a deployable JAR is that the same bytes go to every environment. Only the configuration differs. You change the configuration with Spring profiles and environment variables. Maven profiles are for varying the build, not the product.

A pom that publishes only a set of compatible versions is called a BOM, or bill of materials. When you import a BOM, it sets the versions of a whole family of libraries at once. spring-boot-starter-parent does this for you. Directory.Packages.props does the same in .NET. This pom imports a BOM:

<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>4.0.0</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>          <!-- import, not inherit -->
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
Reading the code
<type>pom</type>

This dependency is a POM, not a JAR.

<scope>import</scope>

This scope copies the managed versions of that POM into your POM. So your own dependencies can leave out their versions.

Note

scope=import with type=pom is the form to remember. Use this form when you cannot inherit from spring-boot-starter-parent. That is common in a multi-module build that already has its own parent. The import gives you the managed versions, but not the plugin configuration of spring-boot-starter-parent.

Two versions of one librarytrap#

Two of your dependencies each bring in jackson-databind, which is a JSON library. Each dependency brings in a different version. Maven puts only one of the two versions on the classpath:

PredictTwo versions of one library in the dependency tree#
Which version of jackson-databind does Maven use?
billing
├── reports-client
│   └── jackson-databind 2.15.0
└── pdf-export
    └── templating
        └── jackson-databind 2.17.0
Show the answer
2.15.0

When two libraries need different versions of a third library, Maven picks the declaration nearest to your project in the dependency tree. Maven does not pick the highest version. When NuGet gets two requested versions, it takes the higher version. So the Maven rule surprises people.

You can force a version in two ways. Declare the library directly in your own <dependencies>, because a direct declaration is always nearest. Or set the version in <dependencyManagement>.

Gotcha

“Nearest wins” means that adding an unrelated dependency can downgrade a dependency of one of its neighbours, and nothing warns you. If something breaks after you add a library, run dependency:tree before anything else. If code calls a method that the older version does not have, the code fails with NoSuchMethodError. For more about this error, see the section Two JARs, one class.

Dependency conflicts#

The dependency:tree goal shows which dependency brings in which library. Here the goal runs for the whole project, and then for one library:

./mvnw dependency:tree
./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind
Reading the code
./mvnw dependency:tree

This command prints every dependency as a tree. The tree also shows the dependencies that each dependency brings in.

-Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind

This option shows only the paths that lead to jackson-databind. Use it to find which dependency brought in an unexpected version.

Check yourself
1
What does ./mvnw package do before it builds the JAR?
It validates, compiles and runs the tests, because running a lifecycle phase runs every phase before it.
2
An expert asksA Spring Boot pom lists spring-boot-starter-test with no <version>. Where does the version come from?
The version comes from the parent POM of Spring Boot. This parent POM sets compatible versions for several hundred libraries. A project that cannot inherit that parent POM imports the same versions as a bill of materials (BOM). The import uses scope=import and type=pom.

Task.NETMaven
Compiledotnet buildmvn compile
Run testsdotnet testmvn test
Build a JAR / dlldotnet buildmvn package
Skip testsdotnet buildmvn package -DskipTests
Cleandotnet cleanmvn clean
Install locallydotnet pack + local feedmvn install
Publish to a repodotnet nuget pushmvn deploy
Run the appdotnet runmvn spring-boot:run

Check for updatesdotnet list package --outdatedmvn versions:display-dependency-updates

Gradle and multi-module builds#

Build and tooling · Chapter 32· 6 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

Gradle is the other build tool for Java. A Gradle build file is a program, written in Kotlin or Groovy. A Maven build file is an XML document. In both tools, a build of several modules together does the same as a solution file in .NET.

KindC#JavaNote
twista .csproj filebuild.gradle.ktsa Gradle build file is a Kotlin or Groovy program, not an XML document Why
newno equivalentMaven or GradleIf you are choosing, pick Maven. Choose Gradle when build times are a real problem. Why
twistPackageReferenceimplementation("org.slf4j:slf4j-api:2.0.16")a dependency is one string that holds the group, artifact and version, separated by colons Why
twistPrivateAssets="compile" on a PackageReferenceimplementation against apian implementation dependency stays off the compile classpath of projects that use yours Why
twistSolution (.sln)aggregator pom with <modules>, or settings.gradle.ktsone file at the root lists the modules that are built together Why
twistProjectReferencea normal dependency on the sibling, or project(":billing-domain")Maven names a sibling module by its coordinates, and Gradle by its path Why
twistDirectory.Packages.props<dependencyManagement>, or a version catalog (libs.versions.toml)versions are declared once at the root, and every module inherits them Why
twistBuild the solutionmvn package at the root, or ./gradlew build at the rootthe root build compiles, tests and packages every module Why
trapBuild one projectmvn -pl billing-api -am package, or ./gradlew :billing-api:buildwithout -am, Maven expects the sibling modules to be installed already Why
twistnuget.orgMaven Central (repo1.maven.org)Maven Central is the public repository, and a company repository fetches from it for you Why
twist~/.nuget/packages~/.m2/repositorythe local repository, where downloaded artifacts are kept on your machine Why
twistnuget.config~/.m2/settings.xmlset it up once, to send every download through the company repository Why
twistAzure Artifacts / GitHub PackagesNexus, Artifactory, GitHub Packagesin a company, every download usually goes through one of these Why
trappackages.lock.jsonMaven has none, so set exact versions, but Gradle has gradle.lockfileMaven has no lockfile by default, and a SNAPSHOT version can change when you have changed nothing Why

Gradle against Mavennew#

A Gradle build file is a program. So Gradle is more powerful than Maven, and it is easier to write a messy build with Gradle. Gradle is also much faster on large builds, because it redoes only the work that changed and can reuse results from a shared cache. Maven and Gradle make different trade-offs:

AspectMavenGradle
FormatXML, declarativeKotlin or Groovy DSL, imperative
Learning curveshallow, because conventions do the worksteeper, with more freedom to make mistakes
Speed on big buildsslowermuch faster, because it is incremental and has a build cache
Customisationwrite or find a pluginwrite code inline
Predictabilityvery highdepends on the author
Ecosystem defaultenterprise, Spring tutorialsAndroid, newer projects

“Write code inline” is meant literally. In Maven, a custom build step needs a plugin. In Gradle, a custom build step is a few lines of Kotlin:

// build.gradle.kts: a custom task is ordinary code
tasks.register("printVersion") {
    doLast { println("version ${project.version}") }
}
Reading the code
tasks.register("printVersion")

This line adds a new build step. In Gradle, a build step is called a task. The name of this task is printVersion. You run the task with ./gradlew printVersion.

doLast { println("version ${project.version}") }

This is the code that the task runs. It prints the project's version.

Note

If you are choosing, pick Maven. Maven is rigid, and on a team that is a strength. The Spring documentation assumes Maven. A Maven build that someone else wrote is always readable. Choose Gradle when build times are a real problem, or when the project is for Android.

The same project, both waystwist#

Maven: pom.xml
<properties>
  <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
</properties>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
    <version>2.0.16</version>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>6.0.3</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
Gradle: build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    java
}

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(25)
    }
}

dependencies {
    implementation("org.slf4j:slf4j-api:2.0.16")
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:6.0.3")
}
Reading the code
plugins {

Plugins give a build its abilities. The java plugin compiles Java code, runs the tests and builds a Java archive (JAR).

languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(25)

This line tells Gradle which Java version to build with, like maven.compiler.release in Maven.

implementation("org.slf4j:slf4j-api:2.0.16")

This is a dependency, written as one string. The string holds the group, the artifact and the version, separated by colons.

testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:6.0.3")

This dependency is available to the tests only, like the test scope in Maven.

A Maven scope is called a configuration in Gradle. This table maps each scope to its configuration:

Maven scopeGradle configurationMeaning
compileimplementationused internally, but NOT exposed to consumers
compile (exported)apiexposed to consumers transitively
providedcompileOnlyneeded to compile, but supplied at run time by the server
runtimeruntimeOnlyneeded only at run time, such as a JDBC driver
testtestImplementationon the test classpath only, so it is never shipped
Gotcha

Maven has no equivalent for the choice between implementation and api. This choice is the best feature of Gradle. An implementation dependency is not added to the compile classpath of the projects that use your project. That speeds up builds and stops accidental coupling. In Maven, every compile dependency is visible to your users. That is how a project comes to depend on things that it never declared.

Multi-module: your solution filetwist#

A multi-module build is called a reactor build in Maven. It is called a multi-project build in Gradle. Gradle lists the modules in settings.gradle.kts. Maven lists the modules in an aggregator Project Object Model (POM):

billing/                       ← aggregator; the "solution"
├── pom.xml                    ← <modules> list + <dependencyManagement>
├── billing-domain/
│   └── pom.xml                ← no dependencies on siblings
├── billing-persistence/
│   └── pom.xml                ← depends on billing-domain
└── billing-api/
    └── pom.xml                ← depends on both; the deployable

Only billing-api is deployed. The aggregator's own pom.xml lists the modules, and declares their versions once:

<!-- billing/pom.xml; the aggregator -->
<packaging>pom</packaging>

<modules>
  <module>billing-domain</module>
  <module>billing-persistence</module>
  <module>billing-api</module>
</modules>

<!-- versions declared once, inherited by every module -->
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
      <artifactId>billing-domain</artifactId>
      <version>${project.version}</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
Reading the code
<packaging>pom</packaging>

This project builds no JAR of its own. It only groups the modules.

<module>billing-domain</module>

Each module is a folder with its own pom.xml, like a project in a solution.

<version>${project.version}</version>

The modules share the aggregator's version, so a dependency on a sibling module always matches.

.NET refresherDirectory.Packages.props: NuGet central package management

One file at the solution root sets the version of every NuGet dependency. Each project then references a dependency without a version.

<!-- Directory.Packages.props -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Serilog" Version="4.1.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
<!-- each .csproj: <PackageReference Include="Serilog" /> -->

In Gradle, a module names a sibling module by its path, for example project(":billing-domain"). A file called a version catalog holds the versions. The name of this file is libs.versions.toml.

Command mapping#

The quick reference lists the everyday commands. You will use these three commands most on a multi-module Gradle build:

./gradlew build                                         # compile, test and package everything
./gradlew :billing-api:bootRun                          # run one module's Boot app
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath # what actually ships
Reading the code
./gradlew build

This command compiles, tests and builds every module, like mvn package at the root.

./gradlew :billing-api:bootRun

The colon path names one module, which is billing-api. bootRun starts the Spring Boot application of that module.

./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath

This command lists the dependencies that are really delivered with the application.

To build one module with Maven, name the module, and also ask for the modules that it depends on:

./mvnw -pl billing-api -am package

-pl billing-api picks one module of the build.

Note

-am means “also make”. It tells Maven to build the dependencies of the named module too. Without -am, Maven expects that the sibling modules are already installed in your local repository. If they are not installed, you get a confusing “could not resolve” error for your own code. -pl module -am is the combination to remember.

Where artifacts come from#

In a company, every download usually goes through a company repository such as Nexus. You set that up once, in settings.xml:

<!-- ~/.m2/settings.xml: send every download through the company repository -->
<mirrors>
  <mirror>
    <id>company</id>
    <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>
    <url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-public/</url>
  </mirror>
</mirrors>
Reading the code
<mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>

This element sends the requests for every repository through this mirror.

<url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-public/</url>

This is the address of the company repository. The company repository fetches from Maven Central for you, and keeps a copy.

.NET refresherpackages.lock.json: NuGet's lock file
<PropertyGroup>
  <RestorePackagesWithLockFile>true</RestorePackagesWithLockFile>
</PropertyGroup>
<!-- restore writes packages.lock.json; CI runs: dotnet restore --locked-mode -->
Gotcha

Maven has no lockfile by default. To get a repeatable build, fix exact versions and never use version ranges. SNAPSHOT versions are allowed to change. For example, Maven downloads 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT again, and the new download can be different when you have changed nothing. Never depend on someone else's snapshot from a release build.

Gradle has dependency locking, but you must first activate it for a build. This command writes the resolved versions into gradle.lockfile:

./gradlew dependencies --write-locks

--write-locks creates or updates the lock file. A later build fails if it would resolve a different version.

Check yourself
1
You are choosing a build tool for a new service. Which one, and when would you choose the other?
Choose Maven. Maven is rigid, and on a team that is a strength. The Spring documentation assumes Maven. A Maven build that someone else wrote is always readable. Choose Gradle when build times are a real problem, or when the project is for Android.

TaskMavenGradle

Testmvn test./gradlew test
Packagemvn package./gradlew build
Cleanmvn clean./gradlew clean
Run a Boot appmvn spring-boot:run./gradlew bootRun
