Modules, JPMS and the missing internal#

Build and tooling · Chapter 33· 6 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens

The Java Platform Module System (JPMS) Java 9 is the nearest thing Java has to an assembly boundary. Most applications do not use it. You need to know what a module-info.java file means when you see one. You do not need to write one.

KindC#JavaNote
twistan assemblymodule com.acme.billing { ... }a module declares what it exports and what it requires, and the JVM enforces both Why
twistan assembly referencerequires java.sqlthe module needs java.sql to compile and to run Why
twistpublic types in the assemblyexports com.acme.billing.apionly the public types in an exported package are usable outside the module Why
twistinternala package the module does not exportits public types cannot be used from outside, but this works per package, not per type Why
twistInternalsVisibleTo("X")exports p to Xa qualified export makes one package visible to one named module Why
twistInternalsVisibleTo, for a test projecttests in the same packagea test in the same package gets package-private access Why
newno equivalentjava -p mods -m com.acme.billing/com.acme.Appthe module path enforces module boundaries, but the classpath enforces nothing Why
trapreflection into private fieldsopens com.acme to a named moduleunder JPMS, Spring, Hibernate and Jackson can reflect only into an opened package Why
newno equivalent--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMEDThe JDK's internals are closed by default since Java 16. Since Java 17, only a flag like this reopens a package. Why
newno equivalentno module-info.java at alla Spring Boot service skips modules, because the fat JAR is its boundary Why

The problem it solvesnew#

Before Java 9, the classpath was one flat namespace. Any class could use any public class in any Java archive (JAR), so public meant public to the whole world. And when two JARs contained a class with the same name, one class hid the other class, and nothing reported it. This well-known problem is called “JAR hell”. C# never had this problem, because assemblies are real boundaries. Inside an assembly, C# has internal.

A module fixes that. A module declares which packages it exports and which modules it requires. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) enforces both declarations. Here the billing module makes these declarations in a file called module-info.java, at the root of its source folder:

// src/main/java/module-info.java
module com.acme.billing {

    requires java.sql;                       // depend on a JDK module
    requires transitive com.acme.domain;     // and re-export it to my consumers

    exports com.acme.billing.api;            // public to everyone
    exports com.acme.billing.spi
        to com.acme.plugins;                 // public only to a named module

    // com.acme.billing.internal is NOT exported: unreachable outside,
    // even though its classes are public

    provides com.acme.billing.api.PaymentProvider
        with com.acme.billing.internal.StripeProvider;   // service loading
}
Reading the code
requires java.sql;

The module needs java.sql. This is one of the modules that the Java Development Kit (JDK) itself is split into.

requires transitive com.acme.domain;

The billing module needs the domain module. Any module that requires billing gets the domain module too.

exports com.acme.billing.api;

The public types in this package can be used outside the module.

to com.acme.plugins;

This package is visible only to the one module named here.

provides com.acme.billing.api.PaymentProvider

This line declares an implementation of a service interface. Other modules can find the implementation while the program runs, through ServiceLoader. This is a small built-in form of dependency injection.

Here is the full set of directives. It includes opens, which frameworks such as Spring, Hibernate and Jackson need:

DirectiveMeans.NET analogy
requires Xthis module needs module X to compile and to runassembly reference
requires transitive Xneeds X, and any module that requires this one gets X tooa public dependency
exports pthe public types in package p are usable outside the modulepublic types in the assembly
exports p to Mpackage p is visible only to MInternalsVisibleTo, inverted
opens plets frameworks reflect into p, private fields includedneeded by Spring, Hibernate, Jackson
uses / providesdeclares a service it looks up, or an implementation it suppliesDI at the platform level

This is the closest thing to internaltwist#

C#: per type, inside an assembly
// visible only within this assembly
internal class StripeGateway { }

// and grant one friend assembly access
[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("Acme.Billing.Tests")]
Java: per package, inside a module
// module-info.java: the package is simply not exported,
// so its public types are unreachable outside the module
module com.acme.billing {
    exports com.acme.billing.api;
    // com.acme.billing.internal stays hidden
}
Reading the code
internal class StripeGateway { }

C# hides one type from other assemblies.

// com.acme.billing.internal stays hidden

Java hides a whole package, by not exporting it.

This table shows each C# visibility and its Java form:

GoalC#Java
Public to my code, hidden outsideinternala non-exported package in a module
Public to everyonepublicexported package + public type
Visible to my testsInternalsVisibleTotests in the same package
Visible to one other componentInternalsVisibleTo("X")exports p to X
Gotcha

In C#, internal works per type or member. A JPMS export works per package, all or nothing. You cannot export a package and hide one class in it. So a design with modules forces you to put the API and the implementation in different packages. That is a good habit, but it can mean a lot of restructuring.

Code that uses a class from a package that is not exported does not compile, even though the class itself is public:

// in module com.acme.app, which requires com.acme.billing
import com.acme.billing.internal.StripeGateway;
// error: package com.acme.billing.internal is not visible
Reading the code
import com.acme.billing.internal.StripeGateway;

The class is public, but the billing module does not export the package of the class. So another module cannot import the class.

Classpath vs module path#

ClasspathModule path
Flat namespaceyesno
Access enforcednoyes
Split packages allowedyesno
Needs module-infonoyes (or it becomes an automatic module)
Most Spring Boot appsthis onerarely
Note

You can place a JAR without a module-info.java on the module path. The JAR is then called an automatic module. Its module name comes from the file name, and it exports everything and reads everything. An automatic module is the bridge for migrating to modules. Most of the ecosystem is still at this stage.

Here is the same application started both ways:

# classpath: one flat namespace, nothing enforced
java -cp "app.jar:lib/*" com.acme.App

# module path: module boundaries enforced; -m names module/main class
java -p mods -m com.acme.billing/com.acme.App
Reading the code
java -cp "app.jar:lib/*" com.acme.App

This line uses the classpath. Every JAR is in one flat namespace, and nothing is enforced.

java -p mods -m com.acme.billing/com.acme.App

-p gives the module path. -m names the module and its main class. On the module path, the module boundaries are enforced.

Why frameworks need opens#

Gotcha

Spring, Hibernate and Jackson all read and set private fields through reflection. Under JPMS, this reflection is blocked unless the package is open. This problem is the main reason why ordinary applications do not use JPMS at all. If you put an application that uses these frameworks into modules, expect this error:

java.lang.reflect.InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field private java.lang.String com.acme.Customer.name accessible: module com.acme.billing does not "opens com.acme" to unnamed module @3af49f1c#
Means
A framework tried to read a private field by reflection. The module that owns the class has not opened the package of the class to the framework.
Fix
Add opens com.acme to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind; to module-info.java, or declare an open module. For a JDK package, pass --add-opens on the command line instead.
What triggers it
// com.acme is exported by com.acme.billing, but not opened
var field = com.acme.Customer.class.getDeclaredField("name");
field.setAccessible(true);      // throws InaccessibleObjectException

Flags you will meet#

FlagDoes
--add-opens M/p=ALL-UNNAMEDgrant deep reflection into a JDK package
--add-exports M/p=ALL-UNNAMEDgrant compile/runtime access to a non-exported package
--add-modules Madd a module not required transitively
--illegal-access=permitremoved in Java 17, so it is no longer available

The flag that you are most likely to type lets an old library reflect into the JDK:

# let an old library reflect into java.lang, for code on the classpath
java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED -jar app.jar
Reading the code
--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED

This flag opens the java.lang package of the java.base module to all code on the classpath. The JDK calls the code on the classpath the unnamed module.

Gotcha

Strong encapsulation of JDK internals is on by default since Java 16. Java 17 removed the single option that disabled strong encapsulation for everything. Some libraries used private parts of the JDK, such as private fields of java.lang classes. These libraries now fail with InaccessibleObjectException instead of printing a warning. sun.misc.Unsafe is the exception to this rule. It can still be used, but since Java 24 its memory methods print a warning that they will be removed. If an old library fails this way after an upgrade, the short-term fix is --add-opens. The real fix is to upgrade the library.

When to bother#

Modules matter for the JDK itself, for libraries, and for jlink. Modules are optional for a Spring Boot service. A library published to Maven Central is the clearest case for modules:

SituationUse JPMS?
Spring Boot service in a containerno, because the fat JAR is the boundary
Library published to Maven Centralyes, publish at least an Automatic-Module-Name
Desktop app shipped with jlinkyes, jlink requires modules
Large internal platform with many teamsmaybe, enforced boundaries help
Anything on Java 8not available
Note

When you publish a library, add an Automatic-Module-Name entry to the manifest of your JAR, even if you do not write a module-info.java. The manifest is the file of settings inside every JAR. The entry takes one line, and it gives your users a stable module name if they do move to modules.

With Maven, the JAR plugin writes the entry for you:

<plugin>
  <artifactId>maven-jar-plugin</artifactId>
  <configuration>
    <archive>
      <manifestEntries>
        <Automatic-Module-Name>com.acme.billing</Automatic-Module-Name>
      </manifestEntries>
    </archive>
  </configuration>
</plugin>
Reading the code
<Automatic-Module-Name>com.acme.billing</Automatic-Module-Name>

This is the module name that your users will write if they move to modules. They can use this name even though the library has no module-info.java.

Check yourself
1
A class is public, yet code in another module cannot import it. Why?
The module of the class does not export the package of the class. A package that is not exported is the closest thing Java has to internal. An export works per package. You cannot export a package and hide one class in it.

Testing#

Build and tooling · Chapter 34· 10 min read· Quick reference

The Java testing tools match the .NET testing tools. JUnit does the same as xUnit. Mockito does the same as Moq. AssertJ does the same as FluentAssertions. The Java Development Kit (JDK) includes none of these three tools, but spring-boot-starter-test from Spring Boot adds all three in one line.

KindC#JavaNote

sameAssert.Equal(expected, actual)assertEquals(expected, actual)The expected value comes first, as in xUnit. The AssertJ form assertThat(actual) removes the doubt.

The stacktwist#

Almost every .NET testing tool has a matching Java tool, often with the same name. The first difference that you meet is where the set-up code goes:

xUnit
public class OrderTests : IClassFixture<DbFixture>, IDisposable
{
    public OrderTests(DbFixture db) { }      // before each test
    public void Dispose() { }                // after each test

    [Fact, Trait("Category", "slow")]
    public void Saves() { }
}
JUnit 5 and 6
class OrderTest {
    @BeforeAll static void startDb() { }     // once per class: IClassFixture
    @BeforeEach void setUp() { }             // before each test
    @AfterEach void tearDown() { }           // after each test

    @Test @Tag("slow")
    void saves() { }
}
Reading the code
@BeforeAll static void startDb() { }

This method runs once, before any test in the class, like an IClassFixture in xUnit. The method must be static, because it runs before any test object exists.

@BeforeEach void setUp() { }

This method runs before every test. In xUnit, the constructor of the test class does that.

@Test @Tag("slow")

@Test marks a test method, like [Fact] in xUnit. @Tag labels the test, like [Trait], so that a build can include or exclude the test.

A testtwist#

Here is the same small test in both frameworks:

xUnit
public class MoneyTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Add_SumsAmounts()
    {
        var a = new Money(10m, "GBP");
        var b = new Money(5m, "GBP");

        var result = a.Add(b);

        result.Amount.Should().Be(15m);
    }
}
JUnit 5 and 6
class MoneyTest {

    @Test
    void add_sumsAmounts() {
        var a = new Money(new BigDecimal("10"), "GBP");
        var b = new Money(new BigDecimal("5"), "GBP");

        var result = a.add(b);

        assertThat(result.amount())
            .isEqualByComparingTo("15");
    }
}
Reading the code
class MoneyTest {

The class has no attribute and no public. JUnit finds the test methods by their @Test annotation.

void add_sumsAmounts() {

The test method returns void and takes no arguments.

.isEqualByComparingTo("15");

This is an AssertJ assertion, like Should().Be(...) in FluentAssertions. It compares BigDecimal values with compareTo, so 15 and 15.00 count as equal.

Note

Test classes and methods are package-private by convention. JUnit 5 and later do not require public. When you leave public out, the tests are not part of your published API. JUnit 4 required public, so older code has it.

Note

assertEquals(expected, actual) takes the expected value first, as Assert.Equal does in xUnit. If you swap the two arguments, the failure message shows the expected value as the actual value. The AssertJ form assertThat(actual).isEqualTo(expected) removes the doubt. That is one reason why most Java teams prefer AssertJ.

Parameterised teststwist#

C#
[Theory]
[InlineData(1, 1, 2)]
[InlineData(2, 3, 5)]
public void Adds(int a, int b, int expected)
    => Assert.Equal(expected, Add(a, b));
Java 25
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({
    "1, 1, 2",
    "2, 3, 5"
})
void adds(int a, int b, int expected) {
    assertThat(add(a, b)).isEqualTo(expected);
}
Reading the code
@ParameterizedTest

This annotation marks a test that runs once for each set of arguments, like [Theory] in xUnit.

@CsvSource({

Each string is one row, like one [InlineData]. JUnit splits the row at the commas, and each part becomes one parameter of the method.

Data can come from other sources too:

SourceProvides
@ValueSource(ints = {1,2,3})one primitive argument
@CsvSource({"a,1", "b,2"})several arguments inline
@CsvFileSource(resources = "/data.csv")from a file
@MethodSource("provider")from a static method returning a Stream
@EnumSource(Status.class)every enum constant
@NullAndEmptySourcenull and empty string

Mockingtwist#

OrderService saves each order that it processes through an OrderRepo. The test replaces the OrderRepo with a mock:

Moq
var repo = new Mock<IOrderRepo>();
repo.Setup(r => r.Find(7))
    .Returns(new Order(7));

var svc = new OrderService(repo.Object);
svc.Process(7);

repo.Verify(r => r.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()), Times.Once);
Mockito
OrderRepo repo = mock(OrderRepo.class);
when(repo.find(7))
    .thenReturn(new Order(7));

var svc = new OrderService(repo);
svc.process(7);

verify(repo, times(1)).save(any(Order.class));
Reading the code
OrderRepo repo = mock(OrderRepo.class);

This line creates the mock. The mock is itself an OrderRepo, so there is no .Object.

.thenReturn(new Order(7));

This line stubs find(7), like Setup(...).Returns(...) in Moq.

verify(repo, times(1)).save(any(Order.class));

This line checks that save was called exactly once, with any order. Moq does this with Verify and Times.Once.

Here is the rest of Moq:

MoqMockito
new Mock<T>()mock(T.class)
mock.Objectthe mock itself, so there is no .Object
Setup(...).Returns(v)when(...).thenReturn(v)
Setup(...).Throws(e)when(...).thenThrow(e)
Verify(..., Times.Once)verify(mock, times(1))
It.IsAny<T>()any(T.class)
It.Is<T>(p)argThat(predicate)
CallbackthenAnswer(invocation -> ...), or an ArgumentCaptor
MockBehavior.Strictno exact equal, so use a default answer that throws, or STRICT_STUBS
Gotcha

Older Mockito could not mock final classes or static methods. Moq has the same limitation, for the same reason. Since Mockito 5 the inline mock maker is the default, so final classes can be mocked. mockStatic exists, but use it only when nothing else works. If a class is hard to mock, that is usually a sign that its design should be improved.

Capturing an argument, and strict mocks#

C# refresherMoq Callback and MockBehavior.StrictC# 8
var repo = new Mock<IOrderRepo>(MockBehavior.Strict);   // any call without a Setup throws
Order? saved = null;
repo.Setup(r => r.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()))
    .Callback<Order>(o => saved = o);                   // capture the argument

Here is how Mockito captures an argument, and how it fails on any call that you did not expect:

// capture what was passed, the usual job of a Moq Callback
var captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class);
verify(repo).save(captor.capture());
Order saved = captor.getValue();

// fail on any call you did not stub, like MockBehavior.Strict
OrderRepo strict = mock(OrderRepo.class, call -> { throw new AssertionError("unexpected " + call); });
Reading the code
ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class)

The captor keeps the argument of the verified call. In Moq, a Callback usually does this.

Order saved = captor.getValue();

This is the order that was passed to save.

mock(OrderRepo.class, call -> { throw new AssertionError("unexpected " + call); })

The second argument is a default answer. It throws for every call that you have not stubbed, like MockBehavior.Strict in Moq.

Gotcha

Stub such a mock with doReturn, not when. when(strict.find(7)) calls find first, and the default answer throws. doReturn(order).when(strict).find(7) stubs the method without calling it.

Testcontainerstwist#

Testcontainers for .NET is the same project in another language. It runs real dependencies in Docker for integration tests. Here the dependency is a PostgreSQL database:

import org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer;

@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer db =
        new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:16")
            .withDatabaseName("billing");

    @Test
    void findsSavedOrder() {
        // db.getJdbcUrl() points at a real Postgres
    }
}
Reading the code
@Testcontainers

This annotation starts and stops the containers that are declared in the class.

import org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer;

This import is from Testcontainers 2, which Spring Boot 4.1 manages. Spring Boot 3.4 manages Testcontainers 1. Testcontainers 1 has only the generic class PostgreSQLContainer<?>, in the package org.testcontainers.containers. That generic class is now deprecated.

static PostgreSQLContainer db =

The field holds a PostgreSQL 16 container. Because the field is static, one container serves every test in the class.

// db.getJdbcUrl() points at a real Postgres

The container reports where it is listening, so the code under test connects to a real database.

Note

Spring Boot works with Testcontainers directly. Put @ServiceConnection on a container field, and Spring Boot sets the data source settings automatically. You do not override any properties yourself. See Testing Spring Boot.

WireMock: faking an HTTP dependencytwist#

WireMock is the Java original, and WireMock.Net copies its features in a separate codebase. WireMock starts a real HTTP server. So all of your client code really runs, and no part of it is replaced by a mock:

WireMock.Net
var server = WireMockServer.Start();
server
  .Given(Request.Create()
      .WithPath("/rates/GBPUSD").UsingGet())
  .RespondWith(Response.Create()
      .WithStatusCode(200)
      .WithBodyAsJson(new { rate = 1.27 }));
WireMock
@WireMockTest
class RatesClientTest {

  @Test
  void fetchesRate(WireMockRuntimeInfo wm) {
    stubFor(get("/rates/GBPUSD")
        .willReturn(okJson("{\"rate\":1.27}")));

    var client = new RatesClient(wm.getHttpBaseUrl());
    assertThat(client.fetch("GBPUSD").rate())
        .isEqualTo(1.27);
  }
}
Reading the code
@WireMockTest

This annotation starts a real HTTP server on a free port for the test class. It passes the details of the server into each test.

stubFor(get("/rates/GBPUSD")

This call tells the server how to answer a GET for /rates/GBPUSD.

new RatesClient(wm.getHttpBaseUrl())

This line gives the real client the address of the fake server.

Note

Spring Boot has a lighter alternative for pure client tests: @RestClientTest with MockRestServiceServer. This alternative intercepts requests at the RestClient level and needs no port. Use WireMock when you want a real socket, a delay, or an injected fault.

JMH against BenchmarkDotNet#

You cannot benchmark Java with a stopwatch loop. The just-in-time (JIT) compiler compiles busy code only after thousands of calls. It also removes work whose result is never used. So a simple loop measures the optimiser, not your code. The Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH) handles warmup, separate runs and dead-code removal for you:

BenchmarkDotNet
[MemoryDiagnoser]
public class ParseBench
{
    [Params(10, 1000)]
    public int N;

    [Benchmark]
    public int Sum() => Enumerable.Range(0, N).Sum();
}

BenchmarkRunner.Run<ParseBench>();
JMH
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5)
@Measurement(iterations = 10)
@Fork(2)
public class ParseBench {

    @Param({"10", "1000"})
    public int n;

    @Benchmark
    public int sum() {
        return IntStream.range(0, n).sum();
    }
}
Reading the code
@Warmup(iterations = 5)

This annotation runs the benchmark five times before it measures, so the JIT has compiled the code by then.

@Fork(2)

This annotation runs everything in two fresh Java Virtual Machine (JVM) processes. So the optimisations of one run do not affect the other run.

return IntStream.range(0, n).sum();

The method returns the result. JMH consumes the result, so the JIT cannot remove the work.

Gotcha

Return the result, or JMH's Blackhole must consume it. The JIT can delete a benchmark entirely if its value is never used. You then measure an empty loop at an impossible speed. The JVM does this far more aggressively than .NET. That is the main reason why hand-written Java benchmarks are usually wrong.

ArchUnit: architecture rules as tests#

ArchUnitNET calls itself the C# fork of ArchUnit. With ArchUnit, a broken layering rule is an ordinary failing test, not a review comment. The billing code has three rules. The domain must not depend on the web layer or the database layer. Controllers must not depend on persistence. Field injection is banned. Here are the three rules as a test class:

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.acme.billing")
class ArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domainIsPure =
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAnyPackage("..api..", "..persistence..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule controllersAreThin =
        classes().that().areAnnotatedWith(RestController.class)
            .should().onlyDependOnClassesThat()
            .resideOutsideOfPackage("..persistence..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule noFieldInjection =
        noFields().should().beAnnotatedWith(Autowired.class);
}
Reading the code
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.acme.billing")

This annotation loads every class in com.acme.billing, and runs each rule against these classes.

noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")

This rule reads almost like English. No class in a domain package may depend on the api packages or the persistence packages. The two dots match any part of a package name.

noFields().should().beAnnotatedWith(Autowired.class);

This rule bans @Autowired on fields, so dependencies come in through constructors.

JaCoCo against coverlet#

Coverage is a Maven plugin, not a separate tool. The plugin can fail the build when coverage is below a threshold. Here the build fails if less than 80% of lines are covered:

<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution>
      <id>check</id>
      <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
      <configuration>
        <rules><rule><limits><limit>
          <counter>LINE</counter>
          <minimum>0.80</minimum>
        </limit></limits></rule></rules>
      </configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
Reading the code
<goal>prepare-agent</goal>

This goal attaches the JaCoCo agent to the test run, so that the agent can note which lines run.

<minimum>0.80</minimum>

This is the threshold. The check goal fails the build if line coverage drops below 80%.

jacoco:report writes an HTML report into target/site/jacoco. ReportGenerator does the same for coverlet.

JUnit 5 and JUnit 6#

Gotcha

Spring Framework 7 baselines JUnit 6. If you are on Spring Boot 4, you are on JUnit 6. If you are on Spring Boot 3, you are on JUnit 5. The programming model stays the same. @Test, @ParameterizedTest and the extension API work as before.

Two things do change. JUnit 6 needs Java 17 or later. JUnit 6 also unifies the version numbers. The Platform, Jupiter and Vintage parts now share one number. Before, the Platform was on 1.x while Jupiter was on 5.x. If you set the versions yourself, and do not inherit them from the Boot parent, the version line is the line to fix. junit-platform-runner and junit-platform-jfr have also been removed.

Import the bill of materials of JUnit only if you set the version of JUnit yourself:

<!-- only when you pin JUnit yourself; the Spring Boot parent already does it -->
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.junit</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit-bom</artifactId>
      <version>${junit.version}</version>   <!-- JUnit 6: one number for Platform and Jupiter -->
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
Reading the code
<artifactId>junit-bom</artifactId>

This is the bill of materials of JUnit. It sets matching versions for all the parts of JUnit.

<version>${junit.version}</version>

One property holds the version, because JUnit 6 uses one number for every part.

LegacyJUnit 4

You can recognise JUnit 4 code by these signs:

  • org.junit.Test in place of org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
  • public test classes
  • @Before in place of @BeforeEach
  • @After in place of @AfterEach
  • @RunWith in place of @ExtendWith

The junit-vintage-engine runs JUnit 4 tests inside newer JUnit. That is how large codebases migrate a little at a time.

Naming#

Java has no single naming convention for tests, but two styles are the most common. The first style is a method name of the form methodUnderTest_condition_expectedResult. The second style is a readable sentence in @DisplayName. The second style looks like this:

@Test
@DisplayName("rejects an order when the cart is empty")
void rejectsEmptyCart() {
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.checkout(emptyCart))
        .isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class);
}
Reading the code
@DisplayName("rejects an order when the cart is empty")

This is the text that test reports show instead of the method name.

assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.checkout(emptyCart))

This is an AssertJ check that the code throws, like Should().Throw<T>() in FluentAssertions.

Check yourself
1
A service moves from Spring Boot 3 to Spring Boot 4. Its plain JUnit tests, with no Spring in them, use @Test and @ParameterizedTest, and nobody edits them. Do they still run, and what do you check first?
Yes. Boot 4 brings JUnit 6 in place of JUnit 5, and both annotations work as before. Check the Java version first, because JUnit 6 needs Java 17 or later. If the build sets the versions of JUnit itself, the build needs one edit, because JUnit 6 has one version number for all its parts.
2
TranslateWrite this Moq test in Java, with Mockito. order is an Order the test has already created: 
var repo = new Mock<IOrderRepository>();
repo.Setup(r => r.FindById(7)).Returns(order);

var service = new OrderService(repo.Object);
service.Cancel(7);

repo.Verify(r => r.Save(order), Times.Once);
OrderRepository repo = mock(OrderRepository.class);
when(repo.findById(7)).thenReturn(order);

var service = new OrderService(repo);
service.cancel(7);

verify(repo, times(1)).save(order);

The mock is the repository itself, so there is no .Object. verify takes the mock and the count. The call that you expect follows verify.

3
An expert asksWhy can a hand-rolled timing loop give a Java benchmark that is orders of magnitude too fast?
The JIT compiles hot code after thousands of iterations. It also deletes work whose result you discard. Use JMH, which handles warmup, forking and dead-code elimination.

Spring Boot orientation#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 35· 8 min read· Quick reference

Spring Boot does the same as ASP.NET Core. It is an application host with dependency injection, configuration, an embedded web server and health endpoints. Spring Boot configures most of itself from the libraries that it finds on the classpath.

KindC#JavaNote
twistthe ASP.NET Core versionBoot 3.x or Boot 4.x, set by the parent in pom.xmlExisting systems and most tutorials use Boot 3. Boot 4 is for new work. Why
twistProgram.csa class marked @SpringBootApplication, with a main methodone class starts Boot, and it holds no list of registered services Why
trapa service registered from any namespacea class in the application class's package, or below ita class in a sibling package is never scanned, so its bean does not exist Why
twista PackageReference for each libraryone starter, such as spring-boot-starter-data-jpaa starter brings a set of libraries and switches on their configuration Why
twistno equivalentspring-boot-starter-web in Boot 3, spring-boot-starter-webmvc in Boot 4Boot 4 renamed its modules, and this is the rename you meet first Why
newbuilder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDb>(), written by youauto-configurationBoot creates the beans a library needs, unless you define your own Why
twistno equivalent--debugprints the conditions evaluation report, which lists what Boot configured and why Why
twistthe folders of a .NET projectsrc/main/java and src/main/resourcesthe application class is in the root package, above every other class Why
twista framework-dependent dotnet publish./mvnw package, then java -jarone runnable JAR holds your code, every dependency and an embedded Tomcat, and needs only a JVM Why
twistMinimal APIs, NativeAOTJavalin, Quarkus, MicronautBoot is the default. Quarkus and Micronaut start faster, and Javalin is tiny. Why

Which versiontwist#

Two version lines of Boot are in use:

LineSpring FrameworkBaselinesUse when
Boot 3.xFramework 6Java 17, Jakarta EE 10existing systems and most tutorials
Boot 4.xFramework 7Java 17 (25 recommended), Jakarta EE 11, Kotlin 2.2, GraalVM 25, JUnit 6greenfield
Note

A minor version arrives every six months, in May and November. Each minor version is supported for at least 12 months. A major version is supported for at least three years from its release, as long as you are on a supported minor version. So plan one upgrade a year.

By September 2026 the 4.x line had reached 4.1. So look for the current release at spring.io/projects/spring-boot, not in a tutorial.

The parent version in pom.xml decides which line you are on:

<!-- pom.xml: this one line decides which Boot line you are on -->
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.0.0</version>      <!-- or a 3.5.x release for the Boot 3 line -->
</parent>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>

This is the parent Project Object Model (POM) of Boot. Your pom.xml inherits from the parent POM. The parent POM sets compatible versions for hundreds of libraries.

This book shows both lines. Where an API differs, the code has one tab for each line. A Boot 4 badge marks what Boot 4 adds.

The entry pointtwist#

ASP.NET Core 8+
// Program.cs
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDb>();

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
Spring Boot
// BillingApplication.java
@SpringBootApplication
public class BillingApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(BillingApplication.class, args);
    }
}
// services are discovered by annotation, not registered here
Reading the code
@SpringBootApplication

This annotation switches on auto-configuration. It also makes Spring search the package of this class, and every package below it, for your classes. That search is called component scanning.

SpringApplication.run(BillingApplication.class, args);

This line starts Boot. Boot creates the beans, which are the objects that Spring manages for you. Then Boot starts the embedded web server and runs until it is stopped, like app.Run() in ASP.NET Core.

// services are discovered by annotation, not registered here

There is no builder.Services list. Spring finds your classes by their annotations, such as @Service.

Which packages are scannedtrap#

PredictA service in a sibling package#
Does the application start?
package com.acme.billing;

@SpringBootApplication
public class BillingApplication { }      // its main method is left out here

package com.acme.billing;

@Service
public class OrderService {
    OrderService(com.acme.audit.AuditService audit) { }
}

package com.acme.audit;

@Service
public class AuditService { }
Show the answer
No. Spring never creates an AuditService, so it cannot build the OrderService.

@SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan. The scan covers the package containing the class and every package under it. com.acme.audit is a sibling of com.acme.billing, so Spring does not see a component in com.acme.audit. Boot reports a bean that could not be found.

Put the application class in your root package, com.acme.billing. Then Spring scans everything under the root package. To fix this example, move AuditService to the package com.acme.billing.audit. This one convention causes more “bean not found” confusion than anything else in Spring.

Starterstwist#

A starter is a dependency that brings a set of libraries that work together. It also switches on their auto-configuration. These are the starters you will meet first:

CapabilityBoot 3 starterBoot 4 starter
Web MVCspring-boot-starter-webspring-boot-starter-webmvc
Reactive webspring-boot-starter-webfluxspring-boot-starter-webflux
JPAspring-boot-starter-data-jpaspring-boot-starter-data-jpa
Flyway migrationsflyway-core, with no starterspring-boot-starter-flyway
Securityspring-boot-starter-securityspring-boot-starter-security
OAuth2 clientspring-boot-starter-oauth2-clientspring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client
Validationspring-boot-starter-validationspring-boot-starter-validation
Testingspring-boot-starter-testspring-boot-starter-test
Actuatorspring-boot-starter-actuatorspring-boot-starter-actuator
SOAP servicesspring-boot-starter-web-servicesspring-boot-starter-webservices
OpenTelemetryn/aspring-boot-starter-opentelemetry

Here one starter brings everything the billing service needs for database access through Jakarta Persistence (JPA):

<!-- one starter: Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, a connection pool, and their configuration -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>

This starter brings Hibernate, which is the library that maps objects to database tables. It also brings Spring Data JPA and a connection pool, and it switches on their auto-configuration. The starter has no version here, because the parent POM sets it.

Gotcha

Boot 4 renamed its modules, so that every module name has the form spring-boot-<technology>. The root package of each module has the form org.springframework.boot.<technology>. The rename that you meet first is starter-web becoming starter-webmvc. This starter is the first dependency in every tutorial you will read.

Auto-configurationnew#

When you add the JPA starter, Boot configures a data source, an entity manager and transactions. You do not write a line of code for this. ASP.NET Core has no equivalent. In ASP.NET Core, you call builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDb>() yourself.

Each starter contains configuration classes. A configuration class switches itself on only when certain conditions are true. This is called auto-configuration. Here is a simplified version of how Boot sets up a database connection:

// roughly what Boot does internally, simplified
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)          // the JDBC classes are present
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)    // and you have not defined your own
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DataSourceProperties.class)
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) { ... }
}
Reading the code
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)

The configuration applies only if the Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) classes are on the classpath. JDBC is the standard database interface of Java.

@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)

And the configuration applies only if you have not defined a DataSource yourself.

@Bean

The return value of the method becomes a bean. Spring can inject this bean into other classes.

Note

The rule that matters is that anything you define yourself replaces what Boot would configure. If you declare your own DataSource bean, Boot does not create the auto-configured DataSource bean. The reason is @ConditionalOnMissingBean. You override an auto-configured bean by defining your own bean, not by unregistering the auto-configured bean.

Boot finds these classes through a file. Each library lists its auto-configuration classes in a file inside its Java archive (JAR). The file is in the META-INF/spring folder, and its name ends in AutoConfiguration.imports. At startup, Boot reads every such file on the classpath.

The pattern behind the file: a service provider interfacedeep dive

This pattern is called a service provider interface (SPI). A library defines a place where other code can add its own classes. At run time, the library finds those classes from files in META-INF. Java itself has a class that works the same way, called ServiceLoader. For more about ServiceLoader, see the modules chapter.

Asking Boot what it configuredtwist#

# what did Boot configure, and why?
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments=--debug
# prints a "CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT": matched and unmatched, with reasons
Reading the code
-Dspring-boot.run.arguments=--debug

This argument passes --debug to the application. Boot then prints its conditions evaluation report. The report lists every auto-configuration that matched and every auto-configuration that did not match, with the reason. java -jar takes the same --debug flag.

Project layout#

A typical Boot service has this layout:

src/main/java/com/acme/billing/
├── BillingApplication.java     ← must be in the root package
├── api/                        ← @RestController
├── domain/                     ← entities, value objects, domain services
├── persistence/                ← repositories
└── config/                     ← @Configuration classes

src/main/resources/
├── application.yml             ← the appsettings.json
├── application-dev.yml         ← per-profile overrides
└── db/migration/               ← Flyway SQL

BillingApplication is in the root package, com.acme.billing. So component scanning finds everything in the folders below the root package. application.yml does the same as appsettings.json in ASP.NET Core. application-dev.yml overrides application.yml when the dev profile is active.

Running it#

Note

On a Boot project, ./mvnw package produces a single JAR that you can run. This JAR is called a fat JAR. It holds your code, every dependency and an embedded Tomcat. java -jar runs the fat JAR anywhere a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) exists.

The closest match in .NET is a framework-dependent dotnet publish. Its output needs the .NET runtime, in the same way that a fat JAR needs a JVM. To compare the forms, see the chapter Packaging. The fat JAR is also the reason why Java web applications no longer need an application server.

Here are both ways of running the billing service:

./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev    # run from source with a profile
java -jar target/billing-1.0.0.jar --server.port=9090    # run the packaged JAR on another port
Reading the code
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev

This command runs the service from source, with the dev profile active.

java -jar target/billing-1.0.0.jar --server.port=9090

This command runs the packaged JAR. You can give any setting on the command line after --. Here the setting is the port.

The quick reference lists the other everyday commands, with their .NET equivalents.

The alternatives#

FrameworkPitchCompared to
Spring Bootthe default, with a vast ecosystemASP.NET Core
Quarkuscompile-time DI, fast startup, native-firstASP.NET Core + NativeAOT
Micronautcompile-time DI, no runtime reflectionsimilar to Quarkus
Javalintiny, explicit, no magicMinimal APIs
HelidonOracle, MicroProfile and NimaMinimal APIs

Quarkus and Micronaut do their dependency injection while the code compiles. They use annotation processors for this. So they do not need the classpath scanning and reflection that Spring does at startup. The result is a startup time in the tens of milliseconds, and much better GraalVM native image support. NativeAOT in .NET makes the same trade-off. Spring Boot has removed much of this difference with ahead-of-time (AOT) processing, but not all of the difference.

Here is a Quarkus endpoint. It uses the Jakarta REST annotations instead of the Spring annotations:

// Quarkus: Jakarta REST annotations instead of Spring's
@Path("/hello")
public class HelloResource {
    @GET
    public String hello() { return "hello"; }
}
Reading the code
@Path("/hello")

@Path sets the path that this class answers, like @RequestMapping in Spring.

@GET

@GET marks a method that handles GET requests, like @GetMapping in Spring.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java, for Spring Boot: 
// Program.cs
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<OrderService>();

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
// BillingApplication.java
@SpringBootApplication
public class BillingApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(BillingApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// OrderService.java
@Service
public class OrderService { }

Nothing is registered in main. The @Service annotation on the class replaces the AddSingleton line. A Spring bean is a singleton unless you say otherwise.

2
What does @SpringBootApplication switch on, besides marking the class that main starts?
@SpringBootApplication switches on two things. The first is auto-configuration, because the annotation includes @EnableAutoConfiguration. The second is component scanning, because the annotation includes @ComponentScan. Component scanning searches the package of the class, and every package under it, for your annotated classes.
3
An expert asksYou added one starter and wrote no configuration, yet a DataSource bean exists. Where did it come from, and how do you replace it?
The library lists its auto-configuration classes in a file under META-INF/spring. Boot applies each class whose conditions are true. One condition is @ConditionalOnMissingBean. So when you declare your own DataSource bean, Boot does not create its own DataSource bean.

Dependency injection and configuration#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 36· 12 min read

Spring does dependency injection in the same way as ASP.NET Core, but Spring has no registration list. You mark a class with an annotation, and Spring finds the class. Configuration works as you expect, but the names are new.

KindC#JavaNote
twistbuilder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>()@Service on the classthe annotation is the registration, so there is no registration list Why
newno equivalent for services, so each is registered by handcomponent scanningat startup Spring finds every annotated class under the application's package and makes a bean of it Why
sameconstructor injectionconstructor injectionA class with one constructor needs no annotation. Older code puts @Autowired on a field instead.
trapAddScoped, chosen every timesingleton, unless you say otherwiseone bean is shared by every request, so a field in it is shared too Why
twistAddSingleton, AddScoped, AddTransientsingleton, @RequestScope, @Scope("prototype")the same three lifetimes, under different names Why
twistAddKeyedScoped<IPaymentGateway, CardGateway>("card")@Service("card"), then @Qualifier("card")when two beans fit one type, a bean name picks between them Why
twistIEnumerable<IPaymentGateway>List<PaymentGateway> or Map<String, PaymentGateway>a List or Map parameter receives every bean of that type Why
twista factory lambda in AddSingletona @Bean method in a @Configuration classfor a class you cannot annotate, such as a library type Why
twistappsettings.jsonapplication.ymlthe same settings in YAML, where indentation shows nesting Why
trapa MongoDB connection string in appsettings.jsonspring.mongodb.uriOn Boot 3 it is spring.data.mongodb.uri. Boot 4 ignores that old name and tries localhost:27017. Why
twistASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENTSPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVEan environment, such as dev or prod, is called a profile in Spring Why

twist--environment Development--spring.profiles.active=deva command-line argument that switches a profile on Why

twistIOptions<RatesOptions>a @ConfigurationProperties record, injected directlybinds one section of the settings to a type, with no wrapper Why
twistRates__TimeoutSecondsRATES_TIMEOUT_SECONDSan environment variable sets rates.timeout-seconds, with one underscore Why
twistdotnet user-secretsapplication-local.yml, gitignoredSpring has no secrets tool, so keep a local profile file out of git Why

Registration by annotationtwist#

The billing service has an OrderService that needs an OrderRepository to load and save orders:

C#
// Program.cs: each class is registered by hand
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();

// OrderService.cs: the repository arrives
// through the primary constructor
public class OrderService(OrderRepository repository)
{
}
Java 25
// OrderRepository.java
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;

@Repository
public class OrderRepository {
    // loads and saves orders; the Data access chapter fills it in
}

// OrderService.java: there is no registration line,
// because the annotation is the registration
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;

    // Spring passes in the OrderRepository
    // when it creates the OrderService.
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
Reading the code
@Repository

This annotation marks OrderRepository as a class that Spring should create. @Repository is for classes that talk to the database.

@Service

This annotation does the same for OrderService. This one line replaces the builder.Services line in C#.

private final OrderRepository repository;

final means that the field is set once, in the constructor, and never changes. A final field is like a readonly field in C#.

public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {

Spring sees that the constructor needs an OrderRepository. It finds the OrderRepository that it created, and passes this object to the constructor.

Beans and component scanningnew#

An object that Spring creates and gives to other objects is called a bean. At startup, Spring searches the package of the application class, and every package below it, for classes with these annotations. Spring creates one bean for each class that it finds. That search is called component scanning. Here the framework creates the objects, and your code does not. This is called inversion of control (IoC).

A class with one constructor needs no further annotation, because Spring uses that constructor. This is called constructor injection, and you already do it in ASP.NET Core. With constructor injection, the field can be final. The constructor lists everything that the class depends on. And a unit test can create the service with new and a fake repository.

These are the annotations that make a class a bean:

AnnotationMeansNote
@Componentany class Spring should create and injectan object that Spring creates and injects is called a "bean"
@Servicea component that holds business logicworks the same as @Component, but the name shows what the class is for
@Repositorya component that does data accessalso converts database errors into Spring's own exception types
@Controller / @RestControllera component that handles web requests
@Configurationa class that declares @Bean methods
@Beana method whose return value becomes a beanuse it for classes you cannot annotate, such as library types
LegacyField injection with @Autowired

Older code often injects into a field instead of a constructor, so you should be able to recognise field injection. Use constructor injection with final fields in new code.

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;

// the older style: avoid it in new code
@Service
public class OrderService {

    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository repository;
}
Reading the code
@Autowired

@Autowired tells Spring to set the field after Spring has created the object. Field injection works, but it hides what the class depends on. Also, a unit test cannot give the class a fake repository without starting Spring.

Lifetimestrap#

PredictA bean that keeps the current order in a field#
Two customers pay at the same moment. What can go wrong?
@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private Order current;

    public void pay(Order order) {
        current = order;
        charge(current);
    }

    private void charge(Order order) { }
}
Show the answer
Both requests can charge the second customer's order.

The defaults are opposite. ASP.NET Core makes you choose a lifetime every time. In Spring, the default lifetime is singleton. So there is one PaymentService for the whole application, and this one object has one current field. Every request reads and writes this one field. The second request can overwrite the field before the first request reaches charge, and nothing warns you.

Keep beans stateless. Hold per-request data in local variables and parameters. Here, that means calling charge(order) directly.

Spring calls a lifetime a bean scope. Spring has the three lifetimes that you know, under different names. It also has two more scopes for web applications:

ASP.NET CoreSpringNote
AddSingletonsingletonthe default in Spring, which gives one shared instance for the whole application
AddScopedrequestone instance per HTTP request, declared with @RequestScope
AddTransientprototypea new instance each time the bean is injected
n/asessionone instance per user's HTTP session
n/aapplicationone per deployed web application

The three lifetimes, side by sidetwist#

C#
// one SystemTime for the whole application
builder.Services.AddSingleton<SystemTime>();

// one Cart for each HTTP request
builder.Services.AddScoped<Cart>();

// a new IdGenerator every time one is injected
builder.Services.AddTransient<IdGenerator>();
Java 25
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Scope;
import org.springframework.web.context.annotation.RequestScope;

// one SystemTime for the whole application
@Service
class SystemTime { }

// one Cart for each HTTP request
@Service
@RequestScope
class Cart { }

// a new IdGenerator every time one is injected
@Service
@Scope("prototype")
class IdGenerator { }
Reading the code
class SystemTime { }

There is no scope annotation, so this bean is a singleton. Spring creates one SystemTime and injects that same object everywhere.

@RequestScope

Spring creates one Cart for each HTTP request, like AddScoped in ASP.NET Core. A singleton can still take a Cart in its constructor. Spring injects a stand-in object, which is called a proxy. Each time you call the proxy, it finds the cart of the current request.

@Scope("prototype")

Spring creates a new IdGenerator every time one is injected, like AddTransient in ASP.NET Core. In Spring, a transient lifetime is called prototype.

Beans for types you do not own#

The billing service calls an exchange-rate service over HTTP. It uses the Spring type RestClient for this. You cannot put @Service on RestClient, because RestClient is not your class. In ASP.NET Core you would register a factory function. In Spring you write a @Bean method inside a @Configuration class:

C#
var url = builder.Configuration["Rates:Url"]!;

builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp =>
    new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(url) });
Java 25
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

@Configuration
public class HttpConfig {

    @Bean
    RestClient ratesRestClient(
            @Value("${rates.url}") String url) {
        return RestClient.create(url);
    }
}
Reading the code
@Configuration

@Configuration marks a class that holds @Bean methods. Spring calls these methods at startup.

@Bean

The object that the method returns becomes a bean. The bean gets the name of the method, which is ratesRestClient. Any class can now take a RestClient in its constructor. Bean names must be unique. Two beans with the same name stop Boot from starting.

@Value("${rates.url}") String url

Spring injects the parameters of a @Bean method, like constructor parameters. This parameter is a single setting from the configuration. For the ${…} form, see the section Single values and precedence.

return RestClient.create(url);

This line builds a client whose requests all start with that address.

Multiple implementationstwist#

Two gateway classes implement one interface, PaymentGateway. So you must tell Spring which gateway CheckoutService gets. C# solves this with keyed services. Spring uses bean names:

C#
// CardGateway and BankGateway both
// implement IPaymentGateway
builder.Services
    .AddKeyedScoped<IPaymentGateway, CardGateway>("card")
    .AddKeyedScoped<IPaymentGateway, BankGateway>("bank");

public class CheckoutService(
    [FromKeyedServices("card")] IPaymentGateway gateway)
{
}
Java 25
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;

public interface PaymentGateway {
    void charge(Order order);
}

@Service("card")
class CardGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public void charge(Order order) { }
}

@Service("bank")
class BankGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public void charge(Order order) { }
}

@Service
public class CheckoutService {

    private final PaymentGateway gateway;

    CheckoutService(
            @Qualifier("card") PaymentGateway gateway) {
        this.gateway = gateway;
    }
}
Reading the code
@Service("card")

This annotation registers the bean under the name card. Without a name, Spring names a bean after its class, with a lower-case first letter. Here that name would be cardGateway.

@Qualifier("card") PaymentGateway gateway

@Qualifier asks for the bean named card, like [FromKeyedServices("card")] in ASP.NET Core. Without @Qualifier, Spring finds two matching beans and fails at startup.

@Qualifier is one of several ways to choose:

NeedSpring
Pick one by name@Qualifier("name")
Prefer one by default@Primary on that bean
Inject all of themList<PaymentGateway> or Map<String, PaymentGateway> parameter
Conditional registration@ConditionalOnProperty, @Profile

Injecting every implementation: List and Map#

A List<PaymentGateway> parameter is like injecting IEnumerable<T> in ASP.NET Core, but the list includes named beans. The .NET version does not include keyed registrations unless you ask for KeyedService.AnyKey. The Map form has no equivalent in ASP.NET Core. It gives you the beans keyed by name. Here the shop uses a Map to find the gateway for the payment method that the customer chose:

import java.util.Map;

@Service
public class PaymentRouter {

    private final Map<String, PaymentGateway> gateways;

    // Spring fills the map with every PaymentGateway bean, keyed by bean name.
    PaymentRouter(Map<String, PaymentGateway> gateways) {
        this.gateways = gateways;
    }

    void pay(String method, Order order) {
        gateways.get(method).charge(order);   // method is "card" or "bank"
    }
}
Reading the code
PaymentRouter(Map<String, PaymentGateway> gateways) {

A Map parameter with String keys receives every bean of that type, keyed by bean name. Here the names are card and bank. A List<PaymentGateway> parameter would receive the same beans, without the names.

gateways.get(method).charge(order);

This line gets the gateway for the customer's choice and charges the order. To add a third gateway, for vouchers, you write a new class and change nothing else.

Configuration filestwist#

Settings are in the file src/main/resources/application.yml. The file is written in YAML. YAML is a format that shows nesting with indentation instead of braces:

appsettings.json
{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "Default": "Server=localhost;Database=billing"
  },
  "Rates": {
    "Url": "https://rates.example.com",
    "TimeoutSeconds": 5
  },
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information" }
  }
}
application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost/billing

rates:
  url: https://rates.example.com
  timeout-seconds: 5

logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.acme.billing: DEBUG
Reading the code
url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost/billing

This is the setting spring.datasource.url. Each level of indentation adds one part to the name. Settings under spring: belong to Spring Boot itself. This setting is the database address, in the form used by Java Database Connectivity (JDBC).

timeout-seconds: 5

Your own settings can have any name. The convention in Boot is lower case with hyphens.

com.acme.billing: DEBUG

This is the log level for one package and everything below it.

Many projects use application.properties instead. This file holds the same settings, one per line, such as rates.timeout-seconds=5. Boot reads either file. A document database has its own setting, spring.mongodb.uri. For this setting, see the section Connecting to Amazon DocumentDB.

The MongoDB setting changed its nametrap#

A document database has a connection setting of its own, and Boot 4 renamed it:

spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://localhost:27017/billing
spring:
  mongodb:
    uri: mongodb://localhost:27017/billing
Reading the code
uri: mongodb://localhost:27017/billing

This is the connection string. Only the path to the setting differs. On Boot 3 the setting is spring.data.mongodb.uri. On Boot 4 the setting is spring.mongodb.uri.

Gotcha

Boot 4 ignores spring.data.mongodb.uri. A service that still sets the old name tries localhost:27017 instead. The first sign of the problem is a MongoTimeoutException. For the full settings, see the section Connecting to Amazon DocumentDB.

Profiles are environmentstwist#

A Spring profile is a named set of settings and beans that you switch on at startup. Examples are dev and prod. Here a fake email sender exists only on a developer's machine:

C#
// run with ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development;
// .NET then also loads appsettings.Development.json
if (builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    builder.Services
        .AddSingleton<IEmailSender, FakeEmailSender>();
Java 25
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Profile;

interface EmailSender {
    void send(String to, String text);
}

// run with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev;
// Boot then also loads application-dev.yml
@Service
@Profile("dev")
class FakeEmailSender implements EmailSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) { }
}
Reading the code
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev

This is an environment variable that switches on the dev profile, like ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT in ASP.NET Core. Boot then also reads application-dev.yml. Its settings override the settings in application.yml.

@Profile("dev")

Spring creates this bean only when the dev profile is active. With any other profile, the bean does not exist.

Several profiles can be active at the same time. You separate the names with commas, as in SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev,local. ASP.NET Core has one environment at a time. It reads Development,Local as a single name.

A bean for every profile except one#

A profile can also be excluded. This fake sender exists everywhere except in production, so no developer or test server has to remember to switch it on:

@Service
@Profile("!prod")           // active in every profile except prod
class FakeEmailSender implements EmailSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) { }
}
Reading the code
@Profile("!prod")

! means not. The bean is created unless the prod profile is active, so production needs a real sender of its own.

IOptions becomes @ConfigurationPropertiestwist#

You describe the whole rates section of the settings as one type. Here the type is a record. Spring fills the record with the values from the settings:

C#
public class RatesOptions
{
    public string Url { get; set; } = "";
    public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; }
}

builder.Services.Configure<RatesOptions>(
    builder.Configuration.GetSection("Rates"));

public class RatesClient(IOptions<RatesOptions> options)
{
}
Java 25
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.*;

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "rates")
public record RatesProperties(
        String url,
        int timeoutSeconds) { }

@Configuration
@EnableConfigurationProperties(RatesProperties.class)
class RatesConfig { }

// the record is injected itself, with no wrapper
@Service
class RatesClient {
    RatesClient(RatesProperties rates) { }
}
Reading the code
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "rates")

This annotation binds the rates section of application.yml to this type.

int timeoutSeconds) { }

A record is an immutable data class. See Records. Spring fills each component from the setting with the matching name, so timeoutSeconds gets the value of timeout-seconds.

@EnableConfigurationProperties(RatesProperties.class)

This annotation tells Spring to create a RatesProperties bean. On a larger service, put @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the application class instead. Spring then finds every such type itself.

RatesClient(RatesProperties rates) { }

Spring injects the record like any other bean.

The binding accepts several spellings of a name. rates.timeout-seconds, rates.timeoutSeconds and RATES_TIMEOUT_SECONDS all fill the same component. This is called relaxed binding. Because of relaxed binding, an environment variable can set any property.

Single values and precedence#

For a single setting, @Value injects the setting directly. @Value is useful in a @Bean method or a small class:

@Service
class RatesClient {

    RatesClient(@Value("${rates.url}") String url,
                @Value("${rates.timeout-seconds:5}") int timeoutSeconds) {
    }
}
Reading the code
@Value("${rates.url}") String url

${rates.url} is a placeholder. Spring replaces the placeholder with the value of the rates.url setting. If there is no such setting, Spring fails at startup.

${rates.timeout-seconds:5}

The text after the colon is a default. Spring uses the default when the setting is missing.

The same setting can come from several places. Here the container platform sets the exchange-rate address as an environment variable, and a startup script passes it again with -D:

export RATES_URL=https://rates.staging.example.com
java -Drates.url=https://rates.example.com -jar billing.jar
Reading the code
export RATES_URL=https://rates.staging.example.com

This line sets the environment variable RATES_URL. Relaxed binding reads RATES_URL as rates.url.

java -Drates.url=https://rates.example.com -jar billing.jar

This line starts the service with a Java system property of the same name. Spring uses the system property, because it is higher in the list below. You can also give an argument, such as --rates.url=…, after the name of the Java archive (JAR). Spring would then use that argument, and not the environment variable or the system property.

When the same setting is given in several places, Spring uses the source that is higher in this list:

PrioritySource
1command-line arguments
2SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON
3Java system properties, set with -D
4OS environment variables
5application-{profile}.yml
6application.yml
7@PropertySource
8defaults in code
Note

SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON is one environment variable that holds many settings, written as JSON. In the list, two more sources are between SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON and system properties. One source is the servlet container. The other source is the Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI), which is a lookup service provided by an old-style application server. These two sources rarely matter in a Boot service. For what a system property is, see the chapter How Java runs your code.

Gotcha

Environment variables are written in upper case with underscores. For example, RATES_TIMEOUT_SECONDS sets rates.timeout-seconds. ASP.NET Core marks each level of nesting with a double underscore, as in Rates__TimeoutSeconds. Spring needs no such convention. In Spring, a single underscore is enough.

Secrets#

The database password of the billing service must never be committed to the repository. Here is the Spring match for each .NET option for secrets:

.NETSpring
User Secretsapplication-local.yml, gitignored
Azure Key VaultSpring Cloud Azure, or HashiCorp Vault through Spring Cloud Vault
AWS Secrets ManagerSpring Cloud AWS
Environment variablesenvironment variables
.NET refresherdotnet user-secrets
dotnet user-secrets init
dotnet user-secrets set "Db:Password" "dev-only-secret"   # stored per user, outside the repo
Gotcha

Spring has no built-in equivalent of dotnet user-secrets. The common pattern is a file called application-local.yml. The file is listed in .gitignore, and a local profile switches it on. Do this on day one, because the alternative is a committed password. A committed password is the most common accident in Spring repositories.

Here is the local file for the billing service:

# src/main/resources/application-local.yml, listed in .gitignore
spring:
  datasource:
    password: dev-only-secret
# activate it with: ./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local
Reading the code
password: dev-only-secret

This is the development password. The file is listed in .gitignore, so git never commits the file.

-Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local

This argument runs the service with the local profile. So Boot also loads application-local.yml, and its settings override the settings in application.yml.

1
TranslateWrite this in Java, for Spring Boot: 
public class RatesOptions
{
    public string Url { get; set; } = "";
    public int TimeoutSeconds { get; set; }
}

builder.Services.Configure<RatesOptions>(
    builder.Configuration.GetSection("Rates"));

public class RatesClient(IOptions<RatesOptions> options) { }
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "rates")
record RatesProperties(String url, int timeoutSeconds) { }

@Configuration
@EnableConfigurationProperties(RatesProperties.class)
class RatesConfig { }

@Service
class RatesClient {

Spring injects the record itself, with no IOptions wrapper. The record is a bean only because @EnableConfigurationProperties names it. If you remove that line, Spring has no RatesProperties to inject.

2
The shop wants a fake email sender on a developer's machine and nowhere else. How do you write that in Spring, and how is it switched on?
Put @Profile("dev") on the bean class. Spring then creates the bean only while the dev profile is active. Switch the profile on with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev or --spring.profiles.active=dev. Boot then also loads application-dev.yml, and its settings override the settings in application.yml.
3
An expert asksOlder Spring code puts @Autowired on a private field. Why does new code take the dependency through the constructor instead?
A constructor parameter can be stored in a final field, and the constructor shows everything that the class depends on. A unit test can also create the class with new and pass a fake to the constructor. An @Autowired field hides the dependency, and a unit test cannot set the field without starting Spring.
