How Spring actually works#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 37· 12 min read· Quick reference

Spring does not change your class. It wraps it. Other classes often receive a stand-in object in place of your bean. The stand-in object is called a proxy. The proxy does what an annotation asks for, such as starting a transaction. Then the proxy calls your object.

KindC#JavaNote
newservices.Decorate<IOrderService, TransactionalDecorator>()an annotation such as @Transactional, and Spring makes the proxythe wrapper is generated while the program runs, and no code shows it Why
trapthis.Place(order) skips a decorator too, but you wrote that decoratorplace(order) from inside the class skips the proxya call that never leaves your object starts no transaction, and no code shows why Why
newno equivalenta CGLIB subclass, OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0Boot generates a subclass as the proxy, even for a bean with an interface Why
trapa method is not virtual unless you say soa final method loses its annotationIt runs on the proxy itself, with no transaction and with null injected fields. A final class stops startup. Why
twistorderService.GetType().FullNameorderService.getClass().getName()prints the generated subclass's name, because you hold the proxy Why
twistIHostedServicea bean that implements ApplicationRunnerBoot calls its run method one time, after the application context has started Why
twistwork in a constructorApplicationRunner, or a @PostConstruct methodwhile a constructor runs, other beans may not exist yet Why
twistthe service providerthe application context, with its BeanPostProcessorsa post-processor can replace a new bean, which is how proxies are made Why
twistmiddleware or an action filteran @Aspect class with @Aroundwraps one behaviour around many bean methods, not only controllers Why
twistno equivalent#{...} in an annotation valueSpEL evaluates an expression, but ${...} only reads a setting Why
twista dependency cycle throwsa cycle stops Boot at startupcycles are rejected by default since Boot 2.6, so extract a third bean Why
twistthe order of registration@Order(1) on the beansets a bean's place in an injected List, not the order of creation Why

What a proxy actually isnew#

The place method of the OrderService is marked @Transactional. This means that the method must run inside a database transaction. Spring cannot add code to your method. Instead, after Spring creates the OrderService, it puts a different object in the place of the OrderService. The different object is an instance of a subclass that Spring generates while the program runs. This object is called a proxy. The proxy starts the transaction, calls your place method, and commits. Every class that has the OrderService injected receives the proxy, not your object.

Think of a receptionist at an office. Visitors speak to the receptionist. The receptionist signs them in and then gives their message to a colleague.

C# has nothing that does this for you. You write the decorator class and register it yourself. In Spring, you write only the annotation:

C#: you wire it yourself
// no built-in support: use a DispatchProxy,
// or the Scrutor library's Decorate method
services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
services.Decorate<IOrderService, TransactionalDecorator>();

// the decoration is visible in your code
Spring: the container wraps it
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    @Transactional
    public void place(Order order) {
        // save the order
    }
}
// nothing here shows that a wrapper exists
Reading the code
services.Decorate<IOrderService, TransactionalDecorator>();

Scrutor wraps OrderService in your own TransactionalDecorator class, so the wrapping appears in Program.cs.

@Transactional

@Transactional asks Spring to run the method inside a transaction. To do this, Spring gives every other class a proxy instead of your object. For more about the transaction itself, see the chapter Transactions, propagation and isolation.

Self-invocation: a call from inside the classtrap#

PredictA method that calls a @Transactional method of its own class#
A controller calls placeAll. Does each call to place run in a transaction?
@Service
public class OrderService {

    public void placeAll(List<Order> orders) {
        for (var order : orders) {
            place(order);
        }
    }

    @Transactional
    public void place(Order order) {
        // save the order
    }
}
Show the answer
No. No transaction starts, and nothing warns you.

The controller reaches placeAll through the proxy. But placeAll has no @Transactional, so the proxy only calls placeAll on your object. Inside placeAll, place(order) means this.place(order). Your object calls itself, so the call never reaches the proxy.

Make the call come from outside, through the proxy. Here the loop moves to its own bean:

@Service
public class BatchService {

    private final OrderService orders;

    BatchService(OrderService orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    public void placeAll(List<Order> batch) {
        for (var order : batch) {
            orders.place(order);   // through the proxy: one transaction per order
        }
    }
}

orders is the injected proxy. So orders.place(order) goes through the proxy, and each order is placed in its own transaction.

When a method calls another method of its own object, this is called self-invocation. In the office picture, one colleague speaks to another colleague, and the receptionist never hears it.

There are four ways to fix this:

FixHowCost
Move the method to another beaninject it and call itbest, and usually better design anyway
Inject yourself@Autowired @Lazy OrderService self; then self.place(order)works but reads oddly, and without @Lazy, Boot rejects it as a cycle
AopContext.currentProxy()cast the result and call through itneeds exposeProxy=true, and is obscure
Use AspectJ weaving instead of proxiescompile-time or load-time weavingpowerful, much heavier
Note

Every annotation that works through a proxy behaves this way. For examples, see the chapters Data access, Security and HTTP clients and resilience. A private method fails too, because only its own class can call it. See the section The proxy trap, again.

Two kinds of proxytrap#

Spring Boot builds a proxy with the Code Generation Library (CGLIB). CGLIB generates a subclass of your class while the program runs.

PredictA final method marked @Transactional#
A controller calls place on the injected OrderService. Does it run in a transaction?
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @Transactional
    public final void place(Order order) {
        orders.save(order);
    }
}
Show the answer
No. It runs on the proxy object itself: no transaction starts, and the proxy's injected fields are null, so orders.save(order) throws NullPointerException.

A CGLIB proxy is a subclass, so final defeats it silently. A subclass cannot override a final method, so the proxy cannot wrap that method. The call runs the method on the proxy object. Spring never set that object's fields. Only your real object has its orders. The one notice is a startup warning that the method “cannot get proxied via CGLIB”. Java methods are virtual by default, and C# methods are not. So a final added for safety breaks the method.

Remove final. A final class does not fail silently. The application stops at startup with “Cannot subclass final class”. This is also why Kotlin needs a Spring plugin. Kotlin classes and methods are final by default. The kotlin-spring plugin opens the classes that carry Spring annotations.

Java also has built-in dynamic proxies, but they only work through an interface. The kind of proxy that you get depends on the bean and on one setting, proxyTargetClass:

KindUsed whenBuilt byLimitation
JDK dynamic proxythe bean implements an interface, and proxyTargetClass is falsejava.lang.reflect.Proxyonly interface methods are proxied
CGLIB proxythere is no interface, or proxyTargetClass is truea generated subclasscannot proxy final classes or final methods
Note

Spring Boot sets proxyTargetClass=true by default. So you almost always get a CGLIB subclass, even for a bean that implements an interface. That is why the bean's class name in a stack trace looks like OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0. It is also why your class needs a constructor that is not private. The generated subclass must be able to see a constructor.

Seeing the proxy for yourself#

You can see the proxy for yourself by printing the class of an injected bean:

@Service
public class OrderService {          // no interface, so Spring subclasses it
    @Transactional public void place(Order order) { }
}

// in any bean that has the OrderService injected:
System.out.println(orderService.getClass().getName());
// prints com.acme.billing.OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
Reading the code
System.out.println(orderService.getClass().getName());

getClass() returns the class of the object that you actually hold. That object is the proxy.

// prints com.acme.billing.OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0

This is the name of a subclass of OrderService that Spring generated. $$SpringCGLIB$$ shows that Spring generated the class. The number at the end keeps generated names unique.

Work at startuptwist#

C# refresherIHostedService: code that runs when the host startsC# 6
public class Warmup : IHostedService
{
    public Task StartAsync(CancellationToken ct) => LoadCachesAsync(ct);   // at startup
    public Task StopAsync(CancellationToken ct) => Task.CompletedTask;     // at shutdown
}

builder.Services.AddHostedService<Warmup>();

Boot calls this bean after the application context is fully started:

import org.springframework.boot.ApplicationArguments;
import org.springframework.boot.ApplicationRunner;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
class Warmup implements ApplicationRunner {

    // Boot calls this once, after every bean is ready.
    // args holds the command-line arguments the application was started with.
    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        loadExchangeRates();
    }

    private void loadExchangeRates() {
        // read today's rates into memory
    }
}
Reading the code
class Warmup implements ApplicationRunner {

Boot finds every bean that implements ApplicationRunner. After startup, Boot calls the run method of each of these beans. The run method is like StartAsync in ASP.NET Core.

Gotcha

Do not use injected dependencies in a constructor body for work that needs the whole context. While your constructor runs, the application is still starting. Other beans may not exist yet, and your own bean has no proxy yet. Put such work, for example loading caches, in an ApplicationRunner.

Work that needs only this bean's own dependencies can go in a method marked @PostConstruct. Spring runs this method after injection. The annotation @PostConstruct is in the package jakarta.annotation. But if this method calls the bean's own @Transactional methods, no transaction starts, because the call is self-invocation.

The bean lifecycle#

The object that creates and holds all the beans is called the application context. The application context is like the service provider in ASP.NET Core. At startup, the application context finds the beans, from component scanning and from @Bean methods. It then creates each bean through the constructor of the bean. This is the point where constructor injection happens. After that, each bean goes through the rest of these steps:

ASP.NET Core builds an object and gives it to you. Spring builds a bean and then shows the bean to every BeanPostProcessor. A BeanPostProcessor is a class that can decorate, replace or reject a bean before any other class sees the bean. The Spring framework extends itself this way. Proxies are made in the step after your initialisation code.

This table shows when each step happens, next to its nearest equivalent in ASP.NET Core:

ASP.NET CoreSpringWhen
constructorconstructordependencies arrive
n/a@PostConstructafter all dependencies are set
n/aInitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()same point, interface form
n/aBeanPostProcessoraround every bean, and this is how the framework extends itself
IDisposable / IAsyncDisposable@PreDestroycontainer shutdown
IHostedService.StartAsyncApplicationRunner, @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent)after the context has started

Here a RateCache bean needs a RatesClient. The bean uses three of those steps:

@Service
class RateCache {

    private final RatesClient client;

    RateCache(RatesClient client) {     // dependencies arrive
        this.client = client;
    }

    @PostConstruct
    void load() { }                     // after all dependencies are set

    @PreDestroy
    void clear() { }                    // at container shutdown
}

@PostConstruct and @PreDestroy mark methods that Spring calls for you. Spring calls load after injection is done. Spring calls clear when the application shuts down.

AOP: writing your own cross-cutting behaviour#

Aspect-oriented programming (AOP) means adding the same behaviour around many methods without editing each one. An example is timing every service call. Spring does this with proxies, and AOP is the API for adding your own behaviour. AOP is like ASP.NET Core middleware, an action filter or a DispatchProxy decorator. But AOP works on any bean method, not only on controllers.

The class that holds the behaviour is called an aspect. Here the billing service logs how long every service method takes:

import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Aspect
@Component
public class TimingAspect {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(TimingAspect.class);

    // every public method in a class marked @Service
    @Around("@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service) && execution(public * *(..))")
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint call) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return call.proceed();          // run the real method
        } finally {
            log.debug("{} took {} ms", call.getSignature(),
                      (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000);
        }
    }
}
Reading the code
@Aspect

This annotation marks the class as an aspect. @Component makes the class a bean, so Spring finds it.

@Around("@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service) && execution(public * *(..))")

This expression says which methods to wrap. execution(public * *(..)) means any public method, with any return type, name and parameters. @within(…Service) limits the match to classes marked @Service.

return call.proceed();

This line runs the real method and returns its result. Without this line, the real method never runs.

} finally {

The finally block runs whether the method returned or threw, as it does in C#. So every call is timed. Each {} in the log message is replaced by the next argument.

The code that an aspect runs is called advice. @Around is one kind of advice. Here are all five kinds:

AdviceRuns.NET analogy
@Beforebefore the methodfilter OnActionExecuting
@AfterReturningafter a successful returnOnActionExecuted
@AfterThrowingonly on exceptionexception filter
@Afteralways, like finallyfinally block
@Aroundwraps the call, and you invoke proceed()middleware

The expression in @Around is called a pointcut. A pointcut selects the methods to wrap. These are the common forms:

Pointcut expressionMatches
execution(* com.acme..*Service.*(..))any method on any *Service under that package
@annotation(com.acme.Audited)any method annotated @Audited
@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)any method in a class annotated @Service
within(com.acme.billing..*)any method in that package tree
args(String, ..)first argument is a String
Gotcha

Aspects are applied by the same proxies, so every limitation above applies to aspects too. Self-invocation skips an aspect. A final method stops an aspect from running. An object that you create yourself with new is never wrapped. When an aspect seems not to run, the cause is almost always one of those three.

AspectJ weaving does not wrap your classes. It changes your compiled classes themselves, so it also covers calls inside a class. But AspectJ weaving needs an extra step in the build or at startup.

SpEL#

Spring Expression Language (SpEL) is a small expression language that runs inside annotation values. It is written #{...}. You will see SpEL in @PreAuthorize for security and in @Cacheable for caching. SpEL also works in @Value. Here SpEL reads a pricing region from a system property:

@Service
class RegionalPricing {

    private final String region;

    // SpEL: the user.region system property, or "eu" when it is not set
    RegionalPricing(@Value("#{systemProperties['user.region'] ?: 'eu'}") String region) {
        this.region = region;
    }
}
Reading the code
#{systemProperties['user.region'] ?: 'eu'}

#{...} marks SpEL. systemProperties['user.region'] reads a Java system property. The operator ?: supplies 'eu' when the property is missing. ?: is like ?? in C#.

In the other annotations, SpEL reads the method's parameters by name, with a # in front:

// in a service with method security: only the order's owner may cancel it
@PreAuthorize("#order.owner == authentication.name")
public void cancel(Order order) { }

// in a service with caching: one cache entry per currency pair and date
@Cacheable(value = "rates", key = "#pair + ':' + #date")
public BigDecimal lookup(String pair, LocalDate date) { ... }
Reading the code
@PreAuthorize("#order.owner == authentication.name")

#order is the order parameter, and authentication is the logged-in user. The method runs only when the owner of the order is the user who calls the method.

key = "#pair + ':' + #date"

This expression builds the cache key from both parameters, for example EURUSD:2026-09-13.

Gotcha

${...} and #{...} are different things. ${...} is called a property placeholder, and it reads configuration. #{...} is SpEL, and it evaluates an expression. If you write one in place of the other, you get a literal string or a startup failure. The error message rarely says which mistake you made.

Circular dependencies#

Say the OrderService needs the BillingService to create an invoice. And the BillingService needs the OrderService to find the order. Then Spring cannot create the first bean without the second bean, and it cannot create the second bean without the first bean:

@Service
class OrderService {
    OrderService(BillingService billing) { }
}

@Service
class BillingService {
    BillingService(OrderService orders) { }
}
Reading the code
OrderService(BillingService billing) { }

To create an OrderService, Spring needs a BillingService. But to create a BillingService, Spring needs an OrderService.

ASP.NET Core throws an exception when it finds a dependency cycle. Spring used to resolve some cycles by injecting a half-built object. This caused bugs that were hard to find. Since Boot 2.6, cycles are rejected by default, and Boot stops at startup with this report:

The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:

┌─────┐
|  billingService defined in file [.../BillingService.class]
↑     ↓
|  orderService defined in file [.../OrderService.class]
└─────┘
Reading the code
┌─────┐

The box draws the loop. Each bean in the box needs the next bean, and the last bean needs the first bean.

There are four things you can try, and only the first one is a real fix:

FixNote
Extract the shared logic into a third beanthe usual fix, because a cycle often hides a missing third responsibility
@Lazy on one of the injection pointsSpring injects a proxy and creates the real bean on first use, but this hides a design problem
spring.main.allow-circular-references=truethis setting enables the old behaviour again, so avoid it
Setter injectionThis no longer works. Since Boot 2.6 a cycle through setters or fields fails too, unless circular references are allowed.
Note

A cycle is a sign of a design problem, not a limitation of the container. It nearly always means that two beans share a responsibility, and that this responsibility should have its own name. The other options in the table exist for legacy code that is being migrated, not for new work.

Ordering and conditional beans#

When a service has many beans, two questions appear. In what order do the beans run? And does a certain bean exist at all? These annotations answer both questions:

NeedAnnotation
Order a list of injected beans@Order(n) on each, or implement Ordered
Force one bean to be built first@DependsOn("otherBean")
Register only if a property is set@ConditionalOnProperty
Register only if a class is present@ConditionalOnClass
Register only if nobody else defined one@ConditionalOnMissingBean
Register only in some profiles@Profile("!prod")

Here checkout runs a list of steps, and the audit step must come before the pricing step:

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

interface CheckoutStep { }

@Component @Order(1) class AuditStep implements CheckoutStep { }
@Component @Order(2) class PricingStep implements CheckoutStep { }

@Service
class Checkout {
    Checkout(List<CheckoutStep> steps) { }   // AuditStep first, then PricingStep
}
Reading the code
@Component @Order(1) class AuditStep implements CheckoutStep { }

A bean with a lower number comes first in any injected List of this type.

Checkout(List<CheckoutStep> steps) { }

The constructor receives every CheckoutStep bean, sorted by @Order.

Gotcha

@Order sets the order of beans within an injected collection, and the order of aspects and filters. It does not set the order in which beans are created. Dependencies decide the order of creation. @DependsOn is the only way to add a dependency that the code itself does not have.

Check yourself
1

builder.Services.AddHostedService<Warmup>();

class Warmup implements ApplicationRunner {

Boot calls run one time, after every bean is ready. Do not do this work in the constructor, because other beans may not exist yet while a constructor runs.

An expert asksA stack trace names the class OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0, although OrderService implements an interface. Why, and why must the class have a constructor that is not private?
This class is the proxy that every other class has injected. Boot sets proxyTargetClass=true by default. So the proxy is a subclass that CGLIB generates while the program runs, even for a bean with an interface. A subclass must be able to see a constructor.

SymptomCauseFix

Controllers, routing and binding#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 38· 11 min read· Quick reference

The web framework of Spring is called Spring MVC. It is named after the model-view-controller (MVC) pattern. Spring MVC does the same as ASP.NET Core MVC. A controller, its routes and its parameter binding each have a direct match in Spring MVC. They are written as annotations.

KindC#JavaNote
twist[ApiController] on a ControllerBase class@RestControllerevery return value is written to the response body, as JSON Why
twist[Route("api/x")]@RequestMapping("/api/x")on the class, as a prefix for every method's path Why
twist[HttpGet], [HttpPost], [HttpPut], [HttpPatch], [HttpDelete]@GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMappingthere is one annotation for each verb, and its path is added to the class prefix Why
twist[HttpGet("{id:int}")]@GetMapping("/{id}")Spring infers the type from the parameter Why
twistroute constraint :inta regular expression: {id:\d+}A path that does not match the expression gets 404. Without an expression, a value that cannot be converted gets 400. Why
twist[Produces("application/json")]produces = "application/json"an attribute of the mapping annotation, not a separate one Why
twist[Consumes(...)]consumes = "..."an attribute of the mapping annotation too, as produces is Why
twist[FromRoute]@PathVariablebinds a part of the URL path, converted to the parameter's type Why
twist[FromQuery]@RequestParambinds one value from the query string, as in ?q=tea Why
trap[FromQuery] int page is 0 when missing@RequestParam int pagerequired by default, whatever the type, so a request without it gets 400 Why
twist[FromHeader]@RequestHeaderbinds a request header, which is also required by default Why
twist[FromBody]@RequestBodybinds the request body, which Jackson reads from JSON Why
twistno equivalentthe compiler's -parameters flagSpring reads a parameter's name from the class file, and Boot's parent POM sets the flag for you Why
twista request or response classa record, such as CreateOrderJackson reads and writes records directly, so a DTO should be one Why
twistOk(x), NotFound() and the other result helpersthe value itself, or a ResponseEntityYou return the value for a plain 200. A ResponseEntity sets any other status, and build() finishes a response with no body. Why
twistmiddleware and action filtersa servlet Filter and a HandlerInterceptora filter sees every request, but an interceptor wraps controller methods only Why
twistAddCors and UseCorsaddCorsMappings in a WebMvcConfigurerthe cross-origin rules are in one configuration class Why
twistversioned routes, such as api/v1/orders@GetMapping(version = "1.0")built-in versioning is new in Boot 4, and Boot 3 uses separate paths instead Why
twistAddSwaggerGen()the springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui dependencythe UI appears with no configuration, generated from your controllers Why

A controllertwist#

ASP.NET Core
[ApiController]
[Route("api/orders")]
public class OrdersController(IOrderService orders)
    : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("{id:int}")]
    public async Task<ActionResult<OrderDto>> Get(int id)
    {
        var order = await orders.FindAsync(id);
        return order is null ? NotFound() : Ok(order);
    }

    [HttpPost]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Create(
        [FromBody] CreateOrder request)
    {
        var created = await orders.CreateAsync(request);
        return CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get),
            new { id = created.Id }, created);
    }
}
Spring MVC
import java.net.URI;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;

    public OrderController(OrderService orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> get(
            @PathVariable long id) {
        return orders.find(id)
                .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
                .orElseGet(() ->
                        ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(
            @RequestBody CreateOrder request) {
        var created = orders.create(request);
        var location =
                URI.create("/api/orders/" + created.id());
        return ResponseEntity.created(location)
                .body(created);
    }
}
Reading the code
@RestController

This annotation makes the class a bean. The return values of its methods are written into the response body as JSON, by Jackson. @RestController does the same as [ApiController] and ControllerBase together.

@RequestMapping("/api/orders")

This is the path prefix for every method, like [Route] in ASP.NET Core.

@PathVariable long id) {

This parameter takes id from the {id} part of the path. Spring converts the text to a long. If Spring cannot convert the text, the request fails with 400 Bad Request.

.map(ResponseEntity::ok)

find returns an Optional. For more about Optional, see the Optional chapter. If the Optional holds an order, the order becomes a 200 OK response. ResponseEntity::ok is a method reference. It is short for order -> ResponseEntity.ok(order).

@RequestBody CreateOrder request) {

This annotation reads the JSON request body into a CreateOrder, like [FromBody] in ASP.NET Core.

return ResponseEntity.created(location)

This line returns 201 Created, with a Location header for the new order, like CreatedAtAction in ASP.NET Core.

Routing and verbstwist#

@RestController
@RequestMapping(path = "/api/orders", produces = "application/json")
class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/{id:\\d+}")                // only digits match
    OrderDto get(@PathVariable long id) { ... }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    OrderDto replace(@PathVariable long id, @RequestBody OrderDto order) { ... }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    void delete(@PathVariable long id) { ... }
}
Reading the code
@RequestMapping(path = "/api/orders", produces = "application/json")

path is the prefix for every path in the class. produces says that every method returns JSON, like [Produces] in ASP.NET Core. In Spring, produces is an attribute of the mapping annotation, not a separate annotation.

@GetMapping("/{id:\\d+}")

The part after the colon is a regular expression. Here the expression means one or more digits, so it works like the route constraint {id:int}. A request for /api/orders/abc gets 404 and does not reach the method. In a Java string, you write the backslash twice.

@PutMapping("/{id}")

There is one annotation for each HTTP verb. @GetMapping, @PostMapping and @PutMapping are three of them. The other two are @PatchMapping and @DeleteMapping.

Model bindingtrap#

PredictA query parameter the client leaves out#
A client sends GET /api/orders/search with no query string. What comes back?
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<OrderDto> search(@RequestParam int page) {
        return List.of();
    }
}
Show the answer
400 Bad Request. search is never called.

@RequestParam is required by default, whatever its type. In an ASP.NET Core controller, a missing int binds to 0, and a missing string? binds to null. Only a non-nullable string is required there. A request without it gets 400, with the message “The q field is required.”

Write required = false, or supply a defaultValue.

Each parameter has an annotation that says where its value comes from:

C#
[HttpGet("search/{region}")]
public List<OrderDto> Search(
    [FromRoute] string region,
    [FromQuery] string q,
    [FromQuery] int page = 0,
    [FromQuery] string? status = null,
    [FromHeader(Name = "X-Tenant")] string tenant = "")
{
    ...
}
Java 25
@GetMapping("/search/{region}")
public List<OrderDto> search(
        @PathVariable String region,
        @RequestParam String q,
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
        @RequestParam(required = false) String status,
        @RequestHeader(value = "X-Tenant",
                required = false) String tenant) {
    ...
}
Reading the code
@PathVariable String region,

This value comes from the {region} segment of the path, like [FromRoute].

@RequestParam String q,

This value comes from the query string, as in ?q=tea, like [FromQuery]. The parameter is required, so a request without q gets 400 Bad Request. A non-nullable string in an [ApiController] behaves the same way.

@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,

This parameter is optional. A missing page becomes 0.

@RequestParam(required = false) String status,

This parameter is optional. A missing status becomes null.

@RequestHeader(value = "X-Tenant",

This value comes from the X-Tenant header, like [FromHeader]. Headers are required by default too, so this header is marked required = false.

Spring Data adds one more kind of parameter, a Pageable. This parameter is filled from the query parameters page, size and sort. This book does not show a Pageable in code.

Where Spring gets a parameter's name#

None of the binding annotations above names its parameter. Spring reads the name, such as q, from the compiled class. This only works when the compiler keeps parameter names. A build that does not keep parameter names gives this error:

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Name for argument of type [long] not specified, and parameter name information not available via reflection. Ensure that the compiler uses the '-parameters' flag.#
Means
Spring needs the parameter's name, here id, to know which part of the request to bind. The class was compiled without the setting that keeps parameter names in the class file.
Fix
The parent Project Object Model (POM) of Spring Boot sets the compiler's -parameters flag for you. So this error appears only in builds that do not use the parent POM. In such a build, add -parameters to the compiler options, or name the value: @PathVariable("id").
What triggers it
// compiled without -parameters
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> get(@PathVariable long id) { ... }

Records as DTOstwist#

Types that only carry data in and out of an API are called data transfer objects (DTOs). In Java, DTOs should be records, because Jackson reads and writes records directly:

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotEmpty;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;

public record CreateOrder(
        @NotBlank String customerId,
        @NotEmpty List<OrderLine> lines) { }

public record OrderLine(String sku, int quantity) { }

public record OrderDto(long id, String status, BigDecimal total) { }
Reading the code
public record CreateOrder(

This record is the request body. Jackson fills each component from the JSON property with the same name, as in {"customerId": "c1", "lines": [{"sku": "A-1", "quantity": 2}]}.

@NotBlank String customerId,

These annotations are Bean Validation rules. They are checked when the parameter is marked @Valid. See the next chapter.

public record OrderDto(long id, String status, BigDecimal total) { }

This record is the response. It is written as {"id":1,"status":"PAID","total":19.99}.

Gotcha

A record has no no-argument constructor. Its accessors have names like id(), not getId(). Modern Jackson handles this. Another library, or a Jackson version older than roughly 2.12, fails to deserialise a record. The failure has a confusing message about missing creators. Check the version before you rewrite the record as a class.

Returning resultstwist#

C#
// valid, deleted, teapot, errors and pdf
// come from earlier in the method
if (!valid) return BadRequest(errors);
if (deleted) return NoContent();
if (teapot) return StatusCode(418);

return File(pdf, "application/pdf", "invoice.pdf");
Java 25
import org.springframework.core.io.ByteArrayResource;
import org.springframework.http.*;

// valid, deleted, teapot, errors and pdf
// come from earlier in the method
if (!valid) return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(errors);
if (deleted) return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
if (teapot) return ResponseEntity.status(418).build();

return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION,
                "attachment; filename=invoice.pdf")
        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
        .body(new ByteArrayResource(pdf));
Reading the code
ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(errors);

This line returns a 400 with the errors as the JSON body, like BadRequest(errors).

ResponseEntity.noContent().build();

build() finishes a response that has no body. Here the response is 204 No Content.

ResponseEntity.status(418).build();

This line sets any status code, by its number.

.body(new ByteArrayResource(pdf));

This line returns a file download, like File(...). The bytes are wrapped as a Resource, and the Content-Disposition header names the file.

Note

If you do not need to set a status or headers, return the value directly. Spring then serialises the value with a 200. Use ResponseEntity<T> only where you actually change the status or the headers. A third option is the annotation @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on the method. It sets a fixed status other than 200.

For an error, ASP.NET Core returns Problem(). Spring returns a ProblemDetail. See the section ProblemDetail.

Middleware#

C# refresherASP.NET Core middleware and action filtersC# 5

Middleware sees every request on its way through the pipeline. A filter wraps only controller actions. A filter has access to the arguments and the result of the action.

app.Use(async (ctx, next) =>            // middleware: every request
{
    ctx.Response.Headers["X-Trace"] = "1";
    await next();
});

public class TimingFilter : IActionFilter   // filter: around controller actions only
{
    public void OnActionExecuting(ActionExecutingContext c) { }
    public void OnActionExecuted(ActionExecutedContext c) { }
}

Java web servers are built on the Jakarta Servlet standard. A class that handles HTTP requests is called a servlet. Spring MVC itself runs as one servlet, the DispatcherServlet. The DispatcherServlet routes each request to a controller method. Code that must see every request runs before the DispatcherServlet. Such code is called a servlet filter. Code that wraps only controller methods is called a HandlerInterceptor:

ASP.NET CoreSpringRuns
app.Use(...) middlewareServlet Filterbefore the dispatcher, and sees every request
IActionFilterHandlerInterceptoraround controller methods
IAsyncActionFilterHandlerInterceptor
IExceptionFilter@ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler
IAuthorizationFilterSpring Security filter chain
Endpoint routingDispatcherServlet

The shop gives every request a correlation id. With this id, all the log lines for one request can be found together. A filter reads the id from a header, or creates a new id:

import jakarta.servlet.*;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class CorrelationIdFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        var id = Optional.ofNullable(((HttpServletRequest) req).getHeader("X-Correlation-Id"))
                         .orElseGet(() -> UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        MDC.put("correlationId", id);        // shows up in every log line
        try {
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } finally {
            MDC.clear();
        }
    }
}
Reading the code
public class CorrelationIdFilter implements Filter {

This class is a servlet filter. Because the class is also a @Component, Spring Boot registers it to run for every request.

MDC.put("correlationId", id);

The mapped diagnostic context (MDC) belongs to the Simple Logging Facade for Java (SLF4J). SLF4J is the logging API that most Java code uses. The MDC holds values for the current thread, and the log format can print these values on every line. The MDC is like a logging scope in Serilog.

chain.doFilter(req, res);

This line sends the request to the next filter, and in the end to Spring MVC. It is like await next() in ASP.NET Core middleware.

MDC.clear();

This line runs in finally. So the next request that this thread handles never sees the id.

A HandlerInterceptor does the same as an action filter in ASP.NET Core. It runs around controller methods only:

class TimingInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, Object handler) {
        req.setAttribute("t0", System.nanoTime());
        return true;                    // false stops the request here
    }
}
Reading the code
public boolean preHandle(

This method runs before the controller method, like OnActionExecuting.

return true;

Returning true lets the request continue. Returning false stops the request here.

Spring Boot registers a filter for you, but you must register an interceptor yourself. You register it in a configuration class that implements WebMvcConfigurer. The cross-origin rules go in the same class.

The shop's web front end runs at https://shop.example.com and calls the API at another address. Browsers block such cross-origin calls unless the API says that the origin of the front end is allowed. This permission system is called cross-origin resource sharing (CORS):

C#
builder.Services.AddCors(o => o.AddDefaultPolicy(p => p
    .WithOrigins("https://shop.example.com")
    .WithMethods("GET", "POST")));

app.UseCors();
Java 25
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.*;

@Configuration
class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                .allowedOrigins("https://shop.example.com")
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST");
    }

    @Override
    public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
        registry.addInterceptor(new TimingInterceptor());
    }
}
Reading the code
registry.addMapping("/api/**")

This line applies the rule to every path under /api. ** matches any number of path segments.

.allowedOrigins("https://shop.example.com")

Only pages from this origin may call the API. The browser first sends a check request, which is called a preflight. Spring answers the preflight. A preflight from any other origin gets 403.

registry.addInterceptor(new TimingInterceptor());

This line registers the interceptor from above, for every controller method.

Gotcha

Do not put @EnableWebMvc on this class in a Boot application. @EnableWebMvc tells Spring that you configure the web layer entirely yourself. This disables Boot's own web setup. Implementing WebMvcConfigurer is enough. For a single controller, @CrossOrigin on the controller class sets the same rule.

API versioning#

The shop's order endpoint changed its format, and old mobile apps still call the old endpoint. Spring Framework 7 added built-in API versioning Boot 4. On Boot 3 you write the versioning yourself, usually with separate paths:

// Boot 3: versioning by path, the common convention
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
class OrderControllerV1 { }

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v2/orders")
class OrderControllerV2 { }
// Boot 4: the version is part of the mapping
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderController {

    @GetMapping(version = "1.0")
    OrderDtoV1 getV1() { ... }

    @GetMapping(version = "1.1")
    OrderDtoV2 getV11() { ... }
}
Reading the code
@GetMapping(version = "1.0")

This method answers requests for version 1.0, and the next method answers requests for version 1.1. Spring selects the method from the version that the request asks for.

On Boot 4, one setting says where the request carries its version, here in a header:

spring:
  mvc:
    apiversion:
      use:
        header: X-API-Version
Reading the code
header: X-API-Version

This setting tells Spring to read the version from the X-API-Version header. The version can also come from a query parameter, a path segment or a media type parameter. The other use settings select these.

Unless you set a default version, a request that sends no version is rejected with 400 Bad Request. A request for a version that no method supports is rejected with 400 Bad Request too.

Note

Boot 4 also supports the version on the client side. RestClient, WebClient and HTTP interface clients can all send a version. Tests can send a version too, through WebTestClient and MockMvc.

OpenAPI#

C# refresherSwashbuckle: OpenAPI for ASP.NET CoreC# 3
builder.Services.AddEndpointsApiExplorer();
builder.Services.AddSwaggerGen();

app.UseSwagger();       // the document, at /swagger/v1/swagger.json
app.UseSwaggerUI();     // the browsable UI, at /swagger
.NETSpring
Swashbuckle / NSwagspringdoc-openapi
[ProducesResponseType]@ApiResponse
[SwaggerOperation]@Operation
XML doc commentsjavadoc, plus annotations
/swagger/swagger-ui.html

Add the springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui dependency, and the UI appears with no configuration. The UI is generated from your controllers, records and Bean Validation annotations. You add annotations only when you want to say more than the code says:

@Operation(summary = "Fetch one order")                      // [SwaggerOperation]
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "no such order")   // [ProducesResponseType]
@GetMapping("/{id}")
OrderDto get(@PathVariable long id) { ... }
Reading the code
@Operation(summary = "Fetch one order")

This is the one-line summary of the operation in the generated document.

@ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "no such order")

This annotation documents a response that the method can give in addition to the normal 200.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this action in Java, for a Spring controller. orders.delete(id) returns true when the order existed: 
[HttpDelete("{id:int}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Delete(int id)
{
    var found = await orders.DeleteAsync(id);
    return found ? NoContent() : NotFound();
}
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable long id) {
    return orders.delete(id)
            ? ResponseEntity.noContent().build()
            : ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
}

noContent() and notFound() return builders, not responses. build() finishes a response that has no body. ResponseEntity<Void> is the return type for such a response.

2
An expert asksA controller method has a long id parameter. Why does GET /api/orders/abc get 400 from @GetMapping("/{id}"), but 404 from @GetMapping("/{id:\\d+}")?
With /{id} the path matches. Spring then fails to convert abc to a long, so the response is 400. The part after the colon is a regular expression. With \\d+ the path does not match at all. No method handles the request, so the response is 404.

Quick reference#

C# refresherA cookie and an uploaded file in an ASP.NET Core actionC# 6

ASP.NET Core has no binding attribute for a cookie, so the action reads the cookie from the request. An uploaded file arrives as an IFormFile parameter.

[HttpGet("theme")]
public string Theme() => Request.Cookies["theme"] ?? "none";

[HttpPost("upload")]
public string Upload(IFormFile file, [FromForm] string note)
    => $"{file.FileName}: {file.Length} bytes, {note}";
ASP.NET CoreSpringNote
[FromForm]@RequestParam / @ModelAttributethe same annotations bind the fields of submitted form data
[FromServices]just take a constructor dependencythe container supplies it, through the controller's constructor
Request.Cookies["theme"]@CookieValueIt binds the value of one cookie to a method parameter. ASP.NET Core has no binding attribute for a cookie.
IFormFile@RequestPartbinds one part of a multipart request, such as an uploaded file, to a method parameter
ASP.NET CoreSpringNote
ActionResult<OrderDto>OrderDto, or ResponseEntity<OrderDto>Spring has no IActionResult hierarchy, so return the value, or wrap it in a ResponseEntity
Ok(value)ResponseEntity.ok(value), or just return the valuea returned value is written as JSON, with status 200
NotFound()ResponseEntity.notFound().build()build() finishes a response that has no body
BadRequest(x)ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(x)answers 400, with x written as the JSON body
NoContent()ResponseEntity.noContent().build()answers 204 No Content, for example after a delete
Created(uri, x)ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(x)answers 201 Created, with a Location header for the new resource

Validation and error responses#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 39· 10 min read

Jakarta Validation is a standard, and it is also called Bean Validation. It does the same as DataAnnotations in .NET. You put constraint annotations on a record, and they are checked before your method runs. Error bodies follow RFC 9457. ProblemDetails in ASP.NET Core follows the same standard.

KindC#JavaNote
trap[Required]@NotNullrejects null only, so an empty string still passes Why
twist[Required] on a string@NotBlankrejects null, empty and whitespace-only strings Why
twist[MinLength(1)] on a collection@NotEmptyrejects null and empty values, on a string or on a collection Why
twist[StringLength(n)]@Size(max = n)sets a length limit, and on a collection or map it limits the size Why
twist[Range(a, b)]@Min(a) @Max(b)or use @Range, which comes from Hibernate Validator Why
twist[EmailAddress]@Emailtreats a missing value as valid, so add @NotBlank to require one Why
twist[RegularExpression(p)]@Pattern(regexp = p)the value must match the regular expression p Why
twist[Compare]no equivalentJakarta Validation has none, so write a class-level constraint Why
newno equivalent@Positive, @Negative, @PositiveOrZeroconstraints on the sign of a number, which .NET lacks Why
newno equivalent@Past, @Future, @PastOrPresentconstraints on dates in the past or future, which work on java.time types Why
trapa nested object is validated without being asked@Valid on the nested fieldwithout it, the constraints inside the nested object are never checked Why
twist[CreditCard]@CreditCardNumberfrom Hibernate Validator, not the Jakarta standard set Why
trap[ApiController] automatic 400@Valid on the parameterwithout @Valid nothing is checked, and nothing warns you Why
twistvalidation of a single query parameter@RequestParam @Min(0) int pagechecked with no @Valid, and fails with a different exception Why
twistAddProblemDetails()spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: trueBoot's RFC 9457 error bodies are switched off by default Why
twistan errors member that lists each fieldno field list in the default bodySpring's default body says only "Invalid request content." Why
twistthe errors member, filled in for youoverride handleMethodArgumentNotValidmost teams add each failing field to the body themselves Why
twistIExceptionFilter@RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandlerone class turns an exception into a response for every controller Why
trapa second handler class for validation errorshandleMethodArgumentNotValid, overridden in the one advice classthe one advice class already handles this exception, and which of two classes answers depends on their names Why
twista FluentValidation validator classan annotation plus a ConstraintValidator classa custom constraint is then used like any built-in one Why

Constraint annotationstwist#

C#
// System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations
public record CreateOrder(
    [Required, StringLength(50)] string CustomerId,
    [Range(1, 100)] int Quantity,
    [EmailAddress] string Email);
Java 25
import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

public record CreateOrder(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 50) String customerId,
        @Min(1) @Max(100) int quantity,
        @Email String email) { }
Reading the code
@NotBlank @Size(max = 50) String customerId,

The value must have at least one character that is not whitespace, and at most 50 characters. A component can have several constraints, like [Required, StringLength(50)] in C#.

@Min(1) @Max(100) int quantity,

The value must be a number from 1 to 100, like [Range(1, 100)] in C#.

@Email String email

The value must look like an email address. Like most constraints, @Email treats a missing value as valid. To require a value, add @NotBlank as well.

Spring Boot checks these annotations with Hibernate Validator. Hibernate Validator is the usual implementation of the standard. The differences table lists the DataAnnotations attribute for each annotation. The table also lists constraints that .NET does not have, such as @Positive and @Past.

@NotNull on a stringtrap#

PredictA required name, marked @NotNull#
The client sends a name that is an empty string. Is the request rejected?
public record CreateCustomer(@NotNull String name) { }
Show the answer
No. An empty string passes. Only a null name is rejected.

@NotNull is not [Required] for strings. @NotNull accepts the empty string "". So {"name": ""} passes, and only {"name": null} is rejected. This is the most common validation mistake.

Use @NotBlank for a string that must contain something other than whitespace. Use @NotEmpty for a collection that must have elements.

Triggering validationtrap#

PredictA controller parameter with no @Valid#
A client posts an order with a blank customer and a quantity of 0. What happens?
public record CreateOrder(
        @NotBlank String customerId,
        @Min(1) @Max(100) int quantity) { }

@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(
        @RequestBody CreateOrder request) {
    ...
}
Show the answer
The order is accepted, and goes straight into your method.

If you forget @Valid, validation is off for that parameter. The annotations are still on the record, but nothing checks them, and there is no warning. If invalid input reaches your code, first check whether @Valid is missing.

Write @Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder request. That one annotation rejects a bad order before any of your code runs.

This is the same method with @Valid on its parameter:

import jakarta.validation.Valid;

@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder request) {
    // runs only when the request passed every constraint
    ...
}

@Valid tells Spring to check the CreateOrder after Spring reads it from the body. If any constraint fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException. The client gets 400 Bad Request, and your method never runs.

You can also put a constraint directly on a query parameter or a path variable. Spring checks these constraints too, and they need no @Valid:

@GetMapping
public List<OrderDto> list(@RequestParam @Min(0) int page) {
    ...
}
Reading the code
@RequestParam @Min(0) int page

A request for page -1 is rejected with 400 Bad Request. This failure arrives as a HandlerMethodValidationException. A failed @Valid raises a different exception, so an error handler should cover both exceptions.

Legacy@Validated on the controller class

Older code puts @Validated on the controller class to get this check. Tutorials written before Spring Framework 6.1 do the same. Spring's documentation now says to remove @Validated from the controller class. With @Validated, the check runs through a proxy. Without @Validated, the check runs through the validation that is built into Spring MVC. Spring MVC is the model-view-controller (MVC) web framework of Spring.

A nested object needs its own @Validtrap#

Each order line holds its price as a Money. Money is a record with its own constraints:

public record Money(
        @NotNull @PositiveOrZero BigDecimal amount,
        @NotBlank String currency) { }

public record OrderLine(
        @NotBlank String productId,
        @Min(1) int quantity,
        @Valid Money unitPrice) { }
Reading the code
@Valid Money unitPrice) { }

This annotation tells the validator to check the constraints inside the Money as well.

Gotcha

Constraints inside a nested object are skipped unless its field carries @Valid. ASP.NET Core checks a nested object without being asked. Jakarta Validation checks a nested object only when you ask. So without @Valid Money unitPrice, a line with a negative amount is accepted. For a list, put @Valid on the element type, as in List<@Valid OrderLine>.

ProblemDetailtwist#

RFC 9457 defines one shape for error bodies. This shape is called problem details. ASP.NET Core has the type ProblemDetails for it. Spring has the type ProblemDetail.

C# refresherProblemDetails in ASP.NET CoreC# 10
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();    // RFC 9457 bodies for unhandled errors

app.MapGet("/orders/{id}", (int id) =>
    Results.Problem(title: "Order not found", statusCode: 404));

In Spring Boot, problem details are switched off by default. One setting switches them on:

# application.yml
spring:
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true
Reading the code
enabled: true

Boot then registers a handler. The handler is a subclass of Spring's ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. It turns Spring MVC's own exceptions into problem details. A failed @Valid is one of these exceptions.

This is the body that ASP.NET Core returns for a failed validation:

{
  "type": "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc9110#section-15.5.1",
  "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
  "status": 400,
  "errors": {
    "Email": ["The Email field is not a valid e-mail address."],
    "Quantity": ["The field Quantity must be between 1 and 100."]
  },
  "traceId": "0HNOHL49BIAAL:00000001"
}

The errors member of this body names each field. The body from Spring Boot names no field. Boot 3 writes a type member, and Boot 4 leaves it out. The two versions also write the members in different orders:

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "Invalid request content.",
  "instance": "/api/orders"
}
{
  "detail": "Invalid request content.",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "status": 400,
  "title": "Bad Request"
}
Reading the code
"detail": "Invalid request content.",

This text names no field. To add the fields, see Returning field-level errors.

"type": "about:blank",

This is the default type. It means that the status code alone describes the problem.

Global exception handlingtwist#

When an order does not exist, the service throws an OrderNotFoundException that carries the missing id:

public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

    private final long orderId;

    public OrderNotFoundException(long orderId) {
        super("No order with id " + orderId);
        this.orderId = orderId;
    }

    public long orderId() { return orderId; }
}
Reading the code
super("No order with id " + orderId);

This is the exception's message. It becomes the detail of the response.

One class turns this exception into a 404 with a problem details body. The class does this for every controller:

C#
app.UseExceptionHandler(...);

// or a filter
public class ApiExceptionFilter : IExceptionFilter
{
    public void OnException(ExceptionContext ctx) { ... }
}
Java 25
@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler
        extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException e) {
        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
        problem.setTitle("Order not found");
        problem.setType(URI.create(
                "https://acme.com/errors/not-found"));
        problem.setProperty("orderId", e.orderId());
        return problem;
    }
}
Reading the code
@RestControllerAdvice

This annotation applies the handlers in this class to every controller. Such a class is called a controller advice.

extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

Your class inherits the problem details that Spring builds for its own exceptions. Your class is now the ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, so Boot does not register its own handler.

problem.setProperty("orderId", e.orderId());

This line adds your own member to the body.

This is the response for order 99. The members come in a different order on each version:

{
  "type": "https://acme.com/errors/not-found",
  "title": "Order not found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "No order with id 99",
  "instance": "/api/orders/99",
  "orderId": 99
}
{
  "detail": "No order with id 99",
  "instance": "/api/orders/99",
  "status": 404,
  "title": "Order not found",
  "type": "https://acme.com/errors/not-found",
  "orderId": 99

Reading the code
"type": "https://acme.com/errors/not-found",

This is a web address that names the kind of problem. So a client does not need to read the text.

These are the pieces that you combine:

NeedSpring
Handle one exception type@ExceptionHandler(X.class)
Handle several@ExceptionHandler({A.class, B.class})
Apply to all controllers@RestControllerAdvice
Apply to some controllers@RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "...")
Override framework error shapesextend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler
Add fields to the responseproblemDetail.setProperty(k, v)

Returning field-level errors#

When validation fails, the default response of ASP.NET Core names the fields that failed. The default response of Spring does not name them. Most teams add the fields. To do this, they override one method in the same ApiExceptionHandler:

@Override
protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(
        MethodArgumentNotValidException e, HttpHeaders headers,
        HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {
    var errors = e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                    FieldError::getField,
                    f -> Objects.requireNonNullElse(f.getDefaultMessage(), "invalid"),
                    (first, second) -> first));

    ProblemDetail problem = e.getBody();
    problem.setTitle("Validation failed");
    problem.setProperty("errors", errors);
    return ResponseEntity.status(status).headers(headers).body(problem);
}
Reading the code
protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(

Spring calls this method when @Valid fails. Overriding this method replaces the default body.

.collect(Collectors.toMap(

This call builds a map from each field's name to its message. For more about toMap, see the chapter Streams.

(first, second) -> first));

This argument keeps the first message when one field has two errors.

ProblemDetail problem = e.getBody();

These are the problem details that Spring had already built for this exception. The method adds to them.

The response now names each field that failed. As before, Boot 3 adds the default type, and the two versions write the members in different orders:

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "Invalid request content.",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "errors": {
    "quantity": "must be greater than or equal to 1",
    "customerId": "must not be blank",
    "email": "must be a well-formed email address"
  }
}
{
  "detail": "Invalid request content.",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "status": 400,
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "errors": {
    "quantity": "must be greater than or equal to 1",
    "customerId": "must not be blank",
    "email": "must be a well-formed email address"
  }
}
Reading the code
"customerId": "must not be blank",

The default messages come from Hibernate Validator. To replace a default message, set the message attribute of the constraint, as in @NotBlank(message = "customer is required").

Gotcha

Collectors.toMap throws on duplicate keys. Two constraint violations on the same field produce a duplicate key. So you must use the three-argument form with a merge function, as this method does.

A failed constraint on a query parameter goes to another method of the same class, handleHandlerMethodValidationException. You override this method in the same way.

One advice class, not twotrap#

It is natural to write a separate handler class for validation errors, next to ApiExceptionHandler:

@RestControllerAdvice
class ValidationAdvice {

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleInvalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) { ... }
}
Reading the code
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)

This method handles a failed @Valid on a request body, in a separate class.

Gotcha

Do not handle the exception in a second advice class. ApiExceptionHandler already handles this exception, through the handleMethodArgumentNotValid method that it inherits. These two classes have no @Order, so the names of the classes decide which class answers. On Boot 4.1, ValidationAdvice never answered. The same class with the name AaaValidationAdvice always answered.

An application with no such subclass has the same problem when problem details are switched on. Boot's own handler is registered at @Order(0). It answered first, whatever the name of the second class was.

Override handleMethodArgumentNotValid in the one class. For an example, see Returning field-level errors.

Custom constraints#

The shop accepts prices only in currencies that exist, and no built-in constraint knows the list of currencies. For a rule like this, Jakarta Validation does what FluentValidation does in .NET. A custom constraint is an annotation, plus a class that does the check.

C# refresherFluentValidation: rules in a validator classC# 3
public class CreateOrderValidator : AbstractValidator<CreateOrder>
{
    public CreateOrderValidator()
    {
        RuleFor(x => x.Currency).Must(c => Currencies.Contains(c));
    }
}
import jakarta.validation.Constraint;
import jakarta.validation.ConstraintValidator;
import jakarta.validation.ConstraintValidatorContext;
import jakarta.validation.Payload;
import java.lang.annotation.*;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Currency;

@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.RECORD_COMPONENT})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Constraint(validatedBy = CurrencyValidator.class)
public @interface ValidCurrency {
    String message() default "unknown currency";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}

public class CurrencyValidator
        implements ConstraintValidator<ValidCurrency, String> {

    @Override
    public boolean isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        return value == null || Currency.getAvailableCurrencies()
                .stream().anyMatch(c -> c.getCurrencyCode().equals(value));
    }
}

// used like any built-in constraint
public record PriceQuote(@ValidCurrency String currency, BigDecimal amount) { }
Reading the code
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.RECORD_COMPONENT})

This line says where the annotation may be used. It may be used on fields, and on record components such as currency.

@Constraint(validatedBy = CurrencyValidator.class)

This line connects the annotation to the class that does the check.

public @interface ValidCurrency {

@interface declares a new annotation type. See the annotations chapter.

String message() default "unknown currency";

This is the message that is used when the check fails. The other two members are groups and payload. Every constraint annotation must have them. Copy them as they are.

return value == null || Currency.getAvailableCurrencies()

A missing value counts as valid, as it does with the built-in constraints. Otherwise the value must be a real currency code, such as EUR. The value ABC is rejected.

In .NET, [Compare] checks a rule that compares two fields. In Jakarta Validation, such a rule is a constraint on the whole class. Give the annotation @Target(ElementType.TYPE) and put the annotation on the record. Then make the record the type that the validator checks, as in ConstraintValidator<SameEmail, Signup>. The isValid method then receives the whole Signup and can compare two of its components.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this exception filter as a Spring class. OrderNotFoundException is the shop's own exception: 
public class ApiExceptionFilter : IExceptionFilter
{

    {
        if (ctx.Exception is OrderNotFoundException e)
        {
            ctx.Result = new ObjectResult(new ProblemDetails
            {
                Status = 404,
                Title = "Order not found",
                Detail = e.Message
            }) { StatusCode = 404 };
        }

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException e) {
        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());

extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler is the piece that is most easily forgotten. It makes this class the one handler for Spring's own exceptions too. So Boot does not register a second handler next to this class.

2
An expert asksWhy must an error handler cover two different exceptions for failed validation?
A failed @Valid on a request body raises MethodArgumentNotValidException. A constraint directly on a query parameter or path variable needs no @Valid. The validation built into Spring MVC checks it, and a failure raises HandlerMethodValidationException.

Data access, JPA and migrations#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 40· 16 min read· Quick reference

Spring Data JPA does the same as EF Core. It maps classes to tables and runs the queries. It is built on Jakarta Persistence (JPA). JPA is the Java standard for an object-relational mapper (ORM). A separate tool runs the migrations, either Flyway or Liquibase.
