Note

If your data is in Amazon DocumentDB, read these three sections of this chapter:

  • An entity
  • Repositories
  • A change is saved with no call to save

For the comparison with these three sections, see the chapter Document data.

The landscapetwist#

EF Core is one product. Java has three layers in its place. You will see the name of each layer in stack traces:

  • Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) does the same as ADO.NET. It is the low-level API that sends SQL and reads rows.
  • Jakarta Persistence (JPA) is a standard for an object-relational mapper (ORM). The standard defines the annotations and interfaces. Hibernate is the implementation that Spring Boot uses. So JPA is the contract, and Hibernate does the work.
  • Spring Data JPA is the top layer. It writes your repository classes for you.

EF Core configures the model in OnModelCreating. JPA uses annotations on the entity classes themselves:

C# refresherOnModelCreating: configuring the model in codeC# 3
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder b)
{
    b.Entity<Order>().ToTable("orders");
    b.Entity<Order>().Property(o => o.CustomerId).IsRequired();
}
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String customerId;
}

@Table does the same as ToTable in EF Core. @Column(nullable = false) does the same as IsRequired.

Everyday EF Core callstwist#

EF Core
// db is your DbContext; db.Orders is a DbSet<Order>
var order = await db.Orders
    .Include(o => o.Lines)
    .AsNoTracking()
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id);

var big = await db.Orders
    .FromSqlRaw(
        "select * from orders where total > {0}", 100)
    .ToListAsync();

db.Orders.Add(newOrder);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
Spring Data JPA
// in the repository interface
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines")  // Include()
Optional<Order> findWithLinesById(Long id);

@Query(value = "select * from orders where total > :min",
       nativeQuery = true)              // FromSqlRaw
List<Order> findBig(@Param("min") BigDecimal min);

// in a service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)         // like AsNoTracking()
Order load(Long id) {
    return orders.findWithLinesById(id).orElseThrow();
}

orders.save(newOrder);  // written by the commit at the latest
Reading the code
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines")

This annotation loads the order's lines in the same query, like Include() in EF Core. Without it, the lines load later, one query at a time.

Optional<Order> findWithLinesById(Long id);

This is a method in a repository interface. Spring Data reads the name and writes the query for you. To learn how, see Repositories.

nativeQuery = true)

This query is plain SQL for your database, like FromSqlRaw in EF Core. :min is a named parameter. Its value comes from the argument marked @Param("min").

@Transactional(readOnly = true)

This annotation runs the method in a read-only transaction. Hibernate then does not watch the loaded objects for changes. This is the nearest thing to AsNoTracking().

orders.save(newOrder);

This call adds the order, like Add() in EF Core. Hibernate sends the insert when it needs to, and at the latest when the transaction commits. In EF Core, SaveChanges writes pending changes in the same way.

An entitytwist#

C#
public class Order
{
    public long Id { get; set; }
    public string CustomerId { get; set; } = "";
    public decimal Total { get; set; }
    public OrderStatus Status { get; set; }
    public DateTimeOffset CreatedAt { get; set; }
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; set; } = [];
}
Java 25
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")   // ORDER is a reserved word in SQL
public class Order {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String customerId;

    private BigDecimal total;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private OrderStatus status;

    private Instant createdAt;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL,
               orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Order() { }   // JPA requires a no-arg constructor

    // getters such as getLines(), and methods such as cancel(), are left out
}
Reading the code
@Entity

This annotation marks a class that Hibernate maps to a table. Such a class is called an entity. Each object is one row.

@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)

The database generates the id. EF Core does the same by default for a numeric key.

@Column(nullable = false)

This annotation is like [Required] in C#. A field without @Column still maps to a column. Boot's default naming turns customerId into customer_id. In the same way, createdAt becomes created_at.

@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)

This annotation stores the enum by its name, such as PAID. The default is a trap.

@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL,

An order has many lines. mappedBy names the OrderLine field that holds the foreign key. Because of cascade and orphanRemoval, saving or removing the order also saves or removes its lines.

protected Order() { }

JPA creates an object through this constructor, and then fills in the fields. protected stops your code from calling the constructor.

Two entity rules: no records, and enum columns by nametrap#

Gotcha

Entities cannot be records. JPA needs a no-argument constructor and fields that can change, so that it can create an object and then fill in its fields. Hibernate also generates subclasses of entities for lazy loading. These subclasses are called proxies. A record is final, and its fields cannot change. Use a class for entities. Use a record for the data transfer object (DTO) that you expose.

Gotcha

@Enumerated defaults to ORDINAL, which stores the enum's declaration position as an integer. If you later insert or reorder a constant, every stored row means something different, and nothing warns you. There is no error and no migration. The data also cannot tell you which mapping was used when a row was written.

@Enumerated                              // ORDINAL by default: NEW=0, PAID=1, SHIPPED=2
private OrderStatus status;

@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)             // always do this: stores "NEW", "PAID", ...
private OrderStatus status;

This is the same danger as storing ordinal(), but here the unsafe option is the default. See the chapter Enums. Always write EnumType.STRING. If you want short values, map an explicit code column with an AttributeConverter instead.

equals and hashCode on entities#

The general contract for equals and hashCode applies to entities too. See the chapter Equality and hashing. But the usual advice fails for entities in three ways. The third way involves Lombok. Lombok is a library that generates code such as equals during compilation:

ProblemWhy
The id is null before persistan entity that is put in a HashSet before it is saved gets a new hash when the id is assigned, so the set cannot find it
Hibernate hands you proxiesa lazy association is an object of a generated subclass, so a comparison with getClass() fails
Lombok @Data on an entityit generates equals over every field, so equals triggers lazy loading and can recurse through both sides of an association

Here are an equals and a hashCode for the Order entity that avoid all three problems:

@Entity
public class Order {

    @Id @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        // instanceof, not getClass(), so a Hibernate proxy still matches
        if (!(o instanceof Order other)) return false;
        // only equal when both have an id, and the ids match
        return id != null && id.equals(other.id);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        // constant, so the hash never changes when the id is assigned
        return getClass().hashCode();
    }
}
Reading the code
if (!(o instanceof Order other)) return false;

A proxy is a subclass of Order, so instanceof accepts a proxy. A comparison with getClass() would not accept it.

return id != null && id.equals(other.id);

Two unsaved orders are never equal. Two saved orders are equal when their ids match.

return getClass().hashCode();

This line returns the same hash for every order. So a set can still find an order after the order gets its id.

Gotcha

A constant hashCode looks wrong, but it is deliberate. With a constant hash, a HashSet can still find the object after the object changes from unsaved to saved. A constant hash makes a hash set of entities as slow as a linear scan. This is acceptable, because entity collections are small. The alternative is to hash the id. But hashing the id breaks the collection at the moment when the entity is saved.

Never put @Data or @EqualsAndHashCode from Lombok on a JPA entity. These two annotations make Lombok generate equals over every field. An equals over every field is the most common cause of unexpected lazy loading. It is also the most common cause of a StackOverflowError from two entities that refer to each other.

Repositoriesnew#

The billing service needs orders by customer, orders by customer and status, and orders above an amount. EF Core builds such queries from LINQ expression trees. Java has no expression trees. So Spring Data builds queries from method names, from query strings, or from a criteria API. You declare an interface, and Spring writes the class at startup:

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.repository.query.Param;

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    // where customer_id = ?
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(String customerId);

    // where customer_id = ? and status = ? order by created_at desc
    List<Order> findByCustomerIdAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc(
            String customerId, OrderStatus status);

    // where total > ?
    List<Order> findByTotalGreaterThan(BigDecimal amount);

    boolean existsByCustomerId(String customerId);
    long countByStatus(OrderStatus status);

    // when the name would get silly, write the query
    @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines where o.id = :id")
    Optional<Order> findWithLines(@Param("id") Long id);
}
Reading the code
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

This is an interface with no implementation. Spring Data creates the class at startup. <Order, Long> gives the entity type and the type of its id.

List<Order> findByCustomerId(String customerId);

This is called a derived query. Spring Data reads the parts of the method name. findBy starts the query. CustomerId names the field. The parameter gives the value.

findByCustomerIdAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc(

Longer names combine conditions with And and Or, and sort with OrderBy. The table below lists the keywords.

@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines where o.id = :id")

This is a query that you write yourself. The query names the entity Order and its field lines, not the tables. join fetch loads the lines in the same query.

That query string is written in the Jakarta Persistence Query Language (JPQL). JPQL looks like SQL, but it works on entities and their fields. Hibernate accepts a larger language of its own, which is called the Hibernate Query Language (HQL). JPQL is a subset of HQL. Here are the keywords that the name of a derived query can use:

KeywordSQL
findBy / getBy / readByselect
And, Orand / or
Between, LessThan, GreaterThancomparisons
Like, StartingWith, Containinglike
In, NotInin
IsNull, IsNotNullis null
OrderBy...Asc/Descorder by
Top, Firstlimit
Distinctdistinct
existsBy, countBy, deleteByexists / count / delete
Note

JpaRepository already gives you save and delete. It also gives you findById, findAll, paging and sorting. You declare only the queries that are specific to your domain.

Counting the queries in a looptrap#

PredictA loop over orders and their lines#
The table holds 100 orders. How many queries does this run, and how do you make it one?
// orders is the OrderRepository; a report counts the lines of every order
int lines = 0;
for (var order : orders.findAll()) {
    lines += order.getLines().size();
}
Show the answer
101. A join fetch in the query, or @EntityGraph on the repository method, makes it one.

Collections load lazily by default. The lines of an order load only when code first uses them. findAll runs one query, and order.getLines().size() runs one more query for each order. The problem is worse than in EF Core, because lazy loading is the default for collections. Also, there is no Include() that you add out of habit.

Load the lines in the same query as the orders. To do this, write join fetch o.lines in a @Query, or put @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines") on the method.

This is called the N+1 problem. The code runs one query for the list, and then one more query for each of the N rows in the list. Here are the fixes, in order of preference:

// 1. JOIN FETCH in the query
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines")
List<Order> findAllWithLines();

// 2. @EntityGraph: declarative, and it works with derived queries
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines")
List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);

// 3. a projection: fetch only the columns you need
interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); BigDecimal getTotal(); }
List<OrderSummary> findSummariesByStatus(OrderStatus status);
Reading the code
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines")

This one query loads every order with its lines.

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines")

This annotation asks for the lines too. It works on a derived query, so you write no JPQL.

List<OrderSummary> findSummariesByStatus(OrderStatus status);

This method returns only the id and the total, through an interface of getters. No entity is loaded, so no lazy collection can run a query later. The word between find and By is only a label.

Counting queries in developmentdeep dive

In development, set spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true. Or add the datasource-proxy library or the Hypersistence Utils library. An N+1 problem then appears as a count of queries, and not as slow pages in production.

Lazy loading and detached entitiestrap#

Inside a transaction, Hibernate keeps every entity that it loads in a persistence context. In EF Core, the DbContext tracks what it loaded in the same way. A lazy field loads only when it is first used. The defaults decide which fields are lazy:

AssociationJPA defaultAdvice
@OneToManyLAZYkeep it lazy, and fetch explicitly
@ManyToManyLAZYkeep it lazy
@ManyToOneEAGERset it to LAZY explicitly
@OneToOneEAGERset it to LAZY explicitly
PredictReading a customer's name after the service has returned#
What happens on the last line?
// application.yml sets spring.jpa.open-in-view to false

// in the Order entity, which here holds its customer as an association
@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
private Customer customer;

// in OrderService
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public Order load(Long id) {
    return orders.findById(id).orElseThrow();
}

// in OrderController
Order order = service.load(id);
String name = order.getCustomer().getName();
Show the answer
It throws LazyInitializationException.

Many orders share one customer, and the customer is lazy here. So nothing loaded the customer inside load. When load returned, its transaction ended and the persistence context closed. So Hibernate can no longer fetch the customer. EF Core behaves in the same way when the DbContext is disposed. With JPA, this happens far more often. The reason is that collections are lazy by default, and the usual advice is to make every other association lazy too.

Fetch what you need inside the transaction, or map the entity to a DTO inside the transaction.

When a transaction ends, its persistence context closes. The entities that the persistence context held are then called detached.

Gotcha

Do not use spring.jpa.open-in-view to avoid this exception. Boot switches this setting on by default in web applications. The setting keeps the persistence context open for the whole request, so the exception does not happen. But the setting also hides N+1 queries, and it holds database connections longer than necessary. Most experienced teams set it to false, and then fix the code that causes each exception.

A change is saved with no call to savetrap#

To cancel an order, the code loads the order and changes its status. In EF Core, a third line writes the change. In Spring, that third line does not exist:

EF Core
// db is your DbContext
var order = await db.Orders.FindAsync(orderId);
order!.Cancel();
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
Spring Data JPA
// in OrderService; orders is the OrderRepository
@Transactional
public void cancel(long orderId) {
    var order = orders.findById(orderId).orElseThrow();
    order.cancel();
    // no call to save
}
Reading the code
order.cancel();

This call sets the order's status to CANCELLED. Hibernate watches every entity that it loads in the transaction. It sends the update when the transaction commits.

// no call to save

Nothing is missing here. The EntityManager of JPA does the tracking. It does the same as the DbContext in EF Core. The repository uses an EntityManager internally, so you rarely see one.

Gotcha

Inside @Transactional, every change to a loaded entity is written on commit. There is no SaveChanges call that you could leave out. So a field that you changed only for a calculation is saved too. Without @Transactional on the method, the same change is lost, and nothing warns you. To add a new entity, call save, like Add() in EF Core.

Transactions#

Saving an order must succeed or fail as a whole. In EF Core, you open a transaction yourself. In Spring, you mark the service method @Transactional:

C#
using var tx = db.Database.BeginTransaction();
db.Orders.Add(order);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
tx.Commit();
Java 25
@Transactional
public Order place(CreateOrder request) {
    var order = new Order(request);
    orders.save(order);
    // committed when the method returns
    return order;
}
Reading the code
@Transactional

Spring starts a transaction before the method runs. It commits the transaction when the method returns. It rolls the transaction back when the method throws an unchecked exception.

Gotcha

@Transactional works through a proxy around the bean. This has two consequences that surprise everyone:

  • Self-invocation does not work. A call to this.other() from inside the same class does not go through the proxy, so @Transactional on other() has no effect. For the reason, see the chapter How Spring actually works. For propagation and isolation, see the chapter Transactions, propagation and isolation.
  • Only unchecked exceptions roll back by default. When the method throws a checked exception, the transaction commits. If you throw checked exceptions, use @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class). Or throw an unchecked exception instead.

Also put @Transactional on the service, not on the repository, because the use case is the boundary of the transaction.

Migrationstwist#

With Flyway you write the SQL yourself, in a numbered file. Flyway runs each file once, in order, and records it in the flyway_schema_history table:

EF Core migrations
dotnet ef migrations add AddOrderStatus
dotnet ef database update

// generated C# with Up/Down methods
Flyway
-- src/main/resources/db/migration/V3__add_order_status.sql
ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW';

-- applied automatically at startup
Reading the code
-- src/main/resources/db/migration/V3__add_order_status.sql

The name of the file identifies the migration. V3 is the version, and the words after the two underscores describe the migration. Boot looks in db/migration by default.

ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW';

This is plain SQL. Existing orders get the value NEW.

-- applied automatically at startup

Boot runs new migrations before it serves requests. Boot 3 needs flyway-core for that. Boot 4 needs spring-boot-starter-flyway. spring-boot-starter-data-jpa does not include it.

AspectEF MigrationsFlyway
Formatgenerated C#plain SQL you write
NamingtimestampedV{version}__{description}.sql
Applieddotnet ef database updateautomatically on app startup
RollbackDown() methodforward-only, so write a new migration
Baseline an existing DBpossible, fiddlyflyway.baselineOnMigrate
Checksum enforcementnoyes, editing an applied migration stops the startup
Gotcha

Flyway checksums every applied migration. If you edit a file that has already run in any environment, startup fails. This is true even if you only add a comment. The fix for a mistake is always a new migration, never an edit.

Two Flyway startup errors#

The checksum is a feature. It guarantees that every environment ran identical SQL. An edited file stops the application with this error:

Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 3#
Means
A migration file was changed after it ran. Flyway stored a checksum of each file that it applied, and the file on disk no longer matches the checksum.
Fix
Undo the edit, and put the change in a new migration, V4. Run flyway repair only when the edit is harmless, such as a comment. This command stores the new checksum.
What triggers it
-- V3__add_order_status.sql, edited after it had been applied
ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW';
-- a comment added later

An existing database that has tables but no Flyway history fails too. It fails the first time that Flyway runs against it:

Found non-empty schema(s) "public" but no schema history table. Use baseline() or set baselineOnMigrate to true to initialize the schema history table.#
Means
Flyway found tables that it did not create. Flyway does not guess which migrations these tables correspond to.
Fix
Set spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrate=true. Flyway then records the existing schema as version 1 and applies only the migrations after version 1.
What triggers it
-- the database already has an orders table, and db/migration holds V1 and V2

ddl-auto: who changes the schematrap#

Hibernate can build or alter tables from your entity classes at startup. In EF Core, a call to Database.EnsureCreated() builds the tables. One setting says whether Hibernate may do this:

# application.yml
spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
Reading the code
ddl-auto: validate

With this value, Hibernate only checks that the mapping agrees with the schema. Hibernate creates nothing and alters nothing, so only your migrations change the schema.

Gotcha

Set spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate in every environment. Hibernate then only checks that the mapping agrees with the schema that Flyway built. Boot's default is none for a real database. For an embedded database such as H2, with no Flyway present, the default is create-drop. This value builds the schema at startup and drops the schema at shutdown. Tutorials often set update, which lets Hibernate alter your schema. This is convenient in a demo and catastrophic in production.

When not to use JPA#

JPA is a good choice for an object model that you load, change and save. Other tools are a better choice for other jobs:

SituationBetter tool
Complex reporting queriesjOOQ, or JdbcTemplate with SQL
You want typed SQL like LINQjOOQ
Simple CRUD, no object graphSpring Data JDBC, which has a much simpler model
Bulk operationsnative SQL, because JPA is poor at bulk operations
Read-heavy projectionsinterface or record projections

For code in the style of Dapper, use Spring's JdbcClient. It runs your SQL and maps each row to a record. It has no entities and no persistence context:

record OrderRow(long id, String customerId, BigDecimal total) { }

List<OrderRow> big = jdbc.sql("select id, customer_id, total from orders where total > :min")
        .param("min", new BigDecimal("100"))
        .query(OrderRow.class)
        .list();
Reading the code
jdbc.sql("select id, customer_id, total from orders where total > :min")

jdbc is a JdbcClient. Boot creates it for you. You write the SQL yourself, with a named parameter.

.query(OrderRow.class)

This call maps each row to an OrderRow. The column customer_id fills the component customerId.

Spring Data JDBC is between JdbcClient and Spring Data JPA. It has repositories, as Spring Data JPA has. But it has no lazy loading and no proxies. An aggregate is loaded and saved as a whole:

// Spring Data JDBC: no lazy loading, no proxies, no session to close
record Order(@Id Long id, String customerId, BigDecimal total) { }

interface OrderRepository extends ListCrudRepository<Order, Long> {
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(String customerId);
}
Reading the code
record Order(@Id Long id, String customerId, BigDecimal total) { }

Spring Data JDBC can map a record, and JPA cannot. The reason is that Spring Data JDBC never needs to make a subclass of the type. It also never needs to fill in an object after creating it.

Note

jOOQ deserves a look if you miss LINQ-to-SQL. It generates a typed domain-specific language (DSL) from your real database schema. So the compiler checks DSL.selectFrom(ORDERS).where(ORDERS.TOTAL.gt(x)), and a renamed column breaks the build. In Java, jOOQ is the closest thing to what EF Core gives you. The code that you write with jOOQ is clearly SQL, and it does not pretend to be objects.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java, as a method of a Spring service. customers is a Spring Data repository of Customer entities: 
var customer = await db.Customers.FindAsync(customerId);
customer!.Email = newEmail;
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
@Transactional
public void changeEmail(long customerId, String newEmail) {
    var customer = customers.findById(customerId).orElseThrow();
    customer.setEmail(newEmail);
}

There is no call to save. Hibernate writes a change to a loaded entity when the transaction commits. If you leave out @Transactional, the change is lost.

2
An expert asksBoot switches spring.jpa.open-in-view on by default, and it makes LazyInitializationException go away. Why do most experienced teams switch it off?
The setting keeps the persistence context open for the whole web request, so a lazy field can still load in the controller. This hides N+1 queries, and it holds a database connection longer than necessary. When the setting is off, the service must fetch what the response needs inside its transaction.

Quick reference#

SettingUse it to
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validatecheck the mapping against the schema Flyway built
spring.jpa.open-in-view=falseclose the persistence context when the service returns
spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrate=trueadopt a database that already has tables
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=truecount queries while developing

Transactions, propagation and isolation#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 41· 10 min read· Quick reference

@Transactional wraps a method in a database transaction. It looks like a checkbox, but it is a policy. It decides which exceptions roll back, and what happens when a transaction is already running. It also decides how much one transaction sees of the work of another transaction.

KindC#JavaNote
twistBeginTransactionAsync, CommitAsync, RollbackAsync@Transactional on the service methodcommits on return, and rolls back on an unchecked exception Why
trapsession.StartTransaction() on a MongoDB sessiona MongoTransactionManager beanon a document database @Transactional does nothing until you declare a transaction manager Why
trapcatch { await tx.RollbackAsync(); throw; }rollbackFor = Exception.classby default a checked exception commits, and only an unchecked exception rolls back Why
trapa call to a method of the same classa call through another bean@Transactional starts no transaction on a self-call, a private method or a final method Why
twistTransactionScopeOption@Transactional(propagation = ...)It says what the method does when a transaction is already running. Spring has seven modes, and .NET has three. Why
twistTransactionScopeOption.RequiresNewPropagation.REQUIRES_NEWa separate transaction, which commits even when the caller rolls back Why
trapa second transaction on the caller's rowsREQUIRES_NEW for independent writes onlyit waits for a lock that the caller holds, and it waits forever if no lock timeout is set Why
twistCreateSavepointPropagation.NESTEDa savepoint inside the same transaction, not a second transaction Why
twistIsolationLevel.ReadCommittedIsolation.READ_COMMITTEDthe level names are the same, and Isolation.DEFAULT uses the default level of the database Why
twistraising the isolation level@Version on the entityoptimistic locking turns a lost update into an exception Why
twistsending a message after Commit succeeds@TransactionalEventListenerruns after the commit, so a rolled-back change sends nothing Why

The defaulttwist#

C#
using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
try
{
    db.Orders.Add(order);
    await db.SaveChangesAsync();
    await tx.CommitAsync();
}
catch
{
    await tx.RollbackAsync();
    throw;
}
Java 25
@Transactional
public Order place(CreateOrder request) {
    var order = new Order(request);
    orders.save(order);
    return order;
}
// commit on normal return,
// rollback on an unchecked exception
Reading the code
@Transactional

Spring starts a transaction before the method runs, and commits the transaction when the method returns. If an unchecked exception leaves the method, Spring rolls the transaction back. Spring does all of this through a proxy around the service.

orders.save(order);

Every database call that is made while the method runs joins the same transaction. This includes calls inside other beans.

Put @Transactional on the service, not on the repository. The transaction boundary is the use case. Everything inside one business operation should commit together or fail together.

readOnly = true is more than a hintdeep dive
Note

readOnly = true is more than a hint on PostgreSQL. Spring marks the connection read-only, so a write inside such a method fails with “cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction”. With Hibernate, the setting has a second effect. Hibernate does not check loaded entities for changes.

The rollback ruletrap#

PredictA transfer that throws a checked exception#
The destination account is closed. What happens to the debit?
// AccountClosed extends Exception, not RuntimeException
@Transactional
public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount)
        throws AccountClosed {
    from.debit(amount);
    if (to.isClosed()) throw new AccountClosed();
}
Show the answer
It is committed.

A checked exception commits. Spring rolls back for RuntimeException and Error only. AccountClosed is a checked exception, so Spring commits the transaction when the exception passes. So the money leaves one account and arrives nowhere.

Tell Spring to roll back for every exception, checked or unchecked:

@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount)
        throws AccountClosed { ... }

In Spring, this behaviour is called the rollback rule. An unchecked exception rolls back, and a checked exception commits. C# has no checked exceptions, so a .NET developer has no habit at all for this rule. Set rollbackFor, or convert checked exceptions to unchecked exceptions at the boundary.

The proxy trap, againtrap#

Gotcha

@Transactional is applied by a proxy. So no transaction starts in three cases:

  • the method is called from inside the same class
  • the method is private
  • the method is final

A final method also runs on the proxy object, and the injected fields of the proxy object are null. For the mechanism, see the chapter How Spring actually works.

The usual case is a batch method that calls a transactional method of the same class. This is called self-invocation. For the code, see the chapter How Spring actually works. That chapter also asks you to predict the result of the code. A private method is the same trap in another form:

@Service
public class OrderService {

    public void place(CreateOrder request) {
        reserveStock(request);
    }

    @Transactional
    private void reserveStock(CreateOrder request) { ... }
}
Reading the code
private void reserveStock(CreateOrder request) { ... }

Only OrderService can call this method. So every call skips the proxy, and no transaction starts.

A document database needs a transaction managertrap#

Gotcha

On a document database, @Transactional does nothing until you declare a transaction manager. Boot sets up a transaction manager for a relational database. For MongoDB, and so for Amazon DocumentDB, Boot sets up no transaction manager, on Boot 3 or Boot 4. The method runs, and a failure rolls nothing back. For what happens without a transaction manager, see the chapter Document data.

The transaction manager for MongoDB is a MongoTransactionManager. One @Bean method declares it. For the method, see the chapter Document data. When the transaction manager is declared, the rollback rule and the proxy trap of this chapter apply to a document database too.

Propagationtwist#

Propagation answers one question. What should happen if a transaction is already running when this method is called? Think of a meeting that is already in progress. You can join the meeting, book a separate room, or refuse to start when no meeting is in progress:

ModeIf a transaction existsIf none existsUse for
REQUIREDjoin itstart onethe default, and almost always right
REQUIRES_NEWsuspend it, start a separate onestart oneaudit rows that must survive a rollback
NESTEDa savepoint inside itstart onepartial rollback, JDBC only
SUPPORTSjoin itrun with noneread-only helpers
NOT_SUPPORTEDsuspend it, run with nonerun with nonelong non-transactional work
MANDATORYjoin itthrowassert a caller opened one
NEVERthrowrun with noneassert nobody opened one

When a payment fails, the audit trail must still show the attempt. So the audit service runs in its own transaction:

@Transactional                                     // REQUIRED
public void placeOrder(CreateOrder request) {
    orders.save(new Order(request));
    audit.record("order placed");                  // see below
    throw new PaymentFailed();                     // rolls the order back
}

@Service
class AuditService {
    // survives the caller's rollback, because it is a separate transaction
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void record(String what) {
        auditRows.save(new AuditRow(what));
    }
}
Reading the code
@Transactional // REQUIRED

REQUIRED is the default mode. It starts a transaction, or joins the transaction that is already running.

audit.record("order placed");

This is a call to another bean, so the call goes through the proxy of that bean.

throw new PaymentFailed();

PaymentFailed is an unchecked exception, so the transaction of the order rolls back.

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)

This mode suspends the transaction of the caller, and runs record in a new transaction. The new transaction commits when record returns. So the audit row stays, although the order is rolled back.

REQUIRES_NEW on the caller's own rowstrap#

The method below ships an order. It updates the row of the order, and then adds a note to the same row through a second bean:

@Transactional
public void ship(long orderId) {
    orders.markShipped(orderId);        // updates the order's row, and so locks it
    notes.add(orderId, "shipped");
}

@Service
class ShippingNotes {
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void add(long orderId, String note) {
        orders.addNote(orderId, note);  // updates the same row
    }
}
Reading the code
orders.addNote(orderId, note);

This line needs the lock that ship already holds on the same row.

Gotcha

REQUIRES_NEW can deadlock against its own caller. The outer transaction is suspended, but it still holds its locks. Suppose the inner transaction writes a row that the outer transaction has already written. Then the inner transaction waits for a lock on that row. The outer transaction will not release the lock until the inner transaction returns.

The database cannot see this as a deadlock, because the outer transaction is only idle. So if you have set a lock timeout, the thread waits until the timeout is reached. On PostgreSQL the error is “canceling statement due to lock timeout”. If you have set no lock timeout, the thread waits forever. Use REQUIRES_NEW for independent writes, such as audit trails, outbox rows and failure logs. Never use it for the rows that the caller is changing.

REQUIRES_NEW and NESTED: connections and savepoints#

Gotcha

REQUIRES_NEW takes a second connection from the pool. With a pool of ten connections and a nested call, only five operations can run at the same time, not ten. Suppose you choose the size of the pool without counting the second connection. Then the pool has no free connection at a load that your calculation did not predict. With a pool of one connection, the inner call cannot get a connection at all:

HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 1006ms (total=1, active=1, idle=0, waiting=0)#
Means
Every connection in the pool is in use. Here the suspended transaction of the caller uses the connection. The inner REQUIRES_NEW transaction waited for a connection until the timeout of the pool.
Fix
Set the size of the pool for the number of connections that one request can hold at the same time. Or remove the REQUIRES_NEW call from the hot path.
What triggers it
// maximumPoolSize = 1
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(CreateOrder request) {
    audit.record("order placed");   // REQUIRES_NEW needs a second connection
}
Note

NESTED is not a second transaction. It is a savepoint inside the existing transaction. A rollback to the savepoint undoes only the inner work, but a rollback of the outer transaction still discards everything. NESTED works with Spring's Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) transaction manager. The Jakarta Persistence (JPA) transaction manager allows NESTED only after you switch on its nestedTransactionAllowed flag. Even then, the savepoint does not undo changes to entities that are already in memory.

Isolation#

Two customers buy the last item at the same moment. Does each transaction see the writes of the other transaction? The isolation level of the transaction decides this. The levels have the same names as in .NET:

LevelPreventsStill allows.NET name
READ_UNCOMMITTEDnothingdirty readsReadUncommitted
READ_COMMITTEDdirty readsnon-repeatable reads, phantomsReadCommitted
REPEATABLE_READnon-repeatable readsphantom readsRepeatableRead
SERIALIZABLEeverythingnothing, but a transaction may abortSerializable
DEFAULTwhatever the database default isdepends on the databaseUnspecified

Each level is defined by the anomalies that it prevents:

AnomalyMeans
Dirty readyou see another transaction's uncommitted write
Non-repeatable readthe same row changes between two reads in your transaction
Phantom readthe same query returns new rows between two reads
Gotcha

Isolation.DEFAULT uses the default level of the database, and the databases have different defaults. PostgreSQL and Oracle default to READ_COMMITTED. MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE_READ. SQL Server defaults to READ_COMMITTED. So code that is correct on MySQL can be wrong on PostgreSQL in a way that is hard to see. If a business rule depends on isolation, set the isolation level explicitly. Do not inherit it from the database.

Note

Prefer optimistic locking to raising the isolation level. Put a @Version field on the entity. Hibernate then checks that the row has not changed since you read it. Optimistic locking scales far better than SERIALIZABLE, and it makes the conflict explicit.

Here the order has a version number:

@Entity
public class Order {
    @Id private Long id;
    @Version private int version;     // Hibernate manages this
}
Reading the code
@Version private int version;

Hibernate adds where version = ? to every update, and increases the number. If another transaction changed the row first, no row matches, and Hibernate throws a StaleObjectStateException. Spring converts this exception to an ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. That class is a subclass of OptimisticLockingFailureException.

Doing something after the commit#

Sending a message from inside a transaction is a classic bug. The message is sent, and then the transaction rolls back. A downstream system now believes something that never happened. The fix is to send the message after the commit:

@Transactional
public void place(CreateOrder request) {
    var order = orders.save(new Order(request));
    events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()));
}

@Component
class OrderPlacedListener {

    // only runs if the transaction actually committed
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    public void on(OrderPlaced e) {
        messaging.send(e);
    }
}
Reading the code
events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()));

This line publishes an application event. events is an ApplicationEventPublisher, which is a Spring type. It is injected like any other bean.

@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)

Spring holds the event until the publishing transaction commits, and then calls the method. If the transaction rolls back, the method never runs.

Gotcha

An event that is published when no transaction is running is dropped. The listener does not run at all. Set fallbackExecution = true on the annotation if the same event can come from code outside a transaction.

The phase decides when the listener runs:

PhaseRuns
BEFORE_COMMITbefore the commit, so it can still fail the transaction
AFTER_COMMITafter a successful commit, and this is the default
AFTER_ROLLBACKonly if it rolled back
AFTER_COMPLETIONeither way
Note

For guaranteed delivery this is still not enough, because the process can stop between the commit and the send. The robust pattern is called the transactional outbox. Write the message to a table in the same transaction, and let a separate poller publish the message. This is the same solution as in .NET.

Check yourself
1
TranslateThis C# rolls back whatever is thrown. Write it in Java, as a method of a Spring service, so that a checked exception rolls back too. orders is the OrderRepository: 
await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
try
{
    db.Orders.Add(order);
    await db.SaveChangesAsync();
    await tx.CommitAsync();
}
catch
{
    await tx.RollbackAsync();
    throw;
}
@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public Order place(CreateOrder request) {
    var order = new Order(request);
    orders.save(order);
    return order;
}

Plain @Transactional matches the catch block for unchecked exceptions only. rollbackFor = Exception.class makes a checked exception roll back as well.

2
Two users save the same order, and one change is lost with no error. What do you add to the entity, and what happens then?
Add a field marked @Version. Hibernate then checks that the row has not changed since it was read. So the second save fails with an OptimisticLockingFailureException. Without the field, the second save overwrote the first save. This is called optimistic locking, and it is preferred to raising the isolation level.
3
An expert asksAn audit row must survive the caller's rollback, so its method is REQUIRES_NEW. Why can that method hang when it writes a row the caller has already written?
REQUIRES_NEW suspends the transaction of the caller and starts a separate transaction. But the suspended transaction still holds its locks. The inner transaction waits for a lock that the caller releases only after the inner transaction returns. The database sees an idle transaction, not a deadlock. So the wait ends only at a lock timeout, if one is set.

Quick reference#

When a transaction does not behave as you expect, the symptom usually points to one of these causes:

SymptomLikely cause
Annotation seems ignoredself-invocation, private method, or final method
Data committed despite an exceptionit was a checked exception, so set rollbackFor
A request hangs, or ends in a lock timeoutREQUIRES_NEW writing a row the caller has already written
Connection pool exhaustedREQUIRES_NEW doubling connection use, or open-in-view holding one for the whole request
Works on MySQL, wrong on PostgreSQLisolation inherited from the database default
Lost update with no errorthere is no @Version, so add optimistic locking
Message sent for a rolled-back changepublish in AFTER_COMMIT, or use an outbox
SettingEffect
rollbackFor = Exception.classroll back for checked exceptions too
noRollbackFor = NotFound.classcommit even though this was thrown
readOnly = truewrites fail on PostgreSQL, and Hibernate does not check for changes
timeout = 5seconds before a running statement is cancelled and the transaction rolled back
Spring.NET
@TransactionalBeginTransaction, SaveChanges and Commit around the method
Propagation.REQUIRES_NEWTransactionScopeOption.RequiresNew
Propagation.NESTEDa savepoint, as with CreateSavepoint in EF Core
Isolation.READ_COMMITTEDIsolationLevel.ReadCommitted
@TransactionalEventListenerwork done after SaveChanges and Commit succeed

Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 42· 17 min read· Quick reference

Amazon DocumentDB is a database from Amazon Web Services (AWS). It stores an order as one document, with the lines of the order inside. It offers the MongoDB API, so the Java code uses Spring Data MongoDB. This chapter does not cover Azure DocumentDB or the open-source DocumentDB.

twist"Status" : 0"status" : "NEW"the two drivers store enums and field names differently by default Why
twist[BsonElement("n")], [BsonIgnore]@Field("n"), @Transientthese attributes and annotations rename a stored field, or leave a member out of the document Why
trapMongoDBRef@DBRefAWS lists DBRefs as unsupported on every engine version (October 2026), so the warning applies to both drivers Why

Note

How this chapter was checked. Its examples were run against a MongoDB 8.0 container on 3 and 4 October 2026. No example was run against an Amazon DocumentDB cluster. The statements of this chapter about Amazon DocumentDB come from the AWS developer guide of October 2026, for engine version 8.0 on an instance-based cluster.

A document, not a rowtwist#

MongoDB .NET driver
using MongoDB.Bson;
using MongoDB.Bson.Serialization.Attributes;

public class Order
{
    [BsonId]
    [BsonRepresentation(BsonType.ObjectId)]
    public string? Id { get; set; }

    public required Customer Customer { get; set; }
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; set; } = [];
    public OrderStatus Status { get; set; }
    public DateTime PlacedAt { get; set; } = DateTime.UtcNow;
}
Spring Data MongoDB
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.Id;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.mapping.Document;

@Document("orders")
public class Order {

    @Id
    private String id;

    private Customer customer;
    private List<OrderLine> lines;
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.NEW;
    private Instant placedAt = Instant.now();

    public Order(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        this.customer = customer;
        this.lines = lines;
    }
}
Reading the code
@Document("orders")

This annotation names the collection. A collection has the same purpose as a table in a relational database. Each order is one document in the collection. The document holds the order, with its customer and its lines inside.

@Id

This @Id is from org.springframework.data.annotation, not from Jakarta Persistence (JPA). It maps the field to the _id of the document.

private String id;

Spring Data generates an id only for a String, an ObjectId or a BigInteger. It stores the generated id as an ObjectId, which is the kind of id that MongoDB itself uses. So the id is a String here, not a long as in the relational chapters.

private List<OrderLine> lines;

This field needs no annotation, because a nested object or list is stored inside the document. For how each type is stored, see What the stored document holds.

A record can be a documenttrap#

In the relational chapter, an entity could not be a record. A document can be a record. Spring Data MongoDB creates the object itself. The reference of Spring Data MongoDB says, “If the type is a Java Record the canonical constructor is used.”

@Document("orders")
public record Order(@Id String id, Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines,
                    OrderStatus status, Instant placedAt) { }

@Document names the collection. @Id on a component marks the id. The rest of this chapter uses this Order record.

Gotcha

Saving a record does not fill in its id. A record cannot change, so save returns a new record that has the generated id:

var order = new Order(null, customer, lines, OrderStatus.NEW, Instant.now());
Order saved = orders.save(order);     // orders is the OrderRepository

System.out.println(order.id());       // prints null
System.out.println(saved.id());       // prints 6ac1845b71b478951620fb72

Continue to work with saved. The .NET driver sets Id on the object that you passed to InsertOne. That habit fails here.

Repositories and derived queriestwist#

MongoDB .NET driver
using MongoDB.Driver;

var client = new MongoClient(connectionString);
IMongoCollection<Order> orders = client
    .GetDatabase("shop")
    .GetCollection<Order>("orders");

await orders.InsertOneAsync(order);

List<Order> paid = await orders
    .Find(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Paid)
    .ToListAsync();

var filter = Builders<Order>.Filter
    .Eq(o => o.Customer.Id, "c-42");
List<Order> hers = await orders.Find(filter).ToListAsync();

List<Order> withProduct = await orders
    .Find(o => o.Lines.Any(l => l.ProductId == "A-1"))
    .ToListAsync();
Spring Data MongoDB
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.repository.MongoRepository;

public interface OrderRepository
        extends MongoRepository<Order, String> {

    // PAID sent the filter {"status": "PAID"}
    List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);

    // "c-42" sent {"customer._id": "c-42"}
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(String customerId);

    // "A-1" sent {"lines.productId": "A-1"}
    List<Order> findByLinesProductId(String productId);
}

// in a service that was given the repository
Order saved = orders.save(order);
List<Order> paid = orders.findByStatus(OrderStatus.PAID);

This is the repository of the JPA chapter again. Spring Data writes the class, and derives each query from the name of the method. Each comment shows the filter that the method sent in the run. A method name can refer to a field of a nested object, as CustomerId does. It can also refer to a field of the items in a list, as LinesProductId does.

save inserts a new document. If the document already exists, save replaces the whole document. There is no persistence context here, so nothing tracks a loaded order. Unlike a loaded JPA entity, a changed order is written only when you call save. In a run, a change that was made in a @Transactional method without save was not stored.

You do not create a MongoClient. Boot builds one from the connection setting.

MongoTemplate for the resttwist#

MongoDB .NET driver
var update = Builders<Order>.Update
    .Set(o => o.Status, OrderStatus.Paid);

await orders.UpdateOneAsync(o => o.Id == id, update);
Spring Data MongoDB
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Criteria.where;
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Query.query;

import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Update;

template.updateFirst(
        query(where("id").is(id)),
        new Update().set("status", OrderStatus.PAID),
        Order.class);
Reading the code
template.updateFirst(

template is the MongoTemplate that Boot creates. The class is in the package org.springframework.data.mongodb.core. This call changes one field in place. A call to save would replace the whole document.

query(where("id").is(id)),

This line does the same as a filter builder in the .NET driver. A field is named by a string, so the compiler does not check the name. The template translates id to _id.

new Update().set("status", OrderStatus.PAID),

In the run, this line sent {"$set": {"status": "PAID"}}. The methods inc, push and pull work in the same way.

Embed or referencetwist#

When you embed an object, it is stored inside the document of the order. When you reference an object, the order stores only the id of that object. Embed an object that is read with its owner. Reference an object that exists without its owner.

Lines are never read without their order, so they are embedded. In the run, orders.save(order) stored them like this:

{
  "_id": { "$oid": "6ac1845b71b478951620fb72" },
  "customer": { "_id": "c-42", "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" },
  "lines": [
    { "productId": "A-1", "quantity": 2,
      "unitPrice": { "amount": { "$numberDecimal": "19.99" }, "currency": "EUR" } }
  ],
  "status": "NEW",
  "placedAt": { "$date": "2026-10-03T22:40:27.22Z" },
  "_class": "com.acme.billing.Order"
}
Reading the code
"lines": [

The lines are an array inside the order. One read returns the whole order, with no join and no lazy loading.

"customer": { "_id": "c-42", "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" },

This is a copy of the customer, made when the order was placed.

"_class": "com.acme.billing.Order"

Spring Data adds the class name, so that it knows which type to create when it reads the document.

A copy does not change when its original changes. When Ada changes her email address, her old orders keep the old address. If that is the wrong behaviour, reference the customer.

Connecting to Amazon DocumentDBtrap#

One setting holds the connection string. A second setting switches on Transport Layer Security (TLS). It names a bundle, and the bundle names the certificate. Boot 4 renamed both settings. spring.data.mongodb.uri became spring.mongodb.uri. spring.data.mongodb.ssl.bundle became spring.mongodb.ssl.bundle. The bundle itself is unchanged:

spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://sample-user:password@sample-cluster.node.us-east-1.docdb.amazonaws.com:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=secondaryPreferred&retryWrites=false
      ssl:
        bundle: docdb
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        docdb:
          truststore:
            certificate: file:/etc/billing/global-bundle.pem
spring:
  mongodb:
    uri: mongodb://sample-user:password@sample-cluster.node.us-east-1.docdb.amazonaws.com:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=secondaryPreferred&retryWrites=false
    ssl:
      bundle: docdb
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        docdb:
          truststore:
            certificate: file:/etc/billing/global-bundle.pem
Reading the code
retryWrites=false

The driver switches retryable writes on by default. As of October 2026, AWS states that Amazon DocumentDB does not support retryable writes before engine version 8.0.2, or on an elastic cluster. The error that AWS quotes is Retryable writes are not supported. Engine version 8.0.2 was released on 28 September 2026. From 8.0.2, you may remove the parameter, within AWS's limits.

bundle: docdb

This line switches TLS on, with the certificates of the bundle below. The connection strings that AWS gives for other languages contain tlsCAFile. In a local run, the Java driver ignored tlsCAFile.

certificate: file:/etc/billing/global-bundle.pem

This is the certificate authority (CA) file that AWS publishes. Without this file, the error is PKIX path building failed. For the other route, see A trust store.

Two parameters that change behaviourtrap#

To a driver, a cluster is a replica set named rs0. One primary instance takes every write, and replicas serve reads.

Gotcha

readPreference=secondaryPreferred gives up reading your own write. This parameter sends reads to the replicas of the cluster. AWS describes the replicas as eventually consistent:

Order saved = orders.save(order);                      // goes to the primary instance
Optional<Order> again = orders.findById(saved.id());   // may go to a replica

So findById can miss the order. If a read must see the write, read from the primary instance. To do that, leave the parameter out.

Gotcha

Through an SSH tunnel, leave out both replicaSet=rs0 and readPreference. AWS states that replica set mode through a tunnel results in an error. AWS also states that a read preference without replica set mode is undefined. So on your laptop, remove both parameters from the connection string that works inside AWS.

Through the tunnel, the host name is localhost, and this name does not match the certificate of the cluster. AWS's shell command adds --sslAllowInvalidHostnames for that. The parameter of the Java driver is tlsAllowInvalidHostnames.

What Amazon DocumentDB does not dotrap#

AWS's developer guide offers no way to run Amazon DocumentDB outside AWS. It says that the service is virtual private cloud (VPC)-only. So this book develops against a MongoDB container. That is the choice of this book, not AWS guidance. AWS's guide says nothing about it.

Gotcha

A MongoDB container accepts features that AWS lists as unsupported on Amazon DocumentDB. DocumentDB emulates the MongoDB API on its own engine, and it lacks some features. AWS lists these features as unsupported on every engine version, as of October 2026:

AWS lists as unsupportedA Spring Data service reaches it throughInstead
DBRefs@DBRefuse @DocumentReference, or a field that holds the id
$wherean @Query string that uses $whereuse the query operators, such as $gt, $in and $elemMatch
Hashed Index, Wildcard index@HashIndexed, @WildcardIndexeduse a single-field or a compound index
2d Index@GeoSpatialIndexed, with its default typeask for a 2dsphere index, which AWS lists as supported
Capped Collections, cursor.tailable()a capped collection, a tailable cursorAWS names no replacement

One difference produces no error. Amazon DocumentDB guarantees no implicit order of results. Name the order in every query that returns a list:

List<Order> findByStatusOrderByPlacedAtDesc(OrderStatus status);

OrderByPlacedAtDesc sends a sort with the filter. For more differences, see the section More differences.

Transactionstrap#

PredictA transactional method that saves, then throws#
What does this print?
// The application declares no transaction manager, and the collection is empty.
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void place(Order order) {
        orders.save(order);
        throw new IllegalStateException("payment failed");
    }
}

// in the caller
try {
    service.place(order);
} catch (IllegalStateException e) { }
System.out.println(orders.count());
Show the answer
1

@Transactional does nothing for MongoDB until you declare a MongoTransactionManager. Spring Data's reference says that without a MongoTransactionManager, “transaction support is DISABLED”. Boot 4.1 creates no MongoTransactionManager. So no transaction started, and the saved order stayed.

Declare a MongoTransactionManager bean. With this bean, the same run printed 0.

In .NET, you pass the session to each call. A call without the session compiles, and it runs outside the transaction. In Spring, declare the manager once:

MongoDB .NET driver
// the session goes to every call
using IClientSessionHandle session = await client.StartSessionAsync();
session.StartTransaction();

await orders.InsertOneAsync(session, order);

await session.CommitTransactionAsync();
Spring Data MongoDB
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.MongoDatabaseFactory;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.MongoTransactionManager;

@Configuration
public class MongoConfig {

    @Bean
    MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(
            MongoDatabaseFactory factory) {
        return new MongoTransactionManager(factory);
    }
}

MongoTransactionManager is an ordinary Spring transaction manager. So the rollback rule and the proxy trap apply. For both, see the chapter Transactions. In the run, MongoTransactionManager needed a replica set.

Gotcha

One point could not be tested. Spring's transaction manager opens a causally consistent session. AWS states that Amazon DocumentDB does not support causal consistency. AWS shows a read in such a session, and the read fails with error 303, Feature not supported: 'causal consistency'. AWS's own examples switch causal consistency off. Test a @Transactional method on your cluster first. AWS also documents limits. As of October 2026, a transaction may run for one minute, and it cannot create a collection.

Indexestrap#

Gotcha

@Indexed(unique = true) enforces nothing by default. Spring Data creates no index unless auto index creation is switched on, and auto index creation is off. In the run, two invoices for one order were both saved:

import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.index.Indexed;

@Document("invoices")
public record Invoice(@Id String id,
                      @Indexed(unique = true) String orderId,
                      Money total, LocalDate issuedOn) { }

invoices.save(new Invoice(null, "o-1", total, today));
invoices.save(new Invoice(null, "o-1", total, today));
System.out.println(invoices.count());        // prints 2

Nothing rejected the second save. One fix is to switch index creation on. The setting has the same name on Boot 3 and Boot 4:

spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      auto-index-creation: true

With auto-index-creation on, the second save threw a DuplicateKeyException. But when the collection already held the two invoices, switching the setting on stopped the application from starting, with the same exception.

Spring Data's reference says, “We generally recommend explicit index creation”. AWS states, as of October 2026, that an index build on Amazon DocumentDB blocks its collection by default. So on a collection that already holds data, create the index yourself, outside the application.

Money: how a BigDecimal is storedtrap#

Gotcha

A BigDecimal is stored as a string on Boot 3, and as a Decimal128 on Boot 4. In the run on Boot 4.1, Money.amount was stored as a Decimal128. AWS lists Decimal128 as a supported type. Boot 3.5 manages Spring Data MongoDB 4.5. Spring Data MongoDB 4.5 states that a BigDecimal “is represented as String instead of Decimal128”. The Boot 3 side was not run.

So after an upgrade, one collection holds old amounts as strings and new amounts as Decimal128 values.

On Boot 4, state the choice:

spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      representation:
        big-decimal: string      # or decimal128

big-decimal: string keeps the Boot 3 form. Spring's upgrade notes offer this value “to retain previous behaviour”. With this value, the run stored "19.99". For decimal128, convert the stored amounts first. Boot 3 has no such setting.

Testing without a clustertwist#

@DataMongoTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static MongoDBContainer mongo = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:8.0");

    @Autowired OrderRepository orders;

    @BeforeEach
    void empty() {
        orders.deleteAll();
    }

    @Test
    void findsByProduct() {
        orders.save(anOrder("A-1"));      // anOrder builds an Order with that product
        assertThat(orders.findByLinesProductId("A-1")).hasSize(1);
    }
}
Reading the code
@DataMongoTest

This is the test slice for document data. Unlike @DataJpaTest, it rolls nothing back. In the run, the next test still saw the order of this test. So each test starts by emptying the collection.

static MongoDBContainer mongo = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:8.0");

Pin the MongoDB version that your cluster is compatible with. To test a transaction, add .withReplicaSet(). In the run, the plain container refused a transaction.

A passing test proves less than it seems, because the container accepts features that AWS lists as unsupported on Amazon DocumentDB. Test against a real cluster before a release.

Referencing a document instead of embedding it#

A customer exists without any one order. To store customers once, give customers a collection of their own, and let the order hold a reference:

import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.mapping.DocumentReference;

@Document("customers")
public record Customer(@Id String id, String name, String email) { }

@Document("orders")
public record Order(@Id String id,
                    @DocumentReference Customer customer,
                    List<OrderLine> lines) { }

@DocumentReference stores only the id of the customer in the order. In the run, reading orders then needed one more query for each order, to load its customer. This is the N+1 problem again. Nothing cascades, so you save the customer yourself.

Gotcha

Do not use @DBRef on Amazon DocumentDB. @DBRef is the other way to reference in Spring Data. It stores a value of the DBRef type. AWS lists that type as not supported on any engine version, as of October 2026.

What the stored document holds: types, names and _class#

A stored document is in BSON. BSON is the format of MongoDB. It has types that JSON lacks, such as ObjectId, Date and Decimal128. Each row below shows what a run on 3 October 2026 stored. The run used Spring Data MongoDB 5.1.1 and the MongoDB .NET driver 3.12.0, both with their defaults:

MemberSpring Data MongoDB storedThe .NET driver stored
the id, a string"_id": an ObjectId"_id": an ObjectId, with [BsonRepresentation]
status, an enum"status": "NEW""Status": 0
placedAt"placedAt": a date, from an Instant"PlacedAt": a date, from a DateTime
amounta Decimal128, from a BigDecimal, but a string on Boot 3a Decimal128, from a decimal
a field's namethe name of the Java field, for example customerthe name of the C# property, for example Customer
the id of a nested object"_id""_id"
the type"_class": "com.acme.billing.Order"nothing

So two services that share a collection must agree on names and on enums. These attributes and annotations make the two services agree:

MongoDB .NET driver
[BsonIgnoreExtraElements]
public class Product
{
    [BsonId]
    public string Id { get; set; } = "";

    [BsonElement("display_name")]
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";

    [BsonIgnore]
    public string Label { get; set; } = "";
}
Spring Data MongoDB
@Document("products")
@TypeAlias("product")
public class Product {

    @Id
    private String id;

    @Field("display_name")
    private String name;

    @Transient
    private String label;
}
Reading the code
[BsonIgnoreExtraElements]

This attribute lets the .NET class read a document that holds a field for which the class has no property, such as _class. Without this attribute, the driver threw a FormatException in the run.

@TypeAlias("product")

This annotation stores product in _class, in place of the class name. So renaming or moving the class does not change what is stored.

@Field("display_name")

This annotation stores the field under another name, as [BsonElement] does.

@Transient

This annotation leaves the field out of the document, as [BsonIgnore] does. It is from org.springframework.data.annotation.

Gotcha

A LocalDate is stored through the machine's time zone. On a machine set to British summer time, the run stored 3 October 2026 as 2026-10-02T23:00:00Z. The date was read back correctly on the same machine. Spring Data's reference recommends the driver's own java.time codecs. These codecs use UTC.

Note

Boot 4 sets no representation for a BigDecimal. In the run, the driver stored a BigDecimal as a Decimal128. AWS lists Decimal128 as a supported type. On Boot 3, a BigDecimal is a string. For what to set when you upgrade, see the section Money: how a BigDecimal is stored.

A trust store made with keytool: one of AWS's two Java routes#

AWS's “Connecting programmatically” page builds a trust store with keytool. The C# tab of that page imports global-bundle.p7b into X509Store(StoreName.Root). AWS's Java guide also shows how to load the PEM file in code, through an SSLContext.

The keytool route splits global-bundle.pem into its certificates. Then it imports each certificate into a Java trust store, because keytool imports one certificate at a time:

curl -sS "https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem" > global-bundle.pem
split -p "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----" global-bundle.pem rds-ca-

for CERT in rds-ca-*; do
  keytool -import -file "$CERT" -alias "$CERT" -storepass changeit \
          -keystore rds-truststore.jks -noprompt
done
Reading the code
split -p "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----" global-bundle.pem rds-ca-

This line writes one file for each certificate. This is the macOS form. AWS's Linux script uses awk.

keytool -import -file "$CERT" -alias "$CERT" -storepass changeit \

keytool is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Each certificate needs an alias of its own. AWS's script takes the alias from the subject of the certificate.

Then tell the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) where the trust store is, or name the trust store in an SSL bundle of the jks kind:

java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=rds-truststore.jks \
     -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit -jar billing.jar

The javax.net.ssl.trustStore route and the jks bundle route both connected in a local run against a MongoDB container that accepts only TLS. The PEM bundle of the connection section also connected to that container, with a file that held two certificates.

Through an SSH tunnel, the host name of the certificate does not match with either route. To find the parameter for that case, see the tunnel gotcha.

More differences: behaviour, engine 5.0 and elastic clusters#

Some features are supported on Amazon DocumentDB but behave differently. AWS states these differences, as of October 2026:

On Amazon DocumentDBWhat it means for your code
$regexuses an index only with hint(), and best for a prefix without options
allowDiskUsenot supported for find, only as part of an aggregation
cursor.noCursorTimeout()not supported, so leave Query.noCursorTimeout() off
The admin and local databasesnot supported
Write concernthe values you send are ignored, and it always writes with majority
Document sizeat most 16 MiB, which is the ceiling for what an order can embed

This chapter describes engine version 8.0 on an instance-based cluster. AWS's table of features by engine version shows what engine 5.0 and elastic clusters lack:

FeatureEngine 5.0Engine 8.0Elastic clusters
ACID transactionsYesYesNo
Retryable writesNoYes (8.0.2+)No
Change streamsYesYesNo
CollationNoYesNo
ViewsNoYesNo
Text IndexV1V2No
Partial indexYesYesNo
$facetNoYes (8.0.2+)No
$set, $unset and $replaceWith stagesNoYesNo
GridFSYesYesNo

An elastic cluster is sharded, and it uses a wire protocol that is compatible with MongoDB 5.0. AWS does not offer elastic clusters on engine version 8.0. So on an elastic cluster, @Transactional has no transactions to use, and retryable writes stay off:

mongodb://sample-user:password@sample-cluster.node.us-east-1.docdb.amazonaws.com:27017/shop?retryWrites=false

The parameter retryWrites=false is required on an elastic cluster, and on every engine version before 8.0.2.

From 8.0.2, some writes are still not retryable. AWS lists these limits, as of October 2026. updateMany and deleteMany are not retryable. Writes inside a transaction are not retryable. No write is retryable on a cluster that uses query planner version 1.0.

Note

Spring Data MongoDB 5.1 states that it is tested against MongoDB 6 to 8. Engine version 8.0 is the only engine version in that range. That is this book's reading of two sources, not a promise by either vendor.

Transactions on Amazon DocumentDB: the documented limits#

AWS documents these limits for a transaction, as of October 2026. None of these limits could be reproduced on a MongoDB container, so none was run:

LimitWhat AWS states
Engine versiontransactions need engine version 4.0 or later
Elastic clustersACID transactions are not supported
New collectionsa transaction cannot create a collection, or query one that does not exist
Durationa transaction has a one minute execution limit
Sizethe transaction log must be smaller than 32 MB
Cursorscursors within a transaction are not supported
Causal consistencynot supported, and AWS's own examples switch it off in the session

The collection limit conflicts with a Spring habit. The first save creates a collection that does not exist. Inside a transaction on Amazon DocumentDB, save cannot create a collection, so create the collection first:

// once, outside any transaction: for example when the application starts
if (!template.collectionExists(Order.class)) {
    template.createCollection(Order.class);
}

collectionExists and createCollection are methods of MongoTemplate. A transaction that runs longer than one minute is aborted. AWS quotes the error that the next command receives. The error is Given transaction number 0 does not match any in-progress transactions.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this in Java, with Spring Data MongoDB. Order is a record, and orders is the OrderRepository: 
Order order = await orders.Find(o => o.Id == id).SingleAsync();
order.Status = OrderStatus.Paid;
await orders.ReplaceOneAsync(o => o.Id == id, order);
Order order = orders.findById(id).orElseThrow();
Order paid = new Order(order.id(), order.customer(), order.lines(),
                       OrderStatus.PAID, order.placedAt());
orders.save(paid);

There is no persistence context. So unlike a loaded JPA entity, a changed order is written only when you call save. A record cannot change, so you build a new record and save the new record.

2
An expert asksInvoice.orderId carries @Indexed(unique = true), yet two invoices for one order are both saved. Why, and why is switching auto index creation on not always the fix?
Spring Data creates no index unless auto index creation is on, and it is off by default. So the annotation alone enforces nothing. When the collection already held duplicates, switching spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation on stopped the application from starting, with a DuplicateKeyException. Spring's reference recommends creating indexes explicitly. AWS states, as of October 2026, that an index build on Amazon DocumentDB blocks its collection by default.
3
An expert asksYour tests pass against a MongoDB container. Why can the same code still fail on Amazon DocumentDB?
Amazon DocumentDB emulates the MongoDB API on its own engine. AWS lists some features as unsupported, such as DBRefs and $where. As of October 2026, Amazon DocumentDB also does not support retryable writes before engine version 8.0.2, and the driver sends retryable writes by default. A container accepts all of these features.

Quick reference#

SettingBoot 4Boot 3
Connection stringspring.mongodb.urispring.data.mongodb.uri

Security#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 43· 10 min read

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters. Every request passes through the chain before it reaches your controllers. The filters identify the caller, and store the result as an Authentication. Authorisation rules then decide what that caller may do.

KindC#JavaNote
twistClaimsPrincipalAuthentication / Principalthe signed-in user, and its authorities do the same as claims in .NET Why
twistUser.Identity.Nameauthentication.getName()the principal's name, such as the JWT subject Why
trapendpoints are open until you add [Authorize]every endpoint needs a login once the security starter is presentBoot supplies a default chain until you declare your own SecurityFilterChain Why
twistAddAuthenticationSecurityFilterChain beanone bean declares how requests are authenticated Why
twistAddAuthorizationauthorizeHttpRequests(...)the URL rules, matched in order inside the same bean Why
twist[AllowAnonymous]permitAll() in the chainusually a path rule in the chain, not an annotation Why
twistCookie authenticationformLogin() + sessionform login backed by an HTTP session Why
