Concept mappingtwist#

Callers prove who they are with a token from an identity provider. The protocols are OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC), as in .NET. The token is called a JSON Web Token (JWT). It is a signed piece of JSON that names the user and lists what the user may do.

C#
// ClaimsPrincipal: the signed-in user and their claims
string? name = User.Identity?.Name;
bool admin = User.IsInRole("Admin");

builder.Services.AddAuthorization(o =>
    o.AddPolicy("ReadsOrders",
        p => p.RequireClaim("scope", "orders")));
Java 25
// Authentication: the signed-in user and their authorities
Authentication auth =
        SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
String name = auth.getName();
boolean admin = auth.getAuthorities()
        .contains(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN"));

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders')")  // a policy
public Order get(long id) { ... }
Reading the code
SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

This is where Spring Security keeps the caller of the request that is being handled.

auth.getName();

This call returns the caller's name. For a JWT, the name is the subject of the token.

.contains(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN"));

An authority is a plain string, such as ROLE_ADMIN. A role is simply an authority whose name starts with ROLE_.

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders')")

This is a rule written as an expression on the method. ASP.NET Core would use a named policy for this. The scopes of a JWT become authorities with the prefix SCOPE_. So the orders scope becomes the authority SCOPE_orders.

The starter locks every endpointtrap#

In ASP.NET Core, an endpoint is open until you add [Authorize]. Spring Boot does the opposite. One dependency is enough to show it:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>

This dependency adds Spring Security and its configuration. Its name is the same on Boot 3 and Boot 4.

Gotcha

Once the security starter is on the classpath, every endpoint needs a login. Boot supplies a default chain until you declare a SecurityFilterChain bean of your own. With the default chain, a request with no credentials gets 401 Unauthorized. A browser is redirected to /login instead. The startup log prints “Using generated security password”. None of your code changed, so the 401 looks like a bug. To write a chain of your own, see the section The filter chain.

The filter chaintwist#

You declare one bean of type SecurityFilterChain. You configure the bean through a domain-specific language (DSL). Here the DSL is a chain of method calls on HttpSecurity. Each call takes a lambda that sets up one part of the configuration.

C#
builder.Services.AddAuthentication()
    .AddJwtBearer();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers().RequireAuthorization();
Java 25
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http)
            throws Exception {
        return http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**")
                    .hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o ->
                o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            // stateless API only
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(
                SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .build();
    }
}
Reading the code
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth

This call holds the URL rules. It is like AddAuthorization and RequireAuthorization together.

.requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()

Anyone may call the health check. This rule is like [AllowAnonymous].

.hasRole("ADMIN")

Paths under /api/admin need the authority ROLE_ADMIN.

.anyRequest().authenticated())

Every other request needs a signed-in caller of any kind.

o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))

This call accepts JWT bearer tokens, like AddJwtBearer. withDefaults() takes its settings from application.yml.

.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())

This line switches off the protection against cross-site request forgery (CSRF). That is safe here only because the API uses tokens, not cookies.

SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))

With this policy, Spring Security never creates an HTTP session. Every request carries its own token.

Where the tokens come fromtwist#

One setting tells Spring where the tokens come from. Spring then fetches the provider's signing keys, and checks each token's signature, issuer and expiry:

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://login.acme.example/realms/shop
Reading the code
issuer-uri: https://login.acme.example/realms/shop

This is the address of the identity provider. It is like Authority in the JwtBearer options.

The oauth2ResourceServer call in the chain needs a starter of its own. On Boot 3, the starter is spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server. On Boot 4, the starter is spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server. With only the security starter, the application fails at startup with a NoClassDefFoundError.

Two chain traps: rule order and CSRFtrap#

Two lines of the chain each hold a trap:

// inside SecurityConfig's chain method; http is its HttpSecurity parameter
http
    .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
        .anyRequest().authenticated())
    .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());
Reading the code
.anyRequest().authenticated())

This is the broadest rule, so it comes last.

.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());

This line switches CSRF protection off for the whole API.

Gotcha

Rules are matched in order and the first match wins. Put anyRequest() last. If a broad rule comes early, the rules after it are never checked, and nothing warns you. An endpoint is then more open than you intended.

Gotcha

CSRF protection is on by default, including for POST requests to a JSON API. It stops one attack. In that attack, another site makes the user's browser send a request with the user's cookies. If your first POST is refused with no useful message, CSRF protection is the reason. Spring Security answers 403. On Boot 4.1, the client saw 401 instead while the /error page of Boot needed a login too. The client saw 403 once /error was open to everyone. Disable CSRF protection only for an API that browsers do not call with cookies. Keep it for anything that uses cookies.

Method-level authorisationtwist#

A rule that depends on the method's arguments goes on the method:

C#
[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
public async Task Delete(int id) { ... }

[Authorize(Policy = "OwnsOrder")]
public async Task<Order> Get(int id) { ... }
Java 25
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public void delete(long id) { ... }

@PreAuthorize("@orderGuard.owns(#id, authentication)")
public Order get(long id) { ... }
Reading the code
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")

This rule is checked before the method runs, like [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]. If the rule fails, Spring refuses the call. A signed-in caller gets 403 Forbidden.

@PreAuthorize("@orderGuard.owns(#id, authentication)")

This rule calls a bean. @orderGuard is the bean named orderGuard. #id is the id parameter of the method. authentication is the caller. This is the Spring form of a custom policy.

The guard is an ordinary bean, so it can use the repository:

@Component
class OrderGuard {

    private final OrderRepository orders;

    OrderGuard(OrderRepository orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    boolean owns(long orderId, Authentication caller) {
        return orders.findById(orderId)
                .map(order -> order.getCustomerId().equals(caller.getName()))
                .orElse(false);
    }
}
Reading the code
class OrderGuard {

The bean name is the class name with a lower-case first letter, so it is orderGuard.

.map(order -> order.getCustomerId().equals(caller.getName()))

The caller owns the order when the customer id of the order equals the caller's name. The caller's name is the subject of the token.

These are the expressions you will use most:

ExpressionMeans
hasRole('ADMIN')requires the authority ROLE_ADMIN, because the prefix is added for you
hasAuthority('orders:write')requires exactly that authority string, with no prefix added
hasAnyRole('A','B')requires at least one of the roles, which means ROLE_A or ROLE_B
isAuthenticated()allows any signed-in user, so anonymous requests are refused
permitAll() / denyAll()always allowed, or always refused, whoever is calling
#idrefers to the method parameter named id
authenticationthe current user's Authentication object
@beanName.method(...)calls a method of a bean, so the rule can hold any policy logic

Three ways a method rule failstrap#

@PreAuthorize puts a rule on one method. Annotations like this one do nothing until one configuration class switches them on:

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity      // required, method annotations do nothing without it
public class MethodSecurityConfig { }
Reading the code
@EnableMethodSecurity

This annotation makes Spring wrap each bean that has @PreAuthorize in a proxy. The proxy checks the rule. Without @EnableMethodSecurity, the annotations are ignored, and nothing warns you.

PredicthasRole and a JWT with a roles claim#
May this caller call delete?
// The caller's JWT holds:   "scope": "orders",   "roles": ["ADMIN"]
// The application declares no JwtAuthenticationConverter bean.

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public void delete(long id) { ... }
Show the answer
No. Spring refuses the call, with 403 Forbidden.

hasRole('ADMIN') checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN. Spring adds the prefix for you in hasRole but not in hasAuthority. If you confuse the two expressions, the rule never matches, and nothing warns you. A JWT adds a second trap. By default, only the scope claim of a JWT becomes authorities, with names of the form SCOPE_…. A "roles": ["ADMIN"] claim is ignored until you map it.

This bean tells Spring to read the roles claim, and to give each role the ROLE_ prefix so that hasRole('ADMIN') matches:

@Bean
JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtAuthenticationConverter() {
    var roles = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    roles.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
    roles.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");

    var converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(roles);
    return converter;
}

setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles") reads authorities from the roles claim instead of the scope claim. This setting replaces the default, so SCOPE_ authorities are no longer produced. setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_") changes ADMIN into ROLE_ADMIN. That is the form that hasRole checks.

Gotcha

@PreAuthorize works through a proxy, exactly like @Transactional. A call from inside the same class is called self-invocation. Such a call does not go through the proxy, and the rule is not checked. So a security check that depends on self-invocation is no check at all. To predict what happens, see the chapter How Spring actually works.

The current user#

An endpoint that returns “my orders” needs the caller's id. In ASP.NET Core you read a claim from User. In Spring, a controller parameter receives the token:

C#
public IActionResult Get()
{
    var id = User.FindFirst("sub")?.Value;
    ...
}
Java 25
@GetMapping
public OrderDto get(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    String id = jwt.getSubject();
    ...
}

// or anywhere, without passing it along
var auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
                                .getAuthentication();
Reading the code
@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt

Spring passes the caller's validated token to this parameter. getSubject() reads the sub claim of the token, which is the user's id.

var auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext()

This line works in any bean, but it hides the dependency. In a controller, use the parameter instead.

Gotcha

SecurityContextHolder keeps the caller in a ThreadLocal. A ThreadLocal is a value that belongs to one thread. So the caller is not available on a thread that you start yourself. The same is true for a task that you submit to an ExecutorService. Whenever you send work to other threads, wrap the executor in a DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor. The wrapper passes the caller to the thread that runs each task.

Passwords#

Some sites sign users in themselves, with a form and a cookie. Such a site calls formLogin() in the filter chain, and keeps the user in an HTTP session. If the shop stores the passwords of its own users, it must hash them. One bean chooses the algorithm:

@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}
Reading the code
PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();

This encoder hashes new passwords with bcrypt. It can still check hashes that were made with older algorithms.

Note

The delegating encoder stores a prefix such as {bcrypt} in the hash. So you can change the algorithm later, and the existing passwords stay valid. The delegating encoder does the same as the versioned password hashes of ASP.NET Identity. It is the right default.

To check a password, Spring Security loads the user by name through a UserDetailsService. The service returns a UserDetails. UserDetailsService is like UserManager in ASP.NET Core Identity. UserDetails is like IdentityUser. But you must build registration, password reset and the rest of account management yourself.

The data protection of ASP.NET Core also has no direct equivalent in Spring. Spring has no built-in key ring, so use a key management service (KMS) or Spring Vault.

Null-safety in the Spring API#

Note

Spring Framework 7 moved its whole API from the Java Specification Request (JSR) 305 annotations to JSpecify Boot 4. If you use a null checker, the signatures of Spring itself now say exactly where null is possible. This includes generics. So the checker is much more useful with Spring than it was on Boot 3. See Nullability.

In the code below, env has the Spring type Environment. It is injected like any bean. Here a configuration lookup may return null, and the checker says so:

String url = env.getProperty("rates.url");   // declared @Nullable in Spring Framework 7
int length = url.length();                   // a null checker such as NullAway flags this line
Reading the code
String url = env.getProperty("rates.url");

getProperty returns null when the setting is missing. Spring 7 declares that with the @Nullable annotation of JSpecify.

int length = url.length();

Using url without a null check could throw, so a checker such as NullAway reports this line when you build.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite the rules for these endpoints in Java, as the authorizeHttpRequests part of a filter chain: 
app.MapControllers().RequireAuthorization();

[AllowAnonymous]
[HttpGet("/api/products")]
public IActionResult Products() => Ok("products");

[Authorize(Roles = "Support")]
[HttpGet("/api/refunds")]
public IActionResult Refunds() => Ok("refunds");
http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
    .requestMatchers("/api/products/**").permitAll()
    .requestMatchers("/api/refunds/**").hasRole("SUPPORT")
    .anyRequest().authenticated())

The two specific rules come first and anyRequest() comes last, because the first rule that matches decides. hasRole("SUPPORT") checks for the authority ROLE_SUPPORT.

2
A service method carries @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), yet every caller gets through, whichever bean calls it. What is missing?
@EnableMethodSecurity is missing on a configuration class. Without it, every @PreAuthorize in the application is ignored, and nothing warns you.
3
An expert asksThe shop's API authenticates callers with bearer tokens, and switches CSRF protection off. Why is that safe there, and not for a site that signs users in with cookies?
In the attack, another site makes the user's browser send a request with the user's cookies. Browsers do not call the shop's API with cookies, because the API uses tokens. So the protection can be switched off. Anything that uses cookies must keep the protection.

HTTP clients and resilience#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 44· 7 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

RestClient in Spring calls another service over HTTP, like HttpClient in .NET. This chapter also covers interface clients, which are like Refit. And it covers what you use in place of Polly when the other service fails.

KindC#JavaNote
twisthttpClientFactory.CreateClient("rates")a RestClient bean, built from RestClient.BuilderRestClient is the default client on Boot 3.2 and later, and it blocks Why
twistGetFromJsonAsync<Rate>(url)get().uri(url).retrieve().body(Rate.class)a blocking call, which is exactly right on a virtual thread Why
twistRefit interfacean @HttpExchange interfaceone method per endpoint, and Spring writes the class that makes the calls Why
twistAddRefitClient<IRatesApi>()Boot 3: HttpServiceProxyFactory. Boot 4: @ImportHttpServicesBoot 4 registers the client bean, but on Boot 3 you build it in a @Bean method Why
twistConfigureHttpClient(c => c.BaseAddress = ...)spring.http.serviceclient.<group>.base-urlon Boot 4, the address of an @ImportHttpServices group is a setting Why
twistPolly's AddRetryBoot 3: @Retry, from Resilience4j. Boot 4: @RetryableSpring Framework 7 has retry in its core, so Boot 4 needs no extra library Why
twista Polly bulkheadBoot 3: @Bulkhead. Boot 4: @ConcurrencyLimit(10)It limits how many calls run at once. Virtual threads have no pool that limits them. Why
twistPolly's AddCircuitBreaker@CircuitBreaker, from Resilience4jcore has no circuit breaker and no rate limiter, on Boot 3 or on Boot 4 Why
twistMaxRetryAttempts = 3@Retryable(maxRetries = 3)Both count only the retries, so 3 means four calls. On Boot 3, maxAttempts counted the first call too. Why
trapa pipeline you call yourself@Retryable, which works through a proxya call from inside the same class skips the proxy, so nothing is retried Why
trapa client with no timeout setsetConnectTimeout(...) and setReadTimeout(...)the defaults are effectively infinite, so a hung service holds the connection Why
twistEnsureSuccessStatusCode()retrieve()a 4xx or 5xx reply becomes an exception, and onStatus replaces it with your own Why
twistHttpClientrestTemplate.getForObject(...), in existing codethe original client is in maintenance mode, so write RestClient in new code Why

The client optionstwist#

Spring offers several clients for an HTTP call:

ClientStyleUse when
RestClientfluent, blockingthe default on Boot 3.2+
WebClientfluent, reactiveyou are in WebFlux, or need streaming
@HttpExchange interfacedeclarativeyou want Refit-style typed clients
RestTemplatefluent, blockinglegacy code, as described below
java.net.http.HttpClientJDK built-inno Spring dependency wanted

The last row is the client built into the Java Development Kit (JDK). Here is the everyday call, in both frameworks:

C#
var client = httpClientFactory.CreateClient("rates");
var rate = await client
    .GetFromJsonAsync<Rate>($"/rates/{pair}");
Java 25
Rate rate = restClient.get()
        .uri("/rates/{pair}", pair)
        .retrieve()
        .body(Rate.class);
Reading the code
.uri("/rates/{pair}", pair)

This is a URI template. The next argument is escaped and put in the place of {pair}. The base address was set when the RestClient was built.

.retrieve()

This call sends the request. A 4xx or 5xx response becomes an exception, as with EnsureSuccessStatusCode in .NET.

.body(Rate.class);

This call reads the JSON body into a Rate. Here Rate is a record, declared as record Rate(String pair, double value).

Note

That call blocks, and on a virtual thread that is exactly right. You no longer need WebClient to scale. Reactive types are for streaming and backpressure. You do not need them to avoid thread starvation. See Threads are cheap now.

Declarative clientstwist#

Refit
public interface IRatesApi
{
    [Get("/rates/{pair}")]
    Task<Rate> GetRate(string pair);

    [Post("/quotes")]
    Task<Quote> CreateQuote([Body] QuoteRequest req);
}

builder.Services
    .AddRefitClient<IRatesApi>()
    .ConfigureHttpClient(c =>
        c.BaseAddress = new Uri(url));
Spring HTTP interfaces
public interface RatesApi {

    @GetExchange("/rates/{pair}")
    Rate getRate(@PathVariable String pair);

    @PostExchange("/quotes")
    Quote createQuote(@RequestBody QuoteRequest request);
}
Reading the code
@GetExchange("/rates/{pair}")

This method sends a GET to that path, like [Get] in Refit. The annotations @PathVariable and @RequestBody say where each argument goes. They are the same annotations as in a controller.

Quote createQuote(@RequestBody QuoteRequest request);

This method sends the QuoteRequest as the JSON body, and reads the reply into a Quote.

Boot 4 added auto-configuration for @HttpExchange interfaces. On Boot 3 you build the client yourself:

// Boot 3: build the proxy factory by hand
@Configuration
class ClientConfig {

    @Bean
    RatesApi ratesApi(RestClient.Builder builder,
                      @Value("${rates.url}") String url) {
        RestClient client = builder.baseUrl(url).build();
        var adapter = RestClientAdapter.create(client);
        var factory = HttpServiceProxyFactory
                .builderFor(adapter).build();
        return factory.createClient(RatesApi.class);
    }
}
// Boot 4: declare the group; Spring registers the client bean
@Configuration
@ImportHttpServices(group = "rates", types = RatesApi.class)
class ClientConfig { }

// configured in application.yml under the group name,
// then injected like any other bean
Reading the code
return factory.createClient(RatesApi.class);

On Boot 3, HttpServiceProxyFactory creates a proxy. The proxy is an object that implements RatesApi. It turns each method call into an HTTP request through the RestClient.

@ImportHttpServices(group = "rates", types = RatesApi.class)

On Boot 4, one annotation does the same. It also puts the interface in a group called rates. The settings of the group are in application.yml.

Boot 4: the settings of a service group#

On Boot 4, the settings of the group are under the name of the group:

spring:
  http:
    serviceclient:
      rates:
        base-url: https://rates.example.com
Reading the code
base-url: https://rates.example.com

This is the address that every RatesApi call starts from, like BaseAddress in .NET.

Resilience: the Polly answertwist#

C# refresherPolly: retry, circuit breaker and timeout as a pipelineC# 5

Polly combines resilience strategies into one pipeline and runs your call through it.

var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder()
    .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions { MaxRetryAttempts = 3 })
    .AddCircuitBreaker(new CircuitBreakerStrategyOptions())
    .AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))
    .Build();

var rate = await pipeline.ExecuteAsync(async ct => await FetchAsync(pair, ct));

Spring Framework 7 added retry support to its core, so on Boot 4 @Retryable needs no separate library:

// Boot 3: Resilience4j, added as a dependency
@Service
class RatesClient {

    @Retry(name = "rates", fallbackMethod = "cached")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "rates", fallbackMethod = "cached")
    @Bulkhead(name = "rates")
    public Rate fetch(String pair) {
        return restClient.get()
                .uri("/rates/{p}", pair)
                .retrieve().body(Rate.class);
    }

    private Rate cached(String pair, Throwable t) {
        return cache.get(pair);
    }
}
// Boot 4: @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit are in
// Spring Framework core; no extra dependency
@EnableResilientMethods
@Configuration
class ResilienceConfig { }

@Service
class RatesClient {

    // core defaults: 3 retries, 1s delay, retries any exception
    @Retryable(includes = RatesUnavailableException.class,
               maxRetries = 4, delay = 200, multiplier = 2,
               jitter = 20, maxDelay = 2000)
    @ConcurrencyLimit(10)
    public Rate fetch(String pair) {
        return restClient.get()
                .uri("/rates/{p}", pair)
                .retrieve().body(Rate.class);
    }
}
Reading the code
@Retry(name = "rates", fallbackMethod = "cached")

This is Boot 3, with Resilience4j. The settings for the rates policy are in application.yml. The method cached is called after every attempt has failed.

@Retryable(includes = RatesUnavailableException.class,

This is Boot 4, with the annotation from core. It retries only when this exception is thrown, and at most 4 more times. The first wait is 200 ms, and each later wait is double the wait before it. Each later wait can be up to 20 ms shorter or longer, but it is never longer than 2 seconds.

@ConcurrencyLimit(10)

At most 10 calls run at once, and the other calls wait. This does the same as a bulkhead in Polly. It is important with virtual threads, because virtual threads have no pool that limits them.

This table shows what each Polly strategy becomes on Boot 3 and on Boot 4:

PollyBoot 3 (Resilience4j)Boot 4 (Spring Framework core)
Retry@Retry@Retryable
Bulkhead@Bulkhead@ConcurrencyLimit
Circuit breaker@CircuitBreakernot in core, so keep Resilience4j
Rate limiter@RateLimiternot in core, so keep Resilience4j
Timeout@TimeLimiter@Retryable(timeout = ...) limits the whole retry, so set a request timeout for each call
FallbackfallbackMethodnot in core, so catch the exception after the last retry fails
ProgrammaticRetryRegistryRetryTemplate with RetryPolicy.builder()

Retries: the count, the proxy and what core leaves out#

On Boot 4, the annotation needs no attributes:

@Retryable
public Rate fetch(String pair) {
    return restClient.get().uri("/rates/{p}", pair).retrieve().body(Rate.class);
}
Reading the code
@Retryable

The core defaults apply. They are 3 retries, 1 second apart, on any exception.

Gotcha

The attribute is maxRetries, not maxAttempts. Spring Retry is the add-on for Boot 3. It uses maxAttempts and counts the first call. The core annotation of Framework 7 uses maxRetries and counts only the retries. So the default of 3 means four calls in total, one second apart, with a retry on any exception. If you paste a Boot 3 snippet into a Boot 4 codebase, it fails to compile, and that is the good outcome. The bad outcome is that you keep the wrong idea of the count.

MaxRetryAttempts in Polly also counts only the retries. With a value of 3, a call that always fails runs four times. So this trap is for code that comes from Boot 3, not from .NET.

Note

Core covers retry and concurrency limiting only. It has no circuit breaker and no rate limiter, so you still use Resilience4j for those on both versions. The timeout attribute of @Retryable limits the whole sequence of attempts, not one call. With the core additions, you need one dependency less for the two cases that most services need.

@Retryable also works on reactive methods. It adds a retry to the returned Mono or Flux. Every failed attempt publishes a MethodRetryEvent. You can listen for this event to log retries.

Gotcha

@Retryable works through a proxy, like @Transactional and @PreAuthorize. So self-invocation does not retry. For the reason, see the chapter How Spring actually works. And be careful when you retry an operation that is not idempotent. A POST that timed out may well have succeeded.

Timeoutstrap#

Gotcha

Set timeouts explicitly. The defaults are effectively infinite. Without a timeout, a downstream service that does not answer holds a connection until the socket dies. This is true of RestClient, of RestTemplate and of the JDK client.

For one client, set the timeouts on its request factory:

@Bean
RestClient ratesClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
                       @Value("${rates.url}") String url) {
    var factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
    factory.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
    factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
    return builder.baseUrl(url).requestFactory(factory).build();
}
Reading the code
factory.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));

The client stops waiting if the connection is not open within 2 seconds.

factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5));

The client stops waiting if the reply does not arrive within 5 seconds. The call then fails with a ResourceAccessException. Its cause is a SocketTimeoutException.

On Boot 4, two settings apply the same limits to every client that Boot builds:

spring:
  http:
    clients:
      connect-timeout: 2s
      read-timeout: 5s
Reading the code
read-timeout: 5s

This setting applies to whichever HTTP library Boot finds. Boot tries Apache HttpClient first, then Jetty, then Reactor Netty, and then the clients of the JDK itself.

Error handling#

By default, a 4xx or 5xx response becomes a Spring exception. To throw your own exceptions instead, add a handler for each status family:

Rate rate = restClient.get()
        .uri("/rates/{p}", pair)
        .retrieve()
        .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError,
                  (req, res) -> { throw new UnknownPairException(pair); })
        .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError,
                  (req, res) -> { throw new RatesUnavailableException(); })
        .body(Rate.class);
Reading the code
.onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError,

For any 4xx reply, Spring runs this handler instead of the default. Here the handler throws the shop's own UnknownPairException.

(req, res) -> { throw new RatesUnavailableException(); })

For any 5xx reply, this handler throws RatesUnavailableException. The @Retryable example above retries on this exception.

Without any handler, these are the defaults:

SituationRestClient default
4xxthrows HttpClientErrorException
5xxthrows HttpServerErrorException
Want the status, not an exceptionuse .exchange(...) instead of .retrieve()

Each exception has a subclass for each status, such as HttpClientErrorException.NotFound for a 404. So you can catch exactly the case you expect.

RestTemplate#

LegacyRestTemplate

RestTemplate is the original Spring HTTP client, and it is still in most existing codebases. It is in maintenance mode. This means that it is not deprecated, but it gets no new features. The documentation recommends RestClient, which wraps the same infrastructure with a better API.

Rate rate = restTemplate.getForObject(
        "/rates/{p}", Rate.class, pair);
Reading the code
restTemplate.getForObject(

RestTemplate has one method for each verb and kind of result. This method sends a GET and reads the body into a Rate. The URI template works as it does in RestClient.

Migration is mostly mechanical. You can build a RestClient from the configuration of an existing RestTemplate with RestClient.create(restTemplate).

Check yourself
1
What takes the place of Polly on Boot 3, and what on Boot 4?
Boot 3 uses the Resilience4j library. On Boot 4, @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit are in Spring Framework itself. For a circuit breaker or a rate limiter you still add Resilience4j, on both versions.

Quick reference#

SettingUse it to
spring.http.clients.connect-timeoutlimit the wait for a connection, for every client
spring.http.clients.read-timeoutlimit the wait for a reply, for every client
spring.http.serviceclient.<group>.base-urlset the address for an @ImportHttpServices group

Messaging and WebSockets#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 45· 7 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens

Messaging between services works in the way you know from MassTransit or the raw client libraries. A Template class sends a message. A method with a listener annotation receives the message. Push to the browser is different, because Spring has no single equivalent of SignalR.

KindC#JavaNote
twistProduceAsync (Confluent.Kafka)kafkaTemplate.send(topic, key, value)records with the same key go to one partition, so they stay in order Why
twistConsume loopa @KafkaListener methodSpring calls the method for each record, so there is no loop to write Why
trapan exception in the consume loopa listener method that throwsredelivered nine more times, then logged and skipped, unless you add a dead-letter topic Why
trapa publish inside a database transactionkafkaTemplate.send inside @Transactionala rollback does not cancel the message that was sent, so use a transactional outbox, as in .NET Why
twist_bus.Publish(new OrderPlaced(order.Id))rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(exchange, routingKey, event)MassTransit chooses the exchange for you, but with Spring AMQP you name the exchange Why
twistIConsumer<T> (MassTransit)a @RabbitListener methodSpring calls the method for each message on the queue Why
twistMassTransit sagas and schedulingno equivalentSpring AMQP does not include these, so you build them yourself. The nearest Java libraries are Spring Integration, Camel and Axon. Why
newno equivalentjmsClient.destination("orders").send(event)Jakarta Messaging is the standard messaging API in Java, and JmsClient needs Boot 4 Why
twistMapHub<PricesHub>("/prices")a STOMP broker over WebSocket, with @MessageMappingno Java framework bundles what SignalR does, so Spring gives you the pieces Why
twistClients.Group(...).SendAsyncmessagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/...", payload)pushes to every client subscribed to that destination Why
trapa SignalR backplaneenableStompBrokerRelay, to RabbitMQ or ActiveMQenableSimpleBroker is in memory, so it works on one instance only Why
twistTypedResults.ServerSentEventsSseEmitter, or a Flux on WebFluxThe C# call needs ASP.NET Core 10. Server-sent events are simpler than WebSocket when only the server pushes. Why

Kafkatrap#

With Kafka, the producer sends to a topic, and the consumer listens on the same topic:

Confluent.Kafka / MassTransit
// producer
await _producer.ProduceAsync("orders",
    new Message<string, string> {
        Key = order.Id, Value = json });

// consumer
_consumer.Subscribe("orders");
while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    var cr = _consumer.Consume(ct);
    Handle(cr.Message.Value);
}
Spring Kafka
// producer
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", order.id(), order);

// consumer
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders",
               groupId = "billing")
public void handle(OrderPlaced order) {
    process(order);
}
Reading the code
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", order.id(), order);

This line sends the event to the orders topic. The key is the id of the order. Events with the same key go to the same partition, so the events of one order stay in order.

@KafkaListener(topics = "orders",

Spring calls this method for each record on the topic. In Kafka, a message is called a record. Spring turns the JSON of the record into an OrderPlaced. You do not write a loop.

groupId = "billing")

This names the consumer group. Each record goes to one listener in the group.

The Kafka settings in application.ymldeep dive

Boot builds the template and the listeners from settings like these:

spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: billing
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      properties:
        spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.acme.billing.events"
    producer:
      acks: all
Reading the code
auto-offset-reset: earliest

A new consumer group starts from the oldest record that is still on the topic. So the group reads the old records too, and not only the new records.

spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.acme.billing.events"

The JSON reader creates classes from this package only. So a message cannot make the JSON reader create an object of any other type.

acks: all

A send is complete only when every in-sync replica has the record.

Gotcha

The listener method commits the offset by returning normally. If the method throws, Spring's default error handler redelivers the record up to nine more times, with no pause. Then the error handler logs the record at ERROR level and continues with the next record. So an unhandled exception drops the message, and only a log line remains. Configure a DefaultErrorHandler with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer. Then a failed record goes to a dead-letter topic and is not lost.

Ordering, retries and the outbox#

These settings become important when a Kafka consumer handles production traffic:

ConcernSpring Kafka
Orderingguaranteed per partition only, so key by aggregate id to keep an entity's events ordered
Concurrencyconcurrency = "3" on @KafkaListener, capped by partition count
Manual acksAckMode.MANUAL plus an Acknowledgment parameter
Retry with backoffDefaultErrorHandler with an ExponentialBackOff
Dead letterDeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, publishes to topic-dlt
Batch consumptionbatch = "true" and a List parameter
TransactionsKafkaTransactionManager, but it does not span Kafka and your database

Here is the dead-letter setup that the gotcha above recommends:

@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
    var toDeadLetter = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);   // failures go to orders-dlt
    return new DefaultErrorHandler(toDeadLetter, new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3));   // 3 retries, 1 s apart
}
Reading the code
var toDeadLetter = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);

When no retries remain, this recoverer publishes the failed record to a dead-letter topic. The name of that topic is the name of the original topic with -dlt added. The record goes to the same partition as in the original topic. So the dead-letter topic needs at least as many partitions as the original topic.

new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3)

This gives three retries after the first delivery, one second apart. That is four deliveries in total.

Gotcha

There is no distributed transaction across Kafka and your database. Suppose you publish inside an @Transactional method, and the method later rolls back. The message is still sent. The standard fix is called the transactional outbox. Write the event to a table in the same transaction. A separate poller then publishes the event. The problem and the solution are the same as in .NET. For more about the outbox, see the chapter Transactions, propagation and isolation.

RabbitMQ#

RabbitMQ uses the Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP). Spring AMQP is the client library for RabbitMQ. The producer publishes to an exchange with a routing key. The consumer listens on a queue:

C#
_bus.Publish(new OrderPlaced(order.Id));

public class Consumer : IConsumer<OrderPlaced>
{
    public Task Consume(
        ConsumeContext<OrderPlaced> ctx) { ... }
}
Java 25
rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(
    "orders.exchange", "order.placed", event);

@RabbitListener(queues = "orders.queue")
public void handle(OrderPlaced event) { ... }
Reading the code
rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(

This call converts the event to a message. Then it publishes the message to the exchange orders.exchange with the routing key order.placed. MassTransit chooses the exchange for you. Here you name the exchange yourself.

@RabbitListener(queues = "orders.queue")

Spring calls this method for each message on the queue. This is like IConsumer in MassTransit.

You declare the rest of the configuration yourself:

ConceptSpring AMQP
Declare topology@Bean Queue / TopicExchange / Binding
SerialisationJacksonJsonMessageConverter, registered as a bean, but Jackson2JsonMessageConverter on Boot 3
Retryspring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.retry.*
Dead letterx-dead-letter-exchange argument on the queue
Manual ackAcknowledgeMode.MANUAL plus a Channel parameter
Note

MassTransit and NServiceBus do much that Spring AMQP does not do, such as saga state, scheduling and conventional routing. With Spring AMQP, you build these yourself. The nearest Java equivalents are Spring Integration, Apache Camel and Axon. But none of these three is a direct replacement for MassTransit or NServiceBus.

JMS and JmsClient#

Java also has a standard messaging API. It is called Jakarta Messaging (JMS). It is used with brokers such as ActiveMQ Artemis and IBM MQ. Spring has wrapped JMS in JmsTemplate for a long time. Spring Framework 7 also adds a fluent JmsClient Boot 4:

jmsClient.destination("orders")
        .send(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()));

Optional<OrderPlaced> next = jmsClient.destination("orders")
        .withReceiveTimeout(1000)
        .receive(OrderPlaced.class);
Reading the code
jmsClient.destination("orders")

This call picks the queue or topic. The calls after it describe the operation on that queue or topic.

.receive(OrderPlaced.class);

This call waits for one message, for at most the timeout. It returns the message as an Optional. The Optional is empty if no message arrived. For a steady stream of messages, mark a method with @JmsListener. This annotation works like @KafkaListener.

WebSockets and the SignalR gapnew#

The web page of the shop shows live exchange rates. The server pushes each rate to the page when the rate changes. In ASP.NET Core, you write this as a SignalR hub:

C# refresherSignalR hubs: server push to groups of clientsC# 6
public class PricesHub : Hub
{
    public Task Subscribe(string pair) =>
        Groups.AddToGroupAsync(Context.ConnectionId, pair);
}

app.MapHub<PricesHub>("/prices");
await hub.Clients.Group("GBPUSD").SendAsync("price", price);   // push to one group
SignalR

No Java framework does everything that SignalR does in one library. SignalR gives you a hub abstraction, automatic transport negotiation and fallback, typed clients, reconnection and backplane scale-out. Spring gives you the separate parts:

SignalR featureSpring equivalent
Hub@Controller with @MessageMapping, over STOMP
Strongly typed hub clientnone, so you send to a destination by name
Transport fallbacknone built in, but SockJS is an optional fallback for WebSocket
GroupsSTOMP destinations, or a broker topic
Backplane for scale-outan external broker, RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ, as a STOMP relay
Automatic reconnectclient-side library concern

The nearest equivalent of a hub is a broker that uses the Simple Text Oriented Messaging Protocol (STOMP) over WebSocket. Clients subscribe to named destinations, such as /topic/prices. The server sends messages to those destinations:

@Configuration
@EnableWebSocketMessageBroker
public class WsConfig implements WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void registerStompEndpoints(StompEndpointRegistry registry) {
        registry.addEndpoint("/ws").setAllowedOriginPatterns("*");
    }

    @Override
    public void configureMessageBroker(MessageBrokerRegistry registry) {
        registry.enableSimpleBroker("/topic");     // in-memory, single instance
        registry.setApplicationDestinationPrefixes("/app");
    }
}

@Controller
class PriceController {

    // client sends to /app/subscribe, replies go to /topic/prices
    @MessageMapping("/subscribe")
    @SendTo("/topic/prices")
    public Price onSubscribe(SubscribeRequest req) {
        return prices.current(req.pair());
    }
}

// push from anywhere in the application
messagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/prices", price);
Reading the code
registry.addEndpoint("/ws").setAllowedOriginPatterns("*");

This line sets the address on which browsers open the WebSocket, like MapHub in SignalR. In production, allow only the origin of your own front end, not *.

registry.enableSimpleBroker("/topic");

This line enables a broker inside the application. The broker takes each message that is sent to a /topic/… destination. It delivers the message to every client that is subscribed to that destination.

@MessageMapping("/subscribe")

This method handles the messages that a client sends to /app/subscribe, like a hub method in SignalR. Here prices is a service that returns the latest price.

messagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/prices", price);

The type of messagingTemplate is SimpMessagingTemplate, which is part of Spring. Spring injects it like any other bean. This call pushes the price to every subscriber of the destination, like Clients.Group(...).SendAsync in SignalR.

Gotcha

enableSimpleBroker creates an in-memory broker. This broker works correctly on one instance. It fails as soon as you run more than one instance. The reason is that a message published on instance A never reaches a client connected to instance B. For more than one instance, you need enableStompBrokerRelay, which points to RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ. This is the equivalent of adding a SignalR backplane.

Server-sent events, the simpler option#

Sometimes you need push from server to client only, and not in both directions. Then server-sent events are much simpler than WebSocket. Server-sent events also pass through most load balancers and firewalls. ASP.NET Core 10 has server-sent events built in. Spring MVC is the model-view-controller (MVC) web framework of Spring. Spring MVC has the class SseEmitter for server-sent events:

C#
// ASP.NET Core 10; Prices(ct) is an IAsyncEnumerable<Price>
app.MapGet("/prices", (CancellationToken ct) =>
    TypedResults.ServerSentEvents(Prices(ct),
        eventType: "price"));
Java 25
@GetMapping(value = "/prices",
    produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public SseEmitter stream() {
    var emitter = new SseEmitter(0L);   // no timeout
    executor.submit(() -> {
        try {
            emitter.send(price);
            emitter.complete();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            emitter.completeWithError(e);
        }
    });
    return emitter;
}
Reading the code
var emitter = new SseEmitter(0L);

This line creates an open response. The method returns the response at once, and the code writes to it later. 0L means that the response never times out.

executor.submit(() -> {

The sending runs on another thread. That thread comes from an executor of virtual threads. The request thread is free during this time.

emitter.send(price);

This line writes one event, data:{"pair":"GBPUSD","value":1.27}, followed by a blank line. send can throw IOException, so the call is inside a try block.

emitter.complete();

This line ends the stream. A real price feed would continue to send events.

Note

WebFlux is the reactive web stack of Spring. On WebFlux, you return a Flux<Price> with the same produces value. On virtual threads, an SseEmitter that a blocking loop writes to is now a reasonable design. Before virtual threads, it was not a reasonable design. See Threads are cheap now.

Check yourself
1
A @KafkaListener method throws every time it receives one record. What happens to that record by default?
Spring redelivers the record up to nine more times, with no pause. Then Spring logs the record at ERROR level and continues with the next record. The message is dropped, unless a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer sends it to a dead-letter topic.

Actuator and observability#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 46· 9 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

Actuator gives you health checks, metrics and diagnostics in one dependency. That is more than ASP.NET Core gives you by default. This chapter also covers metrics, logging and tracing. And it covers Java Flight Recorder (JFR), which is a profiler built into the Java Development Kit (JDK).

KindC#JavaNote
twistAddHealthChecks()/actuator/healthone starter adds health, metrics and diagnostic endpoints under /actuator Why
trapan endpoint is reachable once you map itmanagement.endpoints.web.exposure.includeonly health is exposed over HTTP by default, and you must never expose env or heapdump publicly Why
twisthealth checks for Kubernetes probes/actuator/health/liveness and /readinessBoot 4 adds these two endpoints by default, but Boot 3 adds them only when it detects Kubernetes Why
twistediting appsettings.json, which reloadsPOST /actuator/loggers/com.acme.billingan HTTP call changes the level on one running instance, but ASP.NET Core rereads the file instead Why
twistIHealthChecka HealthIndicator beanAny bean that implements HealthIndicator joins /actuator/health. The package of HealthIndicator moved in Boot 4. Why
twistmeter.CreateCounter<long>("orders.placed")Counter.builder("orders.placed").register(registry)Micrometer is the metrics facade. Prometheus scrapes this counter as orders_placed_total. Why
trapa filter that times each call@Timed on a service methoddoes nothing until you enable observation annotations and add AspectJ Why
twistILogger<T>SLF4J Loggeryour code calls SLF4J, and Logback does the actual writing Why
twist{Named} placeholders{} positional placeholdersSLF4J placeholders are positional, and argument names are not kept Why
twistBeginScopeMDCper-thread key/value pairs that every log line can include Why
twistappsettings logging levelslogging.level.* in application.ymlsets the level for one package and everything below it Why
twistSerilogLogbackLogback is what Spring Boot uses unless you switch Why
twistNLogLog4j2Boot also includes a default configuration for Log4j2 if you switch Why
twista JSON formatterlogging.structured.format.console: ecsBoot 3.4 and later write JSON logs with one setting and no extra library Why
twistOpenTelemetry for .NETspring-boot-starter-opentelemetry, or the Java agentThe starter needs Boot 4. The agent instruments the application with no code changes. Why
twistdotnet-trace and dotnet-counters, installed as separate toolsjcmd <pid> JFR.starta recorder built into the JDK, started against a running process with nothing to install Why

Actuator endpointsnew#

The billing service runs in Kubernetes. Kubernetes must know whether each instance is alive and ready for traffic. The operations team also wants metrics. A single starter named spring-boot-starter-actuator adds a set of HTTP endpoints under /actuator:

EndpointGives you.NET analogy
/actuator/healthliveness and readinessAddHealthChecks
/actuator/metricsevery metric, queryabledotnet-counters
/actuator/prometheusPrometheus scrape formatprometheus-net
/actuator/infobuild and git info
/actuator/envresolved configuration
/actuator/loggersread AND CHANGE log levels at runtimeappsettings.json, reread when it changes
/actuator/threaddumpevery thread's stackdotnet-dump
/actuator/heapdumpa heap dump filedotnet-gcdump
/actuator/mappingsevery route
/actuator/beansthe whole container
/actuator/configpropsbound @ConfigurationProperties

Most of these endpoints are hidden until you list them. Here the service exposes four endpoints, and it shows health details to signed-in callers:

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus,loggers
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized
      probes:
        enabled: true        # /health/liveness and /health/readiness for Kubernetes
Reading the code
include: health,info,prometheus,loggers

This line lists the endpoints that are reachable over HTTP. Without this line, only health is reachable.

show-details: when-authorized

Anonymous callers see only UP or DOWN. Signed-in callers see each check. The default value is never.

enabled: true

This line adds /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness for Kubernetes probes. Boot 4 adds these two endpoints by default, so this line matters on Boot 3. Without the line, Boot 3 adds the two endpoints only when it detects Kubernetes.

The same endpoints can also be published over Java Management Extensions (JMX). JMX is the older management interface that is built into Java. Tools such as JConsole read it. JMX is off in Boot unless you set spring.jmx.enabled=true.

Gotcha

Only health is exposed over HTTP by default. You must list every other endpoint before it is exposed. Do not expose these four endpoints publicly, because they leak configuration and memory contents:

  • env
  • heapdump
  • beans
  • configprops

Put Actuator on a separate port that is not routed from the internet, or secure it. The setting for the port is management.server.port.

The loggers endpoint is useful to know. Here an engineer sets the log level to DEBUG for the billing code on a running production instance:

curl -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.acme.billing \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'
Reading the code
localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.acme.billing

This address names the logger for one package and for everything below that package. The service answers 204, and the new level applies at once.

-d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'

This is the new level. Later, post null to restore the earlier level.

Note

You collect the information that you need, and then you restore the level. You do not restart or redeploy the service. ASP.NET Core also changes a level without a restart, but it uses the file. A running host rereads appsettings.json when the file changes.

Custom health checks#

The billing service depends on the rates service. So the health of the billing service should include the health of the rates service. A health check is a bean that reports up or down:

C#
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck<RatesHealthCheck>("rates");

public class RatesHealthCheck : IHealthCheck
{
    public Task<HealthCheckResult> CheckHealthAsync(
        HealthCheckContext context, CancellationToken ct)
        => Task.FromResult(HealthCheckResult.Healthy());
}
Java 25
@Component
public class RatesHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final RatesClient ratesClient;

    RatesHealthIndicator(RatesClient ratesClient) {
        this.ratesClient = ratesClient;
    }

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try {
            long ms = ratesClient.ping();    // round trip, in ms
            return Health.up()
                    .withDetail("latencyMs", ms).build();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return Health.down(e).build();
        }
    }
}
Reading the code
public class RatesHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

Any bean that implements HealthIndicator joins /actuator/health. The key of this check is the bean name without the suffix: rates.

.withDetail("latencyMs", ms).build();

This line adds extra information to the result. Callers who are allowed to see details see this information, as in "rates": {"details": {"latencyMs": 12}, "status": "UP"}.

return Health.down(e).build();

This line reports the check as down. The message of the exception is included as a detail.

Note

On Boot 4, HealthIndicator and Health are in the package org.springframework.boot.health.contributor. On Boot 3, both types were in org.springframework.boot.actuate.health. Boot registers its own checks for disk space, the datasource, Redis, Kafka and most other configured infrastructure. So you get many of the health checks with no code of your own.

Metricstwist#

Micrometer does the same as System.Diagnostics.Metrics in .NET:

C#
var counter = meter.CreateCounter<long>("orders.placed");
counter.Add(1,
    new KeyValuePair<string, object?>("status", "ok"));
Java 25
private final Counter placed;

OrderService(MeterRegistry registry) {
    this.placed = Counter.builder("orders.placed")
            .tag("status", "ok")
            .register(registry);
}

placed.increment();
Reading the code
OrderService(MeterRegistry registry) {

Boot supplies the MeterRegistry. The registry holds every metric. It gives the metrics to the backend that you use, such as Prometheus.

.tag("status", "ok")

This line puts a key and a value on the metric, like the KeyValuePair in the C# code. Each distinct value is a separate series.

The meter types of Micrometer match the instruments of .NET:

InstrumentMicrometerUse for
CounterCountermonotonic counts
GaugeGaugea current value
HistogramDistributionSummarya distribution of values
Timer / durationTimerlatency
n/aLongTaskTimerin-flight long operations
Gotcha

Never tag a metric with something unbounded, such as a user ID, an order ID or a raw URL. Each distinct combination of tags is a separate time series. A tag that has very many distinct values is called a high-cardinality tag. A high-cardinality tag will make your metrics backend fail before it makes your application fail. Prometheus has the same rule in general. But Micrometer makes the rule easy to break by accident inside a loop.

The Prometheus output, and timing a method with @Timed#

When Prometheus scrapes /actuator/prometheus, the counter looks like this:

orders_placed_total{status="ok"} 1.0
Reading the code
orders_placed_total{status="ok"} 1.0

Micrometer changes the dots into underscores and adds _total. Prometheus expects this form for a counter.

For latency, an annotation can time a whole method:

// declarative timing, the equivalent of a filter
@Timed(value = "orders.place", percentiles = {0.5, 0.95, 0.99})
public Order place(CreateOrder cmd) { ... }
Reading the code
@Timed(value = "orders.place", percentiles = {0.5, 0.95, 0.99})

This annotation measures how long each call takes. The metric is named orders.place. It includes the median, the 95th percentile and the 99th percentile.

Gotcha

@Timed on a service method does nothing by default, and no metric appears. To make it work, do two things. First, set management.observations.annotations.enabled=true. Second, add spring-boot-starter-aspectj, which brings the AspectJ library that the annotation needs. On Boot 3, the same starter is named spring-boot-starter-aop. Controllers and repositories are already timed, so annotating them gives you duplicates.

Loggingtwist#

C#
private readonly ILogger<OrderService> _log;

_log.LogInformation("Placed order {OrderId} for {Total}",
    id, total);
Java 25
private static final Logger log =
        LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);

log.info("Placed order {} for {}", id, total);
Reading the code
LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);

Each class has one logger, kept in a static final field. Your code calls the Simple Logging Facade for Java (SLF4J). Logback is the library that Boot uses, and Logback does the writing.

log.info("Placed order {} for {}", id, total);

Each {} is filled by the next argument, in order. The line in the log is Placed order 42 for 19.99. The placeholders have no names.

C# refresherILogger scopes and appsettings log levelsC# 6
using (_log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["OrderId"] = id }))
{
    _log.LogInformation("charging");    // every line in the scope carries OrderId
}
{ "Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information", "Acme.Billing": "Debug" } } }

In place of BeginScope, Java uses the mapped diagnostic context (MDC). The MDC holds key/value pairs for each thread, and every log line can include them.

Gotcha

SLF4J placeholders are written {}. They are positional, not named. Use placeholders, not string concatenation. log.debug("x is " + value) builds the string even when debug is off. log.debug("x is {}", value) does not build the string when debug is off. In both forms, the arguments themselves are evaluated. So if an argument is slow to calculate, put the call inside if (log.isDebugEnabled()), or pass a Supplier.

logback-spring.xml and JSON logging#

In a container, an application usually writes its logs as JSON. Boot writes JSON itself, with one setting:

logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs
Reading the code
console: ecs

This setting writes each line in Elastic Common Schema format, such as {"@timestamp":"…","log":{"level":"INFO","logger":"com.acme.billing.OrderService"},"message":"Placed order 42 for 19.99"}. The other formats are gelf and logstash.

application.yml can set levels, a console pattern and structured output. For anything more, such as per-appender routing or file rotation, you need a Logback configuration file. Name the file logback-spring.xml, not logback.xml. Boot loads the file that has -spring in its name. So Spring properties and profiles work inside that file.

<!-- src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml -->
<configuration>
  <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/defaults.xml"/>

  <springProfile name="!prod">
    <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/console-appender.xml"/>
    <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/></root>
  </springProfile>

  <springProfile name="prod">
    <appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
      <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
        <includeMdcKeyName>correlationId</includeMdcKeyName>
      </encoder>
    </appender>
    <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="JSON"/></root>
  </springProfile>
</configuration>
Reading the code
<springProfile name="!prod">

This block applies only when the prod profile is not active. It gives plain console output for developers.

<encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">

In production, the Logstash encoder library writes each line as JSON. Each line includes the correlation id from the mapped diagnostic context (MDC).

Each Serilog concept has a Logback equivalent:

Serilog conceptLogback equivalent
Sinkappender
EnricherMDC, or a custom converter
JSON formatterLogstashEncoder, or Boot's own structured logging
Minimum level override per namespacelogging.level.com.acme in application.yml
Rolling fileRollingFileAppender with a TimeBasedRollingPolicy
Environment-specific configspringProfile blocks, as above
Note

Spring Boot 3.4 added built-in structured logging, which the start of this section shows. So JSON output no longer needs the Logstash encoder dependency. On Boot 3.4 or later, prefer the built-in structured logging. Use the XML file only when you need routing or rotation that the built-in logging does not provide.

Tracing#

Micrometer Tracing together with OpenTelemetry gives you distributed tracing. Distributed tracing means that one trace id follows a request across services. Boot 4 adds a dedicated starter for this Boot 4:

<!-- Boot 4 -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry</artifactId>

This starter brings Micrometer Tracing with the OpenTelemetry bridge and exporter, and it configures them. So incoming and outgoing HTTP calls carry trace ids.

Note

The alternative is the OpenTelemetry Java agent, and it is often the better choice. You attach the agent with -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar. The agent rewrites the bytecode of classes when they load. It does this for Spring, Java Database Connectivity (JDBC), HTTP client and Kafka classes. So the agent instruments these classes with no code changes. OpenTelemetry offers a similar zero-code option for .NET. You set up that option through environment variables before the process starts.

JFR: the recorder built into the JDK#

JDK Flight Recorder is an always-on event recorder with low overhead. It is built into the JDK. You can start a recording on a running production process without a restart:

# start a recording on a running process
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/rec.jfr

# or from launch
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=rec.jfr -jar app.jar

jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=diag filename=/tmp/now.jfr
Reading the code
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/rec.jfr

jcmd sends a command to a running Java process, which you name by its process id. This command starts a 60-second recording with the more detailed profile settings.

jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=diag filename=/tmp/now.jfr

This command writes the contents of the recording so far to a file. It does not stop the recording.

Open the file in JDK Mission Control. This tool shows allocation profiles, lock contention, garbage collection (GC) pauses, I/O, thrown exceptions and CPU sampling, all on one timeline. Java 25 added CPU-time profiling Java 25 experimental. Java 25 also added events that time and trace chosen methods.

For each profiling task, here is the .NET tool and the Java tool that matches it:

Need.NETJava
Continuous production profilinglimitedJFR
Deep CPU profileVisual Studio Profiler, PerfViewasync-profiler, JFR
Heap analysisdotnet-gcdumpjmap + Eclipse MAT
Thread dumpdotnet-dumpjcmd Thread.print
GC logsGC ETW events-Xlog:gc*
Check yourself
1
Which Actuator endpoints can be reached over HTTP by default, and which should never be public?
Only health can be reached by default. You expose the other endpoints with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include. The endpoints env and heapdump should never be public. The same is true for beans and configprops. These four endpoints leak configuration and memory contents.

Quick reference#

SettingUse it to
management.endpoints.web.exposure.includechoose the endpoints reachable over HTTP
management.endpoint.health.show-detailsshow each check, set to never, when-authorized or always
management.server.portserve Actuator on a separate port
management.observations.annotations.enabledmake @Timed and @Observed work on any bean
logging.structured.format.consolewrite JSON logs in the format ecs, gelf or logstash
