Caching, scheduling and events#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 47· 7 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

You will meet three features within weeks. They are caching the result of a method, running a method on a timetable, and publishing events inside the process. All three features work through a proxy. So the rules in the chapter How Spring actually works apply.

KindC#JavaNote
twist_cache.TryGetValue then _cache.Set@Cacheable on the methodthe proxy does the lookup, the miss handling and the storing Why
trapAddMemoryCache()@EnableCachingWithout @EnableCaching, every cache annotation does nothing and nothing warns you. @EnableScheduling and @EnableAsync work in the same way. Why
twist_cache.Remove(key)@CacheEvict(value = "rates", key = "#rate.pair()")keys and conditions are written in Spring's expression language Why
trapTimeSpan.FromMinutes(5) on each entryspring.cache.type: caffeine, with a specthe default store never evicts and never expires, so configure Caffeine or Redis Why
twistBackgroundService with a Task.Delay loop@Scheduled(fixedDelay = ...)runs once at startup, then again that long after each run finishes Why
trapa five-field cron line, as in Unixcron = "0 0 3 * * *"Spring cron has six fields with seconds first, so with five fields the application refuses to start Why
trapseveral timers running at oncespring.task.scheduling.pool.sizethe scheduler has one thread by default, so one slow job delays every other job Why
trapa job that must run once@SchedulerLock, from ShedLockevery instance runs every schedule, and there is no built-in leader election Why
twistHangfireQuartzthe choice for jobs with retries, persistence and a dashboard Why
twistINotification and INotificationHandleran event record and an @EventListener methodSpring picks the listener by its parameter type, with no interface to implement Why
twist_mediator.Publish(new OrderPlaced(order.Id))events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()))as with MediatR, listeners run on the caller's thread, and a listener that throws fails the caller Why
twista handler that must wait for the commit@TransactionalEventListenerruns after the transaction commits, so it is the safe default for side effects Why
twistTask.Run(...)an @Async methodThe call returns at once. The method needs @EnableAsync, and it may return only void or a Future. Why
trapa method that calls another in its own classself-invocationThe call skips the proxy, so @Async or @Cacheable does nothing. On a final method, these annotations also do nothing. Why

Cachingtrap#

In ASP.NET Core, you check a cache yourself. On a miss, you call the service and store the result. In Spring, one annotation does all of these steps:

C#
public async Task<Rate> GetRateAsync(string pair)
{
    if (_cache.TryGetValue(pair, out Rate hit))
        return hit;

    var rate = await _client.FetchAsync(pair);
    _cache.Set(pair, rate, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
    return rate;
}
Java 25
@Cacheable("rates")
public Rate getRate(String pair) {
    return client.fetch(pair);
}
// lookup, miss handling and population
// are all done by the proxy
Reading the code
@Cacheable("rates")

Before the method runs, Spring looks in the cache named rates. The key is the argument pair. On a hit, Spring returns the stored value, and the method does not run at all. On a miss, Spring runs the method and stores the value that the method returns.

These are the cache annotations, with the IMemoryCache call that each annotation replaces:

AnnotationDoes.NET equivalent
@Cacheablereturn the cached value, or call the method and cache itGetOrCreate
@CachePutalways call the method, then update the cacheSet
@CacheEvictremove an entryRemove
@CacheEvict(allEntries = true)clear the cacheMemoryCache.Clear(), which IMemoryCache does not have
@Cachingcombine several of the aboveseveral calls
@EnableCachingswitch the whole mechanism onAddMemoryCache
Gotcha

Forgetting @EnableCaching makes every cache annotation do nothing. Nothing warns you. The code still works, because it calls the method every time. The same is true of @EnableScheduling and @EnableAsync. When a caching layer appears to have no effect, the cause is nearly always a missing @EnableCaching.

Cache keys, conditions and eviction#

Here the annotations are used together, on the rates of the billing service:

@Configuration
@EnableCaching          // without this, every annotation below is inert
class CacheConfig { }

@Service
public class RatesService {

    @Cacheable(value = "rates", key = "#pair + ':' + #date")
    public Rate lookup(String pair, LocalDate date) { ... }

    @CacheEvict(value = "rates", key = "#rate.pair()")
    public void invalidate(Rate rate) { }

    @Cacheable(value = "rates", unless = "#result == null")
    public Rate maybeNull(String pair) { ... }

    @Cacheable(value = "rates", condition = "#pair.length() == 6")
    public Rate onlyValidPairs(String pair) { ... }
}
Reading the code
@EnableCaching

This annotation enables caching. You write it once, in any configuration class.

key = "#pair + ':' + #date"

This expression builds the key from both arguments, for example EURUSD:2026-09-13. The key is written in Spring's expression language. In this language, #pair means the parameter pair.

@CacheEvict(value = "rates", key = "#rate.pair()")

This annotation removes the entry for the pair of this rate. Rate is a record, so you read the pair with pair().

unless = "#result == null"

Spring runs the method. Then Spring stores the result only when the result is not null. So a missing rate is fetched again on the next call.

condition = "#pair.length() == 6"

Spring uses the cache only for pairs of six letters, such as EURUSD. With any other argument, Spring does not use the cache at all.

Gotcha

condition and unless are not the same. condition is evaluated before the call. It decides whether caching applies at all. unless is evaluated after the call. It decides whether to store the result. Only unless can see #result.

Choosing the cache store#

The annotations work with any cache store. You choose the store separately:

ProviderAddNotes
Simple (ConcurrentHashMap)nothing, because it is the defaultno eviction and no size limit, so use it in development only
Caffeinecom.github.ben-manes.caffeinethe usual choice for a cache inside the process
Redisspring-boot-starter-data-redisone cache shared by every instance of the service
Hazelcast, Infinispantheir startersa cache spread across a cluster of nodes

Here the service uses Caffeine, which is an in-process cache with a size limit and expiry:

spring:
  cache:
    type: caffeine
    caffeine:
      spec: maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=5m
Reading the code
spec: maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=5m

Each cache holds at most 10,000 entries. Each entry is removed five minutes after it was stored, like the TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5) in the C# version.

Gotcha

The default cache manager is an unbounded ConcurrentHashMap. It never evicts an entry, and an entry never expires. So in practice it is a memory leak, not a cache. Configure Caffeine or Redis before the service goes to production.

Schedulingtrap#

In .NET, you write a BackgroundService with a loop and a delay. In Spring, you write one annotated method:

C#
public class ReconcileService : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken ct)
    {
        while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            await ReconcileAsync();
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30), ct);
        }
    }
}
Java 25
@Component
public class ReconcileJob {

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    public void reconcile() {
        ...
    }
}
Reading the code
@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MINUTES)

Spring runs reconcile once at startup. Then Spring runs it again 30 minutes after each run finishes, like the loop with Task.Delay. The annotation needs @EnableScheduling on a configuration class.

Other attributes choose other timetables:

AttributeMeans
fixedDelaywait this long after the previous run finishes
fixedRatestart this often, regardless of how long a run takes
initialDelayhow long to wait after startup before the first run
cron = "0 0 3 * * *"a cron expression with six fields, and the first field is seconds
Gotcha

Spring cron expressions have six fields, not five. The first field is seconds, so "0 0 3 * * *" means 3:00:00 every day. Suppose you paste a Unix crontab line with five fields, such as "0 3 * * *". Then the application refuses to start, with the message “Cron expression must consist of 6 fields”. Also, fixedRate never overlaps runs by default. If a run takes longer than the interval, the next run waits for it to finish.

Gotcha

The scheduler runs on a single thread by default, so one slow job delays every other job. Set spring.task.scheduling.pool.size to change this. On Java 21 or later, consider virtual threads for jobs that block.

A job that must run once: ShedLock and Quartz#

Gotcha

Every instance runs every schedule. If you deploy three replicas, your nightly reconciliation runs three times. There is no built-in leader election. The standard answer is ShedLock. ShedLock is a library that takes a lock in a shared database or in Redis.

With ShedLock, the nightly job runs on the instance that takes the lock first:

@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 3 * * *")
@SchedulerLock(name = "reconcile", lockAtMostFor = "30m")
public void reconcile() { ... }
Reading the code
@SchedulerLock(name = "reconcile", lockAtMostFor = "30m")

The lock is named reconcile. Only the instance that holds this lock runs the job. If that instance fails in the middle of a run, the lock expires after 30 minutes.

Some jobs need more, such as retries, persistence and a dashboard. For these jobs, Quartz is the equivalent of Hangfire.

Application eventstwist#

Spring has publish and subscribe inside the process. It works like the notifications of MediatR in .NET:

MediatR
public record OrderPlaced(long Id) : INotification;

await _mediator.Publish(new OrderPlaced(order.Id));

public class SendEmail : INotificationHandler<OrderPlaced>
{
    public Task Handle(OrderPlaced n, CancellationToken ct)
        => _email.SendAsync(n.Id);
}
Spring events
public record OrderPlaced(long id) { }

events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()));

@Component
class SendEmail {

    @EventListener
    public void on(OrderPlaced e) {
        email.send(e.id());
    }
}
Reading the code
events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()));

The type of events is ApplicationEventPublisher, which is part of Spring. Spring injects it like any other bean. The event can be any object, and a record is the usual choice.

@EventListener

Spring calls this method for every published OrderPlaced. Spring chooses the method by its parameter type. You do not implement an interface.

Gotcha

@EventListener is synchronous by default, like a MediatR handler. The publisher blocks until every listener returns. Every listener runs on the same thread as the publisher, and inside the same transaction. So a slow listener slows the request, and a listener that throws fails the caller.

Add @Async to run the listener on another thread. The listener then runs outside the transaction. For @TransactionalEventListener, see Transactions.

The annotation has variants:

AnnotationRuns
@EventListenersynchronously, in the caller's thread and transaction
@EventListener(condition = "#e.total > 100")only when the SpEL condition holds
@Async @EventListeneron another thread, and outside the transaction
@TransactionalEventListenerafter the transaction commits, so it is the safe default for side effects

@Async#

Rebuilding the monthly report takes a minute. The request that starts the rebuild should not wait for it. In .NET, you would start a task. In Spring, you mark the method with @Async:

C#
_ = Task.Run(() => _reports.Rebuild());
Java 25
@Async
public void rebuild() { ... }        // returns immediately

@Async
public CompletableFuture<Report> build() {
    return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(...);
}
Reading the code
public void rebuild() { ... }

The call returns to the caller at once. The method runs on another thread.

public CompletableFuture<Report> build() {

To return a result, use the return type CompletableFuture. This type does the same as Task<T> in C#. The caller can wait for the CompletableFuture, or chain more work onto it.

Gotcha

@Async works through a proxy, like the other features in this chapter. So a self-invocation runs synchronously. This failure is very hard to find. The code still works, but on the wrong thread, and the wrong thread matters only under load.

@Async also needs @EnableAsync. An @Async method may return only void or a Future. CompletableFuture is one kind of Future. A method that returns a plain value fails when it is called, with the message “Invalid return type for async method”.

On Java 21 or later, you can make the executor use virtual threads. Then @Async no longer needs a tuned pool size:

spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true
Reading the code
enabled: true

Boot then runs @Async methods and scheduled jobs on virtual threads. By default, Boot uses a pool of eight threads for @Async and one thread for scheduling.

Check yourself
1
A method carries @Cacheable, yet it runs on every call and nothing is cached. What is the most likely cause?
@EnableCaching is missing. Without it, every cache annotation is ignored, and nothing warns you. The code still works, because it calls the method every time. The same is true of @EnableScheduling and @EnableAsync.

Quick reference#

SettingUse it to
spring.cache.typechoose the cache provider, such as caffeine or redis
spring.task.scheduling.pool.sizerun more than one scheduled job at once, because the default is 1
spring.threads.virtual.enabledrun @Async methods and scheduled jobs on virtual threads
Next · ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot48Testing Spring Boot9 min

Testing Spring Boot#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 48· 9 min read· Quick reference

@SpringBootTest does the same as WebApplicationFactory<T> in ASP.NET Core. It starts the real application context for an integration test. Spring also has test slices, such as @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest. A test slice starts only one layer, so the test is faster.

KindC#JavaNote
twistWebApplicationFactory<Program>@SpringBootTeststarts the whole application context for an integration test Why
twistIClassFixture<...>the cached application context, shared automaticallySpring caches a context across test classes with the same configuration Why
twistHttpClient from app.CreateClient()MockMvc, or TestRestTemplate and RestTestClient on a random portMockMvc needs no server, but TestRestTemplate makes a real HTTP call Why
newno equivalent@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest and other slicesA test slice starts only one layer. On Boot 4 each slice has its own test module. Why
twistno equivalent@DataMongoTestIt is the slice for document data. Unlike @DataJpaTest, it rolls nothing back. Why
newno equivalent@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)starts the web layer with this one controller, and provides a MockMvc Why
trapno equivalent@WithMockUser on a @WebMvcTest testwith Spring Security present, the slice applies Boot's default security Why
twista Moq mock in place of a service@MockitoBean, @MockitoSpyBeanThey add a Mockito mock or spy as a bean. Boot 4 removed @MockBean and @SpyBean. Why
twistno equivalent@AutoConfigureMockMvc@SpringBootTest provides no MockMvc without it, on Boot 3 or Boot 4. Boot 4 moved its package. Why
twistno equivalent@AutoConfigureTestRestTemplateBoot 3 gave a @SpringBootTest a TestRestTemplate by itself, but Boot 4 needs this annotation Why
twista database in a container@Testcontainers, @ServiceConnectionBoot reads the container's address and points the datasource at it Why
trapno equivalent@DataJpaTest with a @ServiceConnection containerthe slice rolls back each test, and it uses H2 unless the database comes from such a container Why
twistno equivalent@TestPropertySource, @ActiveProfiles, @TestConfigurationthey adjust the properties, profiles and beans of a test's context Why
twista unit test that starts no hosta plain JUnit test, with no Springconstructor injection lets a test create the service with new Why

Test slicesnew#

Test each layer with a test that starts only what the layer needs, because a test that starts less is faster. These are the choices:

AnnotationStartsUse for
@SpringBootTestthe whole contextend-to-end integration
@WebMvcTest(X.class)web layer only, with no databasecontroller tests
@DataJpaTestJPA and an in-memory or container DBrepository tests
@JdbcTestJDBC onlyJdbcTemplate tests
@JsonTestJackson onlyserialisation tests
@RestClientTestHTTP client + mock serveroutbound client tests
(no annotation)nothing, because the test is plain JUnitunit tests, which should be most of them

On Boot 4, each slice comes from its own test module. The module is named after the technology of the slice:

  • @WebMvcTest comes from the module spring-boot-webmvc-test. Its package is org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.
  • @DataJpaTest comes from the module spring-boot-data-jpa-test.

Each module has a starter that you add to the build. The two starters are spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test and spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test. The starter spring-boot-starter-test alone does not bring these two modules. On Boot 3, all slices came from one module, so the imports change when you upgrade.

Document data has a slice of its own, called @DataMongoTest. See Testing without a cluster.

Testing a controllernew#

The test below checks that GET /api/orders/1 returns the order, and it uses no database. In ASP.NET Core, you start the app in memory and call it with an HttpClient. In Spring, you start only the web layer. You replace the service behind the controller with a mock:

ASP.NET Core
public class OrdersTests
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public OrdersTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> app)
        => _client = app.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task Get_ReturnsOrder()
    {
        var res = await _client.GetAsync("/api/orders/1");
        res.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.OK);
    }
}
Spring Boot 4
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @MockitoBean OrderService orders;    // Boot 4 name

    @Test
    void get_returnsOrder() throws Exception {
        when(orders.find(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(
                new OrderDto(1, "PAID", new BigDecimal("19.99"))));

        mvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))
           .andExpect(status().isOk())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(1));
    }
}
Reading the code
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)

This annotation starts Spring MVC with only this controller. Spring MVC is the model-view-controller (MVC) web framework of Spring. The annotation starts no services, no repositories and no database. It also provides a MockMvc, which the test uses to call the controller.

@MockitoBean OrderService orders;

This line puts a Mockito mock in the context as the OrderService bean, so the controller receives the mock. An unstubbed method of the mock returns an empty value. Here the empty value is Optional.empty(), and the controller turns it into a 404.

when(orders.find(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(

This is Mockito stubbing. From now on, the call orders.find(1L) returns that order. See the chapter Testing.

mvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))

This line sends a request through Spring MVC, without a real server or network. The next two lines check the status and the id in the JSON body.

PredictA @WebMvcTest test with Spring Security on the classpath#
What status does this test get?
// Spring Security is on the classpath, and the application has its own SecurityConfig.
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @MockitoBean OrderService orders;   // stubbed to return order 1

    @Test
    void get_returnsOrder() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))
           .andExpect(status().isOk());
    }
}
Show the answer
401

A @WebMvcTest slice applies Boot's default security. That default requires a login for every endpoint. The slice does not load the application's own SecurityConfig. So the test fails with Status expected:<200> but was:<401>. But the same test passes when Spring Security is not on the classpath.

The annotation @WithMockUser comes from spring-security-test. Add it, and the test passes:

import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithMockUser;

@Test
@WithMockUser
void get_returnsOrder() throws Exception { ... }

The test now passes against Boot's default rules, not against your rules. To test your own rules, add @Import(SecurityConfig.class) to the test class.

Boot 4: @MockBean becomes @MockitoBeantwist#

Gotcha

@MockBean and @SpyBean are removed in Boot 4. They are removed, not deprecated. Replace them with @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean. These two annotations come from Spring Framework. They have been available since Boot 3.4, so you can migrate before you upgrade.

Here is the same test class, before and after the upgrade:

// Boot 3
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @MockBean OrderService orders;
    @SpyBean  AuditService audit;
}
// Boot 4: @MockBean / @SpyBean no longer exist
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @MockitoBean    OrderService orders;
    @MockitoSpyBean AuditService audit;
}
Reading the code
@MockitoSpyBean AuditService audit;

A spy wraps the real bean. Each call still reaches the real bean, and the test can check which calls were made. @SpyBean did the same before Boot 4.

MockMvc and TestRestTemplate under @SpringBootTesttwist#

Gotcha

@SpringBootTest does not provide MockMvc by itself, on Boot 3 or on Boot 4. Add @AutoConfigureMockMvc, or the test fails with “No qualifying bean of type MockMvc”. Under @WebMvcTest, MockMvc is provided. Boot 4 moved the annotation to the package org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure. The class is in the module spring-boot-webmvc-test. The starter that you add is spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test. But Boot 4 did stop providing TestRestTemplate. To get one, add @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate.

The integration test is the same on both versions, except for the import:

// Boot 3
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class OrderIntegrationTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
}
// Boot 4: the annotation moved to the spring-boot-webmvc-test module
import org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureMockMvc;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class OrderIntegrationTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
}
Reading the code
@AutoConfigureMockMvc

This annotation adds a MockMvc bean to the full application context, so the test can call every controller without starting a server.

Full integration teststwist#

This test starts the whole billing service on a random port. It uses a real PostgreSQL database in a container. The container comes from the Testcontainers library:

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate
@Testcontainers
class OrderIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection                       // wires the datasource automatically
    static PostgreSQLContainer db = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:16");

    @Autowired TestRestTemplate rest;

    @Test
    void placesAnOrder() {
        var request = new CreateOrder("c1", List.of(new OrderLine("A-1", 2)));
        var res = rest.postForEntity("/api/orders", request, OrderDto.class);
        assertThat(res.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
    }
}
Reading the code
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)

This annotation starts the real application, with a real web server on a free port.

@AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate

Boot 4 needs this annotation to provide a TestRestTemplate. The TestRestTemplate now comes from the spring-boot-resttestclient module. Boot 3 provided one automatically.

@Container

With @Testcontainers on the class, the JUnit extension starts this container before the tests and stops it after the tests.

@ServiceConnection

Boot reads the container's address, user name and password, and points the datasource at the container. The annotation comes from the spring-boot-testcontainers module.

static PostgreSQLContainer db = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:16");

This is the Testcontainers 2 class, from the org.testcontainers.postgresql package. The older class PostgreSQLContainer<?> in org.testcontainers.containers is deprecated.

What @ServiceConnection replaceddeep dive
Note

@ServiceConnection replaces the old @DynamicPropertySource boilerplate code, which copied container URLs into properties. Annotate the container, and Boot wires the datasource, the Redis connection or the Kafka bootstrap servers for you. @ServiceConnection is one of the most helpful features in modern Boot testing.

Four clients can call the application in a test:

ClientUse for
MockMvcfast, with no real server and no network
TestRestTemplatea real HTTP call against a random port
WebTestClientfluent, works for MVC and WebFlux
RestTestClienta fluent test client built on RestClient, new in Spring Framework 7

Testing repositoriestrap#

This test checks that OrderRepository.findByCustomerId finds a saved order. It starts only Jakarta Persistence (JPA). The database is a PostgreSQL container, as in the section Full integration tests:

@DataJpaTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer db = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:16");

    @Autowired OrderRepository orders;

    @Test
    void findsByCustomer() {
        orders.save(anOrder("cust-1"));      // anOrder builds an Order for that customer
        assertThat(orders.findByCustomerId("cust-1")).hasSize(1);
    }
}
Reading the code
@DataJpaTest

This annotation starts JPA, the repositories and a datasource, and nothing else. Each test runs in a transaction that is rolled back at the end.

@Container @ServiceConnection

Here the database comes from a @ServiceConnection container. Since Boot 3.4, the slice keeps such a database and does not replace it.

assertThat(orders.findByCustomerId("cust-1")).hasSize(1);

This is an AssertJ check that the derived query found exactly one order.

Gotcha

@DataJpaTest has two defaults. It replaces your datasource with an in-memory H2 database, unless the datasource comes from a test container. It also wraps each test in a transaction that rolls back. Both defaults cause trouble. H2 does not behave like PostgreSQL for native queries, JSON columns or sequences. The rollback hides constraint violations that appear only on commit. A database named by a URL in application.yml is still replaced. To keep that database, write @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE).

Test configuration#

Note

Slices are fast because they start only a small part of the context. Spring also caches contexts across test classes with the same configuration. But this also means that every distinct configuration creates a new context. So if many classes use different @TestPropertySource values, the suite takes many times longer to run, and nothing warns you.

These annotations adjust the context that a test starts:

NeedAnnotation
Override properties@TestPropertySource(properties = "x=y")
Activate a profile@ActiveProfiles("test")
Add or replace beans@TestConfiguration + @Import
Replace one bean with a mock@MockitoBean
Reset context after a test@DirtiesContext, but use it rarely because it is slow

Here a test fixes the clock. Code that depends on today's date then gives the same answer on every run:

@TestConfiguration
static class TestClock {
    @Bean Clock clock() {
        return Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    }
}
Reading the code
@TestConfiguration

This is a configuration class for tests only. Import it with @Import(TestClock.class), and its beans are added to the test's context.

return Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);

This line returns a Clock that always says midnight on 1 January 2026. Code that takes a Clock instead of calling Instant.now() can be tested this way.

Gotcha

@DirtiesContext discards the cached application context, so the next test class must start a full context again. One careless @DirtiesContext on a class that runs often can add minutes to a suite. It is better to reset the state explicitly.

Keep most tests plain#

Note

The most common mistake that a team makes with Spring is to test everything through @SpringBootTest. Then context startup takes most of the running time, and the suite takes minutes. The tests also tell you little about your logic.

Test domain logic with plain JUnit and no Spring at all. This is possible because constructor injection makes your services ordinary classes, which you can create with new. Use slices only for the wiring. Use a full @SpringBootTest only for a few end-to-end paths.

Here the pricing rules are tested with no Spring at all:

class PricingTest {                          // no Spring at all: just construct the class
    @Test
    void appliesDiscount() {
        var pricing = new Pricing(new FixedRates(Map.of("GBP", BigDecimal.ONE)));
        assertThat(pricing.total(anOrder())).isEqualByComparingTo("90");
    }
}
Reading the code
var pricing = new Pricing(new FixedRates(Map.of("GBP", BigDecimal.ONE)));

The class under test is created directly, with a simple fake in place of the real rates service. Nothing starts, so the test takes milliseconds.

.isEqualByComparingTo("90");

This method compares BigDecimal values by amount, so 90 equals 90.00.

Check yourself
1
TranslateWrite this test method in Java. It is in a @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) class that has @Autowired MockMvc mvc and @MockitoBean OrderService orders: 
[Fact]
public async Task Get_ReturnsOrder()
{
    var res = await _client.GetAsync("/api/orders/1");
    Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.OK, res.StatusCode);
}
@Test
void get_returnsOrder() throws Exception {
    when(orders.find(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(
            new OrderDto(1, "PAID", new BigDecimal("19.99"))));

    mvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk());
}

The slice starts no real service, so stub the mock first. An unstubbed find returns Optional.empty(), and the controller answers 404.

2
A Boot 3 test class uses @MockBean. It also injects MockMvc under @SpringBootTest with @AutoConfigureMockMvc. What must change on Boot 4?
@MockBean is removed, so write @MockitoBean in its place. @AutoConfigureMockMvc is still needed, as it was on Boot 3, but its import changes. The annotation moved to the package org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure. The class is in the module spring-boot-webmvc-test. The starter spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test brings that module into the build.
3
An expert asksA @DataJpaTest passes, and the same repository fails against the real database. Which two defaults of the slice can hide that?
The slice replaces your datasource with an in-memory H2 database, unless the database comes from a @ServiceConnection container. H2 does not behave like PostgreSQL for native queries, JSON columns or sequences. The slice also rolls back each test. The rollback hides constraint violations that appear only on commit.

Quick reference#

Boot 3Boot 4
@MockBean@MockitoBean
@SpyBean@MockitoSpyBean
@AutoConfigureMockMvc from org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servletfrom org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure, in spring-boot-webmvc-test
TestRestTemplate under @SpringBootTest, automaticallyadd @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate, or use RestTestClient
@WebMvcTest from spring-boot-test-autoconfigurefrom spring-boot-webmvc-test

Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4#

ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 49· 8 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens

Spring Boot 4 is built on Spring Framework 7 and Jakarta EE 11. Moving a Boot 3 service to Boot 4 is not the painful change that the move from Boot 2 to Boot 3 was. That earlier move renamed javax to jakarta across the whole ecosystem.

KindWhat changesBoot 3 becomes Boot 4Note
twistParent version3.5.x becomes 4.xBoot 4 needs Java 17 or later, Spring Framework 7 and Jakarta EE 11 Why
twistTest frameworkJUnit 5 becomes JUnit 6Boot 4 also needs Kotlin 2.2 and GraalVM 25 or later, if you use them Why
twistWeb starterspring-boot-starter-web becomes spring-boot-starter-webmvcmodules now follow one spring-boot-<technology> naming pattern Why
trapFlyway and Liquibaseflyway-core becomes spring-boot-starter-flywayWithout the starter, Boot 4 starts with no error and runs no migration. Liquibase moved in the same way. Why
twistJackson importscom.fasterxml.jackson becomes tools.jacksonevery Jackson import moves, except com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation, which stays as it is Why
twistBoot's Jackson annotations@JsonComponent becomes @JacksonComponent, @JsonMixin becomes @JacksonMixinBoot's own Jackson types were renamed to match Jackson 3 Why
twistMock beans in tests@MockBean becomes @MockitoBean, @SpyBean becomes @MockitoSpyBeanremoved in Boot 4, not deprecated, so switch on Boot 3.4 or 3.5, before you upgrade Why
twistMockMvc in a @SpringBootTest@AutoConfigureMockMvc, from org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigureIt is needed on Boot 3 too. On Boot 4, add the starter spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test, which brings its module. Why
twistTest slices@WebMvcTest comes from the module spring-boot-webmvc-testyou add the starter spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test to the build, and it brings that module Why
twistNullable annotationorg.springframework.lang.Nullable becomes org.jspecify.annotations.Nullablethe old annotation is deprecated, so it still compiles, with a warning Why
twistTestRestTemplate in a @SpringBootTestadd @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplateBoot 3 provided it with a running server, but Boot 4 needs the annotation and spring-boot-resttestclient Why
trapUndertowremoved, so switch to Tomcat, Jetty or Nettya dependency swap rather than a compile error, so it is easy to miss Why
twistRemoved in Spring Framework 7ListenableFuture and javax.inject supportuse CompletableFuture and the jakarta.* equivalents instead Why
trapConfiguration settingsspring.jackson.parser.* becomes spring.jackson.json.read.*Boot 4 ignores the old name and reports nothing, so a missed rename fails silently Why
trapMongoDB connection settingsspring.data.mongodb.uri becomes spring.mongodb.uriBoot 4 ignores the old name and tries localhost:27017. The setting auto-index-creation keeps its old name. Why
trapA BigDecimal stored in MongoDBa string becomes a Decimal128to keep strings on Boot 4, set spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimal to string Why
newNew in Boot 4@Retryable, @ImportHttpServices, JmsClient, RestTestClienteach new feature is shown in the chapter that covers it Why
twistUpgrade orderBoot 3.5 first, then the test annotations, then Boot 4keep each step small, and never upgrade Boot and Java in the same change Why

Baseline requirementstwist#

First, check the versions that Boot 4 needs:

RequirementBoot 3Boot 4
Java17+17+, 25 recommended
Spring Framework6.x7.x
Jakarta EE10 (Servlet 6.0)11 (Servlet 6.1)
Kotlin1.9+2.2+
GraalVM22+25+
JUnit56
Gradle8.x9 supported, 8.14+ still works

Java 17 is enough, so the upgrade itself is a change to the parent version in pom.xml:

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.1</version>
</parent>
<properties>
  <java.version>25</java.version>     <!-- 17 is the minimum; 25 is recommended -->
</properties>
Reading the code
<version>4.1.1</version>

This was the current Boot 4 release when this chapter was written. Check spring.io for a newer release.

<java.version>25</java.version>

This is the Java version that the build compiles for. Boot 4 also runs on Java 17, which is the minimum, so change this value in a separate step. The last gotcha in this chapter explains why.

1. Renamed starterstwist#

Modules now follow one naming pattern, spring-boot-<technology>. The root package of a module is org.springframework.boot.<technology>. As a result, a few starters changed name. Flyway and Liquibase now need a starter:

Boot 3Boot 4
spring-boot-starter-webspring-boot-starter-webmvc
spring-boot-starter-web-servicesspring-boot-starter-webservices
spring-boot-starter-oauth2-clientspring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client
spring-boot-starter-aopspring-boot-starter-aspectj
flyway-core, with no starterspring-boot-starter-flyway
liquibase-core, with no starterspring-boot-starter-liquibase
spring-boot-data-mongodb (health indicators)spring-boot-mongodb

For the billing service, only the web starter changes:

Boot 3 pom
<parent>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.5.x</version>
</parent>

<dependency>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
Boot 4 pom
<parent>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.1</version>
</parent>

<dependency>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>

This is the same web stack under its new name. Test starters follow the same pattern, with one starter for each technology. An example is spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test.

Flyway and Liquibase need their startertrap#

Gotcha

On Boot 4, Flyway on the classpath no longer runs your migrations. Boot 4 moved the auto-configuration of Flyway out of spring-boot-autoconfigure. The auto-configuration is now in the module spring-boot-flyway. In a run on Boot 4.1 with only flyway-core, the application started with no error and ran no migration.

Replace the dependency with the starter:

<!-- Boot 3 needed only flyway-core. Boot 4 needs the starter. -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-flyway</artifactId>
</dependency>

The starter spring-boot-starter-flyway brings two things. It brings spring-boot-flyway, which runs the migrations. It also brings flyway-core itself. Liquibase moved in the same way, so for Liquibase use spring-boot-starter-liquibase.

2. Jackson 2 to Jackson 3twist#

Boot 4 uses Jackson 3 by default. The classes of Jackson 3 are in tools.jackson, not in com.fasterxml.jackson. Only the Jackson annotations did not move. Boot 4 still includes support for Jackson 2, but that support is deprecated. Boot's own Jackson types were renamed to match Jackson 3:

Boot 3Boot 4
com.fasterxml.jackson.*tools.jackson.*, for every package except the annotations
com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.*unchanged, because Jackson 3 still uses these annotations
@JsonComponent@JacksonComponent
@JsonMixin@JacksonMixin
JsonObjectSerializerObjectValueSerializer
JsonValueDeserializerObjectValueDeserializer
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizerJsonMapperBuilderCustomizer
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderdeprecated for removal in Spring Framework 7, so use Jackson's own builders
spring.jackson.parser.*spring.jackson.json.read.*, where Jackson 3 still has the feature
spring.jackson.generator.*spring.jackson.json.write.*, where Jackson 3 still has the feature

Custom JSON for Money shows both changes:

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

@JsonComponent
class MoneyJson { ... }
import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

@JacksonComponent
class MoneyJson { ... }
Reading the code
import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

This is the same class, under the new root package of Jackson 3.

@JacksonComponent

This annotation registers the serializers in MoneyJson with Boot's JSON mapper, as @JsonComponent did. The annotation is in the package org.springframework.boot.jackson.

Gotcha

Do not find-and-replace the whole com.fasterxml.jackson root. Every import moves to tools.jackson, except the imports of one package. The annotations stay in com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation. Examples are @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore and @JsonCreator.

Also check your dependency tree. A library that still exposes Jackson 2 types in its API adds Jackson 2 to the build again, next to Jackson 3.

3. Test annotationstwist#

Several test annotations were removed or moved. For each annotation in code, see the chapter Testing Spring Boot. These are the changes:

Boot 3Boot 4Note
@MockBean@MockitoBeanremoved in Boot 4, not deprecated, so switch before you upgrade
@SpyBean@MockitoSpyBeanremoved in Boot 4, not deprecated, so switch before you upgrade
MockitoTestExecutionListenerMockito's MockitoExtension
@AutoConfigureMockMvc from org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servletfrom org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigureA @SpringBootTest needs it on both versions. Only its package and module changed.
@AutoConfigureMockMvc(htmlUnit-related)@AutoConfigureMockMvc(htmlUnit = @HtmlUnit(...))
@PropertyMappingmoved to org.springframework.boot.test.contextthe same annotation, moved to a new package
@WebMvcTest from spring-boot-test-autoconfigurefrom the module spring-boot-webmvc-testadd the starter spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test to the build, because it brings that module
@SpringBootTest gives TestRestTemplateadd @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplateit also needs the spring-boot-resttestclient and spring-boot-restclient modules
Note

@MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean exist from Boot 3.4 onwards. If you are on Boot 3.4 or 3.5, migrate to these two annotations before you upgrade. Then one whole kind of failure is gone from the upgrade commit.

Gotcha

@SpringBootTest does not provide MockMvc by itself, on Boot 3 or on Boot 4. Add @AutoConfigureMockMvc. Without it, the test has no MockMvc bean to inject, and the test fails with “No qualifying bean of type MockMvc”. Boot 4 changed only the place of the annotation. The annotation is now in the module spring-boot-webmvc-test. To get that module, add the starter spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test to the build. But Boot 4 did stop providing TestRestTemplate.

4. JSpecify null-safetytwist#

Spring moved its whole API from the Java Specification Request (JSR) 305 annotations to JSpecify. If your own code used org.springframework.lang.Nullable, switch the import:

// Boot 3: Spring's own annotation, from the JSR-305 days
import org.springframework.lang.Nullable;

// Boot 4: the JSpecify standard
import org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable;
Reading the code
import org.springframework.lang.Nullable;

This annotation is still present in Spring Framework 7, but it is deprecated, so it compiles with a warning.

import org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable;

This is the replacement. It has the same meaning, and it comes from the JSpecify standard, which null checkers understand.

Note

The move has a benefit. Spring's signatures now say exactly where null is possible, and this includes generic type arguments. So a null checker such as NullAway gives far better results against Spring APIs than it did on Boot 3. See Nullability.

Removals in Spring Framework 7#

Some older APIs are removed, or are deprecated and will be removed:

RemovedReplacement
javax.annotation / javax.inject supportthe jakarta.* equivalents
spring-jclApache Commons Logging 1.3, which Spring now depends on directly
ListenableFutureCompletableFuture
Undertow supportTomcat, Jetty, or Netty
suffixPatternMatch and similar path optionsexplicit mappings
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuildernot removed yet, but deprecated for removal, so use Jackson's native builders
Certificate validity threshold in SSL infon/a
Gotcha

Undertow support is gone. If your service runs on Undertow you must switch to Tomcat, Jetty or Netty as part of the upgrade. This is easy to miss, because it is a change of dependency and not a compile error.

In a Maven build, you make the switch by deleting this dependency:

<!-- remove this before upgrading; Tomcat comes back as the default -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>

Without this dependency, the application uses Tomcat again. Tomcat is the default server of the web starter. If you had excluded Tomcat from the web starter so that Undertow could replace it, remove that exclusion too.

What you gainnew#

The upgrade also brings new features. Each feature is shown in the chapter that covers it:

FeatureDetail
@Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit in coreorg.springframework.resilience.annotation, switched on by @EnableResilientMethods
API versioningspring.mvc.apiversion.*, spring.webflux.apiversion.*
HTTP service client auto-config@ImportHttpServices for @HttpExchange interfaces
BeanRegistrarprogrammatic bean registration, AOT-friendly
JmsClienta unified JMS send/receive API alongside JmsTemplate
spring-boot-starter-opentelemetryfirst-class OTel starter
spring-boot-starter-kotlin-serializationKotlin serialization support
RestTestClienta fluent test client built on RestClient

Configuration property renames#

A few configuration settings moved. Boot ignores a setting that it no longer knows. So a missed rename causes no error at startup, and the setting just has no effect. While you upgrade, Boot's spring-boot-properties-migrator module can report renamed settings at startup. These are the renames:

Boot 3Boot 4
spring.jackson.parser.*spring.jackson.json.read.*
spring.jackson.generator.*spring.jackson.json.write.*
spring.data.mongodb.* (driver-level)spring.mongodb.*
spring.session.redisspring.session.data.redis

Here are two of the renames, before and after:

# Boot 3
spring.jackson.parser.allow-single-quotes=true
spring.session.redis.namespace=billing

# Boot 4
spring.jackson.json.read.allow-single-quotes=true
spring.session.data.redis.namespace=billing
Reading the code
spring.jackson.json.read.allow-single-quotes=true

This is the same Jackson feature. It is a parser setting on Boot 3, and a json.read setting on Boot 4. In a run on Boot 4.1, the old spring.jackson.parser line was ignored, with no error. So single quotes were rejected again.

spring.session.data.redis.namespace=billing

These are the Redis session settings, which are now under spring.session.data.redis.

Note

spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation keeps its name. It is a Spring Data setting, not a driver setting, and the split is deliberate. If a service still sets spring.data.mongodb.uri on Boot 4, Boot ignores that line. The service then tries localhost:27017.

Gotcha

On Boot 4 a BigDecimal is no longer stored in MongoDB as a string. Boot 3.5 manages Spring Data MongoDB 4.5. That version states that a BigDecimal “is represented as String instead of Decimal128”. Spring Data MongoDB 5 sets no default. In a run on Boot 4.1, the amount was stored as a Decimal128. So after the upgrade, one collection holds old amounts as strings and new amounts as Decimal128.

Spring's upgrade notes say you “may choose BigDecimalRepresentation.STRING as default to retain previous behaviour”. To do that, set spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimal to string. Or convert the stored amounts. The statement about Boot 3 comes from Spring's documentation. It was not checked in a run. For the setting, see the chapter Document data.

A suggested ordertwist#

This order keeps each step small:

StepDo
1Get to Boot 3.5 and Java 17+ first, and fix all deprecation warnings
2Replace @MockBean and @SpyBean with @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean
3Replace Undertow if you use it
4Change the parent version to Boot 4. Then fix the starter names, and add the Flyway or Liquibase starter
5Run the build, and fix each Jackson import error
6Fix the import of @AutoConfigureMockMvc, and add @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate where a test injects TestRestTemplate
7Check the property renames above against your application.yml
8Consider replacing Resilience4j with core @Retryable where it fits
Gotcha

Do not combine a Boot 4 upgrade with a Java version upgrade in the same change. Each upgrade produces its own kind of failure. If you separate the two upgrades, both kinds of failure are far easier to diagnose.

Check yourself
1
A service moves from Boot 3 to Boot 4, and so from Jackson 2 to Jackson 3. Which Jackson imports change, and which stay?
Every Jackson import moves from com.fasterxml.jackson to tools.jackson, except the imports of one package. The annotations stay in com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation. An example is @JsonProperty. So a find-and-replace of the whole root package breaks the annotations.
2
A Boot 3 service sets spring.data.mongodb.uri. What becomes of that setting on Boot 4?
Boot 4 reads spring.mongodb.uri. It ignores the old name and tries localhost:27017, so the service cannot reach its database. The settings database and ssl.bundle moved in the same way. spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation kept its name.
Next · Ship it50Packaging and native images8 min

Packaging and native images#

Ship it · Chapter 50· 8 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens· Quick reference

The Java counterpart of dotnet publish is one Java archive (JAR) file. The file holds your code, every dependency and a web server. It is called a fat JAR. A fat JAR needs a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) to run it. GraalVM native-image does the same as NativeAOT in .NET.

KindC#JavaNote
twistdotnet publish, framework-dependent./mvnw package, giving a fat JARone JAR holds your code, every dependency and an embedded web server Why
twistexpecting the libraries merged into one fileeach dependency's JAR, kept whole inside the fat JARmerging JARs lets one META-INF/services file silently replace another, so Boot does not merge Why
twistdotnet billing.dlljava -jar target/billing-1.0.0.jarruns on any machine that has a JVM installed, but the fat JAR does not contain a JVM Why
twista bare dll, a publish folder, an installer, NativeAOTplain JAR, fat JAR, jlink, jpackage, native-imagethere are five ways to ship, but a Spring Boot service almost always starts with the fat JAR Why
twistdotnet publish /t:PublishContainer./mvnw spring-boot:build-imageBuildpacks build a layered container image, with no Dockerfile to maintain Why
twista Dockerfile that copies the publish outputjava -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layersone image layer per JAR layer, so a code change re-sends only your own classes Why
twistdotnet publish --self-containedjlink, a trimmed runtime around your appneeds modular libraries, so it suits desktop and command-line tools more than Spring Boot Why
twistan MSI or dmg installerjpackage --type dmgwraps the JAR and a runtime in a native installer of the type msi, dmg or deb Why
twistPublishAotGraalVM native-imagestarts in milliseconds on a fraction of the resources, GraalVM states, but builds in minutes with lower peak throughput Why
trapa feature toggle that adds a service from configuration@ConditionalOnPropertyThis is not supported in a native image. Beans are fixed at build time, so the toggle does nothing and reports no error. Why
trapreflection with no setup@RegisterReflectionForBinding(OrderDto.class)a native image needs reflection registered, or it fails at run time, not at build time Why
twista faster start without going nativejava -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar app.jarthe AOT cache of Java 24 and 25 reuses the classes a training run loaded, so later starts are faster Why
newsmaller objects on the heap-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeadersThis option is supported since Java 25 and is off by default. It shrinks every object by four bytes. Why
twista site deployed into IISa WAR deployed into an application serverThis is the older model. Spring Boot produces a JAR with the server inside, and each service is one process. Why

The optionstwist#

Java has five ways to ship an application, from a bare JAR to a native binary. Each way has a counterpart in .NET:

ApproachProducesNeeds a JVM installed.NET analogy
Plain JARjust your classesyes, plus the classpatha bare dll
Fat / uber JAReverything in one JARyesframework-dependent publish
jlinka trimmed JVM + your appnoself-contained publish
jpackagea platform installernoMSI / dmg installer
GraalVM native-imageone native binarynoNativeAOT

A Spring Boot service almost always starts with the second row.

The fat JARtwist#

One command builds the billing service, and a second command runs it:

./mvnw package
java -jar target/billing-1.0.0.jar
Reading the code
./mvnw package

This command compiles the code, runs the tests and builds target/billing-1.0.0.jar. That file is a fat JAR. Every dependency and an embedded Tomcat are inside it.

java -jar target/billing-1.0.0.jar

This command starts the service on any machine that has a JVM. It is like dotnet billing.dll in .NET.

For the everyday commands that run the fat JAR, see the quick reference.

Why the fat JAR keeps each dependency's JAR whole#

The Spring Boot plugin does not merge the classes of the dependencies. It keeps the JAR of each dependency whole inside the fat JAR:

billing-1.0.0.jar
  BOOT-INF/classes/     your own classes
  BOOT-INF/lib/         each dependency, as the JAR it arrived in

When the application starts, Spring Boot builds the classpath from the JARs in BOOT-INF/lib/. That avoids the classic shading problem. In that problem, two dependencies each contain a META-INF/services file, and one file replaces the other with no warning.

Containerstwist#

Most services are packaged in a container. Spring Boot can build an optimised image with no Dockerfile at all. To do so, it uses Cloud Native Buildpacks:

./mvnw spring-boot:build-image
Reading the code
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image

This command builds a container image in your local Docker. The buildpacks choose a Java Runtime Environment (JRE) and split the JAR into layers. They also set memory flags for the container, and they set the service to run as a non-root user.

Note

This command is the closest Java match for dotnet publish /t:PublishContainer. It is a good default for a team that does not want to maintain a Dockerfile.

A Dockerfile with layerstwist#

If a Dockerfile copies the fat JAR in one step, every code change makes each server download all the dependencies again. Spring Boot can split the JAR into layers. Each JAR layer becomes one Docker image layer:

# build: compile, then split the jar into layers
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
RUN ./mvnw -B dependency:go-offline          # cached unless pom.xml changes
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw -B package -DskipTests
RUN cp target/*.jar application.jar \
 && java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

# run: one image layer per Boot layer, the least-changing first
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
WORKDIR /application
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /app/extracted/application/ ./
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]
Reading the code
RUN ./mvnw -B dependency:go-offline

This line downloads the dependencies in a separate step. Docker reuses the result of that step until pom.xml changes.

java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

This line runs a tool that is part of Spring Boot. The tool splits the JAR into four folders under extracted. The first two folders are dependencies and spring-boot-loader. The last two folders are snapshot-dependencies and application.

COPY --from=build /app/extracted/dependencies/ ./

Each COPY line makes one image layer. A code change alters only the last layer. So a server downloads a few hundred kilobytes, not the whole service.

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]

The extracted application.jar holds only your code. It refers to the extracted libraries, which are next to it. This layout also starts faster than the fat JAR.

jlink and jpackage#

The Java Development Kit (JDK) has two packaging tools. One tool builds a runtime around your application, and the other tool builds an installer around it:

ToolProducesUse for
jlinka custom runtime image with only the modules you needshrinking a container
jpackagea native installer of the type msi, dmg or debdesktop distribution

Here the runtime of the billing service keeps only the modules that the service uses:

# a minimal runtime containing only what the app uses
jlink --add-modules java.base,java.sql,java.naming \
      --strip-debug --no-header-files --no-man-pages \
      --compress=zip-9 --output custom-jre

# a platform installer around it
jpackage --name Billing --input target/ --main-jar billing-1.0.0.jar \
         --runtime-image custom-jre --type dmg
Reading the code
jlink --add-modules java.base,java.sql,java.naming \

This command builds a runtime from three modules, plus the modules that they depend on, such as java.logging. On JDK 26 the result is about 36 MB. The whole JDK is about 380 MB.

--runtime-image custom-jre --type dmg

jpackage wraps the JAR and that runtime in a macOS disk image. The type msi does the same for Windows, and the type deb does the same for Linux.

Gotcha

jlink requires everything to be modular, or to be an automatic module. Many libraries are still not modular. This is why fat JARs and containers are the most common choice on the server. jlink is much more useful for desktop apps and command-line tools than for Spring Boot services.

GraalVM native-imagetrap#

GraalVM compiles the whole application ahead of time into one native executable. NativeAOT does the same in .NET:

NativeAOT
<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>

dotnet publish -r linux-x64 -c Release
GraalVM native-image
<!-- Maven, with the Spring Boot parent -->
./mvnw -Pnative native:compile
./target/billing

<!-- Gradle -->
./gradlew nativeCompile
Reading the code
./mvnw -Pnative native:compile

This command runs Spring's ahead-of-time processing, and then the GraalVM compiler. It needs an installed GraalVM JDK. It takes minutes, not seconds.

./target/billing

This is an ordinary executable. It needs no JVM to run.

Each choice is better in some ways and worse in other ways:

AspectJVM fat JARNative image
Startupslower"starts in milliseconds", in GraalVM's words
Memory at restlarger"a fraction of the resources", in GraalVM's words
Peak throughputhigher, because the JIT is faster over timelower
Build timesecondsminutes
Reflectionneeds no registrationmust be registered
Debugging in productionJFR, full toolingmore limited
Gotcha

Native image uses closed-world analysis. This means that everything reachable must be known at build time. Reflection, dynamic proxies, resource loading and the Java Native Interface (JNI) all need explicit registration. Without registration, they fail at run time, not at build time.

Spring's own closed-world assumption adds more restrictions. Bean definitions are fixed at build time. So beans cannot appear or disappear while the application runs. @Profile is restricted, and @ConditionalOnProperty is not supported. A feature toggle that switches a bean on through configuration works on the JVM. In a native image, the same toggle does nothing and reports no error.

Choose by workload:

Use native image whenUse the JVM when
Serverless, scale-to-zeroLong-running services
CLI toolsPeak throughput matters
Very high instance countsYou need JFR and full diagnostics
Memory is the binding constraintBuild time matters

Reflection hints for a native image#

Spring Boot's ahead-of-time processing generates most of the required metadata for you. This is the reason that Spring works as a native image at all. A library that does its own reflection may still need a hint:

@RegisterReflectionForBinding(OrderDto.class)
@Configuration
class NativeHints { }
Reading the code
@RegisterReflectionForBinding(OrderDto.class)

This line registers the record OrderDto for the reflection that JSON binding uses. So an OrderDto can still be read and written in the native image.

Startup without going native#

The JVM already shortens startup with a feature that is called class data sharing (CDS). The JDK includes an archive of its own core classes, which are already parsed. When the JVM starts, it maps this archive into memory. Java 24 and 25 extend the idea to your application, with an ahead-of-time (AOT) cache. A training run records the classes that the application loads and links. Later starts reuse those classes:

# Java 25: one-command AOT cache creation
java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -jar app.jar     # training run
java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar app.jar           # subsequent runs start faster
Reading the code
java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -jar app.jar

This command runs the application once as a training run. It writes the cache when the application exits.

java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar app.jar

With this command, every later start reads the cache and does not load and link those classes again. Use the same JDK and the same JAR that made the cache.

Note

Java 25 finalised two features. The first feature is ahead-of-time command-line ergonomics, which is the one-command form above. The second feature is ahead-of-time method profiling Java 25. Java 25 also made compact object headers a supported option Java 25. This option shrinks every object by four bytes. It is off by default. Switch it on with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. Together, these features make JVM startup and footprint on Java 25 noticeably better than on Java 21. The gain is often enough to make native image unnecessary.

LegacyWAR files and application servers

Before embedded servers existed, you built a web application archive (WAR) and deployed it into a shared Tomcat, JBoss or WebSphere. That model is largely gone. Spring Boot produces a JAR with the server inside it, and each service is one process. This form is what containers need.

You will still meet WARs in older enterprise environments. Spring Boot can still produce a WAR. To do so, set <packaging>war</packaging> and extend SpringBootServletInitializer. Do not choose a WAR for anything new.

Check yourself
1
What is the Java equivalent of a self-contained dotnet publish?
The equivalent is jlink. It builds a trimmed runtime around your application, so no JVM needs to be installed. A fat JAR is the counterpart of a framework-dependent publish, because it still needs a JVM. You build a fat JAR with ./mvnw package. A Spring Boot service almost always ships the fat JAR.
2
Why does a feature toggle built on @ConditionalOnProperty stop working in a GraalVM native image?
A native image must know everything reachable at build time. So Spring fixes its bean definitions at build time. @ConditionalOnProperty is not supported, and the toggle does nothing and reports no error.

Quick reference#

TaskCommand
Build it./mvnw package
Run itjava -jar target/app.jar
Run with a profilejava -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
Override a propertyjava -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
Set JVM optionsjava -Xmx512m -jar app.jar
Inspect the layersjava -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar list-layers

The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers#

Ship it · Chapter 51· 8 min read· a look-up chapter: Essentials shows its table, and each section opens

You tune the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) with command-line flags. The JVM needs tuning more often than the CLR does. Two choices matter. The first choice is the size of the heap in a container. The second choice is which garbage collector (GC) runs. The defaults are good, so measure with Java Flight Recorder (JFR) before you change a default.

KindC#JavaNote
trapGCHeapHardLimit-Xmx / -XX:MaxRAMPercentageThese flags cap the heap only. Metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers need 25 to 30 percent more. Why
twistGen0/1/2Young / OldG1 is region-based, not strictly generational Why
twistLOHhumongous regions in G1large objects get their own regions, and collect poorly Why
twist"System.GC.Server": true in runtimeconfig.jsonjava -XX:+UseG1GC -jar app.jarthe .NET GC settings are command-line flags on the JVM Why
twistDOTNET_GCHeapCount-XX:ParallelGCThreadshow many threads the collector uses in parallel Why
twistGC.Collect()System.gc()HotSpot runs a full collection, but the flag -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns this off Why
trap"System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent": 70-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70the default is 25, so a 1 GB container gets a 256 MB heap unless you set a share Why
trapa fixed heap size in the image-XX:MaxRAMPercentage, not -Xmx2g-Xmx2g in an image that later runs with a 1 GB limit gets OOMKilled, but a percentage adapts to the limit Why
trapmemory for loaded classes-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256mmetaspace has no limit by default, so a class-loading leak can consume the container Why
twistServer GCG1 (default)the default, except on very small machines, where Serial is chosen Why
twistWorkstation GCSerialGCa single-threaded collector, for small heaps and tools Why
twistGCSettings.LatencyModechoice of collectorpick ZGC or Shenandoah when pauses matter more than throughput Why
newno equivalent-XX:+UseZGCpauses stay under 1 ms whatever the heap size, but Server GC pauses grow with the heap Why
trapan old start script-XX:+ZGenerationalThe flag no longer exists, so the JVM refuses to start. ZGC is already generational with -XX:+UseZGC. Why
twistdotnet-counters ps, dotnet-gcdumpjcmd -l, jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dumpjcmd inspects the flags, heap, threads and Flight Recorder of a running JVM Why
trapa pool of 500 threads500 platform threads, at about 1 MB of stack eachthe stacks are reserved outside the heap, but a virtual thread keeps its stack on the heap Why
twistBenchmarkDotNetJMHcode is interpreted first and compiled once hot, so benchmarks and new instances need warmup Why

The memory modeltrap#

The container of the billing service has a memory limit, and the JVM must fit inside that limit. This start command looks as if it keeps the service under 512 MB:

java -Xmx512m -jar app.jar

The command does not keep the service under 512 MB. A JVM process uses memory in several regions. -Xmx512m sets the size of the first region only:

RegionLimited byHolds
Heap-Xmx, or -XX:MaxRAMPercentageyour objects, in a young generation for new objects and an old generation for survivors
Metaspace-XX:MaxMetaspaceSizeclass metadata, with no limit by default
Code cache-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSizemachine code compiled while the program runs
Thread stacks-Xssabout 1 MB for each platform thread
GC overheadthe collector itselfthe bookkeeping the collector needs
Direct and native memory-XX:MaxDirectMemorySizeByteBuffers, Netty buffers and JNI allocations
Gotcha

-Xmx is not a limit on the process. It limits the heap only. Sometimes a container is killed with OOMKill while the heap usage looks fine. In that case, the memory is almost always used outside the heap, by metaspace, by the stacks of platform threads, or by direct buffers. Allow roughly 25 to 30 percent above -Xmx for everything else. Or use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, and the JVM calculates the heap size for you.

GC settings are command-line flagstwist#

C# refresherGC.Collect, generations and GCSettings.LatencyModeC# 1
GC.Collect();                                   // force a full collection: rarely wise
int gen = GC.GetGeneration(order);              // 0, 1 or 2
GCSettings.LatencyMode = GCLatencyMode.SustainedLowLatency;   // avoid blocking gen 2 GCs

In .NET you tune the GC in runtimeconfig.json. On the JVM the same choices are command-line flags. Here the service takes 70% of the container's memory for its heap:

runtimeconfig.json / env
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.GC.Server": true,
    "System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent": 70
  }
}
JVM flags
java -XX:+UseG1GC \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 \
     -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \
     -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -jar app.jar
Reading the code
-XX:+UseG1GC \

This flag selects G1, which is the default collector. So the flag only makes the choice visible.

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 \

The heap may grow to 70% of the memory that the container is given. This flag is like HeapHardLimitPercent in .NET.

-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \

This flag caps the memory for class metadata. Without the flag, class metadata has no limit at all.

-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \

With this flag, the process exits on an OutOfMemoryError, so the orchestrator restarts it. Without the flag, the process continues to run in a broken state.

For the other .NET GC settings and their JVM counterparts, see the differences table at the top of this chapter.

Containerstrap#

The JVM has been container-aware since Java 10. This means that it reads the CPU and memory limits of the container, not the limits of the host. But the default heap is only a quarter of the memory limit. The first command below shows the default heap. The second command sets a larger share on purpose:

# a 1 GB container: the default max heap is ~25% of it, i.e. ~256 MB
docker run -m 1g eclipse-temurin:25 java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxHeapSize

# take a deliberate share instead
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar
Reading the code
docker run -m 1g eclipse-temurin:25 java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxHeapSize

This command starts a JVM in a container that is limited to 1 GB, and prints the maximum heap of that JVM. The result is 256 MB, because the default MaxRAMPercentage is 25.

java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar

With 70%, the same container allows a heap of about 718 MB. The rest is left for metaspace, thread stacks and buffers.

Gotcha

In a container, use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, not a fixed -Xmx. Suppose an image has a hardcoded -Xmx2g and later runs with a 1 GB limit. Then the container gets OOMKilled. A percentage adapts to the limit. And always set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize. Metaspace has no limit by default, so a class-loading leak will use all the memory of the container.

It is useful to set these flags in every container:

FlagDoes
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70heap as a share of the container limit
-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=70avoid repeated heap resizing
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256mlimit class metadata
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryErrorexit and let the orchestrator restart the process, not continue in a broken state
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryErrorwrite a dump for analysis
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumpswhere to write it
-Xss512ksmaller platform thread stacks

Choosing a collectornew#

The JVM offers several collectors. Each collector makes a different choice between short pauses and high throughput:

CollectorPause timesThroughputUse when
SerialGChighfine for tiny heapssmall containers, CLI tools
ParallelGChigh, but efficienthighestbatch jobs, where latency does not matter
G1 (default)~10-200 msvery goodalmost everything
ZGCunder 1 msslightly lowerlarge heaps, latency-critical
Shenandoahunder 1 msslightly loweras ZGC, but it is not in every Java build, and generational mode is optional since Java 25

A single flag selects a collector:

java -XX:+UseG1GC        -jar app.jar    # default; leave it alone
java -XX:+UseZGC         -jar app.jar    # generational by default since Java 23
java -XX:+UseSerialGC    -jar app.jar    # small container, single CPU
Reading the code
java -XX:+UseG1GC -jar app.jar

The JVM chooses G1 even without this flag. The exception is a machine with a single CPU or very little memory. On such a machine, the JVM chooses Serial by itself.

java -XX:+UseZGC -jar app.jar

ZGC does almost all its work while your threads keep running. Since Java 24, the generational mode of ZGC is the only mode.

java -XX:+UseSerialGC -jar app.jar

Serial uses one GC thread and has the least overhead. It is meant for tools and tiny containers.

Gotcha

Old start scripts often contain -XX:+ZGenerational. On current versions of the Java Development Kit (JDK), that flag no longer exists, and the JVM refuses to start. The error message is “Unrecognized VM option 'ZGenerational'”. Delete the flag. -XX:+UseZGC alone already gives you generational ZGC.

Note

ZGC's pause times are essentially independent of heap size. A 100 GB heap pauses about as long as a 4 GB heap, because the work is concurrent. There is no equivalent in .NET. Even Server GC with background collection has pauses that grow with the heap. If you have a latency-sensitive service with a large heap, this is a real reason to prefer the JVM.

Diagnosing#

When a service misbehaves, these commands inspect the running JVM. jcmd is part of the JDK, and it finds a JVM by its process id:

jcmd -l                              # list JVMs, like dotnet-counters ps
jcmd <pid> VM.flags                  # what flags are actually in effect
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info              # heap usage now
jcmd <pid> Thread.print              # full thread dump
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram        # what is on the heap, by class
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof      # heap dump for Eclipse MAT
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/r.jfr

jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>   # the older way to take a heap dump

java '-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime' -jar app.jar   # GC logging
Reading the code
jcmd <pid> VM.flags

This command prints the flags that are in effect. The output includes the flags that the JVM chose for itself, such as the collector.

jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram

This command counts the objects of each class, and lists the largest class first. It is the quickest way to see what is filling the heap.

jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof

This command writes every object on the heap to a file. You analyse the file in a tool such as Eclipse MAT. The command is like dotnet-gcdump in .NET.

java '-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime' -jar app.jar

This command logs every collection to gc.log, with the time of day and the time since start. The quotes stop shells such as zsh from treating the * as a file pattern.

For each symptom, the table gives the first place to look:

SymptomLook at
Container OOMKilled, heap looks finemetaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers
Long pausesGC logs, and consider ZGC
High CPU, low throughputJFR CPU profile, or async-profiler
Memory grows steadilyheap dump, then Eclipse MAT dominator tree
Threads climbingthread dump, and look for a leaked executor
Slow startupAOT cache, CDS, or the auto-configuration report
Gotcha

Thread stacks are the hidden cost of platform threads. Each platform thread reserves around 1 MB. So a pool of 500 threads takes 500 MB of address space before your application allocates anything. This is one more reason that virtual threads matter. The stack of a virtual thread is on the heap, and it starts at a few hundred bytes. See Threads are cheap now.

The JIT and warmup#

Note

The JVM starts by interpreting your code. Then its just-in-time (JIT) compiler compiles the methods that run often. First the C1 compiler compiles these methods quickly. Then the C2 compiler compiles the methods that run most often, and it does so thoroughly. So peak performance arrives only after thousands of executions. That is why a Java benchmark that does not warm up is worthless. It is also why the Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH) exists. JMH does the same as BenchmarkDotNet in .NET. It handles warmup, forking and dead-code elimination for you.

In production, the practical consequence is that the first few hundred requests after a deploy are measurably slower. Java 25's ahead-of-time (AOT) method profiling reduces this slowdown. It uses the profile data from a training run. If you run a load balancer with aggressive health checks, give a new instance a moment before you send it full traffic.

You can watch the compiler work:

# watch the JIT at work: each line is a method being compiled as it gets hot
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar app.jar | head
Reading the code
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar app.jar | head

A method that runs often is called a hot method. This command prints one line for each method that the JIT compiles. So you can see which of your methods become hot as the service warms up.

Check yourself
1
Your container is OOMKilled but the heap graph looks flat. Where is the memory?
The memory is outside the heap, in metaspace, thread stacks or direct buffers. -Xmx limits the heap only, so allow 25 to 30 percent more for everything else.
2
Which garbage collector does the JVM use by default, and when do you choose ZGC instead?
The default is G1, except on a very small machine, where the JVM chooses Serial. Choose ZGC when pauses matter more than throughput. The flag for ZGC is -XX:+UseZGC. The pauses of ZGC stay under 1 ms whatever the heap size. Do not add -XX:+ZGenerational, because that flag no longer exists, and the JVM refuses to start.

End of the first read

You have read every teaching chapter. What follows is for coming back: the tours, the review questions and the lookup appendices.
