Appendix A: Java 9 to 25#

Appendices · Chapter 55· 4 min read

This appendix lists the Java release that added each feature. It also gives the status of each feature, and the status is as important as the release. A feature is final, is a preview, or was withdrawn. Roughly half the Java features that people write about in blogs are still preview-only. Preview features need the option --enable-preview, and they can change or disappear between releases.

Releases with long-term support (LTS) are marked. Target an LTS. Most rows name the chapter that shows the feature in code. Search for the title of that chapter to go there.

Note

The entries below for Java 21, 22, 24 and 25 are verified against the project pages of those releases on openjdk.org. The entries for Java 9 to 20 and for Java 23 are widely documented and stable, but they were not verified again for this edition. If you rely on an exact release number, check openjdk.org/projects/jdk/<n>.

Language features#

FeatureReleaseStatusC# analogueChapter
var for locals10finalvarvar, strings and text blocks
Text blocks15finalraw string literalsvar, strings and text blocks
Records16finalrecordsRecords
instanceof pattern16finalis T xSealed types and pattern matching
Sealed classes and interfaces17finalno equivalentSealed types and pattern matching
Switch expressions14finalswitch expressionsSwitch expressions and statements
Pattern matching for switch21finalswitch on patternsSealed types and pattern matching
Record patterns21finalpositional patternsSealed types and pattern matching
Unnamed variables and patterns22finaldiscard _Sealed types and pattern matching
Module import declarations25finalno equivalent, because a using directive imports one namespaceAccess modifiers and packages
Compact source files, instance main25finaltop-level statementsGetting a JDK
Flexible constructor bodies25finalnone, because base(...) is written before the bodyClasses, constructors and initialisation
Primitive types in patterns25PREVIEWrelational patternsSealed types and pattern matching
String templates21, 22WITHDRAWNinterpolation. Java has nonevar, strings and text blocks
Gotcha

String templates were previewed in Java 21 and 22, then withdrawn. They are not in Java 23, 24 or 25. Java has no string interpolation. Any tutorial that shows STR."..." describes a feature that no longer exists. See var, strings and text blocks.

Concurrency#

Each feature was added through a proposal to the Java Development Kit (JDK). Such a proposal is called a JDK Enhancement Proposal (JEP). The two biggest concurrency changes were virtual threads and structured concurrency. Virtual threads are now final. Structured concurrency is still a preview. This table lists the concurrency features:

FeatureReleaseStatusNote
CompletableFuture improvements9finalThe improvements are timeouts and delayed executors. See the chapter CompletableFuture and Task.
Virtual threads21finalJava uses virtual threads for the work that C# does with async and await. See the chapter Threads are cheap now.
Synchronize virtual threads without pinning24finalJEP 491 removes the synchronized trap. See the chapter Threads are cheap now.
Scoped values25finalA scoped value is like AsyncLocal in C#. See the chapter Structured concurrency and cancellation.
Structured concurrency25PREVIEWThis is the fifth preview, and the API has changed. See the chapter Structured concurrency and cancellation.
Stable values25PREVIEWA stable value is like Lazy<T> in C#, and the JIT can treat it as a constant. See the chapter Locks, atomics and the memory model.
Gotcha

Structured concurrency is still preview in Java 25. It is JEP 505, and this is its fifth preview. Virtual threads are final and safe to use. The scope API around virtual threads is not final, and it is not safe to rely on. Any text that you read from 2023 or 2024 uses an earlier form of the API.

Library and API#

FeatureReleaseStatusNote
Collection factories List.of, Map.of9finalThese factories create an unmodifiable collection in one call. See the chapter Collections.
Stream takeWhile, dropWhile, iterate9finaltakeWhile and dropWhile are like TakeWhile and SkipWhile in LINQ. See the chapter Streams vs LINQ.
Optional.stream, ifPresentOrElse9finalThese methods give you more ways to use a value that may be absent. Only stream() is listed in the chapter Nullability.
New HTTP client (java.net.http)11finalThis client is part of the JDK, and it is like HttpClient in .NET. See the chapter HTTP clients and resilience.
String isBlank, lines, strip, repeat11finalThese methods are like IsNullOrWhiteSpace and similar string methods in C#. See the chapter var, strings and text blocks.
Files.readString, writeString11finalThese methods are like File.ReadAllText and File.WriteAllText in C#. See the chapter Files and I/O.
Collectors.teeing12finalThis collector combines two collectors into one result. See the chapter Streams vs LINQ.
Stream.toList()16finalThis method replaces collect(toList()). See the chapter Streams vs LINQ.
Sequenced collections21finalThese collections have the methods getFirst, getLast and reversed(). See the chapter Collections.
Foreign Function and Memory API22finalThis API is like P/Invoke in .NET. See the appendix Going deeper.
Class-File API24finalThis API is like Reflection.Emit in .NET. See the appendix Going deeper.
Stream gatherers24finalGatherers are custom intermediate operations, such as Chunk. See the chapter Streams vs LINQ.
Ahead-of-Time Class Loading and Linking24finalStartup is faster after a training run. See the chapter Packaging and native images.
Permanently disable the Security Manager24finalThe Security Manager was already deprecated. See the appendix The Java you'll inherit.
ZGC: remove non-generational mode24finalGenerational is now the only ZGC mode. See the chapter The JVM at runtime.
Quantum-resistant ML-KEM and ML-DSA24finalpost-quantum key exchange and digital signatures
Key Derivation Function API25finala standard API for deriving keys from shared secrets
PEM encodings25PREVIEWreading and writing keys and certificates as PEM text
Vector API25INCUBATORThis is the tenth incubation. The Vector API is like System.Numerics.Vector in .NET.

Runtime, garbage collection (GC) and tooling#

FeatureReleaseStatusNote
jshell (REPL)9finalThis is the Java REPL, which you use to try an API quickly. See the chapter Getting a JDK.
JPMS modules9finalA module is declared in the file module-info.java. See the chapter Modules, JPMS and the missing internal.
Single-file source launch11finalYou run java Foo.java with no compile step. See the chapter Getting a JDK.
Flight Recorder open-sourced11finalJDK Flight Recorder (JFR) is free to use in production. See the chapter Actuator and observability.
Helpful NullPointerExceptions14finalThe exception message names the expression that was null. The feature has been on by default since Java 15.
Strong encapsulation of JDK internals17finalOld libraries that use JDK internals now fail. See the chapter Modules, JPMS and the missing internal.
Deprecate finalization for removal18deprecatedNever override finalize(). See the chapter Exceptions and resources.
Generational ZGC21finalZGC gained generations, which reduced its memory overhead
Multi-file source launch22finaljava Main.java can now use the other source files beside it
Generational ZGC by default23finalZGC is generational unless you choose the non-generational mode
Compact object headers25finalThe option -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders is off by default. It makes the header of every object smaller.
Ahead-of-time command-line ergonomics25finalOne flag creates the AOT cache. See the chapter Packaging and native images.
Ahead-of-time method profiling25finalProfiles from a training run make warm-up faster. See the chapter The JVM at runtime.
Generational Shenandoah25finalGenerational Shenandoah is a supported option but not the default. The option is -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational.
JFR CPU-time profiling25EXPERIMENTALCPU-time sampling in Flight Recorder, experimental in Java 25
JFR cooperative sampling25finalsafer, lower-overhead stack sampling inside Flight Recorder
JFR method timing and tracing25finaltime or trace chosen methods without changing their code
Remove the 32-bit x86 port25finalthe JDK builds for 64-bit x86 only from Java 25

Release cadence#

ReleaseDateLTSNotes
Java 82014LTSstill widespread, but it lacks almost everything in the tables above
Java 92017modules, jshell, collection factories
Java 112018LTSHTTP client, var refinements, single-file launch
Java 172021LTSsealed types, strong encapsulation
Java 212023LTSvirtual threads, pattern matching, sequenced collections
Java 252025LTSscoped values, compact source files, AOT, compact headers
Note

Java has a new release every six months, in March and September. Every fourth release is an LTS, so a new LTS arrives every two years. A non-LTS release receives updates for six months. Use an LTS in production. Treat a non-LTS release as a way to try preview features early.

This appendix lists every C# construct, keyword, type and library in alphabetical order. Each row gives what Java uses in its place. Use this page when you know the C# word and need the Java word.

Search is faster than this page. Press ⌘K, or Ctrl+K, and type the C# name. Every row of every table in this book is indexed.

Some rows are about runtime concepts, such as assembly probing and the classpath. Those rows name the chapter How Java runs your code. Read that chapter once before you rely on those rows.

Two more places answer questions that this index cannot answer. For the Java tools that have no C# name to search for, see the section Only in Java. For the whole language as one listing of commented code, see the chapter Java in 19 minutes.

where T : X<T extends X>Generics and type erasure

The rows to remember are in the next table. These rows change how you design, and not only how you type:

C#JavaWhy it matters

Appendix C: The Java you'll inherit#

Appendices · Chapter 57· 17 min read· Quick reference

Java almost never breaks old code. So a real codebase holds layers from several eras, with the oldest style at the bottom. This appendix is a guide to those layers. For each old technology, it says what the technology is, roughly when it was written, and what replaced it.

KindC#JavaNote
twist.NET Framework 1.x, WebForms, ASP.NET Core 1-3, .NET 5-10J2EE, Spring XML, Spring Boot, modern Javaeach of the four eras has its own house style, so the style of a file tells you its era Why
twistArrayList and Hashtable, from before 2005import javax.servlet, applicationContext.xml, @Autowired on fieldseach signal dates the code, as ArrayList and Hashtable date C# Why
twistList<Order> orders = new List<Order>();List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<Order>(...);Java 7 added the diamond, <>, in 2011. Code that repeats the type argument is older, or was written from habit. Why
twista constructor parameter@Autowired on a private field, in older codeField injection dates a class to about 2007 to 2016. New code injects through the constructor. Why
trapa namespace that changes in every fileimport jakarta.persistence.EntitySpring Boot 2 uses javax, and Spring Boot 3 and 4 use jakarta. Nothing translates between javax and jakarta. Why
twistwhy the names changedJakarta EE, once Java EEOracle kept the Java trademarks, so Eclipse could not change anything under the javax names Why
trapexpecting XML binding inside the runtimeNoClassDefFoundError: javax/xml/bind/JAXBContextJava 11 removed JAXB from the JDK, and the code fails only when the line that uses it runs Why
twistadding a NuGet packagejakarta.xml.bind-api and jaxb-runtimeadd JAXB back as two dependencies, and change the imports to jakarta.xml.bind Why
twistAPIs you may still see in old codeapplets, Nashorn, the Security Manager, Thread.stopJava 15 removed Nashorn, Java 24 disabled the Security Manager, and Java 26 removed the Applet API and Thread.stop Why
twistorders.Sort((a, b) => a.Total.CompareTo(b.Total))Collections.sort(orders, new Comparator<Order>() { ... })Before Java 8, in 2014, a callback was a whole anonymous class. Today a callback is a lambda. Why
twistservices registered in Program.cs<bean> elements in applicationContext.xmlThis is how Spring was configured before annotations. The XML still loads in Spring 7, often beside annotations. Why
twistMSBuild targetsbuild.xml, for AntAnt is a task runner with no conventions and no dependency management, and Maven replaced it Why
twistIHttpHandler, Web Forms, Silverlightservlets, Struts and JSF, appletsServlets still run under Spring MVC. If you inherit Struts, migrate to Spring MVC. Why
twistCOM+, .NET Remoting and IISEJB 2 and application serversSpring beans replaced EJB 2, and an embedded web server replaced application servers Why
twistASMX and WCF@WebService, WSDL and SOAPthese are XML services, and they are still current in banking, government and telecoms Why
twistdating advice by the C# it assumesdating advice by the Java era it assumesan old answer may still recommend finalize(), which Java 18 deprecated for removal Why

Four erastwist#

The history of Java has four eras, and each era has its own house style. The first era was built on the Java 2 Platform, Enterprise Edition (J2EE). J2EE was a set of standards for business software that ran inside large shared servers. The last column of the table names what .NET developers were using at the same time. That name is often the quickest way to picture an era. These are the four eras:

EraYearsHouse style.NET contemporary
Applets and J2EE1995-2005XML configuration files, heavyweight application servers.NET Framework 1.x
Spring and annotations2005-2014Spring XML, then annotations, and Maven.NET 2.0-4.5, WebForms
Boot and microservices2014-2020Spring Boot, embedded servers, DockerASP.NET Core 1-3
Modern Java2020 onwardrecords, virtual threads, Jakarta.NET 5-10

You rarely need the exact year. It is more useful to recognise the era of a file from its style.

Dating a codebase at a glancetwist#

You can already date C# code by its style. A class full of ArrayList and Hashtable was written before generics arrived in 2005. A class that uses async and await was written after 2012. Java code shows its age in the same way. Two fragments of one file can be enough:

import javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet;     // javax, not jakarta: before 2020

@Autowired
private OrderRepository repository;        // injected into a field: about 2007 to 2016

The javax.servlet import and the @Autowired field are two signals. Each signal in this table points to an era:

If you seeIt was written aroundEra
import javax.servletbefore 2020pre-Jakarta
Struts action classes2001-2008J2EE
EJB with Home interfaces1999-2006J2EE
build.xml (Ant)before 2008J2EE
applicationContext.xml2004-2013Spring XML
Hibernate .hbm.xml mappings2003-2010Spring XML
@Autowired on fields2007-2016annotation era
new StringBuilder() everywhereany era, and it is still right inside loops-
Anonymous inner classes as callbacksbefore 2014pre-lambda
Guava for collections2010-2018pre-Java-9
@SpringBootApplication2014 onwardBoot
records and switch expressions2021 onwardmodern

One class, as written around 2010twist#

This Spring service returns the shop's orders, with the biggest total first. OrderRepository is an interface. Its method findAll() returns a List<Order>:

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class OrderReport {

    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository repository;

    public List<Order> biggestFirst() {
        List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<Order>(repository.findAll());
        Collections.sort(orders, new Comparator<Order>() {
            public int compare(Order a, Order b) {
                return b.getTotal().compareTo(a.getTotal());
            }
        });
        return orders;
    }
}
Reading the code
@Autowired

This is called field injection. Spring creates the OrderReport, then writes the repository directly into the private field. Field injection is typical of the annotation era of Spring, about 2007 to 2016.

List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<Order>(repository.findAll());

<Order> is written twice. Java 7 added the empty brackets <> in 2011, and they are called the diamond. Code that repeats the type is older, or was written from habit.

Collections.sort(orders, new Comparator<Order>() {

This is an anonymous class. It is a whole class written inline, only to pass one method. Java had no lambdas until Java 8, in 2014.

return b.getTotal().compareTo(a.getTotal());

Comparing b with a puts the biggest total first. getTotal() is a getter method on an ordinary class. Before records, a class exposed its data through getter methods like this one.

The same class, written todaytwist#

Today the class uses constructor injection. Order is now a record, so the code reads the total with total(), not with getTotal():

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class OrderReport {

    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderReport(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public List<Order> biggestFirst() {
        return repository.findAll().stream()
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::total).reversed())
                .toList();
    }
}
Reading the code
private final OrderRepository repository;

This is constructor injection. Spring passes the repository to the constructor. So the field can be final, and an OrderReport cannot exist without a repository. A class with one constructor needs no @Autowired.

.sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::total).reversed())

Order::total is a method reference to the total() method of the record. This method reference replaces the whole anonymous class. reversed() changes the order from smallest first to biggest first.

.toList();

This line returns a list that cannot be changed. The toList() method arrived in Java 16.

Both versions are correct. The older version still runs on Java 25 and Spring 7. But a class in the older style tells you that the classes around it were probably written in the same era.

The javax to jakarta renametrap#

When you move a Spring Boot 2 service to Spring Boot 3, nearly every entity, controller and validator stops compiling. The enterprise standards of Java were once called Java Enterprise Edition (Java EE). They are now called Jakarta EE. In 2020, Jakarta EE 9 moved every enterprise API package from javax to jakarta, because of a trademark:

BeforeAfterAffects
javax.servlet.*jakarta.servlet.*every web application
javax.persistence.*jakarta.persistence.*every JPA entity
javax.validation.*jakarta.validation.*every @NotNull
javax.annotation.*jakarta.annotation.*@PostConstruct, @Resource
javax.transaction.*jakarta.transaction.*@Transactional (the JTA one)

Only the import lines change. The classes, annotations and methods keep their names:

// Spring Boot 2 uses the javax names.
import javax.persistence.Entity;
import javax.validation.constraints.NotNull;

// Spring Boot 3 and 4 use the jakarta names for the same classes.
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull;

Entity comes from Jakarta Persistence (JPA), which is the standard behind Hibernate. NotNull comes from Jakarta Validation. The rename never affected the java.* packages, such as java.util.

Gotcha

This is a hard break, not a deprecation. Nothing in the framework translates between javax and jakarta. An upgrade means that you change those imports everywhere, and that you replace any library that still uses javax. Tools such as OpenRewrite and the Eclipse Transformer can do the renaming. But plan the upgrade as a project, not as the work of one afternoon.

Why the packages were renamed#

The cause is not a bug. The cause is a trademark. The enterprise standards of Java were called the Java Enterprise Edition (Java EE). They were in the javax packages. In 2017 Oracle gave Java EE to the Eclipse Foundation, and the Eclipse Foundation later renamed it Jakarta EE. Oracle kept the Java trademarks, and the agreement did not let Eclipse change anything under the javax names. So in 2020, Jakarta EE 9 moved every enterprise API package from javax to jakarta. The servlet class that every web application uses shows the result:

import javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet;     // the Java EE name
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet;   // the Jakarta EE name, from 2020

HttpServlet is the same class under both names. Only the package in front of the class name changed.

What Java removedtrap#

A service that exports invoices as XML moves from Java 8 to Java 11. It starts normally, then fails on its first export:

java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: javax/xml/bind/JAXBContext#
Means
The code uses the Java Architecture for XML Binding (JAXB). JAXB is the library that turns objects into XML and back. Java 8 included JAXB in the Java Development Kit (JDK), and Java 11 removed it. The code was compiled long ago, so nothing reports a problem until the line that uses JAXB runs. The stack trace then reads Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException.
Fix
Add JAXB back as a dependency, and change its imports from javax.xml.bind to jakarta.xml.bind.
Gotcha

The Java EE removals in Java 11 break more upgrades than anything except the Jakarta rename. Java 9 stopped loading JAXB and the other Java EE modules by default. Java 11 then deleted them. The error names a missing class. It does not tell you that a dependency is missing.

Adding JAXB back, and the other removalstwist#

The fix is to add JAXB back as an ordinary dependency. In a Spring Boot 3 or 4 project, Spring Boot chooses the versions, and it chooses the Jakarta versions:

<!-- The JAXB API: JAXBContext and the annotations, now in the package jakarta.xml.bind. -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>jakarta.xml.bind</groupId>
  <artifactId>jakarta.xml.bind-api</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- The implementation that does the work at run time. -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.glassfish.jaxb</groupId>
  <artifactId>jaxb-runtime</artifactId>
</dependency>
Reading the code
<artifactId>jakarta.xml.bind-api</artifactId>

This dependency holds the classes that your code calls. You write no <version> in these dependencies, because Spring Boot supplies it. Spring Boot 4.1 chooses version 4, and version 4 is in the package jakarta.xml.bind. So import javax.xml.bind.JAXBContext must become import jakarta.xml.bind.JAXBContext.

<artifactId>jaxb-runtime</artifactId>

This dependency is the engine behind the API. Without it, the code compiles. But the code then fails when it creates a JAXBContext. The failure is a JAXBException, which says that no implementation of the API was found.

JAXB is the removal you are most likely to meet. The full list is short, and each entry says what to use instead:

RemovedWhenNote
Applet APIJava 26Java 11 removed the browser plugin. Java 17 deprecated the API, and Java 26 removed it.
Java Web StartJava 11it is gone, so ship an installer built with jpackage instead
CORBA and Java EE modulesJava 11JAXB and JAX-WS became separate dependencies, as the JAXB example above shows
Nashorn JavaScript engineJava 15it is gone, so use GraalJS to run JavaScript on the JVM
Security ManagerJava 24it is permanently disabled, so you can no longer enable it
Thread.suspend and resumeJava 23They were removed completely. They were never safe to call.
Thread.stopJava 26It has thrown an exception instead of stopping the thread since Java 20. Java 26 removes it.
32-bit x86 portJava 25the JDK now builds for 64-bit x86 only
Non-generational ZGCJava 24generational mode is now the only mode that ZGC has

Language habits from before Java 8#

LegacyAnonymous inner classes as callbacks

Java 8 arrived in 2014. Before Java 8, you had to write a whole class inline to pass a piece of behaviour. C# has had lambdas since 2007, so the same sort looks very different in C# and in old Java:

C# 3 and later
orders.Sort((a, b) => a.Total.CompareTo(b.Total));
Java before 8
Collections.sort(orders, new Comparator<Order>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(Order a, Order b) {
        return a.getTotal().compareTo(b.getTotal());
    }
});

Both versions sort orders with the smallest total first. The Java version creates an unnamed class that implements Comparator. The class has one method, compare, which does the comparison. Modern Java writes orders.sort(Comparator.comparing(Order::getTotal)). IntelliJ converts the old form for you with Alt+Enter, or ⌥↩ on a Mac.

LegacyGuava and Apache Commons

The JDK did not always have collection factories, Optional and string helpers. Before the JDK had them, two libraries provided them. The two libraries are Guava, from Google, and Apache Commons. Older code is full of calls to these libraries, and most of the calls now have a JDK method that does the same job. For each common call and its replacement, see the Quick reference at the end of this appendix.

Both libraries are still in use. The caches, multimaps and graph types of Guava have no JDK equivalent. But new code should not use Guava or Apache Commons to do what the JDK now does.

LegacyChecked exceptions everywhere

Early Java APIs declared checked exceptions freely. A checked exception is an exception that the compiler forces every caller to catch or declare. The try/catch blocks that result are a large reason why Java is known as a wordy language. Since then, libraries have done the opposite. Spring, Hibernate and the AWS SDK all wrap checked exceptions in unchecked exceptions before the exceptions reach your code. See Exceptions and resources.

Configuration by XML#

LegacySpring XML configuration

In .NET you register services in code, in Program.cs. Before annotations, Spring did this in an XML file, usually called applicationContext.xml. Every Spring bean was declared in that file. A data source is the object that supplies database connections. In this example, the order service gets its repository, and the repository gets its data source:

<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans-3.0.xsd">

  <bean id="orderService" class="com.acme.orders.OrderService">
    <constructor-arg ref="orderRepository"/>
    <property name="auditEnabled" value="true"/>
  </bean>

  <bean id="orderRepository" class="com.acme.orders.JdbcOrderRepository">
    <property name="dataSource" ref="dataSource"/>
  </bean>

  <bean id="dataSource" class="org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.DriverManagerDataSource">
    <property name="url" value="jdbc:postgresql://localhost/shop"/>
  </bean>
</beans>
Reading the code
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"

The header names the XML schema, so tools can check the file. The address contains a version number, here 3.0, and this number dates the file. Spring 7 still accepts the file.

class="com.acme.orders.OrderService">

This element declares one bean. Spring creates an OrderService and registers it under the name orderService. The class name is a plain string, and that is the weakness of the whole approach.

<constructor-arg ref="orderRepository"/>

This line passes the bean named orderRepository to the constructor. ref always means another bean.

<property name="auditEnabled" value="true"/>

This line calls setAuditEnabled(true) after the object is created. value passes a literal value, not a bean.

Large systems had thousands of lines of this XML. The XML held class names as plain strings. So when you renamed a class, the build still passed, and the application failed only at its next start-up. The application loaded the file with new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("applicationContext.xml"), or through a setting in web.xml. Annotations arrived in Spring 2.5, in 2007. @Configuration classes arrived in Spring 3, in 2009. XML still works in Spring 7. You will find it in older modules, often beside annotations in the same application.

LegacyHibernate hbm.xml mappings

If you have used NHibernate in .NET, you know this format already. NHibernate is a port of Hibernate, and it copied the format. Before annotations, Hibernate read the mapping between a class and its table from an XML file. Each class had its own file, with a name like Order.hbm.xml:

<hibernate-mapping>
  <class name="com.acme.orders.Order" table="ORDERS">
    <id name="id" column="ORDER_ID">
      <generator class="native"/>
    </id>
    <property name="total" column="TOTAL"/>
  </class>
</hibernate-mapping>

The class element maps Order to the ORDERS table. The id element names the key column, and it lets the database choose how to generate the key. Each property element maps one field. To rename a field, you had to edit two files. If you forgot the second file, the application failed at run time. The @Entity, @Id and @Column annotations replaced these files in 2006. The engine under the annotations is the same.

Build tools#

LegacyAnt and Ivy

Ant dates from 2000. It is a general-purpose task runner that is configured in XML. Ant is closer to MSBuild than to Maven. Ant has no conventions and no dependency management. So every project invented its own folder layout, and libraries were committed to source control in a lib/ folder. A build.xml file lists targets, and each target is a list of tasks:

<project name="shop" default="compile">
  <property name="src" location="src"/>
  <property name="build" location="build"/>

  <target name="init">
    <mkdir dir="${build}"/>
  </target>

  <target name="compile" depends="init">
    <javac srcdir="${src}" destdir="${build}" classpath="lib/commons-lang-2.6.jar"/>
  </target>
</project>
Reading the code
<property name="src" location="src"/>

This line defines a variable, which is used later as ${src}. Ant assumes nothing about the layout, so every project states its layout in full.

<target name="compile" depends="init">

This is a target, like an MSBuild target. depends runs the target init first.

<javac srcdir="${src}" destdir="${build}" classpath="lib/commons-lang-2.6.jar"/>

This line compiles the sources against a Java archive (JAR) that is checked into the repository. There is no package manager. The file in lib/ is the dependency.

Ivy is a later add-on that gave Ant dependency resolution. Maven dates from 2004. Its real contribution was not its XML. Its real contribution was the conventions, such as src/main/java, and a central repository of libraries. Ant is still used in old builds and inside some Gradle scripts.

Web frameworks, in order of extinction#

LegacyApplets

Applets were Java in the browser, from 1995 to about 2015. An applet was user-interface code that was downloaded as a JAR and run by a browser plugin. Silverlight later worked in a similar way for .NET. Security flaws ended the use of applets. Then browsers dropped the Netscape Plugin API (NPAPI), which the plugin needed. Java 11 removed the browser plugin and Java Web Start. The Applet API itself was deprecated for removal in Java 17 and removed in Java 26.

You will not meet a working applet. You may meet the remains of an applet in an internal tool that nobody dares to delete.

LegacyServlets and JSP

A servlet is a class that handles an HTTP request. A servlet does the same as an IHttpHandler in classic ASP.NET. Servlets date from the late 1990s. Unlike applets, servlets are still in wide use, but they are hidden under Spring. This servlet returns a page of HTML:

import java.io.IOException;

import javax.servlet.ServletException;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;

public class OrderServlet extends HttpServlet {

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        response.setContentType("text/html");
        response.getWriter().println("<h1>Orders</h1>");
    }
}
Reading the code
public class OrderServlet extends HttpServlet {

Every servlet extends HttpServlet. A separate file called web.xml mapped a URL such as /orders to this class.

protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response)

A servlet has one method for each HTTP verb, such as doGet and doPost. The request object and the response object are the whole API. In classic ASP.NET, HttpContext was the whole API in the same way.

response.getWriter().println("<h1>Orders</h1>");

This line writes the HTML of the page directly in code. Nobody does this any more. Today a template or a JSON library produces the response.

Spring MVC is the model-view-controller web framework of Spring, and it is built on this same API. Its DispatcherServlet is a servlet that receives every request and passes it to your controllers. So servlets still run under every Spring MVC application. The only change is that developers no longer write servlets themselves. A WebFlux application is different. It runs on Netty, which is not a servlet server.

JavaServer Pages (JSP) are HTML pages with Java mixed in, and each page is compiled into a servlet. JSP is truly legacy, so use Thymeleaf templates instead.

LegacyStruts 1 and 2

Struts was the leading model-view-controller framework of the early 2000s. Struts did the same job in Java that ASP.NET MVC later did in .NET. Actions were configured in struts-config.xml, and forms were ActionForm classes. Struts 1 reached end of life in 2013. Struts 2 is still maintained but rarely chosen. Struts 2 is best known for CVE-2017-5638. This was the remote-code-execution flaw behind the 2017 Equifax breach.

If you inherit Struts, the migration target is Spring MVC. Treat the Struts version as a security matter, not as a preference.

LegacyJSF and Java EE MVC

JavaServer Faces (JSF) was the official web framework of Java EE. It is a component-based framework that keeps page state on the server. JSF is like ASP.NET Web Forms, and in the end it had the same problems as Web Forms. JSF still exists as Jakarta Faces. It is used mostly in large companies, for internal applications that have been in use for many years.

Java EE MVC is a later standard, and it is now called Jakarta MVC. Some older guides name it as the equivalent of ASP.NET MVC. Few teams use Jakarta MVC. In practice, the equivalent of ASP.NET MVC is Spring MVC, through Spring Boot.

EJB and the application server#

LegacyEJB 2.x

Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) were the central component model of J2EE. An EJB was an object inside a server, and the server gave it transactions, security and remote calls. The closest matches in .NET are COM+ and .NET Remoting. In version 2, every bean needed four pieces:

  • a home interface
  • a remote interface
  • an implementation class
  • an XML deployment descriptor

The home interface and the remote interface alone look like this:

import java.rmi.RemoteException;
import javax.ejb.CreateException;
import javax.ejb.EJBHome;
import javax.ejb.EJBObject;

// The home interface is how a client asks the server for an OrderService.
public interface OrderServiceHome extends EJBHome {
    OrderService create() throws RemoteException, CreateException;
}

// The remote interface lists the methods a client may call.
public interface OrderService extends EJBObject {
    Order place(Order order) throws RemoteException;
}
Reading the code
OrderService create() throws RemoteException, CreateException;

A client never used new. It looked up the home interface on the server, then called create to get an OrderService.

Order place(Order order) throws RemoteException;

Every call might cross the network. So every method declared the checked exception RemoteException, and every caller had to handle it.

Spring exists because EJB needed this much extra code. In his 2002 book, Rod Johnson argued that plain objects could have the same transactions without EJB. The plain objects would run in a container that did not interfere with them. In 2006, EJB 3 switched to annotations and became reasonable. But by then Spring had replaced EJB in most new code.

LegacyApplication servers

WebSphere, WebLogic, JBoss and GlassFish were application servers. An application server is a long-running server that several applications share, and you manage it through a web console. It is like IIS when IIS hosts several sites. You packaged a web application as a web application archive (WAR). You packaged several web applications together as an enterprise archive (EAR). Then you deployed the archive into the server. Deployment was something that you did to a server. It was not a process that you started.

Spring Boot reversed this model. The web server is a library inside your JAR. Each service is its own process. The file that you deploy never changes after it is built. These changes made Java suitable for containers. You will still meet WebSphere in banking and insurance.

SOAP and web services#

LegacyJAX-WS, WSDL and SOAP

If you built services with ASMX or WCF in .NET, you know this technology. Before REST, the contract of a service was a Web Services Description Language (WSDL) document. Each message was a SOAP envelope, which is an XML document sent over HTTP. Tools generated client code from the WSDL, and this gave real type safety across languages. REST lost that type safety, and OpenAPI later restored much of it.

In Java, a class became a SOAP service through annotations from JAX-WS, the Java API for XML Web Services:

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

import javax.jws.WebMethod;
import javax.jws.WebParam;
import javax.jws.WebService;

@WebService
public class InvoiceService {

    private final Map<Long, Invoice> invoices = new HashMap<Long, Invoice>();

    @WebMethod
    public Invoice findInvoice(@WebParam(name = "orderId") long orderId) {
        return invoices.get(orderId);
    }
}
Reading the code
@WebService

This annotation publishes the class as a SOAP service. The server generates the WSDL from the class.

public Invoice findInvoice(@WebParam(name = "orderId") long orderId) {

@WebMethod makes the method an operation of the service. @WebParam names the parameter in the XML. JAXB turns the returned Invoice into XML.

More standards were built on SOAP, such as WS-Security and WS-ReliableMessaging. These extra standards gave “enterprise integration” its reputation. SOAP is still current in banking, government and telecoms. Spring Boot supports SOAP through spring-boot-starter-webservices. The same change happened in .NET, from WCF to ASP.NET Core.

Why any of this matterstwist#

When you know the age of a codebase, you know which advice to trust. A codebase with applicationContext.xml and anonymous classes was probably written before 2014. At that time, virtual threads, records and lambdas did not exist. Search results and forum answers from that time are just as old. Some of them still recommend overriding finalize(), which Java 18 deprecated for removal.

Most of the technology in this appendix still runs. So a Java codebase is not rewritten. It gets new layers on top of the old layers. This is why the skill of reading old Java stays useful.

Check yourself
1
Why does nearly every entity, controller and validator stop compiling when a service moves from Spring Boot 2 to Spring Boot 3?
Spring Boot 2 uses the javax packages, and Spring Boot 3 uses the jakarta packages. Nothing translates between javax and jakarta. So every enterprise import must change, for example from javax.persistence to jakarta.persistence.
2
A service moved from Java 8 to Java 11 fails with NoClassDefFoundError: javax/xml/bind/JAXBContext. What is the fix?
Java 11 removed JAXB from the JDK. Add jakarta.xml.bind-api and jaxb-runtime as dependencies, and change the imports to jakarta.xml.bind.

Quick reference#

Old JavaUse todayThe .NET counterpart of the old one
Appletsa web front endSilverlight, also a browser plugin
Hand-written servletsSpring MVC controllersIHttpHandler in classic ASP.NET
JSP pagesThymeleaf templatesclassic ASP or .aspx pages

Appendix D: Going deeper#

Appendices · Chapter 58· 10 min read

This appendix is a map. It shows where each topic is, and it does not teach the topic in full. Each topic below needs more than a handbook section, and some topics need a whole book. Every topic answers four questions:

  • What is it?
  • What symptom tells you that you need it?
  • Where will a C# habit mislead you?
  • What should you read?

Spring internals get short, real explanations with code, because they are conventions. You can learn a convention in a few hundred words. The internals of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) get signposts only, because they are behaviour that you have to measure. No summary replaces a measurement.

Start here: the symptom index#

Start from what you are seeing. Each row names a symptom, the mechanism that usually explains it, and where this book covers it:

What you are seeingWhat explains itWhere
An annotation silently does nothingthe method was called from inside its own class, which bypasses Spring's proxyHow Spring actually works
A bean is null inside @PostConstructthe order in which Spring creates and initialises beansHow Spring actually works
Data committed despite an exceptionby default, a checked exception does not roll the transaction backTransactions, propagation and isolation
Deadlocks that only appear under loadREQUIRES_NEW holds one connection while it waits for a second, and the pool has no connection leftTransactions, propagation and isolation
Correct on MySQL, wrong on PostgreSQLthe two databases have different default isolation levelsTransactions, propagation and isolation
p99 is spiky, the mean is finethe slowest 1% of requests hit garbage-collection pauses, or the JIT recompiling codeThe JVM at runtime, and the JIT entry below
Works in tests, fails in the app serverthe server's classloaders see a different set of classesClassloaders, below
ClassCastException naming the same class twicetwo classloaders each loaded their own copy of the classClassloaders, below
Slow build, unexplained generated sourcesan annotation processor writing code at compile timeAnnotation processing
A concurrency bug you cannot reproducea missing happens-before rule in the Java Memory ModelThe Java Memory Model, below
Memory grows but the heap looks flatmemory outside the heap, used by metaspace, direct buffers and thread stacksThe JVM at runtime
Startup is slow and you have no idea whytoo many auto-configurations or classes to load, and the conditions report shows which ranSpring Boot orientation, and Spring AOT, below
You need to add behaviour to a class you do not ownrewriting the class's bytecodeBytecode manipulation, below
Your own starter is not auto-configuringa wrong registration file, or a condition that is not metWriting an auto-configuration, below
Native image compiles but fails at runtimereflection metadata that the build could not inferSpring AOT, below, and Packaging and native images

Spring internals#

These three topics explain what Spring Boot does at start-up, and each topic takes an afternoon to learn. The first topic is how Spring Boot's auto-configuration works from the library's side.

Writing an auto-configuration and a starter#

Say that several of the shop's services call the same payment provider. You want to write the client once, as a library. Then each service only adds a dependency and sets a URL. The library needs an auto-configuration. An auto-configuration is a class that creates the beans of the library, but only when certain conditions hold.

RowDetail
What it isA configuration class that creates beans only when its conditions hold. Spring Boot finds it through a registration file inside the library, not by component scanning.
You need it whenYou are packaging shared setup for several services, and want each service to get it just by adding one dependency.
The C# instinctAn extension method such as services.AddPaymentGateway() that every application must call. Spring does the opposite. The library registers itself, and the application does nothing.

The library holds two types. PaymentGatewayClient wraps Spring's RestClient. PaymentGatewayProperties is a record that is bound from the payment.gateway.* settings. The auto-configuration is the first of two parts:

package com.acme.payments.autoconfigure;

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnClass;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnMissingBean;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

import com.acme.payments.PaymentGatewayClient;
import com.acme.payments.PaymentGatewayProperties;

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(RestClient.class)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentGatewayProperties.class)
public class PaymentGatewayAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    PaymentGatewayClient paymentGatewayClient(PaymentGatewayProperties properties) {
        return new PaymentGatewayClient(RestClient.create(properties.url()));
    }
}
Reading the code
package com.acme.payments.autoconfigure;

The class is in a package of its own, which no application will scan. The gotcha below explains why that matters.

@AutoConfiguration

@AutoConfiguration marks a configuration class that Spring Boot loads only through the registration file. Spring Boot loads this class after the application's own configuration. That order allows the class to skip its own bean when the application has defined one.

@ConditionalOnClass(RestClient.class)

Spring Boot skips the whole class unless RestClient is on the classpath. RestClient is on the classpath when the service uses Spring's web client.

@EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentGatewayProperties.class)

This line binds payment.gateway.url to the record and makes the record a bean. Spring can then pass the record to the method below.

@ConditionalOnMissingBean

Spring creates the client only if the application has not defined its own PaymentGatewayClient. The application's own bean always has priority.

The second part is the registration file. It is a plain text file with a fixed folder and a fixed name. It lists the auto-configuration classes, one per line:

# This file lives in src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/ and is named
# org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.
com.acme.payments.autoconfigure.PaymentGatewayAutoConfiguration

At start-up, Spring Boot reads this file from every Java archive (JAR) on the classpath. It loads each class that the file names, which here is PaymentGatewayAutoConfiguration. Lines that start with a # are comments.

A starter is the last piece, and it is optional. A starter is a dependency with no code of its own. It adds the library and everything that the library needs, as spring-boot-starter-webmvc does for web applications. Name your starter payment-gateway-spring-boot-starter, because names that begin with spring-boot are reserved for Spring Boot's own modules.

Gotcha

Three things cause bugs here. First, the folder and the name of the registration file must be exact. A typo gives no error at all. The auto-configuration is simply never loaded.

Second, keep the auto-configuration out of every package that the application scans. @SpringBootApplication skips classes named in a registration file, but a plain @ComponentScan does not skip them. A plain @ComponentScan loads the class as ordinary configuration, before Spring has seen the application's own beans. So @ConditionalOnMissingBean does not find those beans, and the application has two clients.

Third, libraries written for Spring Boot 2 often list their auto-configurations in a file called spring.factories instead. Spring Boot 3 and 4 no longer read that file for auto-configurations. So such a library is ignored, and no error is reported.

Note

Read the Spring Boot reference, section “Creating Your Own Auto-configuration”. Then read the source of any Spring Boot auto-configuration, which is unusually readable.

BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor#

Spring has two hooks into its own start-up. A BeanFactoryPostProcessor sees the bean definitions before any bean exists. A bean definition is the recipe that Spring uses to create a bean. A BeanPostProcessor sees each bean when the bean is created, and can wrap or replace the bean. Spring itself uses a BeanPostProcessor to put a proxy around a bean, and you can use one in the same way.

RowDetail
What it isTwo extension points. A BeanFactoryPostProcessor edits bean definitions before any bean is created. A BeanPostProcessor edits or replaces each bean as it is created. Every proxy in Spring is made by a BeanPostProcessor.
You need it whenYou need the same wrapper around many beans, such as timing or auditing, or you load bean definitions from somewhere other than your code.
The C# instinctThere is no direct equivalent. The nearest is editing the IServiceCollection before Build(), plus decorator registrations. But Spring's hooks run inside the container and see every bean.

Here a post-processor times every call to the shop's PaymentGateway. PaymentGateway is an interface, and its charge method takes an Invoice and returns a receipt number. The post-processor wraps each gateway in a proxy. The Proxy class makes the proxy, and this class is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Proxy does the same as DispatchProxy in .NET:

import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException;
import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.BeanPostProcessor;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class TimingPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(TimingPostProcessor.class);

    @Override
    public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {
        if (!(bean instanceof PaymentGateway gateway)) {
            return bean;
        }
        return Proxy.newProxyInstance(
                PaymentGateway.class.getClassLoader(),
                new Class<?>[] { PaymentGateway.class },
                (proxy, method, args) -> {
                    long start = System.nanoTime();
                    try {
                        return method.invoke(gateway, args);
                    } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
                        throw e.getCause();
                    } finally {
                        long micros = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000;
                        log.info("{}.{} took {} microseconds", beanName, method.getName(), micros);
                    }
                });
    }
}
Reading the code
public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {

Spring calls this method for every bean, once the bean is created and initialised. Other beans receive the object that the method returns.

if (!(bean instanceof PaymentGateway gateway)) {

Every bean that is not a gateway passes through unchanged.

return Proxy.newProxyInstance(

This call builds an object at run time. The object implements PaymentGateway and sends every call to the lambda below. The lambda receives the proxy, the method that is called and the arguments of the call.

return method.invoke(gateway, args);

This line calls the real gateway.

throw e.getCause();

invoke wraps any exception that the gateway throws in an InvocationTargetException. Unwrapping the exception lets the caller catch the original exception, such as an IllegalArgumentException.

log.info("{}.{} took {} microseconds", beanName, method.getName(), micros);

This line runs whether the call succeeded or failed. It logs the bean, the method and the time.

Gotcha

A BeanPostProcessor is itself a bean, and Spring must create it before the beans that it processes. So every bean that the post-processor depends on is created very early too. Such a bean is created before the other post-processors are ready, and it never passes through them. Keep post-processors free of dependencies. Or take an ObjectProvider, and fetch the bean only when it is first needed.

If TimingPostProcessor took an AuditLog in its constructor, to record the timings, Spring would log this warning at start-up:

Bean 'auditLog' of type [com.acme.shop.AuditLog] is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors (for example: not eligible for auto-proxying)#
Means
A post-processor depends on this bean, so Spring created the bean before every post-processor was ready. The bean gets no proxies. So annotations such as @Transactional on the bean can do nothing, and no error is reported.
Fix
Remove the dependency, or take an ObjectProvider<AuditLog> and call getObject() only when the bean is first needed.
Note

Read the Spring Framework reference, section "Container Extension Points".

Spring AOT and native processing#

Normally Spring makes all its decisions at start-up. It decides which configuration applies, which beans to create and how to connect them. Ahead-of-time (AOT) processing makes those decisions during the build instead. AOT processing also makes a native image of a Spring application possible.

RowDetail
What it isA build step that runs Spring's start-up decisions early and writes the result out as generated Java code and reflection metadata. Start-up then does less work, and GraalVM can see everything the application uses.
You need it whenYou are building a native image, or start-up time matters, as on serverless platforms that scale to zero and start instances on demand.
The C# instinctNativeAOT plus source generators, which do the same job for the same reason. Compiling ahead of time needs everything decided before the program runs.
Note

Read the Spring Boot reference, section "Ahead-of-Time Processing". Then read the chapter Packaging and native images in this book.

The rest of this appendix is signposts. Each signpost says what a topic is and when you need it, with no code. Each group is folded until you open it.

JVM internals#

These entries go below Spring, into the JVM itself. They cover how the JVM finds classes, how its just-in-time (JIT) compiler turns bytecode into machine code, and the rules for sharing memory between threads.

Classloaders and the classpath#

RowDetail
What it isJava finds classes through a chain of class loaders, each of which asks its parent first. A class's identity is its name plus the loader that loaded it, so one name loaded twice is two different types.
You need it whenA ClassCastException names the same class on both sides. Or a library works in tests but not in the deployed server. Or you are building plugins or hot reload.
The C# instinct.NET has AssemblyLoadContext, and you almost never touch it. In Java the chain of loaders matters. It appears in ordinary bugs, and it is what "JAR hell" means.
ReadJava Language Specification 12.2, and Oaks, "Java Performance". For the application-server case, read the Tomcat class loader documentation.
Note

For the basics, see the chapter How Java runs your code. That chapter covers the classpath as a search list, the order in which loaders are asked, and the two class-not-found errors. This entry is for when the basics are not enough.

The JIT: tiers, inlining, deoptimisation#

RowDetail
What it isHotSpot, the standard JVM, first interprets your code. It compiles methods that run often with a quick compiler, C1. Then it recompiles the busiest methods with an optimising compiler, C2, guided by what it has seen. It makes bold guesses, and it throws the compiled code away when a guess proves wrong. This is called deoptimisation.
You need it whenThroughput changes minutes after start-up. Or a microbenchmark reports impossible numbers. Or the slowest requests spike and the garbage-collection logs do not explain it.
The C# instinct.NET also recompiles hot methods using profile data. This is tiered compilation, with dynamic PGO on by default since .NET 8. But .NET does not deoptimise as HotSpot does. Because HotSpot deoptimises, the speed of a Java method can change long after start-up.
ReadAleksey Shipilev's blog is the reference. -XX:+PrintCompilation and JITWatch show the compilation as it happens. Always measure with JMH, never with a loop that you wrote yourself.

The Java Memory Model and happens-before#

RowDetail
What it isThe formal rules for when a write by one thread is guaranteed to be visible to another. Everything about volatile, synchronized and the atomic classes follows from them.
You need it whenYou have a concurrency bug that you cannot reproduce. Or you are writing a lock-free structure. Or you need to know whether a field really needs volatile.
The C# instinctThe .NET memory model is weak on paper but stronger in practice, especially on x86. Java's model is precisely specified, and was fixed in Java 5, in 2004. Advice written before that is wrong.
ReadGoetz, "Java Concurrency in Practice", is still the definitive treatment. For the specification, read JSR-133 and its FAQ.

MethodHandle, VarHandle and reflection performance#

RowDetail
What it isFaster, typed alternatives to reflection. A MethodHandle points at a method, and the JIT can optimise a call through it like a normal call. A VarHandle reads and writes a field with a chosen memory ordering. The ordering is plain, opaque, acquire/release or volatile.
You need it whenReflection appears as hot in a profiler. Or you are writing a framework or serialiser. Or you need ordering weaker than volatile but stronger than plain.
The C# instinctExpression trees compiled to delegates, or Unsafe.As. A MethodHandle is closer to a compiled delegate than to reflection.
Readthe java.lang.invoke package documentation, and JEP 193 for VarHandle

Bytecode manipulation#

RowDetail
What it isGenerating or rewriting classes, at build time or as they load. ByteBuddy is the easy library, and ASM is the low-level library. Since Java 24, the Class-File API does the job inside the JDK itself.
You need it whenYou are writing a Java agent, a mocking library or a monitoring tool, or you must add behaviour to a class you cannot change.
The C# instinctIL weaving with Fody or Cecil, at build time. A Java agent rewrites classes as they load. This is how the OpenTelemetry Java agent adds tracing with no code change. The zero-code instrumentation in .NET does the same through the CLR profiling API.
Readthe ByteBuddy tutorial, JEP 484 for the Class-File API, and java.lang.instrument for agents

NIO channels, selectors and memory-mapped files#

RowDetail
What it isThe low-level input and output layer under every HTTP server and database driver. It has buffers, channels, selectors that watch many connections at once, and files mapped straight into memory.
You need it whenYou are implementing a network protocol or a high-throughput file processor, or a driver misbehaves under load and you need to know why.
The C# instinctSpan, Memory and SocketAsyncEventArgs. ByteBuffer is clumsier. Its position and limit change as you use it, which often causes bugs. The modern replacement is MemorySegment, from the Foreign Function and Memory API.
Readthe java.nio package documentation, and Netty's source for how it is really used

Platform#

These are parts of the platform that most services never use, until one day a service must use one of them.

TopicYou need it whenRead
JMX and MBeansyou must read or change a runtime value on a live JVM, or an operations tool demands itthe javax.management docs. Actuator also exposes endpoints over JMX.
ServiceLoader and the SPI patternyou are building plug-in implementations found on the classpath, which is how JDBC drivers are foundjava.util.ServiceLoader, and the provides directive in Modules, JPMS and internal
JCA, JCE, keystores and TLSyou must configure mutual TLS, load a keystore, or pick a cipher suiteJava Security Standard Algorithm Names, and the keytool documentation
Foreign Function and Memory APIyou need to call native code, or manage memory outside the heap preciselyJEP 454. This API is the modern alternative to JNI and, for off-heap memory, to ByteBuffer.
Vector APIyou have measurable number-crunching that suits SIMD instructionsJEP 508. The Vector API is still an incubator in Java 25, so it is not for production.
Locale, charset and i18ntext is garbled, or sorting differs between environmentsalways set the charset explicitly, and use ICU4J for serious internationalisation

Ecosystem, beyond one service#

These are the projects that you use once there are many services, or once one service has grown large.

TopicWhat it isYou need it when
Spring Cloudconfig server, service discovery, gateway, distributed tracingyou run many services and need shared configuration and routing
Spring Batchchunk-oriented batch processing with restartabilityyou have long-running jobs that must resume after failure, not restart
Spring Integration and Camelenterprise integration patterns as a DSLyou are routing and transforming between many systems
Kafka patternsconsumer groups, exactly-once, the transactional outboxyou are building event-driven services and need delivery guarantees
Testcontainers at scaleshared containers, reuse, parallel suitesyour integration tests have become the slowest part of the build
Mutation testing (PIT)mutates your code to check the tests noticecoverage is high and you do not trust it
ArchUnitarchitecture rules enforced as unit testslayering keeps eroding and review is not catching it

The short list#

If you read only a few things after this handbook, read these:

ForRead
Concurrency, properlyGoetz, "Java Concurrency in Practice"
Everyday idiom and API designBloch, "Effective Java"
Performance and the JVMOaks, "Java Performance", and Shipilev's blog for depth
Springthe Spring Boot and Spring Framework reference documentation, which is genuinely good, and better than most books about them
What is comingthe JEP index at openjdk.org/jeps
Note

Remember one point. Java has a severe problem with outdated advice. The language is thirty years old, and search results do not sort by the Java version that you use. An answer that was right in 2011 appears beside an answer that is right today, and both are stated with confidence. So check the date and the Java version. Prefer a JDK Enhancement Proposal (JEP) or the reference documentation over a blog post. Some old guides still recommend overriding finalize(), which Java 18 deprecated for removal.
