Appendix J: About this book#

Appendices · Chapter 64· 3 min read

This appendix says what the book targets, and how and when its facts were checked. It also says what the book does not cover, and where its structure came from.

What it targets#

SideVersionNote
Java25 LTSwhere Java 21 is different in a way that matters, the text says so
.NET10, C# 14all C# code uses the modern style, such as records, patterns and primary constructors
SpringBoot 3 and Boot 4the two versions are shown side by side wherever they differ

Many of the Java features that people write about online are still preview features. A preview feature is finished, but it is not final. You enable a preview feature with --enable-preview, and the feature can still change between releases. So this book marks every preview feature, because you can easily lose an afternoon if you copy a preview API into production code.

On accuracy#

Java is thirty years old. Search results are not sorted by the Java version that you use. An answer that was correct in 2011 appears next to an answer that is correct today. Nothing shows you which answer is the old one. That is the biggest danger when you learn Java from the internet.

So every claim in this book that depends on a version was checked against the original sources:

  • The OpenJDK project pages were used for the features of the Java Development Kit (JDK) releases 21, 22, 24 and 25.
  • The JDK Enhancement Proposals (JEPs) were used for the exact shape of each API. The JEPs are the documents that describe each change to Java.
  • The Spring release notes and migration guides were used for the differences between Spring Boot 3 and Spring Boot 4.

If a claim could not be verified, the book marks it as uncertain or does not include it.

When it was written#

This is the October 2026 edition. The facts that depend on a version were checked against those sources, 9 September to 4 October 2026. Java, .NET and Spring all release on a fixed schedule. So anything that this book calls current, latest or new was true on those dates. Each sentence that says so gives the date.

After those dates, treat version numbers, support dates and preview status as claims that you must check. Check them against the current documentation. When this book and the reference documentation disagree, the documentation is right.

The sidebar shows the date when a copy was built. That date is not the edition. A copy that is rebuilt later from the same text is still the October 2026 edition.

What it does not cover#

This is a transition handbook for server-side Java. It is for someone who builds web services and APIs. Java runs in many other places, and this book covers none of those places.

Not coveredWhere Java is used for itWhy it is out of scope
Mobile developmentAndroid, and Kotlin Multiplatforma different SDK, build system, lifecycle and UI model, so almost none of the Spring Boot part applies
Desktop applicationsJavaFX, Swing, SWTa separate UI stack with no ASP.NET Core parallel to translate from
GameslibGDX, jMonkeyEngineniche on the JVM, and the .NET comparison would be Unity
Embedded and IoTJava ME, embedded JVMsa subset of the platform with different constraints
Big data and analyticsSpark, Flink, Hadoop, Kafka Streamslarge ecosystems in their own right, and the language is the smallest part
Applets and browser pluginsthe plugin went in Java 11, the Applet API in Java 26see Appendix C, which explains what you may still find
Jakarta EE application serversWildFly, WebSphere, Open LibertyAppendix C covers enough to recognise them, and Spring Boot is assumed
Java as a first languageany introductory textthis book assumes you are fluent in C# already

Appendix C is The Java you'll inherit.

Within server-side Java, the book is still selective. It does not teach you the internals of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). The JVM is the program that runs your bytecode. The book does not cover the memory model in depth. For reactive programming, the book covers only the decision of whether to use it.

Kotlin is a language that also runs on the JVM. Kotlin has an appendix and not a chapter, because the platform facts in this book apply unchanged to a Kotlin codebase.

For the expert topics, see Appendix D. For each topic, that appendix says what the topic is and which symptom means that you now need it. It also says where to read about the topic in full. The appendix does not teach the topics. It only points to them, and this is on purpose. For Kotlin, see Appendix E. For an explanation of every Java word that the book uses, see Appendix H.

A note on sources#

The structure of this book was influenced by an older PDF that compared the .NET and Java ecosystems. The PDF was shared freely. It was written for C# 5 and Java 8, and it is now far out of date. No text was taken from the PDF. This book explicitly corrects several recommendations of the PDF. The most important one is the advice to override finalize(). That method has been deprecated for removal since Java 18.

End of the book
